Density = mass / volume of material (solid, no pores). Bulk density includes pores. Specific gravity = density of material / density of water at 4°C. Porosity = volume of voids / total volume × 100. Water absorption: % weight of water absorbed (by dry weight). Always > 0 for porous solids. Hygroscopicity: absorbing moisture from air. Permeability: allowing water to pass under pressure. Weathering resistance: resisting alternate wetting–drying, freezing–thawing. Frost resistance: depends on density and porosity; dense materials are more frost resistant. Refractoriness: withstand high temp without melting/deforming (fire bricks). Fire resistance: withstand fire without losing strength (different from refractoriness). Elasticity: regain shape on unloading. Plasticity: permanent deformation without cracking. Ductility: drawn into wires (tension). Malleability: beaten into sheets (compression). Brittleness: fails suddenly with little deformation (cast iron, glass). Toughness: energy absorbed up to fracture. Resilience: energy absorbed up to elastic limit. Hardness: resistance to scratching/indentation — Mohs scale (1 Talc … 10 Diamond). Creep: increasing strain under constant load over time. Fatigue: failure under repeated loads below ultimate stress. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Mechanical properties: Elasticity, plasticity, ductility (drawn into wires), malleability (beaten into sheets), toughness (energy to fracture), hardness, b

Geological: Igneous (granite, basalt, trap, dolerite), Sedimentary (sandstone, limestone, shale, gypsum, laterite), Metamorphic (marble, quartzite, slate, gneiss). Metamorphism: limestone → marble; sandstone → quartzite; shale/clay → slate; granite → gneiss. Physical: Stratified (sedimentary — layered, can be split), Unstratified (igneous, no layers), Foliated (metamorphic — split in one direction only, e.g. slate). Chemical: Siliceous (granite, quartzite), Argillaceous (clay main: slate, laterite), Calcareous (lime main: limestone, marble).

Stone Type Key points / Use Granite Igneous, siliceous Hard, durable, sp. gr. ~2.6–2.7; strength 100–250 N/mm²; bridge piers, docks, kerbs; poor fire resistance Basalt / Trap Igneous Very hard, dark; road metal, aggregate Sandstone Sedimentary Quartz grains + cementing material; ornamental work Limestone Sedimentary, calcareous CaCO₃; flooring, manufacture of lime & cement Laterite Sedimentary, argillaceous Porous, iron oxide; easily cut, hardens on exposure Marble Metamorphic, calcareous Takes high polish; flooring, decorative; affected by acids Slate Metamorphic, argillaceous Splits in thin sheets; roofing, DPC, sills; water absorption < 1% Quartzite Metamorphic, siliceous Very hard, brittle; rubble masonry, aggregate

Quarrying methods: excavation, wedging, heating, blasting. Explosives: gunpowder, dynamite, gun cotton, cordite. Seasoning: removing quarry sap — keep stone exposed for 6–12 months. Dressing should be done immediately after quarrying (stone is soft then). Natural bed: stone should be placed so load is perpendicular to its natural bed (layers).

Crushing test — min. crushing strength for building stone ≈ 100 N/mm². Water absorption (24-h immersion): as low as possible — generally not more than 5% by weight for a good building stone (granite < 1%; sandstone/limestone up to ≈ 10% by volume). Attrition test (Deval) — resistance to wear by rubbing; Abrasion — Los Angeles test. Impact test — toughness. Hardness test — Dorry's testing machine (coefficient of hardness = 20 − loss/3). Acid test — weathering resistance (HCl); Smith's test — earthy matter; Brard's test — frost resistance; Freezing–thawing test. Crystallisation test — sodium sulphate; determines durability. Durability: dense, compact, uniform texture, low absorption. Specific gravity of good stone > 2.7. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Rock classification: Geological: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic; physical: stratified, unstratified, foliated; chemical: siliceous, argillaceous, calcareous. Metamorphic pairs: Limestone → marble; sandstone → quartzite; shale → slate; granite → gneiss. Granite strength is mainly due to quartz; best stone for piers & abutments: granite; for roofing: slate; for monuments: marble.

Constituent % Function / excess effect Silica (SiO₂) 50–60 Prevents cracking, shrinkage, warping; excess → brittle Alumina (Al₂O₃) 20–30 Gives plasticity; excess → shrinkage, warping, cracks on drying Lime (CaO) < 5 Fuses silica (flux); excess → melting & loss of shape; lumps → splitting (bursting) Magnesia (MgO) < 1 Yellow tint, reduces shrinkage; excess → decay Iron oxide 5–6 Gives red colour, fusibility, strength Harmful ingredients: lumps of lime, iron pyrites (crystallise & disintegrate), alkalis (efflorescence), pebbles, organic matter, carbonaceous matter. Alkalis cause efflorescence (white patches of salts).

Steps: preparation of earth (unsoiling, digging, cleaning, weathering, blending, tempering) → moulding → drying → burning. Tempering in pug mill. Moulding: hand (ground/table) or machine (plastic clay / dry clay). Frog: depression on top face — holds mortar & forms key; size about 100×40×10 mm. Drying: moisture reduced to ~2–3% before burning. Burning: clamp (intermittent, ~60% good bricks) or kiln. Intermittent kiln; Continuous kilns — Bull's trench kiln (most common), Hoffman's kiln (permanent roof, burning in all seasons), Tunnel kiln. Burning temperature ~1000–1200°C. Vitrification ~1100°C.

Standard modular brick (IS): 190 × 90 × 90 mm; nominal with mortar 200 × 100 × 100 mm. Traditional size: 9″ × 4½″ × 3″ (230 × 115 × 75 mm approx.). Weight of one brick ≈ 3–3.5 kg; ~500 bricks per m³ (modular). First class: well burnt, uniform copper colour, metallic ringing sound, sharp edges; absorption ≤ 20%; strength ≥ 10.5 N/mm². Second class: absorption ≤ 22%; strength ~7 N/mm². Third class: absorption ≤ 25%; ~3.5 N/mm². Over-burnt: Jhama bricks (dark, distorted, used as aggregate/road metal). Under-burnt: Pila bricks (yellow, soft). Fire bricks: made from fire clay; withstand ~1800°C; size 230×114×64 mm (approx.). Special bricks: bull-nose, cornice, squint, perforated, hollow (cavity), paving, sand-lime (calcium silicate), fly-ash bricks.

Absorption: 24-hr immersion; first class ≤ 20% of dry weight. Crushing strength: min 3.5 N/mm² (any brick for construction). Hardness: no impression with finger nail. Soundness: two bricks struck together give clear ringing sound. Efflorescence: Nil / Slight (<10% area) / Moderate (10–50%) / Heavy (>50%) / Serious (powdering). Size & shape: 20 bricks stacked — tolerance checks. Structure: broken brick shows uniform, no holes/lumps.

Clay tiles: roofing (Mangalore, pan, flat), flooring, drain tiles, encaustic (decorative). Terracotta: burnt clay, hollow ornamental units. Porcelain: white, glazed, impermeable. Stoneware: hard, partially vitrified (sewer pipes). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Kilns in Pakistan: Traditional Bull’s trench kilns (BTK) are being converted to zig-zag kilns to cut fuel use and smog; brick kilns are a major source of winter smog in Punjab. Tests on bricks: Compressive strength, water absorption, efflorescence, dimension tolerance, hardness (scratch), soundness (ring). Good brick: absorption ≤ 20% (1st class), no efflorescence, ring sound, compressive strength ≥ 10.5 MPa (1st class, Pakistan/IS practice).

Lime is obtained by burning limestone (calcination): CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (~900°C). Quick lime (CaO): product of calcination; slakes with water. Slaking: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + heat; product = hydrated / slaked lime. Setting of lime: Ca(OH)₂ absorbs CO₂ from air → CaCO₃ (carbonation, slow). Lime putty: slaked lime + water (plastic paste). Type Main features Use Fat lime (high calcium / pure / rich) CaO ~95%; slakes vigorously; volume ↑ 2–2.5 times; sets slowly by carbonation; poor strength Plastering, white washing Hydraulic lime Contains clay 5–30%; sets under water; feebly (5–10% clay), moderately (11–20%), eminently (21–30%) Masonry under water, damp places Poor lime (lean / impure) Impurities > 30%; slakes slowly; poor binding Inferior masonry Hydraulicity due to clay (silicates & aluminates of lime). Lime should be stored in a dry place, in a shed, preferably used within short time. Tests: visual (colour — fat lime white), acid test (HCl, effervescence), ball test, heat test, workability test. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 4.1 — Lime cycle: calcination, slaking and carbonation. Fat lime (high-calcium) sets by carbonation only (slow, air needed); hydraulic lime contains clay and sets under water.

Mortar = binding material (cement/lime) + fine aggregate + water. Functions: bind units, distribute load, fill joints, weather-proofing. Types by binder: cement mortar, lime mortar, gauged mortar (lime + cement), surkhi mortar (surkhi = powdered burnt clay, a pozzolana), mud mortar, gypsum mortar. Typical cement mortar ratios: masonry 1:4 to 1:6; plaster 1:4 to 1:6; pointing 1:2 to 1:3. Special: fire-resistant (aluminous cement + fire brick powder), lightweight, sound-absorbing, X-ray shielding (barite), packing mortar. Lime mortar sets slowly; cement mortar should be used within 30 minutes of adding water.

Exogenous (grow outward, annual rings) — conifers/softwood & deciduous/hardwood. Endogenous (grow inward) — bamboo, palm, cane; not used structurally. Softwood (conifers): resinous, light colour, distinct annual rings, light weight, non-porous — pine, deodar, chir, fir. Hardwood (deciduous): dark, close-grained, indistinct rings, heavy, porous — teak, sal, sheesham, oak, mahogany, babul. Cross-section: pith → heartwood (dead, dark, strong, durable) → sapwood (alburnum — living, light, weaker) → cambium layer → inner bark → outer bark. Medullary rays: radial. Felling of trees: at maturity; best season — winter (mid-summer in hills) when sap is at rest. Age of tree = number of annual rings.

Purpose: reduce moisture to ~10–12% (for furniture/joinery 8–10%), prevent decay, shrinkage, warping; increase strength. Green timber moisture ~ 40–100% or more. Fibre saturation point ~ 25–30%. Natural: air seasoning (slow, 2–4 years for hardwood), water seasoning. Artificial: kiln seasoning (fastest, most effective), boiling, chemical (salt) seasoning, electrical seasoning.

Natural: knots (dead/live), shakes (cracks — heart shake, star shake, cup/ring shake, radial shake), twisted fibres, upsets, rind galls, burls, wind cracks. Seasoning defects: bow, cup, twist, check, split, honeycombing, case hardening, warp. Conversion defects: chip mark, diagonal grain, torn grain, wane. Fungi: dry rot (destroys timber into powder, warm damp poorly ventilated places), wet rot (alternate wet & dry). Insects: termites (white ants), beetles, marine borers.

Preservatives: coal tar, creosote oil (most effective oil-type), ASCU (arsenic-copper-chromium; water-borne), chemical salts (zinc chloride, copper sulphate), solignum paint. Methods: brushing, spraying, dipping & steeping, charring (ends buried in ground), hot & cold open tank, pressure treatment (full-cell Bethell, empty-cell Rueping/Lowry). Fire retardants: ammonium phosphate, borax, boric acid.

Plywood: thin veneers glued with grain of adjacent layers at right angles; always odd number of plies (3, 5, 7…). Veneer: thin sheet (0.4–6 mm) of wood cut by rotary cutting, slicing or sawing. Particle board / chip board (wood chips + resin), fibre board (hard board, insulation board), block board, laminated board, batten board, impreg & compreg timber. Strength of timber: max in tension along grain; along-grain compressive > across grain. Strongest when loaded parallel to grain. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 6.1 — Cross-section of a tree: pith, heartwood, sapwood, cambium, bark, annual rings, medullary rays. Fig. 6.2 — Shakes in timber: heart, star, cup/ring and radial shakes. Timbers of Pakistan: Deodar (Himalayan cedar — durable, construction & railway sleepers), Kail (blue pine), Chir pine, Shisham (furniture), Kikar/acacia, Partal/fir. Heartwood is used for structural timber; sapwood is weaker and liable to decay. Seasoning to ≈ 10–12% moisture for joinery.

Metal Carbon % Key properties / use Pig iron 3–4 (up to 4.5) Crude iron from blast furnace; raw material for other forms Cast iron 2–4.5 Brittle, hard, strong in compression, weak in tension, cannot be welded/forged; melting ~1200°C; pipes, columns, manhole covers Wrought iron < 0.15 (0.02–0.12) Purest commercial iron; ductile, malleable, tough, can be welded/forged; fibrous structure Steel 0.1–1.5 (up to ~2) Mild steel 0.1–0.25%; medium 0.25–0.6%; high carbon 0.6–1.5% Mild steel: ductile, weldable; yield ~250 N/mm²; E ≈ 2 × 10⁵ N/mm²; density ≈ 7850 kg/m³. As carbon ↑ → hardness & strength ↑, ductility & weldability ↓. Steel manufacture: Bessemer process, open hearth (Siemens-Martin), electric (arc/induction), L-D (basic oxygen) process, cementation, crucible. Alloying elements: Nickel (toughness, corrosion resistance), Chromium (hardness, stainless — ≥ 11–12%), Manganese (hardness, removes sulphur; Hadfield steel ~12% Mn — wear resistant), Tungsten & Vanadium (tool steels, high-speed steel), Molybdenum, Silicon (electrical/spring steel), Cobalt (magnets). Stainless steel ≈ 18% Cr + 8% Ni (18/8). Heat treatment: Annealing (soften, relieve stress — slow cooling in furnace), Normalising (cool in air; refine grain), Hardening (quench in water/oil), Tempering (reheat after hardening, reduce brittleness), Case hardening/carburising, Nitriding, Cyaniding. Reinforcing steel: mild steel plain bars, HYSD / TMT deformed bars (Fe 415, Fe 500, Fe 550 — number = yield/0.2% proof stress i

Aluminium: light (sp. gr. 2.7), corrosion resistant (oxide film), good conductor; ore — bauxite. Copper: high conductivity, ductile; ore — chalcopyrite. Zinc: galvanising; Lead: heaviest common metal, soft, used for DPC, roofing, X-ray shields; poisonous. Tin: tinning, solder. Brass = Copper + Zinc. Bronze = Copper + Tin. Gun metal = Cu + Sn + Zn. Duralumin = Al + Cu (~4%) + Mg + Mn (aircraft). Solder = Lead + Tin. German silver = Cu + Zn + Ni. Babbitt metal = Tin + Antimony + Copper (bearings). Invar = Fe + 36% Ni — very low thermal expansion (measuring tapes).

Ingredient Function Examples Base Gives body, opacity, protective film White lead, red lead, zinc white, titanium white, iron oxide, aluminium powder Vehicle / carrier Holds ingredients, binds, forms film Linseed oil (most common), tung oil, poppy oil, nut oil Drier Accelerates drying Litharge, lead acetate, manganese dioxide, cobalt Thinner / solvent Makes paint thin for application; evaporates Turpentine, naphtha, benzene, petroleum spirit Pigment Colour Lamp black, ochre (yellow), chrome yellow, Prussian blue Adultrant / extender Reduces cost, improves properties Barium sulphate, gypsum, silica, chalk Coats: priming coat → undercoat → finishing coat. Types: oil paint, enamel paint (gloss, varnish base), emulsion paint (water-based), cement paint, bituminous paint (iron, steel under water), aluminium paint (reflective, oil tanks), anti-corrosive paint, asbestos paint, plastic paint, synthetic rubber paint, cellulose paint, luminous paint, fire-proof paint. Red lead — primer for steel/iron (anti-corrosive). Aluminium primer for timber (resinous). Paint defects: blistering (moisture/vapour trapped), bloom (dull patches), flaking, flashing (glossy patches), grinning (background visible), running/sagging, wrinkling, chalking (powder on surface), saponification (alkali in plaster forms soap), fading, checking/cracking. Varnish: transparent/semi-transparent solution of resin in solvent (oil, spirit, turpentine, water). Types: oil varnish, spirit varnish (French polish = shellac i

Main ingredients: silica (sand) — main; soda/potash (flux, lowers melting point); lime (durability, hardness); cullet (broken glass — helps fusion); colouring agents (metal oxides). Types: Soda-lime glass (cheapest, windows, bottles), Potash-lime glass (hard glass, fusible at high temp), Potash-lead glass (flint glass — high refractive index; lenses, artificial gems), Borosilicate (Pyrex, low expansion, lab ware), common glass. Special glass: wired (fire resisting), laminated (safety, shatter-proof — PVB layer), toughened/tempered (heat treated, 4–5 times stronger, breaks into small blunt pieces), tinted, frosted/ground (translucent), glass wool (insulation), fibreglass, structural glass blocks, bullet-proof, photochromatic, ultraviolet. Annealing of glass: slow cooling to remove internal stresses. Colouring oxides: Cobalt oxide → blue; Chromium oxide → green; Ferrous → green; Ferric → yellow-brown; Manganese → violet/purple; Cuprous → red; Gold chloride → ruby red; Carbon → amber.

Thermoplastics: soften on heating and harden on cooling repeatedly — PVC, polythene, polystyrene, nylon, acrylic (Perspex), polypropylene, Teflon. Thermosetting: harden permanently once set; cannot be remoulded — bakelite (phenol-formaldehyde), urea-formaldehyde, epoxy, melamine, polyester. Properties: light, corrosion resistant, good insulators, easily moulded; but low fire resistance, low stiffness (E), creep, UV degradation. Uses: PVC pipes, water tanks, laminated sheets, doors/windows (uPVC), adhesives (epoxy), sealants, geo-synthetics. Fibre-reinforced plastics (FRP/GFRP/CFRP): strengthening of structures.

Bitumen: obtained by fractional distillation of crude petroleum; black/brown, soluble in carbon disulphide (CS₂). Tar: obtained by destructive distillation of coal or wood; more temperature susceptible; carcinogenic; soluble in toluene. Asphalt: natural or artificial mixture of bitumen with inert mineral matter (rock asphalt, lake asphalt — e.g. Trinidad lake). Cutback bitumen: bitumen + volatile solvent — Rapid curing (naphtha/gasoline), Medium curing (kerosene), Slow curing (light oil). Bitumen emulsion: bitumen dispersed in water with emulsifier; used in wet weather, patch repair. Tests on bitumen: penetration (grading/hardness — 80/100, 60/70 etc.), ductility (≥ 50–75 cm), softening point (ring & ball), flash & fire point (Pensky-Martens), viscosity, specific gravity, loss on heating, solubility. Uses: road surfacing, damp-proofing (DPC), waterproofing roofs, joint fillers, felts.

Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O): heating ~120–160°C gives Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O); sets in 5–10 min; used for false ceilings, plaster boards, mouldings. Keene's cement: anhydrous gypsum + alum; hard, smooth finish plaster. Pozzolanas: fly ash, surkhi, rice husk ash, silica fume, GGBS, metakaolin — react with Ca(OH)₂ in presence of water. Asbestos: fibrous mineral; fire resistant; AC (asbestos cement) sheets & pipes — health hazard, now restricted. Thermal insulating materials: glass wool, mineral/slag wool, cork, vermiculite, thermocol (EPS), asbestos, foam concrete, cellular concrete, air gaps. Sound absorbing materials: acoustic tiles, fibre board, cork, felt, perforated boards. Sabine's formula: T = 0.16V/A (SI). Damp-proofing materials: bitumen/asphalt, bituminous felts, plastic sheets (polythene), metal sheets (lead, copper), mortar with waterproofing compounds, stones (slate). Water-proofing compounds: hydrated lime, calcium chloride, aluminium sulphate, soap, oils, bitumen. Rubber: natural (latex, hevea tree) — vulcanisation with sulphur improves strength & elasticity. Adhesives: animal glue, casein, epoxy, phenolic, synthetic resins. Geosynthetics: geotextiles, geogrids, geomembranes — separation, filtration, reinforcement, drainage.

(CE-216 Concrete Technology, theory + lab) and M.Sc. course material in "University life" Cement • Aggregates • Water • Admixtures • Fresh & Hardened Concrete • Durability • Mix Design • Special Concretes • Testing Coverage note: Old-format .ppt lectures (aggregates, fresh concrete, transporting & handling, weekly lectures) could not be opened; those topics are written from the standard references used by the course (ASTM, ACI, Neville, M.S. Shetty) and cross-checked against the other files on the same topics.

Concrete = hydraulic cement + aggregates (fine + coarse) + water, with or without admixtures/fibres (ACI definition). Composite: binder (cement paste) glues filler (aggregates) into an artificial stone ("man-made stone"). Paste = cement + water; Mortar = paste + fine aggregate; Concrete = mortar + coarse aggregate. Strong in compression, weak in tension (tensile ≈ 10% of compressive) → steel added to take tension and control crack width. Portland cement patented by Joseph Aspdin (1824), England; named after Portland stone (Isle of Portland). Portland cement is a type of cement, not a brand name.

Component % by volume Remark Cement paste 25 – 40% Glue; controls strength & durability Cement 7 – 15% Most expensive ingredient → minimise Water 14 – 21% Only ~1/3 needed for hydration; rest for workability Air 1 – 8% Entrapped 1–2%; entrained 4–8% Aggregates 60 – 75% (some notes 70–80%) Cheap filler; volume stability; abrasion resistance

Cement: fine powder; reacts with water (hydration) to form glue (C-S-H) that binds aggregates. Water: (i) chemical reaction with cement, (ii) workability. Extra water → pores → lower strength, higher permeability, poorer durability; but helps workability and prevents plastic shrinkage. Aggregates: cheap filler, hard, give volume stability, reduce shrinkage/creep, abrasion resistance; density of concrete depends on aggregate density. Admixtures: chemical (retarders, accelerators, water reducers, superplasticizers, air entrainers) and mineral (fly ash, silica fume, slag, RHA).

Versatility of form (fluid when placed), excellent fire resistance (most fire-resistive structural material), low maintenance, lower first cost than steel in many cases, local availability of materials and labour.

Basic elements: Calcium, Silicon, Aluminium, Iron. Calcareous (lime source): limestone, chalk, marl. Argillaceous (silica, alumina, iron): clay, shale, sand. Correctives when needed: mill scale, bauxite, iron ore, fly ash. Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O, ~3–5%) added during final grinding of clinker to control (retard) setting of C₃A.

Quarrying → primary crusher (to baseball size) → secondary crusher (gravel size). Proportioning, blending and raw grinding (roller mill) → raw meal. Preheater tower (cyclones, >60 m tall) uses hot kiln exit gases to preheat raw meal (energy saving). Rotary kiln: sloped steel cylinder lined with firebrick, 1–3 rpm; flame ≈ 1870 °C; material reaches ≈ 1450–1500 °C (clinkering zone) and partially melts → clinker. Zones in kiln: drying (~100 °C) → calcination CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (~900 °C) → clinkering (1400–1500 °C) → cooling. Clinker cooler (forced air; heat recovered) → ball mill grinding with gypsum → silos → bulk/bag dispatch. Wet process: raw materials mixed with water as slurry (35–50% water) → more fuel; Dry process: less fuel, modern, most used. Exam point: Gypsum is added at the grinding of clinker, not in the kiln. Without it, C₃A causes flash set.

Oxide Typical % Function / limit Lime CaO 60 – 67 Main; excess free lime → unsoundness Silica SiO₂ 17 – 25 Forms C₃S, C₂S (strength) Alumina Al₂O₃ 3 – 8 Quick setting; lowers clinkering temp Iron oxide Fe₂O₃ 0.5 – 6 Colour (grey); flux Magnesia MgO 0.1 – 4 Excess (>5–6%) → unsoundness Sulphur trioxide SO₃ 1 – 3 From gypsum; excess → unsoundness Alkalis (Na₂O, K₂O) 0.4 – 1.3 Alkali–aggregate reaction; low-alkali cement ≤ 0.6% Na₂O eq.

Compound Formula / short % in OPC Heat of hydration Role Tricalcium silicate (Alite) 3CaO·SiO₂ = C₃S ~50% (45–55) 502 J/g (120 cal/g) Early strength (first 7 days); high heat Dicalcium silicate (Belite) 2CaO·SiO₂ = C₂S ~25% (15–30) 260 J/g (62 cal/g) Later strength (after 7–28 days); low heat Tricalcium aluminate 3CaO·Al₂O₃ = C₃A ~10% (5–12) 867 J/g (207 cal/g) — highest Flash set, initial set; poor sulphate resistance Tetracalcium aluminoferrite (Felite/Celite) 4CaO·Al₂O₃·Fe₂O₃ = C₄AF ~10% (6–12) 419 J/g (100 cal/g) Little strength; grey colour; flux Gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O ~5% — Retards C₃A (controls set) Only the calcium silicates (C₃S + C₂S, ~75%) give strength. Rate of hydration (fastest → slowest): C₃A > C₄AF > C₃S > C₂S. Heat of hydration (highest → lowest): C₃A > C₃S > C₄AF > C₂S. Exam point: Low-heat cement → reduce C₃A & C₃S, increase C₂S. Sulphate-resisting cement → low C₃A (≤5%). Rapid-hardening → more C₃S + finer grinding.

Hydration = chemical reaction of cement with water; exothermic; continues as long as water and unhydrated cement exist (years). Concrete hardens by hydration, not by drying. Dry concrete stops gaining strength ("dry concrete = dead concrete"). C₃S: 2C₃S + 7H₂O → C₃S₂H₄ (C-S-H gel) + 3Ca(OH)₂ + 173.6 kJ C₂S: 2C₂S + 5H₂O → C₃S₂H₄ + Ca(OH)₂ + 58.6 kJ (slower, less heat, less CH) Products: C-S-H gel (main strength-giving product, ~50–60% of paste solids), Calcium hydroxide CH / portlandite (~20–25%, weak, leachable, gives pH > 12), ettringite & monosulphate (from C₃A + gypsum). pH of pore solution rises above 12 (≈12.5–13) → protects (passivates) steel. C₃S produces about 3× more CH than C₂S → C₂S-rich cements are more durable chemically. Minimum w/c for full hydration ≈ 0.38 (≈0.23 chemically bound + ≈0.15 gel water); slides quote ~0.3 minimum; typical practical w/c 0.4 – 0.6.

Stage Name Key point I Initial hydrolysis Rapid, minutes; temperature rise; Ca²⁺ and OH⁻ released II Dormant (induction) period 1 – 3 h; little heat; concrete stays plastic → transport & placing; ends at initial set III Acceleration C₃S hydration, rapid heat, initial→final set, hardening starts IV Deceleration C-S-H coating thickens; reaction becomes diffusion controlled V Steady state After ~36 h; slow formation of hydrates continues

Setting = change from fluid (plastic) to rigid (solid) state; mainly C₃A (and C₃S). Hardening = gain of strength after setting (C₃S, C₂S). Don't confuse the two. Initial setting time: time from adding water until paste starts losing plasticity (Vicat needle 1 mm² fails to penetrate beyond 5 ± 0.5 mm from bottom). Must not be too short → time for mixing, transport, placing, compacting. Final setting time: time until paste completely loses plasticity (needle with 5 mm annular collar makes an impression but collar does not). Must not be too long → early formwork removal. Standard Initial setting (min) Final setting (max) ASTM C150 (Vicat, C191) 45 min 375 min (6¼ h) IS / ISI (OPC & rapid hardening) 30 min 600 min (10 h) IS low-heat cement 60 min 600 min UiTM slides 45 min 10 h High alumina cement ≈ 3.5 h (≥ 3 h) ≈ 5 h Quick-setting cement ≈ 5 min ≈ 30 min Flash set: rapid irreversible stiffening due to C₃A when gypsum is insufficient; heat evolved; cannot be remixed. False set: premature stiffening due to dehydrated gypsum (hemihydrate) recrystallising; little heat; plasticity regained by remixing without extra water. Setting accelerated by: fineness, high C₃A, high temperature, accelerators (CaCl₂). Retarded by: gypsum, sugar, low temperature, retarders. Approx. setting time of concrete vs temperature (cold-weather notes): 70 °F → 6 h; 60 °F → 8 h; 50 °F → 11 h; 40 °F → 14 h; 32 °F → concrete freezes.

Specific surface: IS ≥ 225 m²/kg; typical OPC 300–400 m²/kg Soundness Le Chatelier (BS EN 196-3) / Autoclave (ASTM C151) Le Chatelier: paste with 0.78 × standard consistency water, 24 h in water at 27 ± 2 °C, then boil 3 h; expansion ≤ 10 mm. Raw materials: calcareous (limestone, chalk) + argillaceous (clay, shale). Gypsum (2–3%) added during grinding to retard setting. Typical OPC oxide composition: CaO 60–67%, SiO₂ 17–25%, Al₂O₃ 3–8%, Fe₂O₃ 0.5–6%, MgO 0.1–4% (max 5–6%), SO₃ 1–3%. Bogue compounds: C₃S (strength early, high heat), C₂S (later strength, low heat), C₃A (flash set, highest heat, sulphate attack), C₄AF (least role, colour). Process: wet process (old) and dry process (modern, less fuel). Kiln — rotary kiln, clinker formed at ~1400–1500°C. Standard tests: fineness (sieve 90 µm residue ≤ 10% OPC; Blaine air permeability ≥ 225 m²/kg), normal consistency (Vicat, ~25–35%), initial setting ≥ 30 min, final setting ≤ 600 min (10 hr), soundness (Le Chatelier ≤ 10 mm; autoclave ≤ 0.8%). Compressive strength test: 1:3 cement-standard sand mortar cubes 70.6 mm (50 cm² face). Grades of OPC: 33, 43, 53 (28-day strength in N/mm²). Types: Rapid hardening (more C₃S, finer), Low heat (less C₃S & C₃A; dams), Sulphate resisting (C₃A < 5%), Portland pozzolana (fly ash 15–35%), Portland slag, White cement (low iron), High alumina (refractory, very fast strength), Quick setting, Expansive, Hydrophobic, Coloured. Unit weight of cement ≈ 1440 kg/m³; one bag = 50 kg ≈ 0.0347 m³. Specific gravity ≈ 3.15.

Aggregates occupy 60–80% of concrete volume; chemically inert fillers held by cement paste. Fine aggregate (FA): passes No. 4 sieve (4.75 mm); sand. Coarse aggregate (CA): retained on No. 4 (> 4.75 mm; slides: > 3/8 in). By origin: natural (river gravel, crushed rock) and artificial (slag, expanded clay, broken brick, recycled concrete). By geology: igneous (granite, basalt), sedimentary (limestone, sandstone), metamorphic (marble, quartzite). Class by weight Examples Use Ultra-lightweight Vermiculite, perlite, ceramic spheres Insulating concrete that can be sawn/nailed Lightweight Expanded clay/shale/slate, pumice, scoria, crushed brick, expanded slag, clinker Lightweight structural & insulating concrete Normal weight Crushed limestone, sand, river gravel, recycled concrete Normal concrete (SG ≈ 2.6–2.7) Heavyweight Barite, magnetite, hematite, steel/iron shot, lead shot Radiation shielding (high density)

Shapes: rounded (river gravel), irregular, angular (crushed), flaky, elongated, flaky-and-elongated. Rounded/smooth → better workability, less water, lower bond. Angular/rough → better bond & strength, need more paste/water. Flakiness index: % by weight of particles whose least dimension < 0.6 × mean size. Elongation index: length > 1.8 × mean size. Both limited (commonly ≤ 15–25%). Bond strength ↑ with surface roughness (mechanical interlock). Smaller max size → larger surface area → higher strength for given w/c.

Property Typical / limit Specific gravity (bulk SSD) 2.5 – 3.0; normal ≈ 2.6 – 2.7 Bulk density (loose / rodded) 1200 – 1750 kg/m³ (normal ≈ 1520 – 1680) Water absorption 0.2 – 4% (good aggregate < 1–2%) Moisture states Oven-dry (OD) → Air-dry (AD) → Saturated surface-dry (SSD) → Wet (moist) Bulking of sand Volume increase of damp sand due to surface moisture films; max ≈ 20–40% at ≈ 4–6% moisture; fine sand bulks more; saturated (inundated) sand shows no bulking Free (surface) moisture Total moisture − absorption; adds water to mix (adjust in mix design) Exam point: SSD condition is the reference state in mix design — aggregate neither absorbs nor gives water to the mix.

A = SSD sample weight; B = pycnometer + sample + water; C = pycnometer + water; D = oven-dry sample. Bulk SG (OD) = D / (C + A − B)  •  Bulk SG (SSD) = A / (C + A − B)  •  Apparent SG = D / (C + D − B) Absorption % = (A − D) / D × 100 Sample ≈ 500 g, soaked 24 ± ½ h at 22–32 °C, dried to free-running (SSD), oven 100–110 °C for 24 h.

A = weight in water (A1 − A2); B = SSD weight in air; C = oven-dry weight in air. Bulk SG (OD) = C / (B − A)  •  Bulk SG (SSD) = B / (B − A)  •  Apparent SG = C / (C − A)  •  Absorption % = (B − C)/C × 100 Sample ≥ 2000 g, washed, immersed 24 h; basket dropped 25 times from 25 mm to remove air.

Grading = particle-size distribution. Well-graded aggregate → fewer voids → less paste, economy, higher strength, less segregation. FA sieves: #4, #8, #16, #30, #50, #100 (4.75, 2.36, 1.18, 0.6, 0.3, 0.15 mm). CA sieves: 1½", 1", ¾", ½", ⅜", #4. Sieve gently in varied directions; do not force material by hand; brush #50 & #100. Fineness modulus (FM) = Σ cumulative % retained on standard sieves (#100 and coarser, incl. 3/8", ¾", 1½" for CA) ÷ 100. FM of FA: fine sand 2.2–2.6, medium 2.6–2.9, coarse 2.9–3.2; FA with FM > 3.2 unsuitable. ASTM C33 limits FA FM to 2.3–3.1. FM of CA ≈ 6.5–8.0. Higher FM = coarser material. FM is used in ACI 211 mix design (Table for volume of CA). Gradation curve: sieve size (log scale, x) vs cumulative % passing (y). D10, D30, D60 = sizes at 10, 30, 60% passing. Cu = D60 / D10 (uniformity coefficient)  •  Cc = (D30)² / (D10 × D60) (curvature). (The class slide wrote Cu = D60/D30 — that is a typo.) Well graded: wide range of sizes, smooth curve, Cu > 4 (gravel) / > 6 (sand) (slide: Cu > 5), Cc 1–3. Gap graded: intermediate sizes missing (step in curve). Uniformly graded: nearly one size, steep curve, Cu ≈ 1. Gap-graded aggregate used for exposed-aggregate finishes; needs close control to avoid segregation.

Not larger than 1/5 of narrowest dimension between forms, 1/3 of slab depth, 3/4 of clear spacing between bars (or bar & form). Usually ≤ 1.5 in (40 mm) except mass concrete; commonly ¾"–1" (20–25 mm). Larger size → less paste & water; smaller size → higher strength at same w/c (high-strength concrete).

Clay, silt and dust (coat aggregate → poor bond); organic matter (retards hydration); coal, lignite, mica; soft/friable particles; salts and chlorides (corrosion, efflorescence); reactive silica (ASR); sulphates. Aggregates should be clean, hard, strong, durable; washed and screened before use. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fineness modulus of sand: Fine sand 2.2–2.6; medium 2.6–2.9; coarse 2.9–3.2 (ASTM range 2.3–3.1). Lawrencepur sand (KP/Punjab) is a well-known high-quality sand; Margalla crush is a common coarse aggregate. Bulking of sand: Damp sand increases in volume up to ≈ 20–30% at ≈ 4–6% moisture — correct volume batching for it. Flakiness index: thickness < 0.6 × mean size; elongation index: length > 1.8 × mean size.

Sand types: pit sand (sharp, angular — best for mortar), river sand (rounded, fine — plaster), sea sand (contains salts — avoid), manufactured (crushed) sand. Bulking of sand: increase in volume due to moisture films; max ~20–40% at about 4–6% moisture; nil for completely dry or saturated sand. Silt content in sand should not exceed ~8% (field test: silt ≤ 8% by volume). Shape: rounded (good workability), angular (good bond & strength), flaky/elongated (undesirable). Tests: crushing value (≤ 30% wearing surfaces, ≤ 45% others), impact value, Los Angeles abrasion, specific gravity (~2.6–2.7), water absorption, flakiness/elongation index, soundness.

Potable water is generally suitable; must be clean, free from injurious oils, acids, alkalis, salts, sugar, organic matter (ACI 26.4.1.4; ASTM C1602). pH commonly ≥ 6 (6–8). Sea water not used for RC/prestressed (chlorides → corrosion). Only about 1/3 of mixing water is needed for hydration; the rest gives workability and later leaves pores.

w/c = weight of water ÷ weight of cement. Abrams' law: for given materials and full compaction, strength depends only on w/c: f = A / B^(w/c) → lower w/c, higher strength (inverse relation). Strength depends on w/c; economy depends on the % of aggregate that still gives a workable mix. Typical w/c 0.4–0.6; HPC can go to 0.25 with superplasticizers. Advantages of low w/c: higher strength, lower permeability, better weathering & freeze-thaw resistance, better bond with steel, less drying shrinkage & cracking, less volume change. Adding water at site raises w/c: e.g., 685 lb cement, 292 lb water (w/c 0.43) + 10 gal (≈ 84 lb) water/yd³ → w/c ≈ 0.55 → big strength loss. Gel/space ratio (Powers): strength = 240 x³ MPa (x = gel/space ratio) — strength depends on how much space hydrates fill. Exam point: Adding water at constant cement content raises slump AND w/c (bad). To raise slump correctly, add water + cement together (constant w/c) or use a water reducer. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 17.1 — Abrams’ law: compressive strength decreases with increasing water–cement ratio. Water needed for complete hydration ≈ 0.23–0.25 by mass plus ≈ 0.15 for gel water — total ≈ 0.38–0.42; extra water creates capillary pores.

Admixture: material other than cement, water and aggregates (and fibres) added to the batch immediately before or during mixing to modify fresh or hardened properties. Reasons: reduce cost, achieve properties more effectively, maintain quality in adverse weather, handle emergencies. No admixture substitutes for good concreting practice; always run trial mixes (compatibility with cement — C₃A content and fineness affect performance).

Type Function Notes A Water reducing Reduces water ≥ 5% (typically 5–10%); lignosulfonates, hydroxylated carboxylic acids, carbohydrates B Retarding Delays set; sugar, borax, lignin, tartaric acid, gypsum, soluble zinc salts C Accelerating Faster set & early strength; CaCl₂ (most common), Ca nitrite, Ca nitrate, Ca formate, triethanolamine D Water reducing + retarding Retards set by 1–3 h E Water reducing + accelerating — F High-range water reducing (HRWR / superplasticizer) Water reduction ≥ 12% (12–30%) G HRWR + retarding — Mid-range WR (no ASTM type) Water reduction 6–12% Introduced 1984; slumps 125–200 mm ASTM C1017 Type 1 / Type 2 Plasticizing / plasticizing + retarding (for flowing concrete) Flowing concrete: slump > 190 mm (7½ in) yet cohesive ASTM C260 Air-entraining admixtures Vinsol resin, synthetic detergents, sulfonated lignin, fatty acid salts

Mechanism: molecules adsorb on cement grains → same-sign surface charge → electrostatic repulsion / dispersion → released trapped water → more workability. Uses: (i) same w/c → higher slump; (ii) same slump → lower w/c → higher strength (28-day strength 10–25% more); (iii) same strength & slump → less cement. Plasticizers: dosage 0.1–0.4% by weight of cement, water reduction 5–15%, slump increase 3–8 cm; good plasticizer entrains < 2% air. Lignosulphonates (Ca, Na, ammonium) most common. Superplasticizers (HRWR): sulphonated melamine formaldehyde (SMF), sulphonated naphthalene formaldehyde (SNF), modified lignosulphonates, polycarboxylate ethers (PCE) — latest. Water reduction 12–30%; strengths > 70 MPa possible; nearly no bleeding/segregation at right dose. Effect of superplasticizer is short-lived: 30–60 min, then rapid slump loss (worse at high temperature) → often added at site. Example: 75 mm slump + plasticizer → ~230 mm slump. Over-dose → segregation, bleeding, excessive retardation. Higher C₃A reduces efficiency. Water reducers may slightly increase drying shrinkage; lignin-based may add 1–2% air. Uses of flowing concrete: thin sections, congested reinforcement, tremie (under-water), pumping, places where vibration impossible. Commercial examples in notes: Chemplast P-200 (plasticizer); Chemrite AG 200, Chemrite NN, Ultra Super Plast 437 (superplasticizers).

Delay setting; used in hot weather (concrete > 30 °C), long hauls, large pours (avoid cold joints), oil-well grouting, exposed-aggregate finishes. Examples: sugar, borax, boric acid, lignosulphonates, tartaric acid, carbohydrate derivatives, gypsum, soluble zinc salts, MgO. Do not lower concrete temperature; increase bleeding; may reduce 1–3-day strength; can increase rate of slump loss. Best hot-weather remedy is cooling the water/aggregates.

Speed setting & early strength; cold weather (< 5 °C / 41 °F), repairs, precast (early demoulding). Calcium chloride (CaCl₂): cheapest, most used (esp. plain concrete). Max 2% by mass of cement; add as solution with mixing water (dry flakes → pop-outs, dark spots). Regular flake ≥ 77% CaCl₂; concentrated ≥ 94%. Side effects: more drying shrinkage, reinforcement corrosion, darkening/discoloration, scaling. Not an anti-freeze. Do NOT use CaCl₂ in: prestressed concrete, parking garages, concrete with embedded aluminium, reactive aggregates, sulphate exposure, dry-shake metallic floor finishes, hot weather, mass concrete. Caution: steam curing, dissimilar metals, galvanized forms, coloured concrete. Non-chloride accelerators: calcium nitrite, calcium nitrate, calcium formate, triethanolamine, sodium thiocyanate. Other ways to accelerate: Type III cement, extra 60–120 kg/m³ cement, water reducer, higher curing temperature. Exam point: ACI 318 max water-soluble chloride ion (% by mass of cement): prestressed 0.06; RC exposed to chloride 0.15; RC dry/protected 1.00; other RC 0.30.

Introduce billions of microscopic, stable, uniformly distributed air bubbles (≈ 10–1000 µm; slides 10–500 µm; 0.0004–0.02 in). Purpose: freeze–thaw durability; water expands ~9% on freezing → pushes into air voids instead of cracking paste. Also resistance to de-icer scaling, better workability, less bleeding & segregation, improved sulphate & ASR resistance. Air content commonly 3–7% (4–8%); bubble spacing factor ≤ 0.2 mm (slide: ≤ 0.01 in). Each 1% air ↓ compressive strength by ≈ 5%; air-entrained concrete ≈ 5% lighter; not for gravity dams where weight is needed. Agents: Vinsol resin, Dadex, natural wood resins & soaps, animal/vegetable fats, alkali salts of sulphonated compounds, calcium lignosulphonate; gas-forming (aluminium/zinc powder, H₂O₂) give aerated concrete. Introduced in 1930s; specs ASTM C260 (admixture), C233 (testing), C226 (for cement).

Admixture Purpose / material Corrosion inhibitors Calcium nitrite, sodium nitrite, amines, ester amines; anodic inhibitors stabilise passive film Shrinkage reducers Propylene glycol, polyoxyalkylene alkyl ether; cut drying shrinkage 25–50% ASR inhibitors Lithium nitrate, carbonate, hydroxide; barium salts Colouring (pigments) Iron oxide, chromium oxide, cobalt blue, carbon black; ≤ 10% of cement (≤ 6% no effect); ASTM C979; avoid CaCl₂ with pigments Dampproofing Calcium/ammonium stearate, butyl stearate, petroleum products — often ineffective under pressure Permeability reducers Latex, calcium stearate; best method: low w/c (< 0.5) + long moist curing Bonding admixtures PVC, PVA, acrylics, SBR latex; 5–20% of cement; bond new to old concrete Gas-forming Aluminium powder — slight expansion before hardening (grouts) or cellular (aerated) concrete Air detrainers Tributyl phosphate, dibutyl phthalate, silicones — reduce air Hydration control Two-part stabiliser + activator; can suspend hydration up to 72 h Antiwashout Cellulose ether, acrylic polymer — under-water placement without tremie Pumping aids Polymers, bentonite, hydrated lime — improve pumpability Foaming agents Surfactants, hydrolysed protein — foamed concrete Fungicidal/germicidal/insecticidal Polyhalogenated phenols, dieldrin, copper compounds

Definition: finely divided siliceous (or siliceous + aluminous) materials added in relatively large amounts, 20–70% by mass of cementitious material. Pozzolan: siliceous/aluminous material with little or no cementing value itself, but in finely divided form reacts with Ca(OH)₂ in presence of water to form C-S-H. Name from pozzolana volcanic ash (Pozzuoli, Italy; Roman concrete = lime + volcanic ash). Pozzolanic reaction: Ca(OH)₂ + SiO₂ + H₂O → C-S-H (consumes weak CH, refines pores). Benefits: lower cost & energy, lower CO₂ (cement production ≈ 7–8% of world CO₂; ~1 t CO₂ per t cement), lower heat, lower permeability, higher long-term strength, better sulphate/chloride/ASR resistance, less bleeding. Drawbacks: slower early strength, need longer curing; very fine SCMs (SF, RHA) increase water demand. Classification: natural (volcanic ash/tuff, pumicite, diatomaceous earth, calcined clay & shale, metakaolin) and by-products/artificial (fly ash, silica fume, GGBS, rice husk ash). SCM Source Key data Effects / uses Fly ash (pulverised fuel ash) — ASTM C618 Residue of powdered-coal combustion in thermal power plants, collected electrostatically from flue gases Spherical glassy particles (cenospheres, plerospheres) ~1–100 µm; Class F (anthracite/bituminous coal): SiO₂+Al₂O₃+Fe₂O₃ ≥ 70%, low lime (< 7–10%), only pozzolanic, dose 15–30%. Class C (sub-bituminous/lignite): ≥ 50%, ~20% lime, pozzolanic + cementitious, dose 15–40% "Ball-bearing" effect → better workability, less water, p

Workability: ease with which concrete can be mixed, transported, placed, compacted fully (100%) and finished without segregation — having regard to the mode of compaction and place of deposition. Consistency: degree of fluidity / mobility (ability to flow); measured roughly by slump. Workability is the wider term. Rheology: fresh concrete is a yield-stress (Bingham) fluid — yield stress governs whether it flows/fills forms; plastic viscosity governs flow speed.

Water content (main factor): more water → more fluidity but bleeding & low strength. Mix proportions / paste content: low paste → harsh mix; high paste → rich mix (lubrication, "ball-bearing effect"). Aggregate size: larger size → less surface area → thicker paste coating → more workable (1" cube: 6 in²; split to ½" cubes: 12 in²; ¼": 24 in²). Shape & texture: rounded/smooth > angular/rough. Grading: well graded → better. Admixtures: plasticizers, air entrainment ↑ workability; fly ash ↑; silica fume ↓. Also: cement content & fineness, temperature (high temp → slump loss), time/transport duration.

Types: true, shear (repeat test), collapse (very wet). Segregation: separation of constituents so the mix is no longer uniform; caused by differences in specific gravity and size (aggregate SG 2.6–2.7, cement 3.1–3.2). Three types: (1) coarse aggregate separates from mortar/mix; (2) cement paste separates from coarse aggregate (grout escapes); (3) water separates from mix = bleeding. Causes: poorly graded aggregate, excess water, badly proportioned/insufficiently mixed mix, free fall > 1.5 m, long transport, under-water placing, congested reinforcement, over-vibration, leaky formwork. Effects: honeycombing, rock pockets, sand streaks, porous layers, low density & strength, non-homogeneous mass, plastic shrinkage cracks. Prevention: proper grading & w/c, correct handling; drop > 1.5 m through chutes/inclined belts (slope 1:3 to 1:2) or tremie; don't let concrete flow laterally; tight formwork; vibrate correct duration; air entrainment, pozzolans; remix segregated concrete before placing (not after initial set).

Bleeding: rise of mixing water to the surface as solids settle (special form of segregation, water lightest). Main cause: high w/c (≈ 0.7); also coarse cement, lack of fines, poor mixing. Types: normal (uniform seepage over whole surface) and channel bleeding (water escapes through localised channels). Laitance: weak, dusty layer of cement & fines carried to the top by bleeding; must be removed before next lift. Effects: loss of homogeneity, permeability, high w/c and weak top layer, water pockets under aggregates & bars → poor bond, delayed finishing, poor pumpability, poor bond between lifts, slip-form pavement edge collapse. Control: reduce water / lower slump, finer cement, more fines in sand, more cement, SCMs (fly ash; silica fume most effective), air entrainment, proper grading. If bleed water rate < evaporation rate → surface dries while plastic → plastic shrinkage cracking. Retarders increase bleeding; superplasticized mixes may bleed slightly more than control at equal w/c.

Air content: pressure method (ASTM C231), volumetric (C173), gravimetric. Unit weight/yield: ASTM C138. Setting time of concrete: penetration resistance on sieved mortar (ASTM C403). Temperature, bleeding (ASTM C232), segregation resistance, heat generation, wet analysis. Slump loss: loss of workability with time (hydration + evaporation + absorption); worse in hot weather and with superplasticizers/retarders. Plastic settlement cracking: cracks over reinforcement as concrete settles.

Batching: by weight (preferred, accurate ±0.1% of batch in lab) or by volume (nominal mixes, adjust for bulking). Lab machine mixing (ASTM C192): CA + part water → start → FA, cement, rest water → mix 3 min, rest 3 min, mix 2 min. Hand mixing: cement + sand dry until uniform colour → add CA → add water. Truck (ready-mixed) concrete (ASTM C94): 70–100 revolutions at mixing speed (6–18 rpm); agitating speed 2–6 rpm; discharge within 1½ h or before 300 revolutions. First ready-mix delivered 1913 (Baltimore). Transporting methods: mortar pans, wheelbarrows/handcarts, buckets & cableways/ropeways, chutes, belt conveyors, skip & hoist, transit/agitator trucks, dumpers, concrete pumps (boom/line), tremie (under water), helicopter. Placing rules: place as near as possible to final position; in uniform layers (150–450 mm); before initial set; avoid cold joints; free drop ≤ 1.5 m; don't move concrete laterally with vibrators. Compaction (consolidation): removes entrapped air (5% voids can cut strength ~30%). Hand: rodding, ramming, tamping. Mechanical: internal (needle/immersion) vibrators (most common; insert vertically, withdraw slowly), external (form) vibrators, surface/screed vibrators, vibrating tables; also centrifugation (spun pipes/poles), pressure & jolting, vacuum dewatering. Poor consolidation → honeycombing, early corrosion, low strength. Over-vibration → segregation, bleeding, laitance. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 19.

Curing: maintaining satisfactory moisture and temperature in concrete for a suitable period immediately after placing & finishing so hydration continues and desired properties develop. Two purposes: (1) retain moisture so strength keeps rising; (2) delay drying shrinkage until concrete is strong enough to resist cracking. Factors: time, temperature, moisture. Longer curing → greater strength, lower permeability, better durability. Concrete must not dry or freeze in the first 7–10 days; if it freezes in first 24 h it may never reach its properties. Dried concrete cannot be re-vitalised fully. Minimum curing: ≈ 7 days for OPC (ACI/IS), ≥ 10 days with mineral admixtures or in hot/dry weather; concrete with fly ash needs longer curing. Curing temperature: higher → faster early gain but lower ultimate strength; best ≈ room temperature (course notes: 28–32 °C range; strongest long-term at ~40 °F but impractical); > 120 °F (≈ 50 °C) harmful.

Category Methods Water curing (adding water) Ponding, immersion, spraying/sprinkling, fogging, wet coverings (hessian/burlap, straw, sand) Membrane curing (sealing in water) Polyethylene sheets, waterproof paper, liquid membrane-forming curing compounds Application of heat Steam curing (live steam at atmospheric pressure; high-pressure autoclave), electrical, infrared, hot-water curing Internal / self-curing Admixtures such as polyethylene glycol (PEG), pre-wetted lightweight aggregate, SAP — useful where water is scarce

Accelerates strength; used in precast/prestressed elements (girders, slabs, piles, blocks). Live steam (atmospheric, ~14 psi): max 40–100 °C, optimum 65–80 °C; higher initial temperature → lower ultimate strength. Autoclave (high pressure): 80–170 psi, 163–190 °C (325–375 °F); small units (blocks, AAC). Cycle: (1) delay/presetting period, (2) heating period, (3) maximum temperature period, (4) cooling period. Advantages: 24-h strength ≈ 28-day normal strength; less creep & shrinkage; better sulphate resistance; no efflorescence; quality control. Disadvantages: costly set-up, not in-situ, unsuitable for large surfaces, skilled labour; CaCl₂ to be used with caution.
7.3 Strength gain with age (Type I, moist cured — ACI 209)

Age (days) 3 7 14 21 28 % of 28-day strength ≈ 46% ≈ 70% ≈ 88% ≈ 96% 100% About 90% of strength develops in first 28 days; concrete continues gaining strength for years if moist. ACI 209: f'c(t) = f'c(28) × t / (4 + 0.85t) for Type I moist cured.

Maximum resistance to axial compressive load per unit area; tested at 28 days (also 7 days); expressed in psi or MPa. Specimens: cylinder 150 × 300 mm (6 × 12 in) (ASTM C39, ACI), cube 150 mm (BS/IS; 100 mm if max aggregate ≤ 20 mm), cores (ASTM C42). L/D of cylinder = 2. Cube strength ≈ 1.25 × cylinder strength (cylinder ≈ 0.8 × cube). Cubes tested on cast sides (not top/bottom), no packing; loading ≈ 140 kg/cm²/min (≈ 14 MPa/min; ASTM C39: 0.25 ± 0.05 MPa/s). At least 3 specimens per age. Most structural concrete: 3000–5000 psi (20–35 MPa); high-rise columns up to 12,000–15,000 psi. High-strength concrete (ACI 363): f'c ≥ 8000 psi (55 MPa). HPC (class notes): 10,000–15,000 psi, w/c ≈ 0.25.

w/c ratio (most important; inverse — Abrams). Degree of compaction (voids/porosity). Curing (time, temperature, humidity). Age. Cement: type (Type III high early), fineness, composition, content (direct relation). Aggregate: strength, texture, shape, grading, size, cleanliness, aggregate/cement ratio (strength ↑ as a/c decreases to ~2). Air content (inverse). Admixtures. Test conditions: specimen shape & size, moisture & temperature of specimen (wet specimens test lower), loading rate (faster → higher), end conditions/capping.

Test Specimen / standard Formula / value Direct tension Difficult; rarely used ≈ 8–12% of f'c Split cylinder (Brazilian) 150 × 300 mm cylinder, ASTM C496; 3 mm plywood strips 25 mm wide; load rate 0.7–1.4 MPa/min T = 2P / (π L D) ; fct ≈ 6.7 √f'c psi (≈ 0.56 √f'c MPa) Modulus of rupture (flexure) — third-point 150 × 150 × 700 mm beam (100 × 100 × 500 if agg ≤ 19 mm); 6 × 6 × 30 in; ASTM C78; load lines 20 cm (or 13.3 cm) apart fr = PL / (b d²) if fracture in middle third (a > 20 cm for 15 cm beam); fr = 3Pa / (b d²) if a between 17 and 20 cm; discard if a < 17 cm. ACI: fr = 7.5 √f'c psi = 0.62 √f'c MPa Modulus of rupture — centre-point ASTM C293 fr = 3PL / (2 b d²) (gives higher values) Order: modulus of rupture > split tensile > direct tensile (for same concrete). Flexural test load rate ≈ 7 kg/cm²/min (400 kg/min for 15 cm, 180 kg/min for 10 cm beams).

Stress–strain curve of concrete is non-linear (no truly linear part); peak at strain ≈ 0.002; crushing strain 0.003 (ACI design). Modulus of elasticity (ACI 318): Ec = 57,000 √f'c psi = 4700 √f'c MPa (normal weight); Ec = 33 w^1.5 √f'c psi (w = 90–160 pcf) = 0.043 w^1.5 √f'c MPa. Range ≈ 15–40 GPa (kN/mm²) at 28 days. Test: ASTM C469 (secant modulus). Modular ratio n = Es / Ec; ≈ 9.3 for 3000 psi concrete. Es = 29,000 ksi (200 GPa). Poisson's ratio of concrete: 0.1 – 0.2 (≈ 0.15–0.20). Unit weight: plain concrete 140–145 pcf (≈ 2300 kg/m³); reinforced 150 pcf (≈ 2400 kg/m³); normal weight ≈ 2200–2400 kg/m³. Coefficient of thermal expansion ≈ 5.5 × 10⁻⁶ /°F (≈ 10 × 10⁻⁶ /°C); e.g., 100 ft slab, 100 °F change → ≈ 0.66 in movement. Voids reduce E, compressive and flexural strength.

Ease with which liquids/gases pass through concrete; governed by capillary porosity and connectivity of pores of the paste. Factors: w/c ratio, curing, compaction, workability, aggregate soundness/porosity & grading, age (permeability ↓ with age as gel fills pores), cement fineness (finer → lower), type of structure. Low permeability → durability, frost & chemical resistance, steel protection; essential for water-retaining structures. Sound dense concrete with w/c < 0.50, properly placed & cured, is watertight. No single ASTM/BS permeability test in notes; common: water penetration (DIN), RCPT (ASTM C1202), sorptivity, air permeability.

Type When / cause Notes & control Plastic shrinkage Before setting, first few hours; surface water evaporates faster than bleed water rises Narrow, short, random/parallel surface cracks. Control: wind breaks, sun shades, cool concrete (ice in mix water), fogging, polythene cover, curing compound, evaporation retarder, fibres; evaporation > ~1 kg/m²/h is critical Drying shrinkage Hardened concrete loses water from gel pores (loss of free/capillary water causes little change) Continues for years at decreasing rate; ~50% of total in first year (other data: 14–34% of 20-yr shrinkage in 2 weeks, 66–85% in 1 year). Paste can shrink ~1% Autogenous shrinkage Self-desiccation from hydration in sealed concrete (no moisture exchange) Very small in normal concrete (notes: 5–10 × 10⁻⁶); important in high-strength low-w/c concrete and dam interiors Carbonation shrinkage CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ (smaller volume) Slow, from surface inward; increases weight of concrete Thermal contraction Cooling after heat of hydration or environment Mass concrete cracking

w/c and water content (↑ shrinkage) — main factor; drying shrinkage ∝ w/c and inversely ∝ aggregate/cement ratio. Aggregate: more aggregate & stiffer (high E), rough aggregate → less shrinkage; lightweight aggregate → more. Relative humidity: no shrinkage at 100% RH; lower RH → more. Member size: larger → less (but slower). Admixtures: pore refinement ↑ shrinkage; CaCl₂ ↑. Cement fineness ↑ shrinkage. Reinforcement restrains shrinkage. Effects: cracking when restrained (tension > tensile strength), opens joints, tile debonding, extra deflection, prestress loss; improves grip on bars (bond). Prevention: low water, max aggregate, early curing, shrinkage reducers, joints, sun shades, dampen sub-grade (not over-wet).

Creep: time-dependent increase in strain under sustained (constant) load; instantaneous (elastic) strain occurs first, then creep. On unloading: instantaneous recovery + creep recovery, leaving residual (permanent) deformation. Total creep = basic creep + drying creep. Creep strain = φ × elastic strain (φ = creep coefficient ≈ 1.5 – 4; higher when loaded young: ~3.7 at 7 days vs ~1.4 at 1 year). In beams, long-term creep deflection can be ≈ 2 × initial elastic deflection; compression steel controls creep. Factors (↑ creep): higher w/c, more/poorer paste, lower strength, young age at loading, poor curing, low humidity, higher stress (creep ∝ stress; no lower limit), higher temperature (up to ~70 °C), lightweight/low-E aggregate, admixtures & pozzolans. Aggregate itself hardly creeps — it restrains paste. Effects: increased deflection of beams, buckling of eccentric columns, loss of prestress, stress redistribution; beneficial: relieves restrained shrinkage & thermal stresses. Harmful in dams (internal cracking). Test: ASTM C512. High-strength concrete: shrinkage ≈ normal concrete; creep coefficient considerably less.

Concrete is the most fire-resistant structural material, but strength & E fall and creep rises at high temperature; steel protected by cover. Notes table (normal weight): min slab/wall thickness for 1, 2, 3, 4 h = 3.5", 4.5", 6", 7"; min column/beam dimension = 8", 10", 12", 14". Cover for fire: slabs ¾" (1 h)–1¼" (3 h); beams/columns 1½" (1–3 h), 2" (4 h). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 21.1 — Strength gain with age for OPC, rapid-hardening and blended cements. Cylinder vs cube: Cylinder strength ≈ 0.8 × cube strength (150 mm cube vs 150 × 300 mm cylinder). 7-day strength ≈ 65–70% of 28-day strength for OPC; tensile strength ≈ 10% of compressive strength.

Durability: ability of concrete to resist weathering, chemical attack, abrasion and other deterioration while performing satisfactorily in its environment for its design life. Internal causes: alkali–aggregate reaction, volume changes (thermal incompatibility of aggregate & paste), permeability, corrosion of steel. External causes: physical (freeze–thaw, abrasion, temperature extremes, weathering), chemical (sulphates, chlorides, acids, leaching, sea water, CO₂), mechanical, electrolytic. Three most common problems (ACI): corrosion of steel, freeze–thaw breakdown, chemical attack (ACI 318 Chapter 19 gives exposure classes & limits). For durable concrete: low w/c, adequate cement content, full compaction, proper curing, adequate cover, suitable cement (SRC, PBFC, PPC), SCMs, good workmanship, low permeability.

Pore type Size Water / significance Gel pores (in C-S-H) 1 – 10 nm Water chemically/physically bound; freezes only ≈ −78 °C Capillary pores 0.01 – 5 µm Excess mixing water; freeze at −1 to −8 °C; govern permeability & frost damage Entrained air voids ≈ 10 – 1000 µm (0.1–0.2 mm typical) Usually empty; relieve freezing pressure Entrapped air voids 10 µm – 1 cm (> 1 mm typically) From poor compaction; reduce strength

Water expands ≈ 9% on freezing; damage when concrete is critically saturated (≈ 91% of pores filled). Mechanisms: hydraulic pressure (unfrozen water forced through capillaries), osmotic pressure, capillary ice growth. Signs: scaling, spalling, D-cracking, pop-outs, crumbling at joints. Locations: pavements, bridge decks, retaining walls in cold climates. De-icing salts (NaCl, CaCl₂; formates) make it more severe (osmotic pressure, saturation) → surface scaling + rebar corrosion. Prevention: air entrainment (4–8%), low w/c, proper curing, frost-resistant aggregate, allow drying before first freeze.

Alkalis (Na⁺, K⁺, OH⁻ from cement) + reactive silica in aggregate + moisture → alkali-silica gel which absorbs water and swells: SiO₂ + 2NaOH + H₂O → Na₂SiO₃·2H₂O. Gel forms at the aggregate–paste transition zone; expansion > tensile strength → cracking; at the surface → map (pattern) cracking; also pop-outs, gel exudation, loss of strength & stiffness. Theories: absorption-swelling and osmotic pressure. Needs RH ≥ ~75–80%. Common in dams, piers, sea walls, pavements. Prevention: low-alkali cement (Na₂O eq ≤ 0.6%), limit cement content & external alkalis (sea water, de-icers), non-reactive aggregate, limit moisture, SCMs (fly ash, GGBS, silica fume, volcanic glass), lithium admixtures, air entrainment (room for gel). Alkali–carbonate reaction is a related type with dolomitic limestone.

Sulphate ions (Na, K, Mg, Ca sulphates) from soils, groundwater, sea water, sewage, industrial waste react with hydration products: CH + sulphate → gypsum; C₃A hydrates (monosulphate) + gypsum → ettringite (calcium sulpho-aluminate) — large volume increase → expansion & cracking. Na₂SO₄ + CH + 2H → CaSO₄·2H₂O + 2NaOH (alkalinity maintained, C-S-H stable). Magnesium sulphate is most aggressive: forms insoluble Mg(OH)₂, lowers pH, attacks C-S-H itself → mushy, non-cohesive mass. Signs: cracking & expansion starting at edges and corners; whitish surface; ettringite in cracks/voids. Prevention: dense low-permeability concrete (low w/c), limit C₃A — Type II (≤ 8%) or Type V (≤ 5%)/SRC, pozzolans/GGBS (for > 1500 mg/L sulphate), protective coatings.

Steel is protected by high pH (> 12) passive oxide film and concrete cover. Chlorides (or carbonation) destroy passivity → rust (volume ↑ 2–6×) → cracking, spalling, loss of bond & section. Chloride attack is responsible for ≈ 40% of concrete structural failures (class presentation). Internal sources: sea water in mixing, CaCl₂ accelerator, unwashed/salty aggregates. External: sea water, de-icing salts, stored chemicals. Prevention: more cover (+1 inch cover can roughly double service life), low permeability (low w/c, SCMs), corrosion inhibitors (Ca nitrite), epoxy-coated/galvanized/stainless-clad bars, cathodic protection, chloride limits (ACI table in 5.4).

CO₂ from air + Ca(OH)₂ (with moisture) → CaCO₃; lowers pore pH from ~12.5 to < 9 → depassivates steel within carbonated depth. Rate ↑ with permeability, high w/c, poor curing; fastest at RH ≈ 50–70%. Lightweight concrete: carbonation depth ≈ 2 × normal → more cover. Test: phenolphthalein spray — pink = uncarbonated (alkaline), colourless = carbonated.
9.7 Other attacks & concreting in sea water

Leaching/efflorescence: soft water dissolves CH → white salt deposits; pozzolans reduce CH and efflorescence. Acid attack: dissolves CH & C-S-H; HAC and dense concrete better. Sea water: salt crystallisation in wet–dry zones, sulphate & chloride attack, abrasion; use max w/c 0.45–0.50, dense well-compacted concrete, adequate cover, GGBS/PBFC or SRC. Abrasion/erosion: hard aggregate, high strength, low w/c, good finishing & curing.

By activity: active (moving in width/length/depth) vs dormant (unchanging). By time: plastic-concrete cracks vs hardened-concrete cracks. Structural cracks: from wrong design, faulty construction or overloading — in beams, columns, slabs, footings; endanger safety. Non-structural cracks: from internally induced stresses (shrinkage, thermal, moisture) — walls, parapets, driveways; mostly aesthetic but allow moisture ingress. IS 456 permissible surface crack width: 0.3 mm (normal, harmless), 0.2 mm (members in contact with moisture/soil), 0.1 mm (aggressive/"severe" environment).

Plastic shrinkage cracks — narrow, nearly invisible, while concrete is plastic. Expansion cracks — thermal expansion pushing against restraints; prevented by expansion joints. Heaving cracks — frozen ground lifting slab; tree roots. Settling cracks — voids/settlement of subgrade; poorly compacted backfill; differential settlement. Overloading cracks — excess weight (e.g., snow, rain loads).

Permeability, thermal movement, corrosion of reinforcement, moisture movement (drying shrinkage — combination of shrinkage + restraint), creep, poor construction practice (poor materials, excess water, inadequate curing, poor joints), poor design/specification, poor maintenance, chemical reactions (ASR), foundation settlement, indiscriminate additions/alterations (e.g., enclosing cantilever balconies). Thermal coefficient of brickwork vertically ≈ 1.5 × horizontal (no vertical restraint).

Procedure: state problem → observe (structural or not; orientation, width, depth, length, age, exposure) → hypothesis → test (dye penetrant, optical comparator; ultrasonic, magnetic particle, electrical potential for sub-surface) → conclusion. Epoxy injection: bonds cracks as narrow as 0.05 mm; restores strength; ports along crack, seal surface, inject under pressure. Routing and sealing: widen crack at surface and fill with sealant; non-structural, flat surfaces (floors, pavements). Stitching: drill both sides, grout U-shaped metal staples ("dogs") across crack — re-establishes tensile strength. Drilling and plugging: drill 50–75 mm hole along straight crack and grout to form a key (vertical cracks in retaining walls). Gravity filling: low-viscosity monomers/resins for cracks 0.03–2 mm. Overlays & surface treatments: fine surface cracks in slabs/pavements with no further movement. Prevention: low water content, max aggregate size, sub-grade prepared & moist, curing plan, shrinkage-reducing admixtures, fibres, control/expansion joints. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 23.1 — Typical time after casting when different types of cracks appear. Plastic shrinkage cracks appear within hours (hot, windy weather) — prevent by fog spraying, wind breaks, early curing; drying shrinkage cracks appear over weeks–months.

Mix design: selecting proportions of cement, water, aggregates, admixtures to obtain required workability, strength and durability at minimum cost. Three phases: specifying, designing, proportioning. Basic considerations: economy (minimise cement: lowest workable slump, good CA/FA ratio, largest practical aggregate, admixtures), workability, strength & durability (w/c limits for exposure). Water demand depends on aggregate (size, shape, grading), not on cement. Improve workability by redesigning mortar fraction, not by adding water. Any method gives a first approximation — confirm with trial batches. Nominal mixes (volume) for quick reference: 1:3:6 (M10), 1:2:4 (M15 ≈ 15 MPa), 1:1.5:3 (M20), 1:1:2 (M25). Dry volume ≈ 1.54 × wet volume (≈ 52–57% extra).

Step 1 — Material data: sieve analysis (FM of FA), dry-rodded unit weight of CA, SG and absorption of aggregates, SG of cement (3.15). Step 2 — Slump: from specification or ACI table; use the lowest slump that permits placement. Step 3 — Max aggregate size: ≤ 1/5 narrowest form dimension, 1/3 slab depth, 3/4 clear bar spacing. Step 4 — Mixing water & air content: from Table (depends on slump, max size, air-entrained or not). Step 5 — w/c ratio: from strength (Table) and durability; take the lower. Step 6 — Cement content = water ÷ (w/c); check minimum cement content. Step 7 — Coarse aggregate: volume fraction (Table, from max size & FM of sand) × 27 ft³ (or 1 m³) × dry-rodded unit weight → OD weight; SSD = OD × (1 + absorption). Step 8 — Fine aggregate: absolute volume method — FA volume = total − (water + cement + CA + air) volumes; volume = weight ÷ (SG × 62.4 pcf or × 1000 kg/m³); air volume = air% × 27 ft³. (Alternatively, weight method.) Step 9 — Moisture adjustment: stockpile weight = OD weight × (1 + MC); reduce mixing water by free (surface) moisture = weight × (MC − absorption). Step 10 — Trial batch: test slump, unit weight, yield, air, segregation, bleeding, finishing; cast strength specimens; adjust.

Type Definition / key data Properties & uses Normal concrete Cement + sand + CA + water; ≈ 2200–2400 kg/m³; setting 30–90 min; slump 1–2 in (notes) Strong in compression, weak in tension; not durable in severe conditions Lightweight concrete (LWC) Density < ≈ 1840–2000 kg/m³ (normal ≈ 2200+); 3 types: (1) aerated/cellular/foamed/gas (large voids, up to 50% air), (2) lightweight-aggregate (pumice, scoria, perlite, vermiculite, expanded clay/shale/slate, sintered fly ash, expanded slag, clinker), (3) no-fines (CA only) Less dead load & seismic force, insulation (heat & sound), fire resistance, easier transport; structural LWC min 17.24 MPa (2500 psi); lower E, more deflection, lower bond & shear strength; carbonation depth ≈ 2× → more cover; porous, water-sensitive, longer mixing. Uses: long-span bridge decks, roof insulation, fillings, fire protection Foam concrete Cement + sand/fly ash + water + preformed foam (≥ 20% foam); dry density 300–1600 kg/m³; 28-day strength 0.2–10 MPa Low thermal conductivity, fire resistant (notes: up to 1450 °C), absorbs energy, self-levelling (no compaction), no lateral load; drying shrinkage 4–10× normal. First used 1923 as insulation Heavyweight concrete Oven-dry density > 2600 kg/m³; aggregate SG > 3.5: barite (≈ 3500 kg/m³ concrete, +45%), magnetite (≈ 3900, +60%), iron shot (≈ 5900), lead shot (≈ 8900); hematite, boron Radiation shielding (hospitals, nuclear plants, PCRV), counterweights, ballast for under-water pipelines, sound/vibration da

Any combination of high concrete/ambient temperature, low humidity, high wind, solar radiation that impairs quality by accelerating moisture loss and hydration (problems when concrete > ~30 °C; placing temperature usually limited to 32–35 °C). Effects: higher water demand, accelerated slump loss, faster setting, plastic shrinkage cracking, cold joints, lower ultimate strength, critical need for early curing. Measures: moisten subgrade, forms & reinforcement; wind breaks & sun shades; cool aggregates and mixing water (ice) — hot cement has minor effect; retarders/WR; place quickly with adequate labour; cover with plastic sheets/evaporation retarders; start curing immediately; concrete at night.

ACI definition: period of more than 3 consecutive days when average daily air temperature < 40 °F (5 °C) and air temperature not > 50 °F (10 °C) for more than half of any 24 h. Problems: fresh concrete may freeze before gaining strength (matrix breaks up); setting very slow below 50 °F; hydration practically stops below ~40 °F. Objectives: prevent early freezing, achieve strength for safe form removal (protect until ≈ 3.5 MPa / 500 psi), maintain curing, limit thermal shock. Measures: Type III cement, hot water, heated aggregates, accelerators (CaCl₂ ≤ 2% where allowed; non-chloride accelerators), air entrainment, low slump/low w/c; insulated forms, blankets, enclosures & heaters; cover immediately after placing; never place on frozen ground. Calcium chloride is not an anti-freeze.

Workability (slump, compacting factor, Vee-Bee, flow, Kelly ball), bleeding, air content, setting time, segregation resistance, unit weight & yield, wet analysis (cement content), temperature, heat generation.

Compressive (cylinder, cube, core), tensile (direct, split), modulus of rupture, density, shrinkage, creep, modulus of elasticity, absorption, permeability, freeze–thaw, chemical resistance, abrasion, bond to steel, cement content analysis. In-situ: rebound (Schmidt) hammer, pull-out, break-off, penetration (Windsor probe), cores, ultrasonic, nuclear/radiographic, load test.

Mould near storage place on rigid vibration-free surface; consolidate by rodding (layers; rod penetrates ~12 mm into lower layer if layer < 100 mm, ~25 mm if ≥ 100 mm; tap mould 10–15 times) or vibration (internal/external); strike off; final layer overfill ≤ 6 mm. Cure first 24 ± ½ h at 27 ± 2 °C and ≥ 90% RH (lab manual), demould, then submerge in water or saturated lime solution (renewed every 7 days) until test; never let dry.

Test Principle / standard Key points Rebound (Schmidt) hammer Surface hardness; ASTM C805 Rebound number correlated with strength; affected by surface finish, moisture, carbonation, aggregate; cheap & quick Ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV) Time of ultrasonic pulse between transducers (20–150 kHz); ASTM C597 High velocity = good quality; low velocity = voids/cracks. Grading (IS 13311): > 4.5 km/s excellent, 3.5–4.5 good, 3.0–3.5 medium, < 3.0 doubtful. Arrangements: direct (best), semi-direct, indirect (surface). Crack depth: readings at 100 mm and 200 mm each side of crack Core test Diamond-bit rotary drill; ASTM C42 Direct evidence of in-situ strength, permeability, carbonation, chemistry; soak, cap (sulphur) ends plane & parallel, test moist; L/D ≈ 2 (correction if less). ACI acceptance: average of 3 cores ≥ 0.85 f'c and none < 0.75 f'c Pull-out / penetration / break-off Partially destructive Strength estimate of in-place concrete Acoustic emission, radiography, cover meter, half-cell potential — Cracks, density, rebar location & corrosion

Strength evaluation of existing structure under gravity loads (not lateral loads); applied in panels to weakest region; measure deflections, stresses, cracks; tells serviceability & capacity; adequate shoring to prevent collapse. Also pile load test.

Strength test = average of 2 cylinders (150 × 300) or 3 cylinders (100 × 200) at 28 days. Acceptable if (a) every average of 3 consecutive tests ≥ f'c, and (b) no single test < f'c − 500 psi (f'c ≤ 5000 psi) or < 0.9 f'c (f'c > 5000 psi). Lab manual: discard specimens that are faulty or differ > 10% from the average.

Setting ≠ hardening: setting = loss of plasticity (C₃A); hardening = strength gain (C₃S, C₂S). Early strength → C₃S; later strength → C₂S; flash set & highest heat → C₃A; least strength role → C₄AF. Gypsum controls setting (added at grinding); not a strength contributor. Unsoundness is due to free lime, MgO, excess SO₃ — not due to fineness. Finer cement: faster strength & more heat, but more shrinkage and cracking risk. Abrams' law: strength depends on w/c (for full compaction) — not on cement content alone. Bleeding is a form of segregation (Type 3). Laitance is the result of bleeding. Air entrainment ↑ workability but ↓ strength; entrapped air is accidental and harmful. Retarders increase bleeding; they do not cool concrete. Calcium chloride is not an anti-freeze and is banned in prestressed concrete. Creep = deformation under sustained load; shrinkage = deformation without load. Young concrete creeps more; high humidity reduces both creep and shrinkage. Compacting factor test suits low-workability concrete; slump test unsuitable for very dry or very wet mixes; Vee-Bee for very dry mixes. Cube strength > cylinder strength (≈ 1.25×) because of platen restraint and lower height/width ratio. Sulphate attack → ettringite & gypsum; best defence low-C₃A cement (Type V) + low w/c; MgSO₄ is the worst. ASR needs all three: reactive silica + alkalis + moisture; sign = map cracking. Carbonation lowers pH (danger to steel), it does not attack concrete strength directly; detected by ph

Substructure: part below plinth level (foundation). Superstructure: part above plinth. Main components: foundation, plinth, walls/columns, floors, doors & windows, sills, lintels, stairs, roof, parapet, finishes, services. Plinth: portion between ground level and ground-floor level; min height ≈ 45 cm above ground. Load-bearing structure: walls carry loads; economical up to 3–4 storeys. Framed structure: beams & columns carry loads; walls are only partitions/panels. Loads: dead, live (imposed), wind, snow, earthquake, thermal. Typical live loads: residential floor 2 kN/m², office 2.5–4 kN/m², accessible roof 1.5 kN/m². Occupancy groups (NBC): A residential, B educational, C institutional, D assembly, E business, F mercantile, G industrial, H storage, J hazardous. Areas: plinth area = built-up covered area at floor level; carpet area = usable area excluding walls, stairs, lifts, verandahs, toilets; circulation area ≈ 10–20% of plinth area. Spread / isolated footing: one column; stepped or sloped. Wall (strip) footing: continuous under load-bearing walls. Combined footing: two or more columns. Rectangular — equal loads; Trapezoidal — larger load near property line. Strap (cantilever) footing: two footings joined by a strap beam; used when exterior column is at property line. Raft / mat: single slab under whole building; used when footings cover > 50% of plan area, low BC, or to reduce differential settlement. Grillage: tiers of steel joists (or timber) embedded in concrete; heavy column loads on low-BC soil. Inverted arch: arches inverted between piers; old practice, now rare.

Pile: when hard stratum is deep, soil is compressible, or uplift / lateral loads exist. Piles by function: end-bearing, friction, compaction, tension (uplift), anchor, batter (inclined loads), fender (protect waterfront structures), sheet piles (retain soil / cut-off). Piles by material: timber, concrete (precast; cast-in-situ — Raymond, Simplex, Franki, Vibro, Pedestal, MacArthur), steel (H, pipe, screw), composite. Under-reamed pile: bulb dia = 2–2.5 × stem dia; spacing ≥ 2 × bulb dia; for black cotton soil. Pile spacing: min 2.5–3 d (friction piles ≥ 3 d). Engineering News formula: Q = WH / [6(S + C)]; C = 2.5 cm (drop hammer), 0.25 cm (steam hammer); FoS = 6. Hiley’s formula — more accurate. Pile group efficiency: Converse–Labarre formula. Negative skin friction: downward drag when soil around pile settles (fill over soft clay). Well (caisson) foundation: bridges/heavy structures in rivers. Shapes — circular (most common), double-D, dumbbell, twin-circular, rectangular. Parts — cutting edge, curb, steining, bottom plug, sand filling, top plug, well cap. Well tilt & shift limits: tilt 1 in 80 (IS 3955 / MoRTH specification; some books quote 1 in 60); shift ≤ 150 mm. Caisson types: box, open (well), pneumatic.

Timbering of trenches: stay bracing (firm soil), box sheeting (loose soil), vertical sheeting (deep, soft soil), runners (very loose), sheet piling (wet/soft). Dewatering: sumps/ditches, well points (sand), deep wells, electro-osmosis (silts/fine soils), freezing, cement/chemical grouting. Causes of foundation failure: unequal settlement, lateral escape of soil, shrinkage of soil, atmospheric action, withdrawal of moisture, tree roots. Stretcher bond: all stretchers; for half-brick (11.5 cm) walls/partitions. Header bond: all headers; for curved walls and footings. Arch terms: intrados (inner curve), extrados (outer curve), soffit, voussoirs (wedge units), keystone (crown), springing line, skewback, span, rise, haunch, spandrel, abutment, pier, impost. By shape: flat, segmental (centre below springing), semi-circular (rise = ½ span), horse-shoe, pointed/Gothic (equilateral, lancet, drop), semi-elliptical (3- or 5-centred), stilted, Venetian, Florentine, Tudor, ogee, relieving. Load on lintel: Masonry above a lintel arches itself; only the triangular portion within 60° lines from the supports is taken as load on the lintel.
