Door size rules: width = 0.4–0.6 × height; height = width + 1.2 m. Common sizes — main door 1.0 × 2.0–2.1 m; internal 0.9 × 2.0 m; bath/WC 0.75 × 2.0 m. Door types: battened & ledged; battened, ledged & braced; framed, ledged & braced; framed & panelled; glazed/sash; flush (solid, hollow, cellular core); louvred; wire-gauzed; revolving; sliding; swing; folding; pivoted; collapsible steel; rolling shutter. Braces: inclined, lower end towards the hanging (hinge) side. Door frame: horns (≈ 10–15 cm projections of head) fixed into wall; holdfasts — 3 per side. Rolling shutters: shops, garages, godowns. Collapsible gates: security without blocking light. Window area: ≥ 1/10 of floor area (bye-laws); ≈ 1/6 in hot-humid climates. Sill height ≈ 75–90 cm. Window types: casement, double-hung sash (counterweights), pivoted, sliding, louvred, bay (projecting), corner, dormer (vertical window on sloping roof), gable, lantern (on flat roof), skylight (on sloping roof plane), clerestory (high on wall), fanlight (above door), ventilator. Hardware: butt, T, strap, counterflap, H/pin and parliament hinges (door opens 180° clear of wall); tower bolt, aldrop, hasp & staple, mortice lock, latch, door closer, door stopper. Term Meaning Frame Fixed part built into the wall: head (top), jambs/posts (sides), sill/threshold (bottom). Horn Projection of the head beyond the jambs (≈ 10–15 cm), built into the wall for fixing. Rebate Recess (≈ 12–15 mm) cut in the frame to receive the shutter. Shutter / leaf Openable part: stiles (vertical) + rails (horizontal) + panels. Hanging stile / shutting stile Stile on the hinge side / stile on the lock side. Top, frieze, lock, bottom rail Rails from top to bottom; lock (middle) rail carries the lock; bottom rail is widest. Muntin Vertical member between two rails dividing panels. Mullion / transom Vertical / horizontal member dividing a window (or door) frame. Sash Frame holding glass panes; sash bars (glazing bars) divide the glass. Architrave Moulded strip covering the joint between frame and wall. Holdfast Mild-steel flat anchor fixing the frame into masonry — 3 per side. Louvres Inclined slats (≈ 45°) allowing air but not rain or view. Location of doors: Near room corners (≈ 20 cm away), minimum number, placed for good circulation and furniture arrangement; opposite openings help cross-ventilation. Flush door cores: Solid core (block board / particle board), hollow core, cellular core (strips with voids). Window glass types: Float/sheet, frosted (obscure), tinted, wired (fire, security), laminated (safety), toughened (≈ 4–5 × stronger, breaks into small blunt pieces), double glazing (heat & sound insulation). Modern frames: Steel, aluminium, uPVC (no paint

Terms: tread (going), riser, nosing, flight, landing, winders, baluster, newel post, handrail, string/stringer, waist (slab thickness), headroom, pitch, scotia. Parameter Residential Public Rise (R) 150–190 mm (≈ 175) ≈ 150 mm Tread (T) 250–300 mm ≈ 300 mm Width 0.9–1.0 m min 1.5–2.0 m Headroom ≥ 2.1 m ≥ 2.1 m Risers per flight 3 min, 12 max (15 common limit) 3 min, 12 max Handrail height 850–900 mm ≈ 900 mm Thumb rules: 2R + T = 550–700 mm (≈ 600); R + T = 400–450 mm; R × T = 40,000–45,000 mm². Pitch: 25°–40°; ideal ≈ 30°–35°. Ramps 1:10–1:12 (wheelchair 1:12). Escalators ≈ 30°. Types: straight, quarter-turn, half-turn (dog-legged — no well between flights; open-newel — well between flights), three-quarter turn, bifurcated, geometrical, circular/spiral (least space), helical. Materials: RCC (most common, fire-resistant), stone, timber, steel, brick. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 9.1 — Stair terms: tread, riser, nosing, waist, pitch line, flight, landing, handrail, baluster, newel post, headroom.

Given: Floor-to-floor height 3.0 m, dog-legged stair, rise 150 mm, tread 250–300 mm. Risers: 3000 ÷ 150 = 20 risers → 2 flights of 10 risers each. Treads: Treads per flight = risers − 1 = 9; going of each flight = 9 × 300 = 2.7 m. Check: 2R + T = 2(150) + 300 = 600 mm ✔ (within 550–700 mm). Requirements of a good stair: Well lit and ventilated; easy to reach (near entrance in public buildings); uniform risers & treads; no winders (if unavoidable, only at bottom); adequate width and headroom; handrails both sides if width > ≈ 1.5 m. Lifts & escalators: Escalator incline ≈ 30° (max 35°), speed ≈ 0.5–0.75 m/s. Lifts needed for buildings over ≈ 4 storeys (bye-laws vary). Winders are tapered steps used to change direction; avoid them. Spiral stair needs least space; dog-legged stair has no well between flights.

Ground floor components: compacted subgrade/fill, base course (lean concrete 1:4:8, ≈ 10 cm), floor finish. Floor finishes: mud, brick, flagstone, cement concrete/IPS, terrazzo, mosaic, ceramic tiles, marble, granite, timber, rubber, linoleum, PVC/vinyl, asphalt, glass. IPS (Indian Patent Stone): 25–50 mm cement concrete finish laid in panels (alternate bays). Terrazzo: marble chips + cement (white/coloured) laid, ground and polished. Linoleum: oxidised linseed oil + cork/wood flour on jute backing. Upper floors: RCC slab (most common), flat slab, ribbed/waffle, hollow block, precast, jack-arch (brick arches on steel joists), timber floors — single joist (≤ 3.6 m), double joist (≤ 7.5 m), framed/triple (> 7.5 m). Selection factors: cost, durability, damp-proofness, sound/heat insulation, hygiene, fire resistance, appearance, maintenance. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Use Suitable flooring Hospitals, labs Terrazzo, vinyl/PVC, epoxy (seamless, hygienic) Libraries, churches, theatres (noiseless) Cork, rubber, linoleum, carpet Industrial / workshops Granolithic, heavy-duty cement concrete, steel-chequered tiles Bathrooms / kitchens Anti-skid ceramic tiles, mosaic, terrazzo Residences (living) Terrazzo, marble, ceramic/porcelain tiles, timber Dance halls, gymnasiums Timber (sprung) flooring Acid-prone areas Acid-resisting tiles, asphalt Granolithic flooring: Hard topping of cement + granite chips (1:1:2), laid on fresh concrete base — for heavy traffic. Mosaic flooring: Small pieces of marble/tile set in cement; ground and polished. Hollow-block / ribbed slabs: Lighter self-weight, better sound and heat insulation, economical for longer spans. Cork flooring = noiseless (libraries, theatres). Granolithic = industrial heavy traffic. Terrazzo = hospitals & residences.

Roof terms: span, rise, pitch (rise/span), ridge, eaves, hip, valley, verge, gable, rafters (common, hip, valley, jack), purlin, cleat, batten, wall plate, ridge piece. Roof type Max. span (approx.) Lean-to 2.4 m Couple roof 3.6 m Couple-close roof 4.2 m Collar-beam roof 4.8–5.0 m Double / purlin roof ≈ 8 m King-post truss 5–8 m Queen-post truss 8–12 m Steel trusses > 12 m Special roofs: mansard (two slopes on each side), gambrel, hipped, gable, north-light / saw-tooth (factories — glazing faces north for uniform light), butterfly, shell, folded plate, dome. Flat roof: RCC slab + terracing (lime concrete / mud phuska + tiles); drainage slope ≈ 1:40–1:100. Roof coverings: thatch, tiles (Allahabad, Mangalore), slates, shingles, AC sheets, GI/CGI sheets, aluminium sheets. GI/AC sheet laps: side lap 1–1½ corrugations; end lap ≈ 15 cm (min 7.5 cm on steep roofs). Rainwater pipes: 75–150 mm dia; roughly one 100 mm pipe per ≈ 40 m² roof area. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 11.1 — Pitched roof terms in plan: ridge, hip, valley, eaves, verge, gable end. Fig. 11.2 — King-post truss (≈ 5–8 m) and queen-post truss (≈ 8–12 m) with their members. Steel truss types: Pratt, Howe, Fink (French), fan, Warren, north-light, bowstring, quadrangular, saw-tooth. Pitch values: ¼ pitch ≈ 26.5°, ⅓ pitch ≈ 33.7°, ½ pitch = 45°. Tiled roofs need steeper pitch than sheet roofs. Roof selection factors: Span, climate (rain/snow), materials available, fire

Causes of dampness: rising ground moisture (capillary), rain penetration, defective construction, condensation, leaking pipes. DPC position: at plinth level, ≥ 15 cm above ground; horizontal DPC continuous over full wall width; vertical DPC in basements. Flexible materials: hot bitumen, bituminous felt, mastic asphalt (semi-rigid), polythene, metal sheets (lead, copper). Rigid materials: dense stone, engineering bricks, cement concrete (1:2:4 / 1:1.5:3, 25–40 mm thick) with waterproofing compound + 2 coats hot bitumen. Methods: membrane DPC, integral (admixtures), surface treatment, cavity walls, guniting (cement-sand sprayed under pressure), pressure grouting, tanking (basements). Anti-termite treatment: chemical soil treatment of trenches and plinth fill before construction. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Requirements of DPC material: Impervious, durable, flexible enough to resist cracking, strong enough for loads, not squeezed out, economical. Mastic asphalt DPC: Laid hot in ≈ 20–25 mm thickness; impervious and durable; may squeeze out under heavy load in hot weather. Bitumen felt DPC: Laid with ≈ 10 cm laps, on a levelled mortar bed; flexible but can be damaged during construction. Anti-termite chemicals: Chlorpyrifos and similar emulsions in trench bottom, sides and plinth fill; older chemicals (aldrin, heptachlor, chlordane) are banned. Tanking: Continuous waterproof membrane on basement floor & walls — external (preferred)

Plaster thickness: external ≈ 20 mm (two coats), internal 12–15 mm, ceiling 6–10 mm; three-coat work 20–25 mm. Mixes: 1:3 (external/ceiling), 1:4, 1:6 (internal); curing ≥ 7 days. Special plasters: stucco (3 coats ≈ 25 mm, decorative), sand-faced, pebble-dash, rough-cast (spatter dash), plaster of Paris, gypsum, Keene’s cement (hard, polished — corners, skirting), barium plaster (X-ray rooms), acoustic plaster, Neeru finish (lime putty). Plaster defects: blistering, cracking, efflorescence, flaking, peeling, popping, rust stains, softness, uneven surface. Pointing: joints raked 10–20 mm deep and refilled with richer mortar (1:1–1:3). Types — flush, recessed, struck, weathered, V, beaded, keyed, rubbed, tuck (projecting band ≈ 3–5 mm). Paint constituents: base (white lead, zinc oxide, red lead, titanium white), vehicle (linseed oil), drier, pigment, thinner (turpentine), extender/inert filler. Types: oil, enamel, emulsion, plastic, distemper, cement paint, bituminous, aluminium, anti-corrosive; whitewash (lime), colour wash. Varnish: oil, spirit (French polish = shellac in spirit), turpentine, water varnish. Paint defects: blistering, chalking, cracking, crawling, flaking, grinning (background visible), saponification (alkali attack), wrinkling, bloom, fading, running, sagging. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 13.1 — Types of pointing (sections through the joint): flush, recessed, struck, weathered, V-groove, beaded, tuck. Dry

Materials: timber, plywood, steel, aluminium, plastic. Slip form — silos, chimneys, towers; jump/climbing form — high-rise cores. Member (OPC, normal weather) Stripping time Vertical faces (walls, columns, beam sides) 16–24 h (IS 456) Slab soffits (props left under) 3 days Beam soffits (props left under) 7 days Props to slabs ≤ 4.5 m span 7 days Props to slabs > 4.5 m span 14 days Props to beams ≤ 6 m span 14 days Props to beams > 6 m span 21 days

Types: single (bricklayer’s / putlog), double (mason’s — stone work), cantilever/needle, suspended, trestle, steel tubular, patented. Parts: standards (vertical, ≈ 2.5–3 m apart), ledgers (horizontal, ≈ 1.2–1.5 m vertical spacing), putlogs (≈ 1.2 m apart, one end in wall), transoms (both ends on ledgers), braces, boarding, guard rail, toe board.

Raking shores: inclined props (60°–75° to ground) supporting unsafe walls. Flying shores: horizontal struts between two parallel walls (≈ up to 9 m apart) when one building is demolished. Dead (vertical) shores: vertical props with needles through wall; for making openings / underpinning.

Purpose: strengthen/deepen existing foundation. Methods — pit method, pile method (jack piles, needle & pile), chemical consolidation (grouting). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 14.1 — Scaffolding parts: standards, ledgers, putlogs, boards, braces, guard rail. Fig. 14.2 — Shoring: raking shore (leaning wall), flying shore (between two walls), dead shore (making openings). Requirements of formwork: Strong for wet concrete + live load, rigid (no deflection), leak-proof joints, easy to remove without damage, re-usable, economical. Loads on formwork: Weight of wet concrete (≈ 24–25 kN/m³), reinforcement, workers & equipment (live load), impact/vibration, lateral pressure of fresh concrete on vertical forms. Release agents: Oil/emulsion applied to form face so it strips cleanly. Underpinning — when needed: Foundation settled, building to be raised, adjacent deeper excavation, change of use with heavier loads. Raking shore: rakers at 60°–75°. Flying shore: no ground support, between walls up to ≈ 9 m apart. Dead shore: vertical props + needles.

Principles of planning: aspect, prospect, privacy, grouping, roominess, furniture requirement, sanitation, flexibility, circulation (horizontal — corridors; vertical — stairs/lifts), elegance, economy, practical considerations. Orientation (northern hemisphere, e.g. Pakistan): long walls facing north–south; minimise east–west exposure; living rooms south for winter sun; kitchen on east (morning sun). FAR / FSI: total covered area of all floors ÷ plot area. Plot coverage: ground-floor covered area ÷ plot area × 100. Typical minimum sizes (NBC): habitable room 9.5 m², width 2.4 m, height 2.75 m; kitchen 5.0 m², width 1.8 m; bath 1.8 m²; WC 1.1 m²; bath/WC height 2.2 m. Open spaces / setbacks: front, rear and side margins fixed by local authority (LDA, CDA, KDA etc.). Building codes: Building Code of Pakistan (BCP) — seismic provisions BCP SP-2007, updated BCP-2021; NBC (India) and IBC often referenced. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) FAR example: Plot 500 m²; building of 3 floors × 250 m² = 750 m² → FAR = 750/500 = 1.5. Ground coverage = 250/500 = 50%. Aspect / prospect / privacy: Aspect = arrangement of doors & windows to get sun, light, breeze; Prospect = view from windows (and impression from outside); Privacy = internal (between rooms) and external (from neighbours/street). Grouping & circulation: Related rooms grouped together (kitchen–dining); circulation area should be short, straight, well lit; ≈ 20–25% of plinth area for co

Fire-resisting materials: brick (best), concrete, asbestos, gypsum. Poor — timber (treat with Abel’s process: sodium silicate), steel (loses ≈ half strength at ≈ 550°C), glass (wired glass better), granite (cracks), limestone (disintegrates — calcines). Fire load: calorific value of combustibles per unit floor area (kJ/m²); decides fire-resistance grading. Fire-safety provisions: fire exits, external fire escape stairs, travel distance limits, fire doors, compartmentation, sprinklers, hydrants, wet/dry risers, smoke detectors, alarms. Fire classes: A — ordinary combustibles (water); B — flammable liquids (foam, CO₂, dry powder); C — gases (dry powder) / electrical in US system (CO₂); D — metals (special dry powder). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Class Burning material Extinguishing agent A Wood, paper, cloth Water, foam, dry powder B Flammable liquids (petrol, oil) Foam, CO₂, dry powder — NOT water jet C Flammable gases (LPG) Dry powder; shut off gas supply D Metals (Mg, Na) Special dry powder Electrical Live equipment CO₂, dry powder — NOT water/foam F / K Cooking oils & fats Wet chemical, fire blanket Fire-resistance rating: Time (hours) for which an element keeps stability, integrity and insulation in a standard fire test. Fire-resistant construction: Adequate concrete cover to steel, encasing steel columns in concrete/gypsum, fire doors (self-closing), compartment walls, protected escape stairs. Concrete in fire: Loses strength progressively above ≈ 300°C; at very high temperature (≈ 1000°C) strength falls to a small fraction of the original. Brick is the best fire-resisting material; granite cracks and limestone calcines; steel loses ≈ half its strength around 550°C.

Sabine’s formula: T = 0.16 V / A (SI); A = Σαs (total absorption, in sabins). 1 open window sabin: α = 1. Ideal reverberation time: speech 0.5–1.0 s; music 1.0–2.0 s. Echo: reflected sound arriving > 1/15 s (≈ 0.067 s) after direct sound; path difference ≈ 23 m (343 m/s × 1/15 s); the classic '17 m' figure is the reflector distance for 1/10 s persistence. Acoustic defects: echo, reverberation, sound foci, dead spots, insufficient loudness, external noise, resonance. Absorbent materials: acoustic tiles, fibre boards, perforated boards, acoustic plaster, curtains, carpets, upholstered seats. Audible range: 20 Hz – 20 kHz. Sound insulation by mass (heavy walls), cavity/double walls, floating floors, sealing gaps. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Sound Approx. level (dB) Threshold of hearing 0 Whisper 20–30 Normal conversation ≈ 60 Busy street traffic ≈ 70–80 Heavy machinery / pneumatic drill ≈ 100 Threshold of pain ≈ 120–130 Inverse-square law: Sound level falls by ≈ 6 dB for every doubling of distance from a point source. Noise Reduction Coefficient (NRC): Average absorption coefficient at 250, 500, 1000 and 2000 Hz. Remedies for defects: Echo — absorbent rear wall; long reverberation — add absorbers; sound foci — avoid concave surfaces; dead spots — reflectors; external noise — insulation and sealing. Sabine: T = 0.16 V/A (V in m³, A in m² sabins). Unit of absorption = sabin (1 m² of open window, α = 1).

Causes of cracks: moisture movement, thermal movement, elastic deformation, creep, chemical action (sulphate attack, steel corrosion, alkali-aggregate reaction), foundation settlement, vegetation (tree roots). Expansion joints: buildings longer than ≈ 45 m (IS 456); joint width ≈ 25–40 mm. Construction joint: where concreting stops; located at points of minimum shear. Earthquake-resistant masonry: plinth, lintel, roof and gable bands; vertical steel at corners and junctions; openings ≥ 600 mm from corners; symmetric plan; avoid heavy roofs and overhangs. Seismic zones (BCP): Zone 1, 2A, 2B, 3, 4 (4 = highest). Soft storey: storey with much lower stiffness (e.g., open ground-floor parking) — vulnerable. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Cause Typical pattern / remedy Foundation settlement Diagonal cracks near corners/openings; wider at top or bottom Thermal movement Cracks at roof–wall junction, long walls; provide expansion joints Shrinkage (drying) Fine map/hair cracks in plaster & concrete; proper curing Corrosion of steel Cracks along bars, spalling cover; adequate cover & dense concrete Sulphate attack Expansion, cracking of brickwork mortar; use SRC/cement low in C₃A Vegetation (tree roots) Cracks near trees; keep trees away from foundations Confined masonry: Masonry walls built first and then confined by RCC tie-columns and tie-beams — good seismic performance for low-rise buildings. Short-column effect: Columns partially restrained by infill/mezzanine attract high shear and fail in brittle manner. Strong column – weak beam: Plastic hinges should form in beams, not columns, to avoid storey collapse. Pakistan seismic code: BCP 2007 Seismic Provisions (based on UBC-97) replaced by Building Code of Pakistan 2021 (based on IBC 2021). Seismic bands in masonry: plinth band, lintel band (most important), roof band, gable band; vertical bars at corners and junctions.

Power shovel: digs above its own level (hard soil). Backhoe (hoe): digs below its level (trenches, basements). Dragline: long reach, below its level, soft/wet soil. Clamshell: vertical, deep, confined excavation in loose material. Bulldozer: push earth ≈ 30–90 m; Scraper: cut, haul, spread (≈ 150–1500 m); Motor grader: levelling, shaping; Ripper: loosens hard ground. Rollers: smooth-wheel (granular, finishing), sheepsfoot (cohesive soils), pneumatic-tyred (most soils), vibratory (granular). Cranes: tower (high-rise), crawler, truck/mobile, derrick, gantry. Hoists, forklifts, concrete pumps, transit mixers, batching plants. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Choice of compactor: Cohesive soil → sheepsfoot / padfoot; granular → vibratory smooth-drum; mixed → pneumatic-tyred; finishing of asphalt → smooth-wheel (tandem). Excavator output (approx.): Output = bucket capacity × fill factor × cycles per hour × job efficiency. Swell & shrinkage of earth: Loose (excavated) volume > bank volume > compacted volume; swell for common earth ≈ 25%. Concrete equipment: Batching plant, transit mixer, concrete pump/boom placer, needle (internal) vibrators, screed (surface) vibrators, shutter (form) vibrators. Power shovel digs above its track level; backhoe below; dragline – soft wet soils at a distance; clamshell – vertical confined digging (wells, cofferdams).

Strongest brick bond: English bond. Best appearance: Flemish bond. Half-brick partition wall: stretcher bond. Curved walls: header bond. Max risers per flight: 12 (min 3). Min headroom: 2.1 m. Dog-legged stair: no well between flights. King post up to ≈ 8 m; queen post up to ≈ 12 m. North-light roof: factories; glazing faces north. Grillage foundation: heavy column loads on poor soil. Under-reamed pile: black cotton soil. Raking shore angle: 60°–75°. Flying shore: between two walls. Lintel bearing: ≥ 15 cm. DPC: at plinth level. Barium plaster: X-ray rooms. Keene’s cement: hard, polished surfaces. Echo time limit: 1/15 s. Sabine: T = 0.16 V/A. Modular brick: 19 × 9 × 9 cm; ≈ 500 bricks/m³. More quick-revision facts (from online MCQ banks) Grillage foundation: Transfers heavy steel-column loads to soil of low bearing capacity. Stairs in public buildings: Located near the entrance. Least bearing capacity: Moist (soft) clay; highest: hard rock. Opening in sloping roof parallel to roof surface: Skylight; vertical window projecting from sloping roof: dormer. Supporting an existing structure from underneath: Underpinning; temporary support of an unsafe structure: shoring. Header: Brick laid with its length perpendicular to the wall face; stretcher — length parallel. Monumental buildings: Marble; bridge piers — granite; roofing — slate. Noiseless floor: Cork flooring.

Traps: P-trap (outlet horizontal, wash basins/WCs on walls), Q-trap (outlet at ≈ 45°, upper floors), S-trap (outlet vertical, floor-connected WC), gully trap (kitchen/bath waste outside), intercepting trap (last manhole before public sewer), floor trap (nahani trap), bottle trap. Water seal: Depth of water in a trap preventing foul gases: ≈ 25–75 mm (≈ 50 mm common for WCs). Loss of seal: Siphonage (self & induced), evaporation, back-pressure, capillary action, wind effect, leakage. Plumbing systems: Two-pipe (separate soil & waste pipes, each with vent), one-pipe (single stack, all traps vented), single-stack (no separate vent), partially vented single stack. Anti-siphonage pipe: Vent connected near the trap crown to preserve the water seal. Vent pipe: Carried ≈ 1–1.5 m above the roof (or above nearby windows), with a cowl. Manholes: At every change of direction, gradient, junction and pipe size; on straight runs at intervals (≈ 30 m for small sewers, larger for big sewers). House drain slopes: 100 mm drain ≈ 1 in 40 to 1 in 60; 150 mm ≈ 1 in 60 to 1 in 100 (self-cleansing velocity ≈ 0.6–0.75 m/s). Septic tank: Detention ≈ 24 hours; length:width ≈ 2:1 to 4:1; effluent to soak pit / dispersion trench. Overhead tank & pipes: GI, PPR, uPVC, HDPE pipes; overhead tank to hold ≈ one day’s demand (≈ 135 L/person/day for residences, a common design value). Intercepting trap is provided in the last manhole of a house drain before it joins the public sewer.

Seasoning: Natural (air) seasoning — slow, cheap; artificial — kiln, chemical, electrical, boiling, water seasoning. Target moisture ≈ 10–12% for joinery. Defects: Knots, shakes (heart, cup, star, radial), rind galls, twisted fibres, upsets, warping, honeycombing; fungal (dry rot, wet rot) and insect (termites, beetles) attack. Preservation: Tar, creosote, ASCU (arsenic–copper–chromium), solignum paints, Ascu treatment; Abel’s process (sodium silicate) for fire-resistance. Joints in carpentry: Lap, butt, mortise-and-tenon (doors), dovetail (drawers, strong in tension), scarf (lengthening a member), bridle, housing, tongue-and-groove (boards/flooring). Wood-based products: Plywood (odd number of veneers, grains at 90°), block board, particle board/chipboard, fibre board (hardboard, MDF), veneers, laminated timber. Plywood always has an ODD number of plies with grains of adjacent plies at right angles — this balances it and prevents warping.

Prefabrication: Members (slabs, beams, wall panels) cast in factory/yard and erected at site — speed, quality control, less formwork; joints are the weak point. Tilt-up construction: Wall panels cast flat on the floor slab and tilted up into position by crane. Slip-form & jump-form: Continuous vertical concreting (silos, chimneys, cores) / climbing forms for tall cores. Shotcrete / guniting: Concrete or mortar sprayed by compressed air — tunnels, slopes, repairs, swimming pools. Light-gauge steel & EPS panels: Fast, light construction systems used for low-rise and rehabilitation housing. BIM: Building Information Modelling — 3D digital model with data for design, quantity take-off, clash detection and facility management. Green building: Energy-efficient envelope (insulation, shading, orientation), rain-water harvesting, solar energy, low-VOC materials, recycled materials. Pakistan: Green Building Code of Pakistan 2023 (PEC, based on IgCC 2021); rating systems such as LEED. Building Code of Pakistan 2021 is based on IBC 2021; BCP Seismic Provisions 2007 were based on UBC 1997.

PART I — MECHANICS OF SOLIDS (INCL. ADVANCED MOM)

Stress σ = P/A; unit N/mm² = MPa. Strain ε = δL/L (dimensionless). Hooke's law: σ = Eε (within proportional limit). Elongation of bar: δ = PL/AE. Tapered circular bar (d1→d2): δ = 4PL / (πE d1 d2). Tapered rectangular bar (width b1→b2, thickness t): δ = PL·ln(b1/b2) / [E t (b1 − b2)]. Bar hanging under self-weight: δ = γL²/2E = WL/2AE (half of same load applied at end). Uniform strength bar: A = A₀·e^(γx/σ). Shear stress τ = P/A; shear strain γ = τ/G. Volumetric strain εv = δV/V = εx + εy + εz. Cylindrical rod: εv = ε − 2(lateral strain) = ε(1 − 2μ). Sphere: εv = 3 × diametral strain. Cube: εv = 3 × linear strain.

Order: proportional limit → elastic limit → upper yield → lower yield → ultimate → breaking (fracture). Nominal (engineering) stress drops after ultimate due to necking; true stress keeps rising. Ductile: % elongation > 5% (mild steel ≈ 25%). Brittle: < 5% (cast iron, concrete, glass). Proof stress (0.2% offset) used where no clear yield point (Al, high-tensile steel). Factor of safety = ultimate (or yield) stress / working stress.

Elasticity: regain shape. Plasticity: permanent deformation. Ductility: drawn into wires. Malleability: hammered into sheets. Toughness: energy absorbed up to fracture (area under full σ–ε curve). Resilience: energy up to elastic limit. Creep: slow deformation under constant load over time. Fatigue: failure under repeated/cyclic load below ultimate. Endurance limit: stress below which fatigue failure does not occur (steel ≈ 0.5 × ultimate). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 1.1 — Stress–strain curves (concrete and mild steel): proportional limit, yield, ultimate, fracture. Elongation of bars: Uniform bar δ = PL/AE; tapering circular bar δ = 4PL/(πEd₁d₂); bar under own weight δ = ρgL²/(2E) = WL/(2AE). Bar of uniform strength under self weight has area varying exponentially: A = A₀ e^(ρgx/σ).

Three fundamental conditions: Every MoM problem uses (1) equilibrium, (2) compatibility (geometry of deformation), (3) constitutive (stress–strain) law. Idealised σ–ε models: Linear elastic, rigid–perfectly plastic, elastic–perfectly plastic (steel), elastic–linear hardening (bilinear), Ramberg–Osgood (power law), concrete parabolic (Hognestad). Ductile vs brittle: Ductile: large plastic strain before fracture (mild steel elongation ≈ 20–25%); brittle: fracture near elastic limit (cast iron, concrete in tension, glass). Strain hardening & Bauschinger effect: Yield in compression reduced after prior tensile yielding.

Poisson's ratio μ = lateral strain / longitudinal strain. Range 0 to 0.5. μ: steel ≈ 0.25–0.30; concrete 0.1–0.2; rubber ≈ 0.5; cork ≈ 0. μ = 0.5 → incompressible material (K = ∞, εv = 0). E = 2G(1 + μ). E = 3K(1 − 2μ). E = 9KG / (3K + G). μ = (3K − 2G) / (6K + 2G). For μ = 0.25: E = 2.5G; for μ = 0.5: E = 3G. Bulk modulus K = direct stress / volumetric strain (hydrostatic loading). Number of independent elastic constants: isotropic = 2; orthotropic = 9; anisotropic = 21. Typical E: steel 200 GPa; aluminium 70 GPa; copper 100–120 GPa; cast iron 100 GPa; concrete 20–35 GPa. G for steel ≈ 80 GPa. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Relations: E = 2G(1 + ν) = 3K(1 − 2ν); E = 9KG/(3K + G). Poisson’s ratio values: Steel ≈ 0.3, concrete ≈ 0.15–0.2, rubber ≈ 0.5 (incompressible), cork ≈ 0. Theoretical limits of Poisson’s ratio: 0 ≤ ν ≤ 0.5 (ν = 0.5 → K infinite, incompressible).
More on this topic — Advanced Mechanics of Materials (MSc): Elasticity: Strain–Displacement, Compatibility & Constitutive Laws

Strain–displacement: εx = ∂u/∂x, γxy = ∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x (small strain). Compatibility (2-D): ∂²εx/∂y² + ∂²εy/∂x² = ∂²γxy/∂x∂y — ensures continuous single-valued displacements. Generalised Hooke's law: εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E; γxy = τxy/G; G = E/(2(1 + ν)); K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)). Plane stress vs plane strain: Plane stress: σz = 0 (thin plates); plane strain: εz = 0 (dams, tunnels, retaining walls — long bodies). Formulations: Displacement (Navier), stress (Beltrami–Michell), Airy stress function φ with ∇⁴φ = 0 (biharmonic) for 2-D problems. Boundary conditions: Displacement (essential/Dirichlet), traction (natural/Neumann), mixed; St Venant's principle. Elasticity vs MoM approach: Elasticity satisfies equilibrium + compatibility at every point (exact); MoM adds kinematic assumptions (plane sections) — simpler, approximate. Plane strain: εz = 0 but σz = ν(σx + σy) ≠ 0.

Free expansion δ = αLΔT (no stress). Fully restrained: thermal stress σ = EαΔT (independent of length and area). Partially restrained (gap Δ): σ = E(αLΔT − Δ)/L. α steel ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C; copper ≈ 17 × 10⁻⁶; aluminium ≈ 23 × 10⁻⁶; concrete ≈ 10–12 × 10⁻⁶. Composite bar under load: strain equal in both: σ1/E1 = σ2/E2; P = σ1A1 + σ2A2. Modular ratio m = E1/E2 → σ1 = mσ2. Composite bar heated: material with higher α goes into compression; lower α into tension. Equilibrium: σ1A1 = σ2A2 (forces equal & opposite). Bars in series: same load, deformations add. Bars in parallel: same deformation, loads add.

Strain energy U = ½Pδ = σ²V / 2E. Resilience = U. Proof resilience = σ_e² V / 2E (at elastic limit). Modulus of resilience = σ_e² / 2E (per unit volume). Shear strain energy = τ²V / 2G. Gradually applied load: σ = P/A. Suddenly applied load: σ = 2P/A (twice gradual). Impact (falling height h): σ = (P/A)[1 + √(1 + 2AEh/PL)]. If h = 0 in impact formula → suddenly applied case (σ = 2P/A). Bending strain energy U = ∫M² dx / 2EI; torsional U = ∫T² dx / 2GJ. Solid shaft in torsion: U = (τ²/4G) × V; hollow: U = (τ²/4G)(D² + d²)/D² × V. Castigliano's theorem: δ = ∂U/∂P. Maxwell's reciprocal theorem: δ_ab = δ_ba (deflection at A due to load at B = at B due to same load at A).

Sign convention: sagging BM +ve; hogging −ve. dM/dx = V (shear force); dV/dx = −w (load intensity). BM is maximum where SF = 0 or changes sign. Point of contraflexure: BM changes sign (BM = 0); occurs in overhanging & fixed beams, not in SS or cantilever. Degree of curves: no load → SF constant, BM linear; UDL → SF linear, BM parabolic (2nd degree); UVL → SF parabolic, BM cubic. Under a point load: SF jumps suddenly; BM has a kink. Couple (moment) applied: BM jumps; SF unchanged. Flexure formula: M/I = σ/y = E/R. Section modulus Z = I/y_max; M = σZ. Higher Z → stronger section. Assumptions: plane sections remain plane; material homogeneous, isotropic; E same in tension & compression; pure bending; R large vs depth. Neutral axis passes through centroid; stress zero at NA, maximum at extreme fibres. Rectangle: I = bd³/12; Z = bd²/6. Solid circle: I = πd⁴/64; Z = πd³/32. Hollow circle: I = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64; Z = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32D. Triangle (about centroidal axis): I = bh³/36; about base: bh³/12. Z (top) = bh²/24. Square with diagonal vertical: Z = a³/(6√2) (less than square with side horizontal, a³/6). Strongest rectangular beam cut from a log of diameter D: d/b = √2; b = D/√3. Stiffest beam from log: d/b = √3. Parallel axis theorem: I = I_G + Ah². Perpendicular axis: J = Ix + Iy.

Shape factor = Zp/Ze = Mp/My. Rectangle 1.5; solid circle 1.7 (16/3π); I-section ≈ 1.12–1.15; triangle 2.34; diamond 2.0; thin hollow circle ≈ 1.27. Plastic modulus rectangle Zp = bd²/4. Section moduli: Rectangle Z = bd²/6; circle Z = πd³/32; hollow circle Z = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32D). Flexure formula: M/I = σ/y = E/R. Strongest rectangular beam cut from a log: d/b = √2; stiffest: d/b = √3.

τ = VAȳ / (Ib). Rectangle: τ_max = 1.5 τ_avg at NA; parabolic distribution. Solid circle: τ_max = (4/3) τ_avg at NA. Triangle: τ_max = 1.5 τ_avg at h/2 (not at NA); τ at NA = (4/3) τ_avg. Thin hollow circle: τ_max = 2 τ_avg. Diamond (square with diagonal vertical): τ_max = 9/8 τ_avg at d/8 from NA. I-section: web carries most of the shear (~95%); flanges carry most of the bending moment; sudden jump in τ at flange–web junction. Shear stress is zero at extreme fibres. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) τmax/τavg: rectangle 1.5; circle 4/3; triangle 1.5 (max at mid-height, not at centroid).

Governing equation: EI d²y/dx² = M. Slope = dy/dx; flexural rigidity = EI. Methods: double integration, Macaulay's, moment-area, conjugate beam, strain energy (Castigliano), unit load. Moment-area theorem I: change in slope between two points = area of M/EI diagram between them. Moment-area theorem II: deflection = moment of M/EI area about the point. Conjugate beam: slope at a point = SF in conjugate beam; deflection = BM in conjugate beam. Conjugate supports: fixed ↔ free; simple support ↔ simple support; internal hinge ↔ internal support. Fixed-end moments (FEM): central load WL/8; UDL wL²/12; eccentric point load Wab²/L² (near end A), Wa²b/L² (end B). Sinking of support by δ: FEM = 6EIδ/L². Rotation θ at one end: moment = 4EIθ/L at that end; carry-over to far fixed end = ½ (2EIθ/L). Stiffness: far end fixed 4EI/L; far end hinged 3EI/L. Carry-over factor: ½ (far end fixed); 0 (far end hinged). Clapeyron's three-moment theorem used for continuous beams. Points of contraflexure in fixed beam with UDL: 0.211L from each support; with central load: L/4.

Torsion equation: T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L. Polar MI: solid J = πd⁴/32; hollow J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32. Polar modulus Zp = J/r: solid πd³/16; hollow π(D⁴ − d⁴)/16D. Torque: T = (π/16) τ d³ (solid). Power P = 2πNT/60 (W, with N in rpm, T in N·m). Torsional rigidity = GJ; torsional stiffness = GJ/L. Shear stress zero at centre, maximum at outer surface (linear). Hollow shaft is stronger & stiffer than solid shaft of same weight. Shafts in series: same torque, angles add (θ = θ1 + θ2). In parallel: same angle, torques add. Combined bending & torsion: Equivalent BM Me = ½[M + √(M² + T²)]; Equivalent torque Te = √(M² + T²). Brittle shaft in torsion fails along 45° helix (tensile); ductile shaft fails on plane ⟂ to axis (shear). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Hollow vs solid shaft: For the same weight, a hollow shaft is stronger and stiffer (material away from centre). Torsion formula: T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L; J (solid) = πd⁴/32; torsional section modulus Zp = πd³/16.

Euler's load: P = π²EI / Le². Effective length Le: both ends hinged L; one fixed, one free 2L; both fixed L/2; one fixed, one hinged L/√2. Crippling load ratio (hinged : fixed-free : fixed-fixed : fixed-hinged) = 1 : 1/4 : 4 : 2. Slenderness ratio λ = Le / k; k = √(I/A) (use least I). Euler's formula valid for long columns only; mild steel: λ > ~80 (≈ 89 for some data). Euler's assumptions: initially straight, axial load, homogeneous material, failure by buckling only, self-weight neglected. Rankine's formula: 1/P = 1/Pc + 1/Pe → P = σc A / [1 + a(Le/k)²]; a = σc / π²E (Rankine's constant). Rankine constant for mild steel ≈ 1/7500; cast iron 1/1600; timber 1/750. Short columns fail by crushing; long by buckling; intermediate by both (Rankine). Other formulae: Johnson's parabolic, straight-line, Perry-Robertson (initial curvature/eccentricity), secant formula (eccentric load).

Short column fails by crushing; long column fails by buckling. Euler's load: P = π²EI / Le². Euler valid only for slenderness ratio λ = Le/r > critical value (≈ 80–100 for mild steel). Rankine formula: P = σc A / (1 + a λ²) — for all columns (empirical). Buckling occurs about axis of least I (least r). Slenderness ratio λ = Le / r_min, r = √(I/A). σ = P/A ± M/Z = P/A (1 ± 6e/b) for rectangle (eccentricity about one axis). No tension condition: e ≤ b/6 (rectangle) → middle-third rule. Core / kern of rectangle: rhombus with diagonals b/3 and d/3. Circular section: e ≤ d/8 → kern circle of diameter d/4. Hollow circular: e ≤ (D² + d²)/8D. Dams/retaining walls: resultant within middle third to avoid tension at heel. Max stress = 2× average when e = b/6 (stress at other face = 0).

Principal stresses: σ1,2 = (σx + σy)/2 ± √[((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²]. Principal planes: tan 2θp = 2τxy / (σx − σy); shear stress on principal planes = 0. Max shear stress τmax = (σ1 − σ2)/2, on planes at 45° to principal planes. Normal stress on max-shear plane = (σ1 + σ2)/2. Uniaxial σ: τmax = σ/2 at 45°. Pure shear τ: principal stresses ±τ at 45°. Equal like stresses (σx = σy): Mohr's circle reduces to a point; τ = 0 on every plane. Sum of normal stresses on two perpendicular planes is constant (σx + σy = σ1 + σ2).

Centre at ((σx + σy)/2, 0); radius = √[((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²] = τmax. An angle θ on the element = 2θ on the circle. Radius of Mohr's circle for strain gives (ε1 − ε2)/2 = γmax/2. Principal strains: ε1 = σ1/E − μσ2/E. Strain rosettes (rectangular 45°, delta 60°) used to find principal strains experimentally. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 13.1 — Mohr’s circle for plane stress: principal stresses and maximum shear stress.

Given: σx = 80 MPa, σy = 20 MPa, τxy = 40 MPa. Answer: Centre 50, R = √(30² + 40²) = 50 → σ₁ = 100 MPa, σ₂ = 0, τmax = 50 MPa; tan 2θp = 2τ/(σx − σy) = 1.33 → θp ≈ 26.6°. Principal planes carry no shear; planes of max shear are at 45° to principal planes; σx + σy = σ₁ + σ₂ (invariant).
More on this topic — Advanced Mechanics of Materials (MSc): 3-D Stress & Strain Transformation

Fig. 13.2 — 3-D Mohr's circles; the largest circle gives the absolute maximum shear stress. Stress tensor: 9 components (6 independent due to τij = τji). Stress on an oblique plane: Traction t = [σ]{n}; σn = Σ σij ni nj; τn = √(|t|² − σn²) (direction cosines l, m, n with l² + m² + n² = 1). Principal stresses: Roots of σ³ − I₁σ² + I₂σ − I₃ = 0; invariants I₁ = σx + σy + σz, I₂ = σxσy + σyσz + σzσx − τxy² − τyz² − τzx², I₃ = det[σ]. Absolute maximum shear: τabs,max = (σ₁ − σ₃)/2 — even for plane stress, compare with σ₃ = 0 (can exceed in-plane maximum when σ₁, σ₂ have the same sign). Octahedral stresses: σoct = I₁/3 (mean/hydrostatic); τoct = ⅓√[(σ₁−σ₂)² + (σ₂−σ₃)² + (σ₃−σ₁)²]. Mean & deviatoric parts: σij = σm δij + sij; deviatoric stress causes distortion (yielding), mean stress causes volume change. Strain transformation: Same as stress with γ/2 replacing τ; principal strains, strain invariants; strain rosettes (0°–45°–90°, 0°–60°–120°). Three methods for plane-stress transformation — equations, matrix (tensor) rotation [σ′] = [T][σ][T]ᵀ and Mohr's circle — must give identical results.

Max principal stress theory (Rankine): σ1 = σy. Suitable for brittle materials. Max shear stress theory (Guest/Tresca): σ1 − σ2 = σy (τmax = σy/2). Ductile; conservative. Hexagon in σ1–σ2 plane. Max principal strain theory (St. Venant): σ1 − μσ2 = σy. Ellipse-like rhombus. Total strain energy theory (Haigh/Beltrami): σ1² + σ2² − 2μσ1σ2 = σy². Ellipse. Max distortion energy / shear strain energy theory (von Mises–Hencky): σ1² + σ2² − σ1σ2 = σy². Ductile; best agreement with tests. Ellipse. Pure shear yield: Tresca τy = 0.5σy; von Mises τy = 0.577σy (1/√3). Hydrostatic stress does not cause yielding (distortion energy = 0). Brittle → max principal stress theory; ductile → Tresca / von Mises. Max normal stress (Rankine): Brittle materials: σ₁ = σult. Max shear stress (Tresca): σ₁ − σ₃ = σy; conservative for ductile materials (hexagon). Max strain (St Venant): ε₁ = σy/E → σ₁ − ν(σ₂ + σ₃) = σy. Max strain energy (Beltrami–Haigh): σ₁² + σ₂² + σ₃² − 2ν(σ₁σ₂ + σ₂σ₃ + σ₃σ₁) = σy². Distortion energy (von Mises): (σ₁−σ₂)² + (σ₂−σ₃)² + (σ₃−σ₁)² = 2σy² — same as octahedral shear theory (ellipse); best for ductile metals. Mohr–Coulomb: Materials with different tension/compression strengths (soils, rocks, concrete). Shaft under axial force + torque: σ = P/A, τ = Tr/J → principal stresses σ/2 ± √((σ/2)² + τ²); compute radius for each theory (2023 final paper). Von Mises: τy = σy/√3 ≈ 0.577σy; Tresca: τy = 0.5σy.

Thin if t < d/20 (d/t > 20). Hoop (circumferential) stress σc = pd/2t. Longitudinal stress σl = pd/4t (σc = 2σl). Max in-plane shear = pd/8t; absolute max shear (thin) = pd/4t. Thin spherical shell: σ = pd/4t (all directions). Hoop strain εc = (pd/4tE)(2 − μ); longitudinal εl = (pd/4tE)(1 − 2μ). Volumetric strain (cylinder) = 2εc + εl = (pd/4tE)(5 − 4μ). Volumetric strain (sphere) = 3 × diametral strain = (3pd/4tE)(1 − μ). Joint efficiency η: σc = pd/2tη_l; σl = pd/4tη_c (longitudinal joint governs hoop stress). Wire-wound cylinders: initial compressive hoop stress increases pressure capacity.

Lamé equations: σr = b/r² − a; σc = b/r² + a (σc tensile, σr compressive under internal pressure). Max hoop stress at inner surface; σr = −p at inside, 0 at outside. Hoop stress varies hyperbolically across wall. Compound cylinders (shrink fit) reduce max hoop stress. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Thin cylinder: hoop σh = pd/2t, longitudinal σl = pd/4t (hoop = 2 × longitudinal); thin sphere: σ = pd/4t. Thin if t < d/20.

Close-coiled helical spring: deflection δ = 64WR³n / (Gd⁴) = 8WD³n / (Gd⁴). Max shear stress τ = 16WR/πd³ = 8WD/πd³ (× Wahl factor K for curvature). Wahl factor K = (4C − 1)/(4C − 4) + 0.615/C; spring index C = D/d. Stiffness k = W/δ = Gd⁴ / (64R³n). Springs in series: 1/k = 1/k1 + 1/k2. In parallel: k = k1 + k2. Cutting a spring into halves doubles stiffness of each half. Close-coiled spring under axial load: wire is in torsion. Open-coiled: torsion + bending. Leaf (laminated) spring: σ = 3WL / 2nbt²; δ = 3WL³ / 8Enbt³ (semi-elliptic, central load W, span L). Quarter-elliptic leaf spring: σ = 6WL/nbt²; δ = 6WL³/Enbt³.
Unsymmetrical Bending, Shear Centre, Torsion & Plates

Fig. 17.1 — Shear centre of a channel lies outside the web; load through S causes bending without twisting. Unsymmetrical bending: σ = −(My Iz + Mz Iyz)y/(IyIz − Iyz²) + … or use principal axes; neutral axis not perpendicular to load plane. Shear flow: q = VQ/I; shear stress in thin walls τ = q/t. Shear centre: Point through which load must pass for no twisting: channel e = b²h²t/(4I) from web; angle, tee — at intersection of legs/flanges; symmetric I — at centroid. Torsion of non-circular sections: Rectangle τmax = T/(αbt²); thin open sections J ≈ Σbt³/3 (weak in torsion); closed thin-walled (Bredt–Batho): τ = T/(2At), J = 4A²/∮(ds/t); Prandtl membrane analogy. Plates: Kirchhoff thin-plate theory: D∇⁴w = q, D = Et³/(12(1 − ν²)); membranes carry in-plane forces only; shells — membrane + bending action. Shell postulates: Thickness small vs radius; normals remain normal & inextensible; transverse normal stress negligible. Closed thin-walled tubes are far stiffer in torsion than open sections of the same material (J ∝ A² vs bt³).

Unit of stress, pressure, E, G, K and modulus of resilience: N/m² (same dimension). Strain, Poisson's ratio: dimensionless. Area under load–deflection curve = strain energy. Shear stress in beam max at NA (rectangle, circle); bending stress zero at NA. Ratio of max bending stress, square vs circle of same area: circle is weaker in bending (Z_square/Z_circle ≈ 1.18). For same weight & material: hollow shaft > solid in strength and stiffness. Doubling diameter of solid shaft → torque capacity × 8; angle of twist ÷ 16 (same T). Doubling length of SS beam (UDL) → deflection × 16; (central load) × 8. Doubling depth of rectangular beam → bending strength × 4; stiffness × 8. Kern/core of section is the area where load causes no tension. Point of contraflexure is read from the BMD (BM = 0 and changes sign), not the SFD. Bauschinger effect: loading in tension lowers yield in compression. St. Venant's principle: effect of load distribution is local; stresses uniform a short distance away. Principle of superposition valid only within elastic limit (linear behaviour). Rivet/bolt in double shear carries twice the load of single shear. Hydrostatic stress state: only volume change, no shape change.

2D: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0 → 3 equations. 3D: 6 equations (3 forces + 3 moments). Two-force member: forces equal, opposite, collinear (along member). Three-force member: forces concurrent or parallel. Internal hinge gives 1 extra equation (M = 0 at hinge).

Beam: carries transverse load mainly by bending. Truss: pin-jointed, members carry axial force only (loads at joints). Frame: rigid joints, members carry axial + shear + moment. Arch: curved; load carried mainly by compression (thrust). Cable: carries tension only; takes funicular shape of loading. Roller = 1 reaction, hinge = 2, fixed = 3; an internal hinge releases moment (adds one equation of condition).

Structure Formula Beam Ds = r − 3 − (releases) Plane truss Ds = m + r − 2j Space truss Ds = m + r − 3j Plane rigid frame Ds = 3m + r − 3j  (or 3C − R for closed loops) Space rigid frame Ds = 6m + r − 6j m = members, r = external reactions, j = joints, C = closed loops, R = releases. Ds = 0 → determinate; Ds > 0 → indeterminate; Ds < 0 → unstable (mechanism). Ds ≥ 0 is necessary, not sufficient — check geometric stability too. Each closed loop in a plane frame is 3 times indeterminate. Hinge release in plane frame = (members meeting − 1).

Structure Formula Plane truss Dk = 2j − r Space truss Dk = 3j − r Plane frame Dk = 3j − r  (− m if axial deformation neglected) Space frame Dk = 6j − r Fixed support: Dk = 0 at that joint; hinge: 1 (rotation); roller: 2. Force (flexibility) methods → unknowns = Ds; displacement (stiffness) methods → unknowns = Dk. Prefer force method when Ds < Dk, displacement method when Dk < Ds.

All reactions concurrent → unstable (rotation possible). All reactions parallel → unstable (sway possible). Fewer than 3 reactions (plane) → unstable. Assumptions: pin joints, loads at joints, members straight, self-weight neglected. Perfect truss: m = 2j − 3; deficient: m < 2j − 3; redundant: m > 2j − 3. Method of joints: max 2 unknowns per joint. Method of sections: cut max 3 unknown members (not concurrent); best for force in a few members. Graphical: Maxwell diagram (Bow's notation).

Two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint → both zero. Three members at an unloaded joint, two collinear → third is zero. Used to simplify analysis; not removable in practice (stability, load reversal).

Pratt: diagonals in tension, verticals in compression (steel bridges). Howe: diagonals in compression, verticals in tension (timber). Warren: equilateral triangles, diagonals alternate T/C. K-truss, Fink (roofs), Baltimore, Parker (curved top chord). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Zero-force member rules: At an unloaded joint with two non-collinear members, both are zero; with three members, two collinear → the third is zero. Methods: Method of joints (all members), method of sections (few members — ≤ 3 unknowns per cut), graphical (Maxwell diagram).

Three-hinged arch: statically determinate (4 reactions, 3 eq. + 1 hinge). Two-hinged arch: indeterminate to 1st degree. Fixed (hingeless) arch: indeterminate to 3rd degree. Three-hinged parabolic arch with UDL over full span: H = wL²/8h, BM = 0 everywhere. Three-hinged arch, central point load W: H = WL/4h. Eddy's theorem: BM at any section = vertical intercept between linear arch (thrust line) and actual arch centre line × H. Temperature rise: no stresses in three-hinged arch; causes stresses in two-hinged/fixed arch. Linear arch: shape of BMD of the loading; BM = 0 at all sections.

Cable carries pure tension; shape = funicular polygon of loads. UDL on horizontal span → parabolic shape; self-weight along cable → catenary. Horizontal tension: H = wL²/8d (d = central sag). Max tension (at supports): T = √(H² + V²) = (wL/2)√(1 + L²/16d²). Length of parabolic cable ≈ L + 8d²/3L. Suspension bridge: stiffening girder distributes load; anchor cables via guide pulley or saddle (roller). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 23.1 — Three-hinged parabolic arch under UDL: pure compression, H = wL²/8h. Cables: Under UDL a cable takes a parabolic shape; under own weight — catenary; horizontal tension H = wL²/(8d) (d = sag). Two-hinged arch is indeterminate to degree 1; fixed arch to degree 3; three-hinged arch is determinate.

Strain energy (axial): U = P²L/2AE; bending: U = ∫M²dx/2EI; shear: U = ∫ kV²dx/2GA; torsion: U = T²L/2GJ. Castigliano's 1st theorem: P = ∂U/∂δ. Principle of least work: ∂U/∂R = 0 for redundant R (indeterminate structures). Maxwell's reciprocal theorem: δij = δji (linear elastic). Betti's law: work by set P through deflections due to Q = work by Q through deflections due to P. Principle of virtual work basis for unit load method. Clapeyron's theorem: work done = ½ × load × deflection (gradually applied). Suddenly applied load: stress = 2 × gradually applied stress. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Castigliano’s 1st theorem: 1st theorem: P = ∂U/∂δ; 2nd theorem: δ = ∂U/∂P (deflection in the direction of P); ∂U/∂M = rotation. Maxwell–Betti: Reciprocal deflections: δij = δji (linear elastic structures). Unit-load method: δ = ∫ M m dx / EI (beams) and Σ P k L/(AE) (trusses).

ILD: variation of a response (R, SF, BM) at a fixed section as a unit load moves across. BMD shows BM at all sections for fixed load; ILD shows BM at one section for moving load. Müller-Breslau principle: ILD shape = deflected shape when the restraint for that response is removed and unit displacement given. Determinate structures → ILDs are straight lines; indeterminate → curved. Value due to point load W = W × ordinate; due to UDL w = w × area under ILD.
Standard ILDs (SS beam span L, section at distance a from left, b from right)
Reaction RA: triangle, 1 at A, 0 at B. SF at section: −a/L just left, +b/L just right (jump of 1). BM at section: triangle, max ordinate ab/L at section.

Single point load: max BM at section when load is at the section. UDL longer than span: max BM at section when span fully covered. UDL shorter than span: max BM when section divides load in same ratio as it divides span. Max SF: load placed on one side of section only (+ve or −ve). Train of loads, max BM at a section: average load on left = average load on right. Absolute max BM (train of loads): place resultant and nearest heavy load equidistant from centre; max BM under that load. Single load: absolute max BM = WL/4 at midspan; UDL: wL²/8. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 25.1 — Influence lines for reaction, shear and moment in a simply supported beam. Rolling loads: Max BM under a UDL longer than span: cover the whole span; shorter than span: section divides the load in the same ratio as it divides the span. Absolute max BM (train of loads): Occurs under the load nearest the resultant when the beam centre lies midway between that load and the resultant. Müller-Breslau principle: ILD of a reaction/force = deflected shape when that restraint is removed and a unit displacement is applied.

Unknowns: redundant forces. Method of consistent deformation: compatibility of displacements. Clapeyron's three-moment theorem (continuous beams): M_A L₁ + 2M_B(L₁+L₂) + M_C L₂ = −6A₁x̄₁/L₁ − 6A₂x̄₂/L₂. Column analogy method (fixed arches, frames). Least work (Castigliano).

Unknowns: joint displacements/rotations. Slope deflection: M_AB = M_FAB + (2EI/L)(2θA + θB − 3Δ/L). Moment distribution (Hardy Cross): iterative; no simultaneous equations. Kani's method: iterative, handles sway easily. Matrix stiffness method: basis for computer programs (FEM).

Flexibility matrix [F]: displacement due to unit force; stiffness matrix [K]: force due to unit displacement. [K] = [F]⁻¹ (for same coordinates). Both are square and symmetric (Maxwell's reciprocal theorem). Stiffness matrix diagonal elements always positive. Stiffness matrix of unsupported structure is singular. Member stiffness (beam): [4EI/L 2EI/L; 2EI/L 4EI/L]. Axial stiffness of bar: AE/L. Stiffness method is preferred for computers (systematic, independent of redundancy choice).

Steps: (1) number nodes & DOFs; (2) element stiffness in local axes; (3) transform to global [k] = [T]ᵀ[k′][T]; (4) assemble [K]; (5) apply loads & boundary conditions; (6) solve {D} = [K]⁻¹{F}; (7) member forces. Truss element: k = (AE/L)[[c², cs, −c², −cs], …] with c = cos θ, s = sin θ. Beam element: k = (EI/L³)[[12, 6L, −12, 6L], [6L, 4L², −6L, 2L²], …]. Frame element: 6 × 6 (2-D) combining axial and flexural terms; 12 × 12 for 3-D. Properties of [K]: Symmetric, banded, singular before supports are applied, positive diagonal terms. Equivalent nodal loads: Fixed-end actions reversed (wL/2, wL²/12 for UDL). Flexibility method: Unknowns are redundant forces; [F]{R} = −{Δ}; preferred for few redundants. Stiffness matrix is singular until supports are imposed (rigid-body motion).

Fig. 28.1 — 1-D bar element and a 2-D CST mesh. Idea: Discretise a continuum into elements connected at nodes; approximate field variable by shape functions; minimise potential energy (Rayleigh–Ritz) or weighted residual (Galerkin). Element types: 1-D: bar/truss, beam; 2-D: CST (3-node, constant strain), LST (6-node), Q4 bilinear quad, Q8; 3-D: tetrahedra, hexahedra (bricks); plate & shell elements. Shape functions: Sum to 1 at any point (partition of unity); Ni = 1 at node i and 0 at other nodes; must give rigid-body & constant-strain states (completeness) and inter-element continuity (compatibility). Element stiffness: [k] = ∫ [B]ᵀ[D][B] dV; [B] = strain–displacement matrix, [D] = constitutive matrix. Isoparametric formulation: Same shape functions for geometry and displacement; numerical (Gauss) integration — 2-point Gauss rule integrates cubic polynomials exactly. Convergence: h-refinement (smaller elements) or p-refinement (higher order); displacement-based FEM is stiffer than real → displacements converge from below. Errors & checks: Shear locking (linear elements in bending), hourglassing (reduced integration), aspect ratio < 5, mesh refinement study, patch test. Software: SAP2000/ETABS (frames & shells), ABAQUS, ANSYS, Midas, PLAXIS (geotechnical). CST element: linear displacement, constant strain/stress within element — needs fine mesh in bending zones.

Assumes material elastic–perfectly plastic (mild steel). Plastic hinge: section fully yielded, rotates at constant Mp. Plastic moment Mp = σy × Zp; yield moment My = σy × Z. Shape factor S = Zp/Z = Mp/My. Collapse: enough hinges form to create a mechanism; hinges needed = Ds + 1 (for complete collapse). Load factor = collapse load / working load. Upper bound (kinematic) theorem: load from assumed mechanism ≥ true collapse load. Lower bound (static) theorem: load from safe & statically admissible BMD ≤ true collapse load. Uniqueness theorem: both satisfied → true collapse load. Principle of superposition valid only for linear elastic, small deflection behaviour. Maxwell–Mohr method = unit load method. Slope deflection method developed by G.A. Maney; moment distribution by Hardy Cross. Kani's method is a relaxation (iterative) method. Three-moment equation given by Clapeyron. In a portal frame with sway, number of shear equations = number of sway degrees. Approximate frame analysis: portal method (lateral loads, low-rise) and cantilever method (tall frames). Substitute frame method: gravity load analysis of multi-storey frames. In portal method, inflection points assumed at mid-height of columns and mid-span of beams. Interior columns take twice the shear of exterior columns (portal method). Rigid joint in frame: members meeting keep the same rotation. Stiffness of a member ∝ EI/L. Flexibility = 1/stiffness. Strain energy is always positive (quadratic in load). Settlement of support induces moments only in indeterminate structures. Temperature change causes stresses only in indeterminate structures. For symmetric structure under symmetric load: antisymmetric quantities (e.g. SF at centre) are zero.

PART III — STRUCTURAL DYNAMICS & EARTHQUAKE ENGINEERING

Dynamic load: load whose magnitude, direction or position varies with time; inertia forces become significant. Static vs dynamic: static has one solution; dynamic response is time-dependent (a solution for every instant). Dynamic analysis needed when: load period < ~3 × natural period of structure (rule of thumb). Types of dynamic loads: Periodic – harmonic (rotating machinery), non-harmonic (propeller, wave). Non-periodic – impulsive/short duration (blast, impact), long duration/random (earthquake, wind). Deterministic load: time variation fully known. Random (stochastic): described statistically (earthquake, wind, waves). Three essential properties: mass (m), stiffness (k), damping (c). Vibration: oscillatory motion about equilibrium. Free vibration: no external force after initial disturbance. Forced vibration: under external excitation. Period T: time for one cycle (s). Frequency f = 1/T (Hz). Circular frequency ω = 2πf (rad/s). Amplitude: maximum displacement from mean position.

DOF: number of independent coordinates needed to define displaced position of all masses. SDOF: single coordinate (e.g., single-storey shear frame, water tank on pedestal). MDOF: finite number of coordinates (multistorey shear building – 1 DOF per floor). Continuous system: infinite DOF (beams, plates, chimneys). Discretisation methods: lumped mass, generalised (assumed shape) coordinates, finite element. Lumped mass: mass concentrated at nodes → diagonal mass matrix. Consistent mass (FEM): uses same shape functions as stiffness → non-diagonal mass matrix. Shear building assumptions: rigid floors (no rotation), mass lumped at floors, columns axially inextensible, axial forces ignored.

Newton's 2nd law / D'Alembert's principle: inertia force (−m·ü) treated as an external force → dynamic equilibrium. Other methods: principle of virtual work, Hamilton's principle, Lagrange's equation, energy (Rayleigh) method. m·ü + c·u̇ + k·u = p(t) Inertia force = m·ü; damping force = c·u̇; spring force = k·u. Support (ground) excitation (earthquake): m·ü + c·u̇ + k·u = −m·üg(t)      (u = relative displacement) Effective earthquake force = −m·üg; response depends on m only through ω. Weight does not affect equation when measured from static equilibrium position. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 34.1 — Idealised SDOF system: mass, spring, viscous damper and dynamic load. D’Alembert’s principle: inertia force m ü is added as a fictitious force to write dynamic equilibrium.

m·ü + k·u = 0   →   u(t) = u0·cos ωt + (u̇0/ω)·sin ωt ωn = √(k/m)      fn = ωn/2π      Tn = 2π√(m/k) ωn = √(g/δst)    (δst = static deflection under weight)   →   fn ≈ 15.76/√δst(mm) Hz Amplitude A = √[u0² + (u̇0/ω)²]      Phase φ = tan⁻¹[u̇0/(ω·u0)] Motion is simple harmonic; amplitude constant (energy conserved). Natural frequency ↑ with stiffness, ↓ with mass. Doubling k → ω × √2; doubling m → ω ÷ √2. Simple pendulum: ω = √(g/L).  Compound pendulum: ω = √(mgd/I0). Max velocity = ωA; max acceleration = ω²A. Energy: KE max = PE max = ½kA² (basis of Rayleigh method). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Given: Water tank: m = 20,000 kg on a column with lateral stiffness k = 2 × 10⁶ N/m. Answer: ωn = √(2 × 10⁶/20,000) = 10 rad/s; fn = 1.59 Hz; T = 0.63 s. Springs: Parallel: k = k₁ + k₂; series: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂. Natural period increases with mass and decreases with stiffness: T = 2π√(m/k). Static deflection method: fn = 15.76/√δst (δst in mm).

Viscous: force ∝ velocity (F = c·u̇); most used in analysis. Coulomb (friction): constant force opposing motion; amplitude decays linearly (by 4F/k per cycle); motion stops when kx < F. Structural / hysteretic: force ∝ displacement, in phase with velocity; energy loss per cycle independent of frequency. Radiation damping: energy lost into soil (soil–structure interaction).

Critical damping  cc = 2mωn = 2√(km) Damping ratio  ζ = c / cc Damped frequency  ωD = ωn√(1 − ζ²)      TD = Tn / √(1 − ζ²) Case ζ Response Underdamped ζ < 1 Oscillatory, exponentially decaying (all real structures) Critically damped ζ = 1 Returns fastest to rest without oscillation Overdamped ζ > 1 Non-oscillatory, slow return Undamped ζ = 0 Oscillation with constant amplitude u(t) = e^(−ζωn t)·[u0 cos ωDt + ((u̇0 + ζωn u0)/ωD) sin ωDt]

δ = ln(un / un+1) = 2πζ / √(1 − ζ²) ≈ 2πζ   (small ζ) Over j cycles:  ζ ≈ ln(un / un+j) / (2πj) Cycles to reduce amplitude by 50%: j50% ≈ 0.11/ζ (≈ 2 cycles for ζ = 5%). Typical damping: welded steel 2–3%, bolted steel 5–7%, RC 5% (code default), prestressed 2–3%, masonry 5–10%. Damping has negligible effect on natural frequency for ζ < 20% (ωD ≈ ωn). Rayleigh (proportional) damping: c = a0·m + a1·k (mass- and stiffness-proportional). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 36.1 — Free vibration responses: under-damped, critically damped and over-damped. Typical damping: Steel structures ≈ 2–3%, RC buildings ≈ 5% (design spectra use 5%), masonry ≈ 7–10%. Damped frequency ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) ≈ ωn for small ζ; logarithmic decrement δ ≈ 2πζ.

Load: p(t) = p0 sin ωt.  Frequency ratio r = ω / ωn. Total response = transient (decays due to damping) + steady state (at forcing frequency). Steady-state amplitude  u0 = ust · Rd ,   ust = p0 / k Dynamic magnification factor  Rd = 1 / √[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²] Phase angle  φ = tan⁻¹[2ζr / (1 − r²)] Frequency ratio Behaviour Rd Phase φ r << 1 Stiffness-controlled (quasi-static) ≈ 1 ≈ 0° r = 1 (resonance) Damping-controlled 1 / 2ζ 90° r >> 1 Mass-controlled → 0 → 180° Resonance: forcing frequency = natural frequency; undamped amplitude grows linearly with time (unbounded). Peak Rd occurs at r = √(1 − 2ζ²) (slightly below 1); Rd,max = 1 / [2ζ√(1 − ζ²)]. Half-power (band-width) method: ζ = (f2 − f1) / (2fn), where f1, f2 are frequencies at Rd,max/√2. Quality factor Q = 1/(2ζ) = response at resonance. Velocity factor Rv = r·Rd; acceleration factor Ra = r²·Rd.
p0 = me·e·ω²   →   amplitude = (me·e / m) · r² · Rd

TR = √[1 + (2ζr)²] / √[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²] TR = 1 at r = √2 for all ζ. Isolation (TR < 1) only when r > √2 → use soft mounts (low k) so ωn is small. For r > √2, damping increases TR (undesirable); for r < √2, damping reduces TR. Same TR expression applies to force transmitted to foundation and to support motion transmitted to mass. Isolation efficiency = (1 − TR) × 100%. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 37.1 — Dynamic amplification factor vs frequency ratio for different damping ratios. Transmissibility: TR = √[1 + (2ζr)²] / √[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²]; vibration isolation only when r > √2. At resonance (r = 1): Rd = 1/(2ζ), phase angle = 90°; damping matters most near resonance.

Periodic load: expand by Fourier series → sum of harmonic responses (superposition, linear systems only). Unit impulse response: h(t) = (1 / mωD) · e^(−ζωn t) · sin ωDt Duhamel's integral (convolution) – response to arbitrary load, zero initial conditions: u(t) = (1/mωD) ∫₀ᵗ p(τ) e^(−ζωn(t−τ)) sin ωD(t − τ) dτ Valid only for linear elastic systems (uses superposition). Step (suddenly applied constant) load p0: umax = 2·ust → dynamic factor = 2 (undamped). Rectangular pulse of duration td: if td/Tn ≥ 0.5, DLF = 2; shorter pulse → smaller DLF. Short impulse (td < Tn/4): response depends on impulse area only, umax = I·ωn / k = I / (mωn). Shock spectrum: plot of max response vs td/Tn for a given pulse shape.

Central difference: explicit; conditionally stable (Δt < Tn/π). Newmark-β: average acceleration (γ = ½, β = ¼) – unconditionally stable; linear acceleration (γ = ½, β = 1/6) – conditionally stable (Δt ≤ 0.551Tn). Wilson-θ (θ ≥ 1.37): unconditionally stable. Accuracy guideline: Δt ≤ Tn/10.

Newmark-β family: u̇ₙ₊₁ = u̇ₙ + Δt[(1 − γ)üₙ + γüₙ₊₁]; uₙ₊₁ = uₙ + Δt u̇ₙ + Δt²[(½ − β)üₙ + βüₙ₊₁]. Average acceleration: γ = ½, β = ¼ — unconditionally stable, no numerical damping (Newmark 1959 paper on your Drive). Linear acceleration: γ = ½, β = ⅙ — conditionally stable (Δt/Tn ≤ 0.551). Accuracy: Choose Δt ≤ Tn/10 (and ≤ ground-motion record step). Other methods: Duhamel integral (linear SDOF), Wilson-θ, HHT-α, modal superposition (linear MDOF), response-spectrum analysis (SRSS, CQC combination). Constant (average) acceleration Newmark method is unconditionally stable — the default in SAP2000/ETABS time-history analysis.

Response spectrum: plot of peak response (D, V, A) of SDOF systems vs natural period Tn for a given ζ and ground motion. Pseudo-velocity  V = ωn·D        Pseudo-acceleration  A = ωn²·D Tripartite (D–V–A) plot: shows all three on four-way log scale. Very short period (Tn → 0, rigid): A → peak ground acceleration (PGA). Very long period (flexible): D → peak ground displacement; A → 0. Regions: acceleration-sensitive (short T), velocity-sensitive (intermediate), displacement-sensitive (long T). Design spectrum: smoothed, enveloped spectrum used by codes. Peak base shear  Vb = m·A = (A/g)·W ;   Equivalent static force  fs = k·D = m·A

T = Ct · hn^x System (ASCE 7 / BCP) Ct (h in m) x Steel moment frame 0.0724 0.8 RC moment frame 0.0466 0.9 Eccentrically braced steel frame 0.0731 0.75 All other systems 0.0488 0.75 UBC-97 (h in ft): Ct = 0.035 steel MRF, 0.030 RC MRF/EBF, 0.020 others; x = 3/4. Rule of thumb: T ≈ 0.1 N (N = number of storeys). Base shear (equivalent lateral force): V = Cs·W, distributed over height roughly ∝ wx·hx^k (k = 1 for T ≤ 0.5 s, 2 for T ≥ 2.5 s). Seismic weight W: dead load + part of live load (e.g., 25% storage live load). Ductility μ = umax / uy; response modification factor R reduces elastic forces. Equal displacement rule (long T): R = μ.  Equal energy rule (short/intermediate T): R = √(2μ − 1). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 40.1 — Shape of a design response spectrum (ASCE 7 / BCP 2021). Equivalent lateral force: Base shear V = Cs W, Cs = SDS/(R/Ie) (with upper & lower limits); distributed up the height ∝ wi hiᵏ. Approximate period: Ta = Ct hnˣ (e.g., RC moment frame Ct = 0.0466, x = 0.9 in m units); rule of thumb T ≈ 0.1 N (N = storeys). Pakistan seismicity: Highest hazard in the north and north-west (Hindu Kush–Himalaya, e.g., 2005 Kashmir earthquake, Mw 7.6) and parts of Balochistan (1935 Quetta). Response modification factor R reduces elastic forces for ductile systems (special RC moment frame R = 8); importance factor Ie raises them for essential buildings.

Seismic hazard in BCP 2021: Mapped spectral accelerations Ss and S₁ (MCE, 2% in 50 years ≈ 2475-yr return); site classes A–F by Vs30; design spectrum SDS = ⅔ Fa Ss, SD1 = ⅔ Fv S₁. Seismic design categories: SDC A–F from SDS, SD1 and risk category; SDC D+ requires special moment frames/special shear walls. Equivalent lateral force: V = Cs W; Cs = SDS/(R/Ie) ≤ SD1/(T R/Ie); Cs ≥ 0.044 SDS Ie ≥ 0.01. Vertical distribution Fx = Cvx V with Cvx ∝ wx hxᵏ (k = 1 for T ≤ 0.5 s, 2 for T ≥ 2.5 s). R, Ω₀, Cd: Special RC moment frame R = 8, Ω₀ = 3, Cd = 5.5; ordinary RC frame R = 3; special RC shear wall (building frame) R = 6. Irregularities: Horizontal (torsional, re-entrant corner, diaphragm discontinuity, out-of-plane offset, non-parallel); vertical (soft storey, weight/mass, geometric, in-plane discontinuity, weak storey) — trigger dynamic analysis. Drift limits: Storey drift ≤ 0.020 hsx (risk category I/II, typical buildings); design drift Δ = Cd δe/Ie. Performance-based design: Immediate Occupancy, Life Safety, Collapse Prevention (ASCE 41); pushover (nonlinear static) and nonlinear time-history analyses. Seismic isolation & damping: Lead-rubber bearings, friction pendulum, viscous dampers, tuned mass dampers (Taipei 101). Soft storey (e.g., open ground-floor parking) is the most common vertical irregularity causing collapse.

[M]{ü} + [C]{u̇} + [K]{u} = {p(t)} Shear building: [M] diagonal; [K] tri-diagonal (banded). Free vibration eigenvalue problem: ([K] − ω²[M]){φ} = 0   →   det([K] − ω²[M]) = 0   (frequency equation) n-DOF system → n natural frequencies & n mode shapes. Fundamental mode: lowest frequency (longest period); usually dominates response. Mode shapes give relative (not absolute) amplitudes; normalised (e.g., top = 1 or mass-normalised φᵀMφ = 1). Number of nodes (zero-displacement points, excluding base) in mode n = n − 1.
φmᵀ[M]φn = 0  and  φmᵀ[K]φn = 0   (m ≠ n) Allows uncoupling of equations → modal analysis. Generalised (modal) mass Mn = φnᵀMφn; generalised stiffness Kn = φnᵀKφn; ωn² = Kn/Mn.

{u} = Σ φn · qn(t)    → each qn solved as an SDOF system Valid only for linear systems with classical (proportional) damping. Modal participation factor  Γn = φnᵀ[M]{1} / φnᵀ[M]φn Effective modal mass  Mn* = (φnᵀ[M]{1})² / φnᵀ[M]φn ;   Σ Mn* = total mass Codes require enough modes for ≥ 90% cumulative effective mass.

ABSSUM: sum of absolute values – upper bound, very conservative. SRSS: √(Σ rn²) – good for well-separated frequencies. CQC: includes cross-correlation; used when frequencies are closely spaced (within ~10%). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 42.1 — First three mode shapes of a 3-storey shear building. Modal combination: SRSS (well-separated modes) and CQC (closely spaced modes) to combine peak modal responses. Orthogonality: modes are orthogonal w.r.t. mass and stiffness matrices; number of modes = number of degrees of freedom.

Rayleigh method: equates max KE = max PE using an assumed shape; gives upper bound on fundamental frequency. ω² = Σ Wi·yi · g / Σ Wi·yi²   (yi = static deflection under weights) Rayleigh–Ritz: combination of several assumed shapes; improves higher modes too. Dunkerley's method: gives lower bound of fundamental frequency. 1/ω1² ≈ 1/ω11² + 1/ω22² + …   (ωii = frequency with mass i alone) Stodola (matrix iteration): iterative; converges to fundamental mode (uses flexibility matrix). Holzer method: trial frequency tabular method; used for torsional & shear building systems. Exact frequency lies between Dunkerley (lower) and Rayleigh (upper). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Rayleigh’s method gives an UPPER bound on the fundamental frequency; Dunkerley’s method gives a LOWER bound.

Infinite DOF; governed by partial differential equations. Beam (Euler–Bernoulli):  EI ∂⁴u/∂x⁴ + m̄ ∂²u/∂t² = p(x,t) Natural frequency  ωn = (βnL)² · √(EI / m̄L⁴)    (m̄ = mass per unit length) Beam support (β1L)² (β2L)² (β3L)² Simply supported π² = 9.87 39.48 88.83 Cantilever 3.516 22.03 61.70 Fixed–fixed 22.37 61.67 120.9 Free–free 22.37 61.67 120.9 Fixed–pinned 15.42 49.96 104.2 Simply supported beam: ωn = n²π²√(EI/m̄L⁴); frequency ratios 1 : 4 : 9 (∝ n²). Cantilever: frequency ratios 1 : 6.27 : 17.55. Taut string: ωn = (nπ/L)√(T/m̄); ratios 1 : 2 : 3. Axial vibration of bar: fixed–free ωn = (2n − 1)(π/2L)√(E/ρ); wave speed c = √(E/ρ). Timoshenko beam: includes shear deformation & rotary inertia → lower frequencies (important for deep beams, higher modes). Axial compression reduces flexural natural frequency; tension increases it.

Types: block, box/caisson, wall, framed foundations. Design criteria: avoid resonance; amplitude within permissible limits; bearing pressure safe. Frequency ratio: keep machine operating frequency at least ±20–30% away from natural frequency. Under-tuned (low-tuned): ωn < ω (passes through resonance at start-up). Over-tuned (high-tuned): ωn > ω. Typical permissible amplitude: ~0.2 mm for low-speed machines; ~0.02–0.04 mm for high-speed turbines. Modes of block vibration: vertical, sliding (horizontal), rocking, pitching, yawing (torsional) – 6 DOF. Methods: Barkan (elastic half-space springs), Lysmer's analog, IS 2974 / codal coefficients. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Design rule: Keep machine operating frequency away from foundation natural frequency (≥ ± 20–30%); ‘low-tuned’ (fn < operating) or ‘high-tuned’ (fn > operating). Block foundations for reciprocating machines; frame foundations for turbo-generators; vibration isolators (springs, pads) for light machines.

Unit of ω: rad/s; of f: Hz (cycles/s); of c: N·s/m. ωn = √(g/δst) – no need for m or k separately. Suddenly applied load → deflection doubles (DLF = 2). At resonance, Rd = 1/(2ζ); phase = 90°; applied force balanced by damping force. Vibration isolation needs r > √2; TR = 1 at r = √2. Logarithmic decrement δ ≈ 2πζ. Critical damping cc = 2√(km); real structures ζ ≈ 2–10%. Damping reduces amplitude but hardly changes natural frequency. Coulomb damping → linear decay; viscous → exponential decay. Lumped mass → diagonal [M]; consistent mass → full [M]. Rayleigh method → upper bound; Dunkerley → lower bound. Mode n has (n − 1) nodes. Modal superposition & Duhamel integral: linear systems only. SRSS for well-separated modes; CQC for closely spaced modes. Rigid structure (T → 0): spectral acceleration = PGA. Taller / more flexible building → longer period → lower seismic acceleration (typically). Average-acceleration Newmark → unconditionally stable. Simply supported beam frequency ∝ n²; string frequency ∝ n. Stiffness in parallel adds; in series reciprocals add. Cantilever k = 3EI/L³; fixed–fixed column sway k = 12EI/h³.

PART I — GEOTECHNICAL ENGINEERING (INCL. FOUNDATIONS & ADVANCED SOIL MECHANICS)

Soil: unconsolidated material formed by weathering of rocks (physical + chemical). Residual soil: remains at place of formation (e.g. laterite). Transported soils: alluvial (water), aeolian (wind), glacial (ice – till/drift), lacustrine (lake), marine (sea), colluvial (gravity – talus). Loess: wind-blown silt; collapses on wetting (collapsible soil). Black cotton soil: expansive clay rich in montmorillonite; large swell–shrink. Laterite: residual, red due to iron oxide; tropical climates. Bentonite: montmorillonite clay from volcanic ash; used in drilling mud and diaphragm walls. Varved clay: alternate thin layers of silt and clay (glacial lakes). Marl: calcareous clay. Caliche: soil cemented by calcium carbonate. Hardpan: dense cemented layer. Peat/muck: highly organic, very compressible. Father of soil mechanics: Karl Terzaghi. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Soils of Pakistan: Indus plains — alluvial silts & sands (often loose, liquefiable, high water table); Potohar/Islamabad — silty clays & loess-like deposits; Karachi — marine clays and limestone; Thar & Cholistan — aeolian sands; northern areas — glacial/moraine deposits and boulders. Weathering: Physical (temperature, frost, abrasion) gives coarse soils; chemical (oxidation, hydration, carbonation) gives clay minerals. Loess (wind-blown silt) collapses on wetting; black cotton soil (montmorillonite) swells and shrinks; varved clays show alternate silt/clay layers (glacial
More on this topic — Engineering Geology & Seismology: Weathering & Soil Formation

Weathering: in-place breakdown of rock. Erosion: removal and transport. Physical: frost wedging (water expands ≈ 9% on freezing), exfoliation (onion-skin), thermal expansion, salt crystallisation. Chemical: oxidation, hydration, hydrolysis (feldspar → kaolinite clay), carbonation (limestone dissolves), solution. Biological: root wedging, burrowing, organic acids. Chemical weathering dominant in hot humid climate; physical weathering in cold/arid climate. Residual soil: formed in place. Transported soils: alluvial (river), lacustrine (lake), marine, aeolian/loess (wind), glacial/till (ice), colluvial/talus (gravity). Soil profile: O (organic) → A (topsoil) → B (subsoil, accumulation) → C (weathered rock) → R (bedrock).

Three phases: solids, water, air. Dry and fully saturated soils are two-phase. Water content w = Ww/Ws × 100 (can exceed 100%). Void ratio e = Vv/Vs (can exceed 1). Porosity n = Vv/V (always < 1). n = e/(1+e);  e = n/(1−n). Degree of saturation S = Vw/Vv (0 dry, 1 saturated). Air content ac = Va/Vv;  S + ac = 1.  Percentage air voids na = Va/V = n·ac. Key relation: Se = wG. Bulk unit weight γ = (G + Se)γw/(1+e). Dry unit weight γd = Gγw/(1+e) = γ/(1+w). Saturated unit weight γsat = (G + e)γw/(1+e). Submerged unit weight γ′ = γsat − γw = (G−1)γw/(1+e)  (≈ half of γsat). Zero air voids line: γd = Gγw/(1 + wG). Specific gravity G: sands ≈ 2.65; clays 2.7–2.8; organic soils lower. Pycnometer (coarse), density bottle (fine). Relative density Dr = (emax − e)/(emax − emin) × 100 = [(γd − γdmin)/(γdmax − γdmin)]·(γdmax/γd) × 100. Dr classes: very loose 0–15, loose 15–35, medium 35–65, dense 65–85, very dense 85–100%. Water content: oven drying at 105–110 °C for 24 h (standard); 60 °C for organic/gypsum soils. Quick methods: sand bath, calcium carbide, alcohol, pycnometer, torsion balance. Field density: core cutter (soft cohesive soils), sand replacement (gravelly/stony soils), water displacement, rubber balloon, nuclear gauge.
