Given: w = 20%, G = 2.70, e = 0.65. Saturation: S = wG/e = 0.20 × 2.70/0.65 = 0.83 (83%). Unit weights: γd = 2.70 × 9.81/1.65 = 16.05 kN/m³; γ = γd(1 + w) = 19.26 kN/m³; γsat = (2.70 + 0.65)9.81/1.65 = 19.92 kN/m³; γ′ = 10.11 kN/m³. Porosity: n = e/(1 + e) = 0.394. Se = wG is the most-used relation; for a fully saturated soil e = wG.

Sieve analysis for coarse fraction (> 75 µm); sedimentation (hydrometer/pipette) for fines (< 75 µm). Stokes' law: v = (γs − γw)D²/(18μ); valid for 0.2 mm to 0.0002 mm. Dispersing agent: sodium hexametaphosphate. Coefficient of uniformity Cu = D60/D10; coefficient of curvature Cc = D30²/(D10·D60). Well graded: gravel Cu > 4, sand Cu > 6, and Cc = 1–3 for both. D10 = effective size (Hazen). Uniform soil: Cu ≈ 1. Gap graded: some sizes missing.

States: liquid → LL → plastic → PL → semi-solid → SL → solid. Liquid limit: water content at which groove (Casagrande device) closes over 13 mm in 25 blows; cone method – 20 mm penetration. Plastic limit: water content at which soil thread crumbles at 3 mm diameter. Shrinkage limit: water content below which no further volume reduction on drying (mercury used to find volume). Plasticity index PI = LL − PL. Shrinkage index = PL − SL. Liquidity index LI = (w − PL)/PI;  Consistency index CI = (LL − w)/PI;  LI + CI = 1. LI > 1: soil in liquid state; LI < 0 (CI > 1): semi-solid/very stiff. Flow index If = slope of flow curve (w vs log N). Toughness index It = PI/If. Plasticity: PI = 0 non-plastic; < 7 low; 7–17 medium; > 17 high. Activity A = PI / (% clay < 2 µm): inactive < 0.75; normal 0.75–1.25; active > 1.25. Kaolinite ≈ 0.4, montmorillonite highest. Sensitivity St = qu (undisturbed) / qu (remoulded, same w): 1 insensitive; 1–2 low; 2–4 medium; 4–8 sensitive; 8–16 extra-sensitive; > 16 quick clay. Thixotropy: regain of strength with time after remoulding at constant water content. Free swell index > 50% indicates high swelling (expansive) soil. Particle sizes (IS): boulder > 300 mm; cobble 80–300; gravel 4.75–80; sand 0.075–4.75; silt 0.002–0.075; clay < 0.002 mm. Sand subdivisions (IS): coarse 2–4.75, medium 0.425–2, fine 0.075–0.425 mm. USCS (Casagrande): coarse-grained if > 50% retained on 75 µm (No. 200) sieve. Gravel if > 50% of coarse fraction retained on 4.75 mm (No. 4) sieve; otherwise sand. Symbols: G gravel, S sand, M silt, C clay, O organic, Pt peat, W well graded, P poorly graded, L low, H high plasticity. USCS: L if LL < 50, H if LL > 50. IS adds I (intermediate): L < 35, I 35–50, H > 50. Dual symbols (e.g. SW-SM) when fines are 5–12%. Plasticity chart A-line: PI = 0.73(LL − 20). Above = clays; below = silts and organic soils. U-line (upper limit): PI = 0.9(LL − 8). Hatched zone PI 4–7 → CL-ML. AASHTO (HRB): A-1 to A-7 (A-8 peat); A-1 best subgrade. Group index GI = 0.2a + 0.005ac + 0.01bd; range 0–20; higher GI = poorer subgrade. Field identification of fines: dilatancy (shaking), toughness, dry strength. Silt – quick dilatancy, low dry strength; clay – no dilatancy, high dry strength. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 4.1 — Casagrande plasticity chart with A-line and U-line; CL/CI/CH above, ML/MH below.

Given: 62% passes 75 µm; LL = 46, PL = 22. Fine-grained: > 50% fines → fine-grained soil. Plasticity: PI = 24; A-line PI = 0.73(46 − 20) = 19 → above A-line → clay; LL between 35 and 50 → CI (IS) / CL (USCS). Soils above the A-line are clays (C); below are silts (M) or organic (O). LL 50 separates low (L) from high (H) compressibility.

Basic units: silica tetrahedron; alumina (gibbsite) or magnesia (brucite) octahedron. Kaolinite: 1:1 layer, strong hydrogen bond; stable, least swelling, low activity. Illite: 2:1 layer bonded by potassium ions; intermediate behaviour. Montmorillonite (smectite): 2:1 layer, weak bond with water between layers; maximum swelling, highest specific surface and activity. Halloysite: hydrated kaolinite, tubular. Cation replacing power: Li < Na < H < K < NH4 < Mg < Ca < Al. Adsorbed water / diffuse double layer gives clays plasticity and cohesion. Structures: single-grained (sands), honeycomb (silts), flocculated (edge-to-face; marine clays, compacted dry of optimum), dispersed (face-to-face; remoulded, compacted wet of optimum). Flocculated: higher strength and permeability than dispersed. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Mineral Structure / bond Swelling Specific surface (m²/g) Kaolinite 1:1, strong H-bond Very low ≈ 10–20 Illite 2:1, K⁺ bond Moderate ≈ 80–100 Montmorillonite 2:1, weak van der Waals / water Very high ≈ 700–800 Montmorillonite: highest swelling, LL, PI, activity and cation exchange capacity; kaolinite: the most stable.

Darcy's law: v = ki (valid for laminar flow, Re < 1). Seepage velocity vs = v/n (vs > v). Hazen: k = C·D10² (C ≈ 100 with k in cm/s, D10 in cm). Kozeny–Carman: k ∝ e³/(1+e). k ∝ γw/μ → k increases with temperature. Factors: grain size, void ratio, viscosity, degree of saturation, soil structure, adsorbed water, entrapped air, organic matter. Absolute permeability K = kμ/γw (depends only on soil; unit m² or darcy). Constant head test (coarse soils): k = QL/(Aht). Falling head test (fine soils): k = 2.303 (aL/At) log10(h1/h2). Pumping test, unconfined aquifer: k = q·ln(r2/r1) / [π(h2² − h1²)]. Pumping test, confined aquifer (thickness b): k = q·ln(r2/r1) / [2πb(h2 − h1)]. Indirect: from consolidation test k = cv·mv·γw. Typical k (cm/s): gravel > 1; clean sand 1–10⁻³; fine sand/silt 10⁻³–10⁻⁵; silty clay 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁷; clay < 10⁻⁷. Layered soils, flow parallel: kh = Σ(ki·Hi)/ΣHi. Layered soils, flow normal: kv = ΣHi / Σ(Hi/ki).  Always kh > kv. Anisotropic flow net: equivalent k′ = √(kh·kv); transform x by √(kv/kh). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Given: Standpipe a = 1 cm², sample A = 50 cm², L = 10 cm; head falls 50 → 25 cm in 300 s. k: k = 2.303 (aL/At) log(h₁/h₂) = 2.303 × (1 × 10)/(50 × 300) × log 2 = 4.6 × 10⁻⁴ cm/s. Layered deposit: Horizontal permeability always ≥ vertical permeability (kh ≥ kv). Constant-head test → coarse soils (sands, gravels); falling-head test → fine soils (silts, clays).

Terzaghi: σ = σ′ + u. Strength and compressibility are controlled by effective stress. Capillary rise hc = 4T cosα/(γw d) ≈ 0.3/d cm (d in cm, pure water). Hazen: hc = C/(e·D10). In capillary zone pore pressure is negative → effective stress increases. Upward seepage: σ′ = z(γ′ − iγw). Downward seepage: σ′ = z(γ′ + iγw). Seepage force per unit volume = iγw (acts in direction of flow). Critical hydraulic gradient ic = γ′/γw = (G − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1. Quick sand: σ′ = 0 under upward flow at i = ic; a hydraulic condition, not a soil type (fine sands/silts). Flow net: solution of Laplace equation; flow lines ⟂ equipotentials; elements are curvilinear squares. Seepage q = kH·(Nf/Nd); Nf/Nd = shape factor. FS against piping = ic / iexit (3–4 recommended). Weir/barrage theories: Bligh's creep theory; Lane's weighted creep (horizontal creep weighted 1/3); Khosla's theory. Earth dam phreatic line: base parabola (Casagrande) with focus at the toe filter; entry correction at upstream face. Filter criteria (Terzaghi): D15(filter)/D85(soil) < 4–5 (no piping) and D15(filter)/D15(soil) > 4–5 (free drainage). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Quick condition example: G = 2.65, e = 0.65 → ic = (G − 1)/(1 + e) = 1.0. Piping & heave: Prevented by cut-offs, longer seepage path, filters, relief wells, weighted filters (inverted filters) at exit. Quicksand is a hydraulic condition (σ′ = 0), not a type of soil; it happens in fine sands/silts under upward seep

Boussinesq (homogeneous, isotropic, elastic, semi-infinite): σz = (3Q/2πz²)·[1/(1 + (r/z)²)]^(5/2). Directly below point load: Boussinesq σz = 0.4775 Q/z². Westergaard (stratified soil, thin rigid layers, μ = 0): σz = (Q/πz²)·[1/(1 + 2(r/z)²)]^(3/2); below load 0.3183 Q/z². Westergaard value ≈ 2/3 of Boussinesq below the load. Line load: σz = (2q/πz)·[1/(1 + (x/z)²)]². Centre of uniformly loaded circle: σz = q[1 − {1/(1 + (R/z)²)}^(3/2)]. Rectangular area: σz = q·I at corner; centre = 4 × corner of quarter rectangle (superposition). Newmark's chart: 200 blocks, influence value 0.005 → σz = 0.005·N·q. 2:1 method: σz = Q / [(B + z)(L + z)]. Pressure bulb: zone of significant stress; ≈ 1.5–2B deep for square footings, deeper (≈ 3B or more) for strip footings. Contact pressure, rigid footing: clay – maximum at edges; sand – maximum at centre. Flexible footing: uniform pressure; settlement maximum at centre on clay, at edges on sand. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Isobar: Line joining points of equal vertical stress; bulb of 0.2q extends ≈ 1.5B below square footing and ≈ 3B below strip footing. Boussinesq influence (point load): σz = (3Q/2πz²)[1/(1 + (r/z)²)]^(5/2).

Compaction: densification by expulsion of air (dynamic, instant). Consolidation: expulsion of water under static load over time. Standard Proctor: 2.5 kg rammer, 305 mm drop, 3 layers, 25 blows, 1000 cm³ mould; energy ≈ 600 kJ/m³. Modified Proctor: 4.89 kg rammer, 457 mm drop, 5 layers, 25 blows; energy ≈ 2700 kJ/m³ (≈ 4.5 × standard). Higher compactive effort → higher γd,max and lower OMC (curve shifts up and left). Dry of optimum: flocculated structure, higher strength, higher permeability, more swelling, brittle. Wet of optimum: dispersed structure, lower permeability, more shrinkage, flexible – preferred for earth dam cores. Well-graded coarse soils: high γd,max, low OMC. Clays: low γd,max, high OMC. Smooth wheel roller: granular bases, asphalt, finishing. Sheepsfoot roller: cohesive soils (kneading action). Pneumatic tyred roller: sandy and silty soils, wide range of soils. Vibratory rollers/plates: cohesionless soils. Rammers/tampers: confined areas. Relative compaction RC = γd(field)/γd,max(lab), usually ≥ 95%. Approx. RC = 80 + 0.2 Dr. Field control: Proctor needle (water content), core cutter, sand replacement. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 9.1 — Compaction curves: standard vs modified Proctor, OMC and zero-air-voids line. Field density tests: Sand replacement (most common), core cutter (soft cohesive), nuclear density gauge (rapid), balloon method, water displacement. Specs: Embankments typically ≥ 95% of modified

Total settlement = immediate (elastic) + primary consolidation + secondary compression. Primary: due to expulsion of pore water (dissipation of excess pore pressure). Secondary: creep after excess pore pressure is zero. Spring analogy explains transfer of load from pore water to soil skeleton. Terzaghi 1-D assumptions: homogeneous, fully saturated, incompressible solids and water, Darcy's law valid, 1-D flow and compression, k and mv constant, small strains. Coefficient of compressibility av = −Δe/Δσ′. Coefficient of volume change mv = av/(1 + e0). Compression index Cc = Δe / log10(σ2′/σ1′) (slope of e–log σ′ line). Skempton (remoulded): Cc = 0.007(LL − 10). Terzaghi–Peck (undisturbed NC): Cc = 0.009(LL − 10). Swelling/recompression index Cs ≈ Cc/5 to Cc/10. NC clay settlement: Sc = [Cc·H/(1 + e0)]·log10[(σ0′ + Δσ)/σ0′]. Also Sc = mv·H·Δσ. OC clay: use Cs up to preconsolidation pressure σp′, then Cc beyond it. OCR = σp′/σ0′: NC = 1; OC > 1; under-consolidated < 1. σp′ found by Casagrande's graphical method. Coefficient of consolidation cv = k/(mv·γw). Time factor Tv = cv·t/d². Drainage path d = H/2 (double drainage), H (single drainage). t ∝ d² → double drainage is 4 times faster. U ≤ 60%: Tv = (π/4)U². U > 60%: Tv = 1.781 − 0.933 log10(100 − U%). Tv for U = 50% = 0.197; U = 90% = 0.848. Square-root-of-time (Taylor): cv = 0.848 d²/t90. Log-time (Casagrande): cv = 0.197 d²/t50. Oedometer: fixed or floating ring; load increment ratio 1; each load ≈ 24 h. Secondary compression i

Given: NC clay 4 m thick, e₀ = 1.0, Cc = 0.30, σ₀′ = 80 kPa at mid-depth, Δσ = 40 kPa. Settlement: Sc = (0.30 × 4/2.0) log(120/80) = 0.6 × 0.176 = 0.106 m ≈ 106 mm. Time (double drainage): d = 2 m; for U = 90%, t = 0.848 d²/cv. Time for given U ∝ d² — doubling drainage path quadruples consolidation time; single drainage takes 4× longer than double for the same layer.

Terzaghi 1-D theory: ∂u/∂t = cv ∂²u/∂z²; Tv = cv t / Hdr²; Tv(50%) = 0.197, Tv(90%) = 0.848; Tv = (π/4)U² for U < 60%. Lab-to-field time: t_field/t_lab = (Hdr,field/Hdr,lab)² (same U). Example: 20 mm sample (double drainage, Hdr = 10 mm) 50% in 10 min → 5 m single drainage layer: 10 × (5000/10)² min ≈ 4.75 years. Determining cv: Casagrande log-time (t50) and Taylor root-time (t90) fitting methods. Pre-consolidation pressure: Casagrande construction on e–log σ′ curve; OCR = σ′p/σ′₀. Settlement equations: NC: Sc = Cc H/(1 + e₀) log(σ′f/σ′₀); OC with σ′f ≤ σ′p: use Cs. Secondary compression: Ss = Cα H log(t₂/t₁)/(1 + ep); significant in organic soils/peat. Acceleration: Preloading/surcharge + vertical (sand/PVD) drains — radial consolidation (Barron); drain spacing controls time. Double drainage halves Hdr → time reduces to one quarter for the same degree of consolidation.

Mohr–Coulomb: τf = c + σ tanφ; effective: τf = c′ + σ′ tanφ′. Failure plane inclined at 45° + φ/2 to the major principal plane. σ1 = σ3·tan²(45° + φ/2) + 2c·tan(45° + φ/2). Maximum shear stress acts on a 45° plane, but failure plane coincides with it only when φ = 0. Direct shear test: failure plane predetermined, non-uniform stress, poor drainage control, no pore pressure measurement. Triaxial test: drainage controlled, pore pressure measured; types UU, CU, CD. UU: φu = 0 for saturated clay. CU: gives total and effective parameters. CD: slow test, gives c′, φ′. Unconfined compression: special triaxial with σ3 = 0; for clays cu = qu/2. Vane shear: in-situ undrained strength of soft/sensitive clays. T = πD²c(H/2 + D/6) (both ends shearing). UU applications: end-of-construction of embankments/footings on saturated clay. CU applications: rapid drawdown, staged construction. CD applications: long-term stability; granular soils. Sands: c = 0, φ ≈ 28–45°. Dense sand shows peak strength and dilation; loose sand contracts. Critical void ratio: void ratio at which shearing causes no volume change. Liquefaction: loose saturated fine sand under cyclic (earthquake) loading; pore pressure rises, σ′ → 0. Skempton: Δu = B[Δσ3 + A(Δσ1 − Δσ3)]. B = 1 saturated, 0 dry. Af: NC clay 0.5–1; heavily OC clay negative; sensitive clay > 1. NC clay: c′ ≈ 0. Residual strength used for long-term stability of old slip surfaces. Stress path: p = (σ1 + σ3)/2, q = (σ1 − σ3)/2. Kf line: tanα = sinφ; intercep
Given: Sand (c = 0), φ = 30°, σ₃ = 100 kPa. Answer: σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(60°) = 100 × 3 = 300 kPa; deviator stress = 200 kPa. Unconfined compression: cu = qu/2 for saturated clay (φ = 0).

Triaxial tests: UU (quick, total stress, φu = 0 for saturated clay), CU (with pore-pressure measurement → c′, φ′), CD (slow, drained — sands, long term). Back pressure: Applied to saturate the specimen (dissolve air) — check by Skempton B ≥ 0.95 (CE-335 question). Skempton pore-pressure parameters: Δu = B[Δσ₃ + A(Δσ₁ − Δσ₃)]; B = 1 for saturated soil; Af ≈ 1 (NC clay), ≈ 0 to −0.5 (heavily OC clay). Dense vs loose sand (direct shear): Dense: peak then softening, dilation (volume increase); loose: no peak, contraction; both reach the same critical (constant-volume) state. Stress paths: MIT: p = (σ₁ + σ₃)/2, q = (σ₁ − σ₃)/2; Cambridge: p′ = (σ′₁ + 2σ′₃)/3, q = σ′₁ − σ′₃. Kf-line: a = c cos φ, tan α = sin φ. Sensitivity & thixotropy: St = qu(undisturbed)/qu(remoulded); quick clays St > 16; thixotropy = regain of strength with time. For a CD test with σ₃ = 100 and deviator 250 kPa: σ₁ = 350; sin φ′ = (350 − 100)/(350 + 100) → φ′ ≈ 33.7°.

Fig. 12.1 — Critical state line, yield surfaces and NCL in q–p′ and e–ln p′ spaces. Critical state: Soil sheared continuously at constant volume, constant stresses: q = M p′ and e = eΓ − λ ln p′. M: Triaxial compression M = 6 sin φ′cs / (3 − sin φ′cs). Normal consolidation line: e = eN − λ ln p′; unloading–reloading lines slope κ (Cc ≈ 2.3λ, Cs ≈ 2.3κ). Wet vs dry side: Lightly OC (wet of critical): contract, positive pore pressure, hardening. Heavily OC (dry of critical): dilate, negative pore pressure, peak then softening. Cam-Clay models: Original & Modified Cam Clay (elliptical yield surface) — basis of advanced FE soil models. Critical-state friction angle is a material constant independent of initial density.

At rest (no wall movement): Jaky K0 = 1 − sinφ′ (NC). Elastic: K0 = μ/(1 − μ). OC: K0 = (1 − sinφ′)·OCR^sinφ′. Active (wall moves away from soil) < at rest < passive (wall moves towards soil). Passive state needs much larger wall movement than active. Rankine (smooth vertical wall, horizontal backfill): Ka = (1 − sinφ)/(1 + sinφ) = tan²(45° − φ/2); Kp = 1/Ka. For φ = 30°: Ka = 1/3, Kp = 3. Active failure plane at 45° + φ/2 to horizontal; passive at 45° − φ/2. Active thrust Pa = ½ Ka γ H², acting at H/3 above base. Surcharge q: uniform pressure Ka·q; resultant acts at H/2. Submerged backfill: p = Ka γ′ z + γw z. Cohesive soil: pa = Ka γ z − 2c√Ka. Depth of tension crack zc = 2c/(γ√Ka); for φ = 0, zc = 2c/γ. Critical height of unsupported vertical cut Hc = 4c/(γ√Ka); φ = 0: Hc = 4c/γ. Coulomb wedge theory: includes wall friction δ, inclined wall, sloping backfill; plane failure surface. Coulomb overestimates passive pressure (actual surface curved). Graphical methods: Rebhann, Culmann. Rankine ignores wall friction → conservative (higher) active pressure. Retaining wall checks: overturning (FS ≥ 1.5–2), sliding (FS ≥ 1.5), bearing pressure, no tension (e ≤ B/6). Provide weep holes/drainage to avoid water pressure behind the wall. Anchored sheet piles: free earth support and fixed earth support methods. Braced cuts: Peck's apparent pressure diagrams. Given: Wall 6 m high, dry sand γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 30°. Thrust: Pa = ½ × ⅓ × 18 × 6² = 108 kN/m, acting 2 m above the base. With water table at surface: p = Ka γ′ z + γw z → water pressure often exceeds the soil pressure — hence weep holes and drainage. Movement needed: active ≈ 0.1–0.5% of H (small); passive ≈ 2–5% of H (large).

Types: Gravity, semi-gravity, cantilever (economical up to ≈ 6–7 m), counterfort (> 7 m), buttressed, crib, gabion, MSE (reinforced earth), anchored. Earth pressure at rest: K₀ = 1 − sin φ′ (Jaky) — wall restrained against yielding (CE-335 question). Rankine: Ka = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ); Kp = 1/Ka; Pa = ½ Ka γ H² at H/3; cohesive soil tension depth zc = 2c/(γ√Ka). Water table in backfill: Undrained backfill: use γ′ below WT + full hydrostatic pressure; thrust much larger → provide weep holes & drains. Coulomb: Considers wall friction δ and inclined back/backfill; gives smaller Ka than Rankine for δ > 0. Stability checks: Overturning FS ≥ 2.0; sliding FS ≥ 1.5; bearing (qmax ≤ qa) with e ≤ B/6; overall (deep-seated) stability FS ≥ 1.5. Proportioning (cantilever): Base width ≈ 0.5–0.7 H; toe ≈ B/3; stem top ≥ 200–300 mm; base thickness ≈ H/10–H/12; shear key to improve sliding resistance. Passive pressure in front of the toe is often ignored in sliding checks (soil may be removed).

Cantilever sheet piles: Rely on passive resistance below dredge line; economical up to ≈ 6 m retained height. Anchored sheet piles: Free-earth support method (shallower, anchor carries more) vs fixed-earth support (deeper embedment); Rowe's moment reduction for flexibility. Braced cuts: Peck's apparent pressure diagrams: sand 0.65 Ka γ H (uniform); soft–medium clay γH − 4cu (or 0.3γH min) trapezoid; stiff clay 0.2–0.4 γH. Base heave (soft clay): FS = cu Nc / (γH + q) (Bjerrum–Eide); stability number N = γH/cu > 6–8 indicates heave risk. Dewatering: Well points (≤ 5–6 m lift per stage), deep wells, electro-osmosis for silts. Strut loads in braced cuts are found from apparent pressure envelopes, not Rankine triangles.

Infinite slope, dry cohesionless: FS = tanφ/tanβ; stable up to β = φ (angle of repose). Same for fully submerged. Infinite slope with seepage parallel to slope: FS = (γ′/γsat)·tanφ/tanβ ≈ ½ of dry value. Infinite slope, c–φ soil: critical depth Hc = c / [γ cos²β (tanβ − tanφ)]. Culmann's method: plane failure surface; steep/vertical slopes. Swedish circle / ordinary method of slices (Fellenius): ignores interslice forces; conservative. Bishop's simplified method: includes horizontal interslice forces; more accurate; iterative. Non-circular surfaces: Janbu; rigorous methods: Spencer, Morgenstern–Price. Friction circle method (Taylor) for c–φ soils. Taylor's stability number Sn = c/(F·γ·H); critical height Hc = c/(Sn·γ). Failure circles: toe, slope (face) and base failure (soft layer below toe). FS defined w.r.t. cohesion (Fc), friction (Fφ) and height (FH). Usual minimum FS ≈ 1.5. Earth dam critical cases: upstream slope – sudden drawdown; downstream slope – steady seepage (reservoir full); both – end of construction. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 15.1 — Slip circles: toe, slope (face) and base failure. Typical FS required: Long-term slopes ≈ 1.5; end-of-construction ≈ 1.3; rapid drawdown ≈ 1.2–1.3; seismic ≈ 1.0–1.1. Landslides in Pakistan: Frequent along KKH, Murree–Kohala, Swat & Kohistan roads; remedies — drainage (horizontal drains), retaining/breast walls, rock bolting, slope flattening, bio-engineering. Infinite slope

Shallow foundation: Df ≤ B (Terzaghi). Gross ultimate qu; net ultimate qnu = qu − γDf; net safe qns = qnu/F; safe qs = qnu/F + γDf. F usually 2.5–3. Allowable bearing pressure = lesser of safe bearing capacity and pressure for permissible settlement. Terzaghi strip: qu = cNc + γDf·Nq + 0.5γB·Nγ. Terzaghi square: qu = 1.3cNc + γDf·Nq + 0.4γB·Nγ. Terzaghi circular: qu = 1.3cNc + γDf·Nq + 0.3γB·Nγ (B = diameter). φ = 0: Terzaghi Nc = 5.7, Nq = 1, Nγ = 0. Skempton (clay): Nc = 5.14 strip, 6.2 square/circle at surface; increases with Df/B up to 7.5 (strip) and 9 (square). General shear failure: dense sand, stiff clay; well-defined surface, heaving, tilting. Local shear: medium soils; Terzaghi uses c′ = (2/3)c, tanφ′ = (2/3)tanφ. Punching shear: loose sand, soft clay, deep footings; no heave. Water table at base of footing: Nγ term reduced (≈ half). At ground surface: both γ terms reduced → large loss of capacity. Clay (φ = 0): bearing capacity independent of width B. Sand: increases with B and Df. Meyerhof, Hansen, Vesic, IS 6403: add shape, depth and inclination factors. Eccentric load: q = (P/A)(1 ± 6e/B); no tension if e ≤ B/6 (middle third). Meyerhof effective width B′ = B − 2e. Rankine minimum depth: Df = (q/γ)·[(1 − sinφ)/(1 + sinφ)]². Immediate settlement: Si = qB(1 − μ²)If / E. Permissible settlement (Terzaghi–Peck): 25 mm for footings on sand. Angular distortion 1/500 safe limit for buildings (Bjerrum). Plate load test: plate ≥ 300 mm; pit width ≥ 5 × plate width. Plate t
Worked example — Terzaghi strip footing on clay

Given: B = 2 m, Df = 1.5 m, cu = 50 kPa, φ = 0, γ = 18 kN/m³. Ultimate: qu = 5.7 × 50 + 18 × 1.5 × 1 = 285 + 27 = 312 kPa; net qnu = 285 kPa; safe (FS = 3) qs = 285/3 + 27 = 122 kPa. Local shear (Terzaghi): c′ = ⅔c and tanφ′ = ⅔ tanφ. Water table rising to the ground surface roughly halves the Nq and Nγ contributions (γ′ ≈ γ/2) in sands.

Fig. 16.2 — Failure zones under a strip footing (Terzaghi's general shear failure). Failure modes: General shear (dense sand, stiff clay — clear peak, heave), local shear (medium dense), punching shear (loose sand/soft clay, deep footings) — Vesic. Terzaghi (strip): qu = c Nc + q Nq + 0.5 γ B Nγ; square: 1.3cNc + qNq + 0.4γBNγ; circular: 1.3cNc + qNq + 0.3γBNγ. φ = 0 (undrained clay): Nc = 5.7 (Terzaghi) / 5.14 (Prandtl–Skempton); Nq = 1, Nγ = 0 → qu = 5.14 cu + q (strip). Meyerhof general equation: qu = c Nc sc dc ic + q Nq sq dq iq + 0.5 γ B′ Nγ sγ dγ iγ (shape, depth, inclination factors). Inclination factors (Meyerhof): ic = iq = (1 − α°/90)²; iγ = (1 − α/φ)². Eccentric load (Meyerhof effective area): B′ = B − 2e, L′ = L − 2e_L; use A′ = B′L′; keep e ≤ B/6 for no tension (qmax/min = (Q/BL)(1 ± 6e/B)). Water table: WT at base: use γ′ in the Nγ term; WT at ground: γ′ in both q and Nγ terms; WT deeper than B below base: no effect. Factor of safety: FS = 2.5–3 on net ultimate: qnet,safe = (qu − γDf)/FS + γDf for gross safe capacity. Short vs long term (stiff clay): Check both undrained (cu, φu = 0) and drained (c′, φ′) cases — for stiff OC clays the drained case often governs (CE-321 mid-term question). In-situ correlations: SPT (Meyerhof/Bowles: qa ∝ N for 25 mm settlement), plate load test (scale effects: sand settlement ratio, clay capacity independent of size). Nc = 5.14, Nq = 1, Nγ = 0 for φ = 0. Bearing capacity in sand increases with B (Nγ term); in clay it is independ

Elastic settlement: Si = q B (1 − μ²) If / Es; flexible footing: centre settlement > corner; rigid footing ≈ 0.8 × flexible centre value. Schmertmann (sand): S = C₁C₂ Δq Σ (Iz/Es) Δz; strain-influence peak at B/2 depth. Permissible settlement (typical): Isolated footings on sand 40 mm (rafts 40–65 mm); on clay 65 mm (rafts 65–100 mm); angular distortion ≤ 1/300 (cracking), 1/500 safe limit for frames. Differential settlement: Controls structural damage; mats & rigid rafts reduce it. Angular distortion 1/150 → structural damage; 1/300 → cracking of panel walls; 1/500 → safe limit (Bjerrum).

Fig. 18.1 — Isolated, combined, strap and mat footings (plan views). Combined footing: When columns are close or an exterior column is at the property line; make the centroid of the footing coincide with the resultant of column loads → uniform pressure. Rectangular or trapezoidal. Strap (cantilever) footing: Exterior footing connected by a rigid strap beam to an interior footing; strap transfers moment, does not bear on soil. Mat / raft: When footings cover > 50% of building area, weak soil, or to reduce differential settlement; types: flat plate, thickened under columns, beam-and-slab, cellular, piled raft. Compensated (floating) foundation: Net pressure qnet = Q/A − γDf → zero when excavated soil weight = building load (fully compensated). Analysis: Rigid (conventional) method vs flexible (Winkler / modulus of subgrade reaction ks; beam on elastic foundation, FEM). Mat is economical when the combined footing area exceeds about half of the plan area.

Piles used for: weak upper strata, heavy loads, uplift, lateral loads, scour, expansive soils. By function: end bearing, friction, compaction, tension (uplift), anchor, fender, batter, sheet piles. By installation: driven (displacement), bored (replacement), driven cast-in-situ. Cast-in-situ types: Franki, Raymond, Simplex, MacArthur. Under-reamed piles: expansive (black cotton) soils; bulb diameter ≈ 2.5 × stem diameter. Static formula: Qu = Qb + Qs = qb·Ab + Σ fs·As. Clay: Qb = 9cu·Ab; Qs = α·c·As (α = adhesion factor). Sand: Qb = σ′v·Nq·Ab; Qs = Kσ′v tanδ·As; σ′v assumed constant below critical depth (≈ 10–20D). Engineering News formula: Qa = WH/[6(S + C)]; C = 2.5 cm (drop hammer), 0.25 cm (steam hammer); FS of 6 built in. Hiley formula: more rational dynamic formula. Dynamic formulas unreliable in clays. Pile load test (IS 2911) safe load: least of 2/3 of load at 12 mm settlement, and 1/2 of load at settlement = 10% of pile diameter. Cyclic load test separates skin friction and end bearing. Initial test (design) vs routine test (working piles). Group efficiency η = Qg/(n·Qs). Converse–Labarre: η = 1 − θ[(n−1)m + (m−1)n]/(90mn), θ = tan⁻¹(d/s) in degrees. Minimum spacing: ≈ 2.5D (end bearing), 3D (friction piles). Clay group: check block failure Qg = cNc·Ab + c·P·L (Nc = 9). Sand (driven): η may exceed 1. Group settlement in clay: equivalent raft at 2L/3 depth with 2V:1H load spread. Negative skin friction: settling fill/soft clay drags pile down; Fn = c·P·L (clay); reduc

Given: Bored pile D = 0.5 m, L = 15 m, cu = 60 kPa (uniform), α = 0.45. Capacity: Qb = 9 × 60 × 0.196 = 106 kN; Qs = 0.45 × 60 × (π × 0.5 × 15) = 636 kN; Qu = 742 kN; Qsafe (FS 2.5) ≈ 297 kN. Pile integrity: Low-strain integrity test (PIT), cross-hole sonic logging, high-strain dynamic test (PDA). In clay, most of the capacity of friction piles comes from skin friction; negative skin friction reduces the capacity.

Fig. 19.1 — Load transfer in a pile: skin friction plus end bearing. Classification: By function: end-bearing, friction, compaction, tension (uplift), anchor, batter (inclined loads), sheet. By material/installation: driven (displacement) vs bored/cast-in-situ (non-displacement). Static capacity: Qu = Qb + Qs = qb Ab + Σ fs As. Clay: qb = 9 cu; fs = α cu (α-method), β-method fs = β σ′v, λ-method. Sand: qb = σ′v Nq* (limited), fs = K σ′v tan δ. Critical depth (sand): Skin friction & end bearing assumed constant below ≈ 15–20 D (Meyerhof/Vesic). Dynamic formulas: Engineering News: Qa = W h / (6(s + c)) (c = 25 mm drop hammer, 2.5 mm steam); Hiley formula; wave-equation & PDA for modern practice. Pile groups: Group efficiency (Converse–Labarre) η = 1 − θ[(n−1)m + (m−1)n]/(90mn), θ = tan⁻¹(d/s); clay block failure: Qg = 9cu·B·L + 2(B + L)·Lp·c̄. Spacing: Minimum 2.5–3 D (friction piles ≥ 3 D). Negative skin friction: Downdrag when surrounding soil settles relative to pile (fill over soft clay, lowering WT); Qn = perimeter × length × α cu. Load tests: Maintained load test; failure load: settlement = 10% of D or double-tangent; allowable (IS 2911) = lesser of ⅔ of the load at 12 mm settlement and ½ of the load at settlement = 10% of D; cyclic test separates skin & tip. Wells/caissons: Open, box, pneumatic caissons; well foundations for bridge piers in rivers (grip length ≥ ⅓ of maximum scour depth). Pile group in clay: capacity = smaller of (n × single pile) and block failure. Nega

Stages: reconnaissance, preliminary exploration, detailed exploration. Methods: test pits (shallow), auger boring, wash boring (disturbed samples), percussion drilling (boulders), rotary drilling (rock). Depth of exploration: till stress increase becomes negligible (≈ 10% of applied); ≈ 1.5–2B for isolated footings. Area ratio Ar = (Do² − Di²)/Di² × 100; ≤ 10% for undisturbed sampling (thin-walled). Inside clearance 1–3% (reduces wall friction); outside clearance 0–2%. Recovery ratio = length of sample / penetration (≈ 0.96–0.98 good). Samplers: split spoon (disturbed, SPT), Shelby/thin-walled tube (soft clays), piston sampler (very soft/sensitive clays), Denison (stiff clays), core barrels (rock). RQD = Σ core pieces ≥ 100 mm / length of run × 100: < 25 very poor; 25–50 poor; 50–75 fair; 75–90 good; 90–100 excellent. SPT: 63.5 kg hammer, 750 mm drop, split spoon 50.8 mm OD; N = blows for last 300 mm of 450 mm penetration. SPT corrections: overburden, energy (N60), dilatancy N′ = 15 + ½(N − 15) for N > 15 in fine/silty sand below WT. N (sand): 0–4 very loose; 4–10 loose; 10–30 medium; 30–50 dense; > 50 very dense. Static cone (CPT): 60° cone, 10 cm² base, pushed at 2 cm/s; cone resistance qc and friction ratio identify soil type. Dynamic cone test: continuous record of blows; quick, approximate. Seismic refraction: works only if wave velocity increases with depth. Electrical resistivity (Wenner array, 4 equally spaced electrodes): ρ = 2πaR. Groundwater table recorded at least
More on this topic — Engineering Geology & Seismology: Site Investigation

Stages: desk study & reconnaissance → preliminary investigation → detailed investigation → construction-stage checks. Direct methods: test pits, trenches, shafts, adits, borings. Boring types: auger, wash, percussion, rotary; core drilling (diamond bit) for rock samples. Core recovery (%) = length of core recovered / length drilled × 100. RQD (Deere) = Σ length of core pieces ≥ 10 cm / total run length × 100. RQD (%) Rock quality < 25 Very poor 25 – 50 Poor 50 – 75 Fair 75 – 90 Good 90 – 100 Excellent

Seismic refraction: wave velocities → depth to bedrock, rippability. Works when velocity increases with depth. Electrical resistivity (Wenner, Schlumberger arrays): groundwater, clay layers, depth to rock. Dry rock = high resistivity; saline water/clay = low. Gravity & magnetic: cavities, ore bodies, buried structures. GPR: shallow utilities, voids. Geophysical results must be confirmed by boreholes.

RMR (Bieniawski): 5 parameters – UCS, RQD, joint spacing, joint condition, groundwater – plus adjustment for joint orientation. Classes: I very good (81–100), II good (61–80), III fair (41–60), IV poor (21–40), V very poor (< 21). Q-system (Barton, NGI): Q = (RQD/Jn) × (Jr/Ja) × (Jw/SRF); range 0.001 – 1000. GSI (Hoek): based on structure and surface condition of joints. Other tests: UCS, point load index, slake durability (shale), Schmidt hammer.

CBR plunger 50 mm diameter, penetration rate 1.25 mm/min. Standard loads: 1370 kg at 2.5 mm; 2055 kg at 5.0 mm. CBR normally taken at 2.5 mm; if value at 5 mm is higher, repeat test; if still higher, use 5 mm value. Specimen soaked 4 days; surcharge weights (2.5 kg each) represent pavement load. Modulus of subgrade reaction k = p/0.125 cm (75 cm diameter plate). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Typical CBR values: Clay ≈ 2–5%; silt ≈ 5–10%; sand ≈ 10–40%; gravel ≈ 30–80%; crushed stone base ≥ 80%. CBR = test load ÷ standard load × 100 at 2.5 mm (1370 kg) and 5.0 mm (2055 kg) penetration; plunger area 19.6 cm² (50 mm dia).

Expansive soils: montmorillonite; remedies – under-reamed piles, CNS (cohesive non-swelling) layer, sand cushion, lime stabilization, moisture control. Collapsible soils (loess): sudden settlement on wetting; remedy – prewetting, compaction, chemical stabilization. Mechanical stabilization: blending soils to good gradation. Cement stabilization: best for sandy/granular soils. Lime: clayey soils (reduces PI, swelling). Bitumen: waterproofing/binding granular soils. Chemicals: CaCl2, NaCl, sodium silicate. Electro-osmosis: drainage of silts and clays. Thermal: heating/freezing. Vibroflotation: densifying deep loose sands. Stone columns: soft clays. Sand drains / prefabricated vertical (wick) drains: accelerate consolidation by radial drainage (Barron); smear zone reduces efficiency. Drain influence radius: R = 0.564s (square pattern), 0.525s (triangular pattern). Preloading/surcharging: induce settlement before construction. Dynamic compaction (Ménard): heavy weight dropped from height. Grouting: cement, chemical, jet grouting. Dewatering: well points, deep wells. Reinforced earth (Henri Vidal), soil nailing, geosynthetics. Geosynthetic functions: separation, reinforcement, filtration, drainage, containment. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Lime stabilisation: Best for clays (reduces PI, swelling); cement for sandy/granular soils; bitumen for sands (waterproofing). Geosynthetics: Geotextiles (separation, filtration, drainage), geogri

Liquefaction: Loss of strength of loose, saturated, clean/silty sands under cyclic loading as pore pressure rises to σ′v (effective stress → 0). Susceptibility: Loose (N₁,60 < 15–20), saturated, uniformly graded fine sands, shallow WT, strong shaking (M > 5.5). Evaluation: Seed–Idriss simplified: CSR = 0.65 (amax/g)(σv/σ′v) rd vs CRR from SPT/CPT/Vs; FS = CRR/CSR. Mitigation: Densification (vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction), stone columns (drainage), grouting, deep soil mixing, piles to non-liquefiable layer. Machine foundations: Avoid resonance: operating frequency should differ from natural frequency by ≥ 20–30%; block foundation mass ≈ 2–3 × machine mass. Liquefaction is most likely in loose saturated fine sand with high water table during strong earthquakes.

γw = 9.81 kN/m³; G (sand) ≈ 2.65; ic ≈ 1. 75 µm sieve divides coarse and fine soils; 4.75 mm divides gravel and sand. A-line PI = 0.73(LL − 20); LL 50 divides L and H (USCS). Tv: U50 = 0.197, U90 = 0.848. Terzaghi Nc (φ = 0) = 5.7; Skempton strip = 5.14; pile end bearing Nc = 9. Rankine φ = 30°: Ka = 1/3, Kp = 3; failure plane at 45° + φ/2. Standard Proctor: 2.5 kg / 305 mm / 3 layers / 25 blows. Modified: 4.89 kg / 457 mm / 5 layers / 25 blows. SPT: 63.5 kg / 750 mm / last 300 mm. CBR plunger 50 mm at 1.25 mm/min. Boussinesq 0.4775 Q/z²; Westergaard 0.3183 Q/z²; Newmark influence 0.005. Middle-third rule: e ≤ B/6 for no tension.

Often confused Key difference Void ratio vs porosity e = Vv/Vs (can exceed 1) vs n = Vv/V (< 1) Density index vs relative compaction Dr from e (sands) vs RC = γd field/γd max Consistency vs liquidity index CI = (LL − w)/PI vs LI = (w − PL)/PI; CI + LI = 1 Compaction vs consolidation Expulsion of AIR (quick, by machines) vs expulsion of WATER (slow, under load) Cc vs Cv Compression index (slope of e–log p) vs coefficient of consolidation (rate) NC vs OC clay OCR = 1 vs > 1; heavily OC clay has negative pore pressure at failure UU vs CU vs CD Short-term / rapid drawdown / long-term analyses Boussinesq vs Westergaard Homogeneous vs stratified (laminated) soil; W ≈ ⅔ B at centre line Active vs passive Wall away (Ka, small movement) vs wall into soil (Kp, large movement) Rankine vs Coulomb Smooth wall, no wedge vs wall friction, trial wedge General vs local vs punching shear Dense/stiff vs medium vs loose/soft Engineering News vs Hiley Simple dynamic (FS 6) vs more rational dynamic formula

Geology: science of the Earth – its materials, structure and processes. Engineering geology: application of geology to the location, design, construction and maintenance of civil works. Age of Earth: ≈ 4.54 billion years. Mean radius: ≈ 6371 km. Crust: oceanic 5–10 km (basaltic, SIMA = Si + Mg); continental 30–70 km (granitic, SIAL = Si + Al). Moho (Mohorovičić) discontinuity: crust–mantle boundary. Mantle: Moho to ≈ 2900 km. Gutenberg discontinuity: mantle–core boundary (2900 km). Outer core: liquid (2900–5150 km) – proved because S-waves do not pass through it. Inner core: solid Fe–Ni (5150–6371 km). Lehmann discontinuity: outer–inner core boundary. Lithosphere: crust + upper rigid mantle (≈ 100 km); rests on the plastic asthenosphere. Abundant elements in crust: O (46.6%) > Si (27.7%) > Al (8.1%) > Fe (5%) > Ca > Na > K > Mg. Abundant minerals: silicates ≈ 90% of crust; feldspars are the most abundant group.

Eon / Era Periods Remark Precambrian — ≈ 88% of Earth history Paleozoic Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous, Permian Age of fishes; coal formation (Carboniferous) Mesozoic Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous Age of reptiles (dinosaurs) Cenozoic Paleogene, Neogene, Quaternary Age of mammals; Himalaya uplift; humans (Quaternary) Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 26.1 — Internal structure of the Earth and its discontinuities. Moho (crust–mantle), Gutenberg (mantle–core; S-waves disappear), Lehmann (outer–inner core). Outer core is liquid.

Mineral: naturally occurring, inorganic, solid with definite chemical composition and crystal structure. Physical properties: colour, streak (colour of powder – more reliable than colour), lustre, hardness, cleavage, fracture, specific gravity, crystal form. Cleavage: breaking along definite planes; fracture: irregular breaking (quartz shows conchoidal fracture). Quartz (SiO₂) – H 7, no cleavage, most resistant to weathering. Calcite (CaCO₃) – H 3, effervesces with cold dilute HCl. Dolomite CaMg(CO₃)₂ reacts only with warm/powdered HCl. Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) – H 2; harmful in foundations (soluble, swelling). Mica – perfect cleavage in one direction. Clay minerals: kaolinite (least swelling), illite, montmorillonite (highest swelling – expansive soils).

H Mineral H Mineral 1 Talc (softest) 6 Orthoclase feldspar 2 Gypsum 7 Quartz 3 Calcite 8 Topaz 4 Fluorite 9 Corundum 5 Apatite 10 Diamond (hardest) Field tests: fingernail ≈ 2.5, copper coin ≈ 3.5, knife / glass ≈ 5.5. Scale is relative, not linear. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Mohs hardness Mineral 1 Talc 2 Gypsum 3 Calcite 4 Fluorite 5 Apatite 6 Orthoclase feldspar 7 Quartz 8 Topaz 9 Corundum 10 Diamond Fingernail ≈ 2.5, copper coin ≈ 3, knife/glass ≈ 5.5; quartz (7) scratches glass.

Intrusive / plutonic: cool slowly at depth → coarse grained (granite, diorite, gabbro). Extrusive / volcanic: cool fast at surface → fine grained / glassy (rhyolite, andesite, basalt, obsidian, pumice). Hypabyssal: medium depth → medium grained (dolerite). By silica: acid > 66% (granite), intermediate 52–66% (diorite), basic 45–52% (basalt, gabbro), ultrabasic < 45% (peridotite). Intrusive forms: dyke (discordant, vertical), sill (concordant, horizontal), batholith (largest), laccolith (dome), lopolith (saucer), phacolith (in fold crests/troughs). Granite: high strength, good foundation and building stone; basalt: strong, used as aggregate, may show columnar joints.

Cover ≈ 75% of Earth’s land surface but only ≈ 5% of crust volume. Clastic: conglomerate (rounded gravel), breccia (angular fragments), sandstone, siltstone, shale (most abundant sedimentary rock). Chemical: limestone, rock salt, gypsum. Organic: coal, chalk, coquina. Features: stratification (bedding), fossils, ripple marks, mud cracks, cross-bedding. Sandstone strength depends on cement: siliceous (best) > ferruginous > calcareous > argillaceous (weakest). Shale: weak, slakes and swells with water – poor for dams/tunnels. Limestone: solution cavities (karst) → leakage, sinkholes.
Metamorphic Rocks (change by heat, pressure, fluids)

Contact (thermal): heat near intrusion – non-foliated. Regional (dynamothermal): heat + pressure over large area – foliated. Foliated: slate → phyllite → schist → gneiss (increasing grade). Non-foliated: marble, quartzite, anthracite. Parent rock Metamorphic rock Shale / mudstone Slate → phyllite → schist Granite Gneiss Limestone Marble Sandstone Quartzite (very hard, durable) Bituminous coal Anthracite / graphite Basalt Greenstone / amphibolite Rock cycle: igneous ⇄ sedimentary ⇄ metamorphic through weathering, deposition, metamorphism and melting.

Strike: direction of line formed by intersection of bed with a horizontal plane. Dip: maximum inclination of bed from horizontal; measured perpendicular to strike. Apparent dip < true dip. Measured with clinometer / Brunton compass. Outcrop: exposure of rock at surface. Inlier: older rocks surrounded by younger. Outlier: younger rocks surrounded by older.

Parts: hinge, limbs, axial plane, crest, trough, plunge. Anticline: up-arched, oldest beds at core. Syncline: down-folded, youngest beds at core. Other types: monocline (one-limbed step), symmetrical, asymmetrical, overturned, recumbent (axial plane ~horizontal), isoclinal (parallel limbs), chevron, plunging, dome, basin. Formed by compression.

Fault type Movement of hanging wall Stress Normal (gravity) Down relative to footwall Tension Reverse Up relative to footwall (dip > 45°) Compression Thrust Up, low-angle reverse fault (dip < 45°) Compression Strike-slip / transcurrent Horizontal along strike (dextral/sinistral) Shear Oblique-slip Combination of dip and strike slip Mixed Horst: up-thrown block between two normal faults; graben: down-dropped block (rift valley). Throw: vertical displacement; heave: horizontal displacement. Evidence: slickensides, fault breccia, fault gouge, offset beds, springs in a line, scarps. Faults are zones of weakness and seepage → avoid for dams, tunnels and heavy structures; active faults cause earthquakes.

Joint: fracture with no displacement – tension, shear, columnar (basalt), sheet joints (granite). Unconformity: surface of erosion/non-deposition (time gap) in the rock record. Angular unconformity: younger beds over tilted/folded older beds. Disconformity: parallel beds with erosion surface. Nonconformity: sedimentary rocks over igneous/metamorphic rocks. Paraconformity: parallel beds, gap hard to detect. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 29.1 — Normal, reverse (thrust) and strike-slip faults. Fig. 29.2 — Anticline and syncline. Strike & dip: Strike = direction of a horizontal line on the bed; dip = maximum inclination, measured ⊥ to strike (clinometer/Brunton compass). Normal fault → tension (hanging wall down); reverse/thrust → compression (hanging wall up); strike-slip → horizontal shear (Chaman fault, Pakistan–Afghanistan).

Porosity (n) = Vv / V; permeability = ability to transmit water. Aquifer: porous and permeable (sand, gravel, jointed rock). Aquiclude: porous but impermeable (clay). Aquitard: poorly permeable, leaky (silt, sandy clay). Aquifuge: neither porous nor permeable (massive granite). Unconfined aquifer: upper surface is water table. Confined / artesian: between impermeable layers, water under pressure (flowing well if piezometric surface above ground). Perched water table: local water body above main water table on a lens of clay. Darcy’s law: v = k·i, Q = k·i·A. Porosity = specific yield + specific retention. Pumping produces a cone of depression. Springs occur where water table meets ground surface. Groundwater effects: uplift, reduced effective stress, slope failure, tunnel inflow, liquefaction potential.
Geology of Dams, Reservoirs, Tunnels & Slopes

Ideal site: narrow valley, sound impervious bedrock at shallow depth, no active faults, low seismicity, construction material nearby. Gravity dam: needs strong rock foundation. Arch dam: narrow V-shaped gorge with strong abutments. Earth/rockfill dam: can be built on weaker foundations. Beds dipping upstream (steeply) = favourable. Beds dipping downstream = sliding and leakage risk. Avoid: faults/shear zones, cavernous limestone, soluble gypsum, swelling shale, highly jointed rock. Treatments: curtain grouting (reduce seepage), consolidation grouting (strengthen rock), cut-off walls/trenches, drainage galleries, relief wells.

Must be watertight, with stable rim slopes and low sediment inflow. Problems: leakage through limestone/faults, siltation, rim landslides (e.g. Vajont 1963, Italy), reservoir-induced seismicity (e.g. Koyna 1967, India).

Best in massive, hard, unjointed rock; tunnel axis preferably perpendicular to strike. Tunnel along a syncline axis → water inflow and high pressure; along an anticline axis → beds arch, less load but crown rock is fractured. Problems: overbreak, squeezing ground (plastic soft rock), swelling ground (montmorillonite, anhydrite), running ground (loose sand), rock burst (hard brittle rock at great depth), groundwater, gases, high temperature. Support: rock bolts, shotcrete, wire mesh, steel ribs, lining; NATM (New Austrian Tunnelling Method) uses rock as part of support.

Types (Varnes): falls, topples, slides (rotational / slump; translational / planar), spreads, flows (debris flow, mudflow, earthflow), creep (slowest – tilted poles, trees). Main trigger: water (rise in pore pressure). Others: undercutting of toe, slope steepening, earthquakes, deforestation, loading of crest. FOS = resisting forces / driving forces (FOS < 1 → failure). Control: drainage (most effective & economical), slope flattening/benching, retaining walls, gabions, rock bolts/anchors, toe berms, vegetation. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Pakistan examples: Tarbela (Indus) on alluvium with huge upstream blanket against seepage; Mangla on sandstone–clay (Siwalik) rocks; tunnels in KKH region face squeezing ground and rock bursts. Best dam site rock: massive, unweathered igneous rock (granite); worst: cavernous limestone, highly jointed or soluble rocks (gypsum).

Continental drift: Alfred Wegener (1912); supercontinent Pangaea, ocean Panthalassa; split into Laurasia (N) and Gondwana (S). Sea-floor spreading: Harry Hess (1960s). Plate tectonics unified both theories. Driving force: mantle convection, slab pull, ridge push. Divergent boundary: plates move apart – mid-ocean ridge, rift valley (East African Rift). Convergent boundary: plates collide – oceanic–continental (subduction, trench, volcanic arc e.g. Andes), oceanic–oceanic (island arcs, Japan), continental–continental (Himalaya, Indian–Eurasian plates). Transform boundary: plates slide past – San Andreas Fault (USA), Chaman Fault (Pakistan–Afghanistan). Indian plate moves north at ≈ 4–5 cm/year.

Main Karakoram Thrust (MKT), Main Mantle Thrust (MMT), Main Boundary Thrust (MBT), Salt Range Thrust – northern collision zone. Chaman Fault – left-lateral (sinistral) transform fault, western boundary of Indian plate. Ornach–Nal Fault – southern continuation towards Makran. Makran Subduction Zone – Arabian plate subducting under Eurasian plate (tsunami source).

Earthquake: sudden shaking of ground due to release of strain energy in the Earth. Causes: tectonic (most common), volcanic, collapse (caves/mines), induced (reservoirs, mining, fluid injection, explosions). Elastic rebound theory: H.F. Reid, after 1906 San Francisco earthquake – rocks store strain and snap back on rupture. Focus / hypocentre: point of origin inside Earth. Epicentre: point on surface vertically above focus. Focal depth: shallow < 70 km (most damaging, most common), intermediate 70–300 km, deep 300–700 km. Foreshock → main shock → aftershocks. Seismic belts: Circum-Pacific “Ring of Fire” (≈ 80% of earthquakes), Alpide / Mediterranean–Himalayan belt (≈ 15–17%, includes Pakistan), mid-oceanic ridges. Wadati–Benioff zone: inclined zone of earthquakes along a subducting slab.

Wave Type of motion Medium Remarks P (Primary) Compressional / longitudinal (push–pull) Solid, liquid, gas Fastest (≈ 5–8 km/s in crust); arrives first S (Secondary) Shear / transverse Solids only ≈ 3–4.5 km/s; absent through outer core → liquid core Love (L) Horizontal shear, side to side Surface Faster of the surface waves Rayleigh (R) Rolling, elliptical (retrograde) Surface Slowest; large amplitude, very damaging Body waves = P & S; surface waves = Love & Rayleigh (cause most damage). Order of arrival: P → S → Love → Rayleigh. Shadow zones: S-wave shadow 103°–180° from epicentre; P-wave shadow 103°–142°. For Poisson’s ratio 0.25, Vp/Vs ≈ √3 ≈ 1.73. Locating epicentre: S–P time interval gives distance (roughly ≈ 8 km per second of S–P lag); minimum 3 stations needed (triangulation). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 34.1 — Particle motion of P, S, Love and Rayleigh waves. Order of arrival: P → S → Love → Rayleigh. S–P time difference gives the distance to the epicentre (≈ 8 km per second of S–P lag).

Seismograph / seismometer: records ground motion; record = seismogram. Accelerograph: records strong-motion acceleration (used in design). Magnitude: measure of energy released – one value per earthquake, instrumental. Intensity: measure of effects/damage at a place – varies with distance, soil and construction; observational. Richter scale (ML): Charles Richter, 1935, logarithmic; open-ended (no upper limit). One unit increase in magnitude = 10× amplitude and ≈ 32× energy (two units ≈ 1000× energy). Other magnitudes: mb (body wave), Ms (surface wave), Mw (moment magnitude) – Hanks & Kanamori 1979; does not saturate for large events. Seismic moment: M₀ = μ·A·D (rigidity × fault area × average slip). Mw = (2/3)(log₁₀ M₀ − 9.1), M₀ in N·m. Intensity scales: Modified Mercalli (MMI, I–XII, Roman numerals), MSK-64, EMS-98, JMA (0–7). Isoseismal lines: lines joining points of equal intensity. Peak ground acceleration (PGA): expressed as fraction of g. Largest recorded earthquake: 1960 Valdivia, Chile – Mw 9.5. Magnitude Class < 2.0 Micro 2.0 – 3.9 Minor 4.0 – 4.9 Light 5.0 – 5.9 Moderate 6.0 – 6.9 Strong 7.0 – 7.9 Major ≥ 8.0 Great

Ground shaking (main cause of damage), surface fault rupture, landslides, fires, dam failure. Liquefaction: loose, saturated, fine/uniform sand loses strength as pore pressure rises and effective stress → 0. Signs: sand boils, tilting/sinking buildings (Niigata, Japan 1964). Susceptible: low SPT N, shallow water table, young deposits. Remedies for liquefaction: densification (vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction), stone columns, drains, grouting, deep foundations. Site amplification: soft soil deposits amplify shaking (Mexico City 1985). Resonance: damage peaks when natural period of building ≈ period of ground motion. Natural period roughly ≈ 0.1 × number of storeys (s). Tsunami (Japanese: “harbour wave”): caused by vertical sea-floor displacement in undersea earthquakes; very long wavelength, speed ≈ √(g·d). Examples: 2004 Indian Ocean (Mw 9.1), 2011 Tohoku (Mw 9.0), 1945 Makran (hit Pasni). Seiche: oscillation of water in enclosed basins (lakes, reservoirs).

Keep building light, simple, symmetric and regular in plan and elevation; provide a continuous load path. Avoid: soft storey (open ground floor), short columns, plan irregularity (L, T shapes → torsion), re-entrant corners, heavy overhangs, abrupt stiffness/mass changes. Provide seismic gap / separation joints between adjacent blocks to prevent pounding. Ductility: ability to deform inelastically without collapse – key to absorbing seismic energy. Strong column – weak beam philosophy: plastic hinges form in beams, not columns. Design philosophy: no damage in minor, repairable damage in moderate, no collapse in major earthquakes (life safety).

Moment-resisting frames (OMRF, IMRF, SMRF), shear walls, braced frames (concentric, eccentric), dual systems. Base isolation: lead–rubber bearings, friction pendulum – lengthen period, reduce forces. Energy dissipation: viscous, friction, yielding dampers; tuned mass damper (e.g. Taipei 101).

Closely spaced ties/stirrups near beam–column joints and column ends (confinement zone). Ties with 135° seismic hooks; no lap splices in plastic hinge zones. Adequate anchorage and joint reinforcement.

Horizontal RC bands: plinth, sill, lintel (most important), roof bands. Vertical reinforcement at corners and junctions; limit size and number of openings; avoid openings near corners. Use good-quality mortar and through-stones; light roofs tied to walls.

Design base shear: V = (Cv · I / R · T) · W Upper limit: V ≤ 2.5 · Ca · I · W / R Lower limit: V ≥ 0.11 · Ca · I · W Cv, Ca = seismic coefficients (zone + soil profile); I = importance factor; R = response modification factor; W = seismic weight; T = fundamental period. Fundamental period: T = Ct · (hn)^¾ ; Ct = 0.0853 (steel MRF), 0.0731 (RC MRF), 0.0488 (other) with hn in metres. Base shear distributed over height as storey forces; part applied at top as Ft = 0.07·T·V (when T > 0.7 s). Analysis methods: equivalent static (seismic coefficient), response spectrum (dynamic), time-history (most accurate). Response spectrum: plot of peak response (acceleration/velocity/displacement) of SDOF systems vs natural period for a given damping (usually 5%).

Softest mineral – talc; hardest – diamond. Mineral that fizzes with cold dilute HCl – calcite. Most abundant mineral group – feldspar; most resistant to weathering – quartz. Granite is intrusive, acidic; basalt is extrusive, basic. Marble from limestone; quartzite from sandstone; slate from shale; gneiss from granite. Oldest beds in core – anticline; youngest in core – syncline. Hanging wall moves down – normal fault (tension); up – reverse/thrust (compression). Clay is an aquiclude; massive granite is an aquifuge. Best rock for dam foundation – massive igneous (granite); worst – cavernous limestone, shale, gypsum. RQD uses core pieces ≥ 10 cm; RQD > 90% = excellent. P-waves are fastest; Rayleigh waves are slowest; S-waves do not pass through liquids. Magnitude = energy (one value); intensity = damage (varies with place). Richter scale introduced in 1935; open-ended; logarithmic. Minimum 3 seismograph stations needed to locate an epicentre. Pakistan seismic code – BCP SP-2007 (based on UBC-97); highest zone – 4 (Quetta). 2005 Kashmir earthquake – Mw 7.6, 8 October 2005. Chaman Fault – transform fault; Makran – subduction zone. Soft storey, short column and pounding are major causes of building collapse. Lintel band is the most important band in masonry buildings.

Estimate: probable cost of a work, calculated before construction. Quantity surveying: working out quantities of items of work and their cost. Bill of Quantities (BOQ): itemised list of quantities with rates; basis of tender. Abstract of estimate: quantities × rates → cost of each item; totals. Specification: describes quality of materials and workmanship (general / detailed). Measurement sheet: records item, No., L, B, H/D, quantity. Lump sum (L.S.): provision for items whose quantities cannot be worked out (e.g. electrification). Contingencies: 3–5% of estimated cost, for unforeseen expenses. Work-charged establishment: 1.5–2% (some departments up to 2.5%), staff paid from works. Centage charges: 10–15% added for departmental establishment, T&P and design. Prime cost (P.C.): cost of articles bought from market (fittings, sanitary ware). Provisional sum: amount kept for work not fully defined at tender stage. Day work: work paid on actual labour/material/time basis.

Preliminary / approximate / rough estimate: for administrative approval; based on cost of similar works. Plinth area estimate: plinth area × plinth area rate. Plinth area = covered built-up area at floor level (outer dimensions of walls). Cube rate estimate: plinth area × height × cube rate; height = floor top to roof top (more accurate than plinth area method for multi-storey). Approximate quantity method: cost per running metre of wall (foundation + superstructure). Detailed estimate: item-wise quantities × rates; for technical sanction and tender. Revised estimate: when original sanctioned estimate is exceeded by more than 5% or design changes. Supplementary estimate: for additional works found necessary during execution. Annual repair / maintenance estimate: for upkeep of existing structure (≈1–1.5% of capital cost). Complete estimate: total cost including land, roads, services, etc.

Plinth area: built-up area at floor level incl. wall thickness (excludes open courtyards, cornices, chajjas). Carpet area: usable area = plinth area − (walls, verandahs, corridors, stairs, kitchen, toilets…). ≈ 50–65% of plinth area (residential). Circulation area: corridors, stairs, lobbies (≈10–20% of plinth area). Built-up area: floor area + wall area (practically = plinth area). Approval forums: Projects approved by DDWP/PDWP (provincial), CDWP and ECNEC (federal) depending on cost thresholds. Contingencies ≈ 3–5% and work-charged establishment ≈ 1.5–2% are added to the detailed estimate (departmental practice).

Long wall – short wall method (out-to-out / in-to-in): long walls taken out-to-out, short walls in-to-in. Most accurate for unequal wall thickness. Long wall L (c/c) = centre-to-centre length + one breadth. Centre line method: total centre line length × breadth × height. Fast; best for walls of same section. Correction in centre line method: deduct ½ × breadth × no. of T-junctions (for each junction) from total centre line length. No deduction at corners (L-junctions) in centre line method. Crossing / partly centre-line method: used where walls of different thickness meet. Lead: horizontal distance for carrying excavated earth. Normal lead = 30 m (CPWD: 50 m). Lift: vertical height through which earth is lifted. Normal lift = 1.5 m. Extra lead/lift charged separately beyond normal values. Initial lead and lift included in the rate of earthwork. Foundation trench excavation = L × B × D (B = width of base concrete). Shrinkage / settlement allowance in filling: 10% (consolidated filling deducted for voids). Swell/bulking of earth after excavation: ordinary soil ≈ 10–25%, rock ≈ 40–60%. Earthwork quantity in pits: 'dead man' (mud pillars) left to check depth; borrow pits used for embankment.

Cross-sectional area (level ground, bank): A = Bd + sd² (B = formation width, d = depth/height, s:1 = side slope H:V). Mid-sectional area method: Q = L × A at mean depth (dm = (d1+d2)/2). Most commonly used. Mean-sectional (average end area) method: Q = L × (A1 + A2)/2. Gives larger quantity; less accurate. Trapezoidal formula: Q = d[(A1 + An)/2 + A2 + A3 + … + An−1]. Prismoidal formula (most accurate): Q = (d/3)[(A1 + An) + 4(even areas) + 2(remaining odd areas)]; needs odd number of sections. Prismoidal correction: Cp = (L/6) × s × (d1 − d2)² (for level sections). Curvature correction applied for earthwork on curves (Pappus's theorem). Simpson's rule (areas): A = (d/3)[(O1+On) + 4ΣO_even + 2ΣO_odd]; requires odd no. of ordinates. Trapezoidal rule (areas): A = d[(O1+On)/2 + O2 + … + On−1]. Given: B = 10 m, side slope 2:1, depths 1.0 m and 2.0 m at 100 m apart. Areas: A₁ = 10 × 1 + 2 × 1² = 12 m²; A₂ = 20 + 8 = 28 m²; mid depth 1.5 m → Am = 15 + 4.5 = 19.5 m². Volumes: Prismoidal = 100/6 (12 + 78 + 28) = 1966.7 m³; mean-area = 100 × 20 = 2000 m³. Prismoidal formula is the most accurate; trapezoidal (end-area) generally over-estimates; prismoidal correction = L/6 · s(d₁ − d₂)².

Rate analysis: determining rate per unit of an item = materials + labour + T&P + overheads + profit. Purpose: fix contract rates, check contractor's rates, compare tenders, prepare estimates. Factors: specifications, quantity/quality of materials, labour output, location, lead, season, profit. Materials cost includes: cost at source + carriage + loading/unloading + storage + wastage. Tools & plant (T&P): ≈ 1–3% of labour cost (sundries). Water charges: ≈ 1–1.5% of total cost. Contractor's profit: ≈ 10% (with overheads ≈ 15%). Overheads: ≈ 2.5–5% (office, supervision, insurance, establishment). Task / out-turn: work done by one labourer per day (e.g. mason brickwork ≈ 1.25 m³/day; earthwork ≈ 2.8–3 m³/day per labourer). Schedule of rates (SOR / MRS / CSR): standard rates by PWD / department (Pakistan: Composite Schedule of Rates – CSR; Market Rate System – MRS). Rate analysis normally done for 1 unit or a standard quantity (e.g. 10 m³ concrete, 100 m² plaster).

General (brief) specification: short description of type & quality; used in preliminary estimates. Detailed specification: full description of materials, proportions, method of construction, curing, measurements; used in detailed estimate & contract. Standard specification: published by departments (PWD, CPWD, BIS). Writing order: same as sequence of construction (earthwork → foundation → DPC → superstructure → finishing). In conflict: specification > drawings (generally detailed drawing > general drawing; written dims > scaled dims).

Tender: written offer by contractor to execute work at stated rates/amount, within time. NIT (Notice Inviting Tender): advertisement of work, cost, earnest money, time, documents. Earnest money (bid security): 1–2% of estimated cost (commonly 2%); refunded to unsuccessful bidders. Security deposit (performance security): 5–10% of contract amount (commonly 10%, incl. earnest money); refunded after defect liability period. Retention money: % deducted from each running bill (≈ 5–10%) until completion/defects liability. Defect liability (maintenance) period: usually 6–12 months after completion. Mobilization advance: ≈ 10% of contract value, recovered from bills. Single tender, limited tender, open tender, global tender, two-envelope (technical + financial) tender. Unbalanced tender: some item rates too high, others too low. Lowest tender usually accepted (L1), subject to competence; tender committee evaluates.

Lump sum contract: fixed total amount for whole work; extra items paid as per schedule. Suitable where design is complete. Item rate (unit price / schedule) contract: payment on measured quantities × quoted unit rates. Most common in PWD. Percentage rate contract: contractor quotes % above/below the department's schedule of rates. Cost plus percentage: actual cost + agreed % profit (no incentive to economise). Cost plus fixed fee: actual cost + fixed fee. Cost plus variable fee / target cost: fee varies with performance vs target. Labour contract: department supplies materials; contractor supplies labour only. Material supply contract: supply of materials only. Turnkey (design & build / EPC): contractor responsible for design, construction, commissioning. BOT / BOOT: build-operate-transfer (public–private partnership). Piece-work agreement: small works, no tender, payment for completed work (limited amount).

Work order: written order for small works without formal contract. Measurement Book (MB): official record of measurements; basis of all payments. Running (on-account) bill: periodic payment for work done; final bill after completion. Muster roll: record of daily labour attendance and wages. Extra item: item not in original contract; Substituted item: replaces a contract item. Deviation: variation in quantity beyond permitted limit (often ±10–20%). Liquidated damages: penalty for delay (e.g. ≈ 0.5–1% per week, capped ≈ 10%). Arbitration: settlement of disputes by arbitrator (Arbitration Act). Force majeure: unforeseeable events (war, flood, earthquake) releasing liability. Escalation clause: allows rate adjustment for price rise of materials/labour. Imprest: advance cash to field officer for petty expenses. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Public procurement in Pakistan: PPRA Rules 2004 (federal) and provincial rules (e.g., KPPRA, PPRA Punjab); e-Pak Acquisition & Disposal System (e-PADS) for e-procurement. Standard contract forms: Pakistan Engineering Council (PEC) Standard Forms of Bidding Documents (based on FIDIC) for civil works. Bid security & performance security: Bid security ≈ 1–5% of estimated cost (as specified); performance security ≈ 5–10% of contract price. Item-rate contract = most common in public works; lump-sum = fixed total price for defined work; cost-plus = cost + fee (emergency works).

Contract – agreement enforceable by law (Contract Act, 1872) Essentials – offer & acceptance, lawful consideration, lawful object, free consent, competent parties Parties – Employer (Client/Owner), Contractor, Engineer (Consultant) Void contract – not enforceable by law; Voidable – enforceable at option of one party

Type Key Points Lump Sum Fixed total price for complete work; suitable when drawings/specs complete; risk on contractor Item Rate (Unit Price) Rate quoted per unit of each item (BOQ); payment on measured quantity – most common Percentage Rate Contractor quotes % above/below schedule of rates Cost Plus Percentage Actual cost + % profit; no incentive to reduce cost Cost Plus Fixed Fee Actual cost + fixed fee Cost Plus Variable Fee Fee varies with performance (incentive) Target Cost Savings/overruns shared between owner and contractor Labour Contract Owner supplies material; contractor supplies labour only Turnkey / EPC Engineering, Procurement, Construction by one party; "ready to use" Design–Build Single entity designs and constructs BOT / BOOT / BOO Build-Operate-Transfer / Build-Own-Operate-Transfer / Build-Own-Operate (PPP)

Sequence – Administrative approval → Technical sanction → Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) → Prequalification → Bid submission → Opening → Evaluation → Award (Letter of Acceptance) → Agreement → Work order Open tender – advertised publicly; Limited (selective) – invited from prequalified firms; Single tender – one firm (specialised/emergency) Single-stage one-envelope – technical + financial together Single-stage two-envelope – technical and financial in separate envelopes; financial opened only for technically qualified Bid security (Earnest money) – submitted with bid; guarantees bidder will not withdraw; refunded to unsuccessful bidders Performance security – submitted by successful bidder; guarantees performance (commonly ~5–10%) Retention money – % deducted from running bills (commonly 5–10%); released after defects liability period Mobilization advance – advance to contractor for starting work; recovered from bills Lowest evaluated bid – bid awarded to the "lowest evaluated responsive" bidder Bid validity – period for which bid remains open for acceptance Pakistan – PPRA (Public Procurement Regulatory Authority) Rules 2004; PEC (Pakistan Engineering Council) standard bidding documents

Liquidated damages – pre-agreed compensation for delay by contractor Defects liability period – period after completion for contractor to rectify defects (commonly 12 months); called Defects Notification Period in FIDIC Variation order – change in scope/quantity ordered by engineer Escalation (price adjustment) – payment for rise in material/labour prices Extension of time (EOT) – extra time for delays not caused by contractor Running Account (RA) bill – interim payment; Final bill – after completion Measurement book (MB) – record of measured work – basis of payment Arbitration – dispute resolution outside court (Arbitration Act 1940 in Pakistan) Taking-over certificate – issued when works substantially complete

Book Use Red Book Construction – design by Employer (re-measurement) Yellow Book Plant and Design-Build – design by Contractor Silver Book EPC / Turnkey projects Green Book Short form – small / simple works White Book Client–Consultant agreement Gold Book Design, Build and Operate (DBO) FIDIC – Fédération Internationale des Ingénieurs-Conseils (International Federation of Consulting Engineers), Geneva Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Pakistan procurement: PPRA Rules 2004 (federal), KPPRA (KP), PPRA Punjab; PEC standard bidding documents (FIDIC-based); e-PADS for e-bidding. PEC role: Pakistan Engineering Council registers engineers (RE/PE) and constructors/operators (categories C-A to C-6) — only PEC-registered firms can bid for engineering works. FIDIC books: Red Book (employer-designed construction), Yellow Book (design-build), Silver Book (EPC/turnkey), Green Book (short form). Single-stage one-envelope, single-stage two-envelope, two-stage bidding — procedures under PPRA Rules.

Valuation: determining present fair value of a property. Purposes: sale/purchase, mortgage/loan, taxation, rent fixation, insurance, compensation (acquisition), betterment levy. Market value: price obtainable in open market at a given time (varies). Book value: original cost − depreciation to date (as per account books). Scrap value: value of dismantled materials (≈ 10% of cost for buildings). Salvage value: value at end of useful life without dismantling (property used for other purposes). Distress value: value under forced sale (lower than market value). Speculative value: purchase with future gain in mind. Potential value: value considering possible future development. Sentimental value: personal attachment; not market-based. Accommodation value: extra value to a particular buyer. Monopoly value: due to unique location/no competition. Replacement value: cost of replacing existing property with similar one. Reversionary value: value receivable after expiry of lease. Gross income: total income from property; Net income = gross income − outgoings. Outgoings: taxes, repairs (≈ 10–12% of gross rent), insurance, management, sinking fund, loss of rent. Annuity: fixed annual payment for a fixed period. Obsolescence: loss of value due to outdated design/technology (functional loss, not physical). Freehold: absolute ownership; Leasehold: right to use for fixed period under lease. Easement: right of a person over another's land (light, air, way). Mortgage: transfer of interest in pro

Year's purchase (YP), perpetuity: YP = 100 / rate of interest (%) = 1/i. YP for n years (single rate): YP = 1 / (i + is), where is = sinking fund coefficient. Capitalised value = Net annual income × YP. Sinking fund coefficient: Ic = i / [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]. Annual sinking fund instalment: I = S × i / [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1], S = amount to be accumulated. Present value of ₨1 due after n years: PV = 1 / (1 + i)ⁿ (deferred value). Amount after n years (compound): A = P(1 + i)ⁿ. Rent fixation: Rent = (interest on capital + sinking fund + outgoings) per year.

Straight line method: equal annual depreciation; D = (C − S)/n (C = cost, S = scrap, n = life). Constant percentage / declining balance method: fixed % on reduced book value each year; D = 1 − (S/C)^(1/n). Never reaches zero. Sinking fund method: annual amount set aside with compound interest to accumulate (C − S) at end of life. Quantity survey method: depreciation based on assessed remaining life/condition. Sum of years' digits method: higher depreciation in early years. Life of buildings (approx.): RCC framed 75–100 yrs; load bearing brick 50–75 yrs; temporary 5–10 yrs.

Rental method: net income × YP (for rented properties). Direct comparison with capital value: comparing recent sales of similar properties. Valuation based on profit: hotels, cinemas, shops (net profit capitalised). Development method: for land/building with development potential. Depreciation method (cost method): present cost − depreciation (land value added). Belting method: for land with road frontage; land divided in belts parallel to road. Belt depths ratio front:middle:rear values ≈ 100% : ⅔ (some texts ¾) : ½; front belt depth ≈ 15–25 m. Land value usually determined by comparison; building value by depreciation. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Depreciation methods: Straight-line, constant percentage (declining balance), sinking fund, quantity survey methods. Year’s purchase: YP = 1/(rate of interest) for perpetual income; capitalised value = net income × YP. Scrap value = value of dismantled materials; salvage value = value of an item for use elsewhere (without dismantling).
