Often confused Key difference Preliminary vs detailed estimate Approximate (plinth area/cubic rate) for sanction vs item-wise for technical sanction Plinth area vs carpet area Covered built-up area vs usable area Supplementary vs revised estimate Additional work vs cost exceeds sanctioned estimate by > ≈ 5% Lead vs lift Horizontal haul distance vs vertical height Scrap vs salvage value Dismantled material value vs value for re-use elsewhere Item-rate vs lump-sum contract Paid per measured item vs fixed total Bid security vs performance security With bid (forfeited if bidder withdraws) vs from contractor after award Prime cost vs provisional sum Cost of specified materials/items vs allowance for undefined work

Project – temporary endeavour with a definite start and end, producing a unique product, service or result Operation – ongoing, repetitive work (opposite of a project) Project management – application of knowledge, skills, tools and techniques to meet project requirements Programme – group of related projects managed together; Portfolio – collection of projects/programmes to meet strategic goals Triple constraint (Iron triangle) – Time, Cost, Scope (Quality at centre); change in one affects the others Characteristics of a project – temporary, unique, progressive elaboration, definite objective, limited resources, risk & uncertainty

Phases – Initiation (Conception) → Planning → Execution → Monitoring & Controlling → Closing Cost and staffing – low at start, peak during execution, drop at closing Influence of stakeholders / ability to change – highest at start, decreases with time Cost of changes – lowest at start, increases with time Risk & uncertainty – highest at start

Fayol – Planning, Organizing, Commanding, Coordinating, Controlling (14 principles of management) POSDCORB (Luther Gulick) – Planning, Organizing, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting, Budgeting Planning – first and most basic function; Controlling – last function, compares actual with planned F.W. Taylor – Father of Scientific Management; Henri Fayol – Father of Modern (Administrative) Management Peter Drucker – Management by Objectives (MBO) Span of control – number of subordinates a manager can effectively supervise Unity of command – one subordinate reports to one boss only

Type Key Points PM Authority Functional (Line) Grouped by speciality; clear reporting; slow cross-department coordination Little / none Line & Staff Line officers give orders; staff give advice Low Weak Matrix PM acts as coordinator / expediter Low Balanced Matrix Power shared between PM and functional manager Low – moderate Strong Matrix Full-time PM and project staff Moderate – high Projectized Team works only for the project; team disbands at completion High – almost total Matrix organisation – two bosses (violates unity of command) – main drawback Projectized – best for large, long, complex projects; problem of "no home" after project ends

PMBOK – Project Management Body of Knowledge, published by PMI (Project Management Institute, USA) 5 Process Groups – Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing 10 Knowledge Areas – Integration, Scope, Schedule (Time), Cost, Quality, Resource (HR), Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder Integration management – only knowledge area present in all 5 process groups Project charter – formally authorises the project and the project manager; issued by sponsor; output of initiation Project management plan – how the project will be executed, monitored and closed WBS (Work Breakdown Structure) – hierarchical decomposition of total scope into deliverables; lowest level = work package 100% rule – WBS includes 100% of work defined by the scope Scope creep – uncontrolled expansion of scope without adjustment of time/cost Gold plating – adding extra features not asked by the client Baseline – approved version of scope, schedule or cost used for comparison RACI matrix – Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed Communication channels – n(n − 1)/2, where n = number of people

Developed by – Henry L. Gantt (≈1917) Horizontal bars – length of bar ∝ duration of activity; x-axis = time Advantages – simple, easy to read, useful for progress monitoring Limitations – does not show interdependency of activities, no critical path, no float, unsuitable for large projects Milestone chart – improvement of bar chart; shows key events (milestones) on bars – still no interdependency

Activity – task consuming time and resources; shown by arrow (AOA) Event (node) – instant of time; start or end of activity; consumes no time or resources Dummy activity – zero time and zero resources; shown by dashed arrow; maintains logic / avoids two activities with same i-j Merge event – two or more activities end at it; Burst event – two or more activities start from it AOA (Activity on Arrow) – i-j method; used in CPM/PERT; may need dummies AON (Activity on Node) – precedence diagram method (PDM); no dummies needed Fulkerson's rule – method of numbering events (i < j for every activity) Network rules – only one initial and one final event; no looping; no dangling activity; time flows left to right Looping (cycling) – error – activity loops back to an earlier event Dangling – error – activity not connected to final event

FS (Finish-to-Start) – most common; B starts after A finishes SS (Start-to-Start) – B starts after A starts FF (Finish-to-Finish) – B finishes after A finishes SF (Start-to-Finish) – least common Lag – delay between activities; Lead – overlap (negative lag)

Used for – repetitive works – highways, pipelines, housing units, tunnels, high-rise floors Also called – linear scheduling method / vertical production method Originated – US Navy (1940s) for production control Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 18.1 — Gantt chart of the CPM example: critical activities and floats. Line of balance (LOB): For repetitive work (housing units, highways) — shows rate of progress of each crew. Bar chart (Gantt) shows time but not interdependencies; network methods (CPM/PERT) show logic and critical path.

Developed – 1957 by E.I. du Pont & Remington Rand (Kelley and Walker) Nature – deterministic (single time estimate), activity-oriented Used for – repetitive / well-known projects (construction); time-cost trade-off

EST (Earliest Start Time) – forward pass – take MAXIMUM at merge events EFT – EST + t LFT (Latest Finish Time) – backward pass – take MINIMUM at burst events LST – LFT − t Event slack – L − E (latest occurrence − earliest occurrence time) Critical path – longest path in network; zero total float; determines project duration Critical activity – any delay delays the whole project Sub-critical path – path next to critical in length More than one critical path – possible

Float Formula Meaning Total Float (TF) LST − EST = LFT − EFT Max delay without delaying project Free Float (FF) EST(j) − EST(i) − t = TF − Sj Delay without delaying any following activity Independent Float (IF) EST(j) − LFT(i) − t = FF − Si Delay without affecting preceding or following activity Interfering Float TF − FF = Sj (head event slack) Portion of TF shared with following activities Relation – IF ≤ FF ≤ TF Si, Sj – slack of tail (i) and head (j) events Negative float – project behind schedule / deadline earlier than computed duration Independent float – can be negative – taken as zero Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 19.1 — CPM network (activity-on-node) with critical path B–D–E. Activity Duration ES EF LS LF Total float A 3 0 3 2 5 2 B 5 0 5 0 5 0 (critical) C 4 3 7 7 11 4 D 6 5 11 5 11 0 (critical) E 2 11 13 11 13 0 (critical) Float types: Total float = LS − ES; free float = ES(successor) − EF; independent float = ES(succ) − LF(pred) − duration. Critical path = longest path through the network; any delay on it delays the project. Dummy activities (AOA) have zero duration.

Full form – Programme Evaluation and Review Technique Developed – 1958, US Navy – Polaris missile project (with Booz Allen Hamilton) Nature – probabilistic, event-oriented; for R&D / new projects with uncertain durations Three time estimates – optimistic (to), most likely (tm), pessimistic (tp) Distribution of activity time – Beta (β) distribution Distribution of project duration – Normal distribution (Central Limit Theorem) Expected time – te = (to + 4tm + tp) / 6 Standard deviation – σ = (tp − to) / 6; Variance = σ² Project variance – sum of variances of activities on critical path; σ(project) = √Σσ² Probability factor – Z = (Ts − Te) / σ  (Ts = scheduled time, Te = expected time) Z = 0 – 50% probability; Z = 1 – 84.13%; Z = 2 – 97.72%; Z = 3 – 99.87%; Z = −1 – 15.87% Range (6σ) – tp − to covers ≈ 99.7% of outcomes

CPM PERT Deterministic Probabilistic Activity-oriented Event-oriented Single time estimate Three time estimates Repetitive / known jobs (construction) New / R&D jobs (defence, research) Time-cost trade-off (crashing) possible No crashing concept Uses "float" Uses "slack" Du Pont, 1957 US Navy, 1958 Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 20.1 — PERT β-distribution: optimistic, most likely, pessimistic and expected time.

Given: Critical path te = 40 days, σ = 4 days. Probability of finishing in 44 days? Answer: Z = (44 − 40)/4 = 1.0 → P ≈ 84%. PERT is event-oriented & probabilistic (R&D); CPM is activity-oriented & deterministic (construction).

Crashing – reducing project duration by adding resources to critical activities Normal time / cost – duration at minimum direct cost Crash time / cost – minimum possible duration at maximum direct cost Cost slope – (Crash cost − Normal cost) / (Normal time − Crash time) Rule – crash the critical activity with the LEAST cost slope first Parallel critical paths – crash both paths simultaneously Direct cost – labour, material, equipment – INCREASES as duration decreases Indirect cost – overheads, supervision, establishment – DECREASES as duration decreases Total cost – Direct + Indirect; U-shaped curve Optimum duration – duration at minimum total cost Fast tracking – doing activities in parallel instead of sequence (increases risk, not cost directly) Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 21.1 — Time–cost trade-off: direct, indirect and total cost; optimum duration. Cost slope: Cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost)/(normal time − crash time); crash critical activities with the lowest cost slope first. Crashing shortens the project; indirect costs fall with time, direct costs rise — optimum where total is minimum.

Resource histogram – bar diagram of resource requirement vs time Resource smoothing – project duration remains FIXED; activities shifted within floats to reduce peaks Resource levelling – resources LIMITED; project duration may INCREASE Resource allocation – assigning available resources to activities Ideal histogram – rectangular (uniform demand) Resource-constrained scheduling – levelling; time-constrained scheduling – smoothing

EOQ (Wilson formula) – √(2DS / H)  [D = annual demand, S = ordering cost per order, H = holding cost per unit per year] At EOQ – ordering cost = holding (carrying) cost ABC analysis – A = ~10% items, ~70% value (strict control); B = ~20% items, ~20% value; C = ~70% items, ~10% value VED analysis – Vital, Essential, Desirable (criticality) Lead time – time between placing and receiving an order Reorder level – Lead time demand + Safety stock

Work study – Method study + Work measurement Method study – finds the best way of doing work Work measurement – finds standard time for the work (time study) Standard time – Normal time + allowances Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Resource smoothing vs levelling: Smoothing: within project duration using floats; levelling: resource limit fixed, duration may extend. A resource histogram should be as uniform as possible — fluctuations raise hiring/firing and idle costs.

Term Formula / Meaning Interpretation PV (BCWS) Planned Value – budgeted cost of work scheduled – EV (BCWP) Earned Value – budgeted cost of work performed – AC (ACWP) Actual Cost of work performed – CV EV − AC − ve = over budget SV EV − PV − ve = behind schedule CPI EV / AC < 1 = over budget SPI EV / PV < 1 = behind schedule BAC Budget at Completion Total planned budget EAC BAC / CPI (typical); AC + (BAC − EV) (atypical) Forecast total cost ETC EAC − AC Cost to finish VAC BAC − EAC − ve = overrun expected TCPI (BAC − EV) / (BAC − AC) > 1 = harder to finish within budget Memory tip – EV always comes first; Variance = subtraction, Index = division S-curve – cumulative cost/progress vs time; used for monitoring progress Updating – revising network with actual progress; frequency depends on project size Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 23.1 — Earned value S-curves (PV, EV, AC) and indices.
Given: PV = 100, EV = 85, AC = 95 (million Rs). Answer: CV = −10 (over budget), SV = −15 (behind schedule), CPI = 0.89, SPI = 0.85; EAC = BAC/CPI. CPI < 1 → over budget; SPI < 1 → behind schedule.

Smooth wheel roller – granular soils, bituminous / sub-base finishing Sheepsfoot roller – cohesive (clayey) soils; kneading action Pneumatic-tyred roller – both cohesive & granular; kneading action Vibratory roller – granular / cohesionless soils (sand, gravel) Grid roller – rocky soils, breaking boulders Rammers / plate compactors – confined areas

Cranes – tower crane (high-rise), mobile crane, crawler crane, gantry crane Derrick – guy derrick, stiff-leg derrick Concrete equipment – batching plant, transit mixer, concrete pump, vibrators Pile driving – drop hammer, single/double acting steam hammer, diesel hammer, vibratory driver

Output (production) – bucket capacity × (60 / cycle time in min) × efficiency × fill factor Cycle time – fixed time (load, dump, turn) + variable time (haul, return) Owning cost – depreciation, interest, insurance, taxes, storage Operating cost – fuel, lubricants, repairs, tyres, operator wages Straight line depreciation – D = (P − S) / n Declining balance – constant % of book value each year; double declining = 2/n Sum-of-years digits – D(year m) = (n − m + 1)/[n(n+1)/2] × (P − S) Sinking fund method – annual deposit grows with interest to equal (P − S) Book value – original cost − accumulated depreciation; Salvage value – value at end of useful life

Term Formula Simple interest I = P × i × n Compound amount (F/P) F = P(1 + i)^n Present worth (P/F) P = F / (1 + i)^n Uniform series compound amount (F/A) F = A[(1 + i)^n − 1] / i Sinking fund (A/F) A = F · i / [(1 + i)^n − 1] Present worth of series (P/A) P = A[(1 + i)^n − 1] / [i(1 + i)^n] Capital recovery (A/P) A = P · i(1 + i)^n / [(1 + i)^n − 1] Effective interest rate ieff = (1 + r/m)^m − 1 Capitalised cost (perpetual) P = A / i NPV (Net Present Value) – PW of benefits − PW of costs; accept if NPV > 0 IRR – rate at which NPV = 0; accept if IRR > MARR (minimum attractive rate of return) B/C ratio – PW of benefits / PW of costs; accept if > 1 Payback period – time to recover initial investment (ignores time value of money) Break-even point – Fixed cost / (Selling price − Variable cost per unit); total revenue = total cost Sunk cost – past cost – not considered in decisions; Opportunity cost – value of best forgone alternative Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Interest formulas: F = P(1 + i)ⁿ; P = F/(1 + i)ⁿ; annuity A = P·i(1 + i)ⁿ/[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]. Decision tools: NPV (> 0 accept), IRR (> MARR accept), B/C ratio (> 1 accept), payback period (shorter better, ignores time value). Straight-line depreciation D = (C − S)/n; declining-balance applies a fixed % to book value each year.

QA (Quality Assurance) – process-oriented, preventive; QC (Quality Control) – product-oriented, inspection/detection TQM – Total Quality Management – continuous improvement, customer focus, involvement of all Deming cycle – PDCA – Plan, Do, Check, Act Kaizen – continuous small improvements (Japanese) Six Sigma – 3.4 defects per million opportunities; DMAIC – Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control ISO 9001 – quality management system; ISO 14001 – environmental; ISO 45001 – occupational health & safety Pareto principle – 80% of problems from 20% of causes Ishikawa (Fishbone / Cause-and-effect) diagram – identifies root causes Control chart – monitors process; limits = mean ± 3σ 7 QC tools – check sheet, Pareto chart, histogram, cause-effect diagram, scatter diagram, control chart, flow chart/stratification Cost of quality – prevention + appraisal (conformance) + internal & external failure (non-conformance) Juran – quality = fitness for use; Crosby – zero defects, quality is free Value engineering – Lawrence D. Miles (General Electric); Value = Function / Cost

Risk – uncertain event that may have positive (opportunity) or negative (threat) effect Process – Plan → Identify → Qualitative analysis → Quantitative analysis → Plan responses → Implement → Monitor Identification tools – brainstorming, Delphi technique, checklists, SWOT analysis Qualitative – probability–impact matrix Quantitative – Monte Carlo simulation, sensitivity analysis (tornado diagram), decision tree, EMV EMV (Expected Monetary Value) – Probability × Impact Threat responses – Avoid, Transfer (insurance, contract), Mitigate, Accept (+ Escalate) Opportunity responses – Exploit, Share, Enhance, Accept (+ Escalate) Contingency reserve – for known risks ("known unknowns"); Management reserve – for unknown risks ("unknown unknowns") Risk register – document listing all identified risks, owners and responses

Heinrich's accident triangle – 1 major injury : 29 minor injuries : 300 no-injury accidents (near misses) Domino theory (Heinrich) – accidents result from a chain of events; ~88% due to unsafe acts Hierarchy of controls – Elimination → Substitution → Engineering controls → Administrative controls → PPE (least effective) PPE – helmet, safety shoes, gloves, goggles, harness, high-visibility vest, ear protection Major hazards in construction – falls from height (most common cause of fatal accidents), struck-by, electrocution, caught-in/between (excavation collapse) Excavations – deeper than ~1.5 m need shoring/sloping OSHA – Occupational Safety and Health Administration (USA) HSE – Health, Safety and Environment; Toolbox talk – short safety meeting at site

Maslow's hierarchy – Physiological → Safety → Social → Esteem → Self-actualisation Herzberg – two-factor theory – hygiene factors and motivators McGregor – Theory X (people dislike work) and Theory Y (people like work) Ouchi – Theory Z (Japanese management) Vroom – Expectancy theory McClelland – needs for achievement, affiliation, power Conflict resolution – Problem solving / confronting (best), compromising, smoothing, forcing, withdrawing Tuckman team stages – Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning Most common source of conflict in projects – schedules (then priorities, resources)

Law: Pakistan Engineering Council Act 1976 — PEC regulates engineering education and profession; CPD Bye-laws 2008 introduced the Professional Engineer (PE) route through the Engineering Practice Examination (EPE). Registration: Graduate of a PEC-accredited programme → Registered Engineer (RE). Only registered engineers may perform professional engineering work; engineering firms are registered as consulting engineers or constructors/operators (categories C-A, C-B, C-1 … C-6). Professional Engineer (PE): RE with ≥ 5 years of relevant experience after registration and ≥ 17 CPD points (10 from work experience + 7 from other CPD activities) may sit the EPE; passing gives the PE title. CPD points are also needed for renewal of registration. International recognition: PEC is a full signatory of the Washington Accord (2017) — accredited Pakistani engineering degrees are recognised by other signatories. Accreditation: Engineering Accreditation Board (EAB) of PEC accredits programmes on outcome-based education (OBE) — graduate attributes / programme learning outcomes. Framework: PPRA Ordinance 2002 and Public Procurement Rules 2004 (federal); provinces have their own: Punjab PPRA Rules 2014, KPPRA Rules 2014, Sindh SPPRA Rules 2010, Balochistan BPPRA Rules 2014. Response time (Rule 13): Not less than 15 days for national competitive bidding and 30 days for international competitive bidding, counted from first publication. Advertisement: Above the threshold: PPRA website + newspapers (one English, one Urdu national daily); e-PADS for e-procurement. Bid security: Not more than 5% of the estimated value (fixed amount, so as not to reveal the estimate). Performance security: Commonly up to 10% of contract price, valid until completion/defects liability. Bid validity extension: May be extended once, by not more than the original validity period; bidders refusing may withdraw without forfeiting bid security. Repeat order: Not to exceed 15% of the original order value. Bidding procedures: Single-stage one-envelope (simple works), single-stage two-envelope (technical + financial, opened separately), two-stage, two-stage two-envelope (complex/turnkey). Evaluation: Lowest evaluated bid (not necessarily lowest price) is awarded; evaluation report published before award; grievance redressal committee for complaints. PPRA: 15 days national / 30 days international; bid security ≤ 5%; repeat order ≤ 15%.

Forms: PC-I (project proposal/cost), PC-II (feasibility/survey), PC-III (progress monitoring), PC-IV (completion report), PC-V (annual operational report for 5 years after completion). Fig. — Project cycle: PC-II → PC-I → approval forum → PSDP/ADP funding → PC-III → PC-IV → PC-V. Budgets: PSDP — Public Sector Development Programme (federal); ADP — Annual Development Programme (provincial). Forum Level Approval limit (federal, from Aug 2022) DDWP Departmental Development Working Party up to Rs 1 billion CDWP Central Development Working Party (Planning Commission) above Rs 1 bn up to Rs 7.5 bn ECNEC Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (chaired by Finance Minister) above Rs 7.5 billion PDWP Provincial Development Working Party (P&D Dept.) provincial limit; larger projects go to ECNEC Note: Limits are revised from time to time (e.g., ECNEC threshold was Rs 3 bn → Rs 10 bn in 2020 → Rs 7.5 bn in 2022). Quote the latest notification in the exam. PC-I = proposal, PC-II = feasibility, PC-III = monitoring, PC-IV = completion, PC-V = operation. ECNEC is the highest approval forum.

Sequence: Rough cost estimate → Administrative Approval (AA, by the administrative department/forum) → detailed estimate → Technical Sanction (TS, by the competent engineer — XEN/SE/CE by limit) → funds allocation → tender (NIT) → comparative statement → acceptance → work order/agreement → execution → measurement → bills → completion → final bill & completion certificate. AA vs TS: AA = formal acceptance of the need and cost by the administrative authority; TS = engineer’s guarantee that the design and detailed estimate are sound and economical. No work starts without both and allotment of funds. Rates: Punjab: Market Rate System (MRS) issued periodically by the Finance Department for each district (material, labour, hire charges) + Composite Schedule of Rates (CSR) analysed rates; KP and other provinces have their own schedules. Non-schedule items are rated by rate analysis. Measurement Book (MB): Government record of every measurement — the basis of all payments; entries in ink, no erasures (cut and initial); measurements test-checked by SDO/XEN as per departmental rules. Bills: Running (on-account) bill — interim payment for work measured so far, subject to final adjustment; final bill — after completion and final measurement. Deductions: income tax, sales tax, retention money/security, recovery of advances. Stopping Sight Distance (SSD) = lag distance + braking distance = 0.278 V t + V²/(254 f)  [V in km/h, t = 2.5 s, result in m]. With gradient: SSD = 0.278 V t + V²/[254 (f ± 0.01n)]; + for ascending, − for descending. Two-way single-lane road: sight distance = 2 × SSD. Overtaking Sight Distance (OSD) = d1 + d2 + d3 = 0.278 Vb t + (0.278 Vb T + 2s) + 0.278 V T. OSD terms: t = 2 s reaction; s = 0.7 Vb + 6 (m); T = √(4s/a); Vb = V − 16 km/h (if not given). Overtaking zone min length = 3 × OSD; desirable = 5 × OSD. Intermediate Sight Distance (ISD) = 2 × SSD. Eye height 1.2 m; object height 0.15 m (SSD), 1.2 m (OSD). Perception–reaction time (PIEV): Perception, Intellection, Emotion, Volition; total 2.5 s for SSD.

Superelevation: e + f = V²/(127 R)  [V km/h, R m]. IRC design: e = (0.75V)²/(127R) (75% speed, f neglected); max e = 7% (plains/rolling), 10% (hilly, non-snow), 4% urban with frequent intersections. Ruling min radius: R = V²/[127 (e + f)]. Overturning vs skidding: overturning if f > b/2h (rare); skidding governs when f < b/2h. Methods of attaining superelevation: rotation about centre line, inner edge, or outer edge. Extra widening: We = mechanical + psychological = n l²/(2R) + V/(9.5 √R)  [n lanes, l wheelbase]. Transition curve: ideal shape = spiral (clothoid) — IRC recommends; lemniscate, cubic parabola also used. Length of transition (IRC, max of 3 criteria): (1) rate of change of centrifugal acceleration Ls = 0.0215 V³/(C R), C = 80/(75+V), 0.5 ≤ C ≤ 0.8; (2) rate of superelevation; (3) empirical Ls = 2.7 V²/R (plain), V²/R (hilly). Shift of curve S = L²/(24R). Set-back distance (curve sight): m = R − (R − d) cos(θ/2); θ/2 = S/[2(R − d)] radians, for L > S.

Grade compensation on curves = (30 + R)/R %, max 75/R %; not needed below 4%. Vertical curve shape: square parabola (uniform rate of change of grade). Summit curve (L > S): L = N S²/4.4 (SSD); L = N S²/9.6 (OSD). N = deviation angle = |n1 − n2|. Valley curve: designed for comfort (centrifugal acceleration ≤ 0.6 m/s³) and headlight sight distance. 3 Es of traffic: Engineering, Enforcement, Education (+ Environment, Emergency). Traffic studies: volume, speed (spot & journey), O–D, flow characteristics, parking, accident. Spot speed: radar gun, enoscope (mirror box), pressure tubes. Journey speed: moving car (floating car) method. Geometric design speed = 98th percentile speed (IRC); safe/upper speed limit for regulation = 85th percentile; lower speed limit = 15th percentile. (AASHTO practice also uses the 85th percentile as operating speed.) O–D survey methods: road-side interview, licence plate, home interview, return post card, tag on car. PCU (Passenger Car Unit): car = 1, bus/truck = 3, motorcycle = 0.5, cycle = 0.5, bullock cart = 8 (IRC values vary with speed). AADT = annual average daily traffic; 30th highest hourly volume used as Design Hourly Volume (DHV). Peak Hour Factor (PHF) = hourly volume / (4 × peak 15-min volume) ≤ 1.

Fundamental relation: q = k × v  (flow = density × speed). Greenshields model: v = vf (1 − k/kj); max flow qmax = vf kj / 4 at v = vf/2, k = kj/2. Headway h = 1/q; spacing s = 1/k. Theoretical capacity C = 1000 V / S  (veh/h/lane), S = spacing in m = SSD + vehicle length. Level of Service (HCM): A (free flow) to F (forced/breakdown flow). Capacity of lane: basic (ideal), possible (prevailing), practical (design).

Signs (3 types): Regulatory/mandatory (circular), Warning/cautionary (triangular), Informatory (rectangular). STOP sign: octagonal, red; GIVE WAY: inverted triangle. Road markings: white generally; yellow = no parking/no overtaking restrictions. Intersections: at-grade (unchannelized, channelized, rotary, signalised) and grade-separated (interchange). Conflict points, 4-legged intersection (two-way roads): 16 crossing (major) + 8 merging + 8 diverging = 32 total. Rotary: design speed 40 km/h (rural), 30 km/h (urban); suitable traffic 500–3000 veh/h; weaving length 45–90 m (rural), 30–60 m (urban). Rotary capacity (Wardrop): Qp = 280 w (1 + e/w)(1 − p/3) / (1 + w/L). Interchanges: trumpet (3-leg), diamond, cloverleaf (full/partial), rotary, directional. Signal types: fixed-time, vehicle-actuated, traffic-actuated, coordinated (simultaneous, alternate, flexible progressive). Webster optimum cycle: Co = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − Y); L = total lost time, Y = Σ (critical q/s). Green time split: gi = (yi / Y)(Co − L). Amber time: 2–4 s (clearance). Pedestrian green ≥ crossing width / walking speed (≈1.2 m/s).

Parking: on-street (parallel, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°) and off-street (lots, multi-storey, underground). 90° parking: max vehicles per kerb length; parallel: min; 45° accepted best compromise for accidents. Parking studies: in–out survey, licence plate (patrol) method. Parking index = (occupied bays / total bays) × 100. Accident studies: collision diagram & condition diagram; spot maps; accident rate per 100 million veh-km. Accident rate R = (A × 10⁸) / (365 × T × V × L). CBR test: penetration at 2.5 mm (standard load 1370 kg) and 5.0 mm (2055 kg); CBR = test load / standard load × 100. Use higher CBR; if 5 mm value higher, repeat test — if still higher, adopt it. Plate bearing test: modulus of subgrade reaction K = p / 0.125 cm (for 75 cm plate); correction for plate size & soaking. Group Index GI = 0.2a + 0.005ac + 0.01bd; range 0 (good) to 20 (poor).

Bitumen: petroleum product, soluble in CS₂. Tar: from destructive distillation of coal/wood, soluble in toluene. Cutback = bitumen + volatile solvent: RC (rapid, gasoline/naphtha), MC (medium, kerosene), SC (slow, oil). Emulsion = bitumen + water + emulsifier; RS (rapid), MS, SS. Cationic preferred for wet aggregates. Modified bitumen: polymer (SBS, EVA), crumb rubber (CRMB) — better temperature susceptibility. Marshall method: specimen 101.6 mm dia × 63.5 mm; compaction 75 blows each face (heavy traffic), 50 blows (medium). Marshall test at 60°C, loading 50.8 mm/min; outputs stability (kN) & flow value (0.25 mm units). Volumetrics: Gm (bulk), Gt (theoretical), Vv air voids 3–5%, VMA = Vv + Vb, VFB = Vb/VMA × 100. Optimum bitumen content = average of bitumen contents at max stability, max density, and 4% air voids. Superpave: newer performance-based design (gyratory compactor). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Bitumen tests: Penetration (hardness; 100 g, 5 s, 25 °C, units of 0.1 mm), ductility (cm at 27 °C), softening point (ring & ball), flash & fire point (safety), viscosity, specific gravity, loss on heating, solubility (CS₂/trichloroethylene). Penetration grades: 80/100 (softer, cold areas), 60/70 (common in Pakistan’s hot plains), 40/50 (very hot areas, heavy traffic). Aggregate tests: Crushing value (strength), Los Angeles abrasion (hardness), impact value (toughness), soundness (durability, Na₂SO₄/MgSO₄), shape (flakiness/elongation), stripping value (bitumen adhesion), specific gravity & water absorption. Marshall criteria (typical): Stability ≥ 8–9 kN, flow 2–4 mm, air voids 3–5%, VMA ≥ 13–15%, VFB 65–75%. Bitumen is soluble in CS₂; tar is obtained by destructive distillation of coal/wood. Cutbacks: RC (naphtha/gasoline), MC (kerosene), SC (oil).

Flexible: load transferred by grain-to-grain contact; layers — subgrade, sub-base, base, binder, surface (wearing) course. Rigid: slab action (flexural strength); PCC slab on base/subgrade. Semi-rigid: lean concrete / soil-cement bases; composite: flexible over rigid. Methods: Empirical (CBR, Group Index, California resistance), Semi-empirical (Triaxial – Kansas), Theoretical (Burmister layered system). IRC:37 — based on CBR & cumulative standard axles (msa); mechanistic-empirical (latest IRC:37-2018). Standard axle load: 80 kN (8.16 t) single axle dual wheel. Fourth power law (VDF): damage factor = (axle load / standard axle)⁴. Cumulative standard axles: N = 365 A [(1+r)ⁿ − 1] × D × F / r; r = growth rate, D = lane distribution, F = VDF. Lane distribution factor (IRC:37): single lane 1.0; two-lane single carriageway 0.5; four-lane single carriageway 0.4; dual carriageway — 2-lane 0.75, 3-lane 0.6, 4-lane 0.45. ESWL (equivalent single wheel load): by equal stress (Boyd & Foster) or equal deflection criterion. Critical strains: horizontal tensile strain at bottom of bituminous layer (fatigue cracking); vertical compressive strain on subgrade (rutting). Burmister: Δ = 1.5 p a F / E (two-layer system). Boussinesq (single layer, flexible plate): Δ = 1.5 p a / E; rigid plate: 1.18 p a / E.

Westergaard: stresses at interior, edge, corner. Edge = critical (wheel load); corner = highest at night (warping). Radius of relative stiffness: l = [E h³ / (12 K (1 − μ²))]^0.25. Equivalent radius of resisting section: b = √(1.6a² + h²) − 0.675h if a < 1.724h; b = a otherwise. Warping (temperature) stress: Ste = (E α t / 2) × C (Bradbury coefficient). Critical combination: day — edge load + warping (bottom tension); night — corner load + warping (top tension). Frictional stress Sf = W Lc f / (2 × 10⁴)  (W = unit wt of concrete). Joints: Expansion (dowel bars, 20–25 mm gap), Contraction (spacing 4.5 m), Construction, Warping/hinge. Dowel bars: load transfer across transverse joints (plain round). Tie bars: hold longitudinal joints (deformed bars, not load transfer). Concrete flexural strength ≥ 4.5 MPa (M40 typical); IRC:58 governs design.

Flexible failures: alligator/fatigue cracking, rutting, shoving, corrugation, bleeding, ravelling, potholes, reflection cracking. Rigid failures: scaling, joint spalling, faulting, pumping, warping cracks, shrinkage cracks, D-cracking. Benkelman beam: measures rebound deflection of flexible pavement → overlay design. Bump integrator: measures surface unevenness (roughness, mm/km). Good surface < 2000 mm/km. IRI (International Roughness Index) in m/km. Overlay types: flexible over flexible, flexible over rigid, rigid over flexible, rigid over rigid. Given: A = 2000 CVPD, r = 7.5%, design life 15 years, VDF = 3.5, lane distribution D = 0.75. Formula: N = 365 × A × [(1 + r)ⁿ − 1]/r × D × F. Answer: [(1.075)¹⁵ − 1]/0.075 ≈ 26.1 → N ≈ 365 × 2000 × 26.1 × 0.75 × 3.5 ≈ 50 million standard axles (msa). AASHTO 1993 (NHA): Structural number SN = a₁D₁ + a₂D₂m₂ + a₃D₃m₃ (layer coefficients, thicknesses, drainage coefficients). Fourth-power law: Doubling axle load increases damage ≈ 16 times — overloading is the main cause of premature failure on Pakistani highways. Flexible pavement critical strains: horizontal tensile at bottom of bituminous layer (fatigue) and vertical compressive on top of subgrade (rutting).

WBM (water-bound macadam): stone aggregate + screenings + binding material, rolled with water. WMM (wet mix macadam): premixed graded aggregate + water; better than WBM. Prime coat: low-viscosity bitumen on porous (granular) surface. Tack coat: bitumen on existing bituminous/concrete surface for bonding. Seal coat: top layer to make surface impervious. Surface dressing: bitumen + chips. Bituminous layers: BM (bituminous macadam), DBM (dense bituminous macadam), BC (bituminous concrete — wearing), SDBC, Mastic asphalt. Mastic asphalt: no rolling required; used on bridge decks. Earthwork compaction: smooth-wheeled roller (granular, bituminous), sheep-foot (cohesive soils), pneumatic-tyred (mixed), vibratory (granular). Surface drainage: camber, side drains, catch water drains (hill roads, uphill side). Sub-surface drainage: lowering water table (longitudinal drains), intercepting seepage, control of capillary rise (capillary cut-off). Rational formula for runoff: Q = C I A / 360  (Q m³/s, I mm/h, A hectares). Hill roads: hair-pin bends (min radius 14–15 m), retaining walls (valley side), breast walls (hill side), catch water drains. Gauge Width Notes Standard 1435 mm Most common worldwide Broad (BG) 1676 mm Pakistan & India main lines Metre (MG) 1000 mm — Narrow (NG) 762 / 610 mm Hilly areas Permanent way: rails, sleepers, ballast, formation (subgrade) + fixtures/fastenings. Rail types: double-headed, bull-headed, flat-footed (Vignoles) — most used. Rail length: 12.8 m (42 ft) BG; 11.89 m (39 ft) MG. Long welded rails (LWR) reduce joints. Coning of wheels: slope 1 in 20; prevents wheel flange rubbing & keeps vehicle central. Rails tilted inward at 1 in 20 (adzing of sleepers). Creep: longitudinal movement of rails. Measured by creep indicator; prevented by anchors/creep anchors. Wear of rails max on outer rail on curves; side wear. Sleeper density = n + x (n = rail length in m); e.g., M + 7 for BG main lines. Sleeper types: wooden (best elasticity), steel, cast iron, concrete (prestressed, most used now). Ballast: broken stone (best), size 50 mm for BG; functions — load distribution, drainage, elasticity. Min depth of ballast cushion: 250 mm (BG). Fish plates: join rails at ends. Expansion gap provided for temperature.

Equilibrium cant: e = G V² / (127 R)  (G gauge in mm, V km/h, R m) → e in mm. Max cant: BG 165 mm (185 mm for special); MG 100 mm. Cant deficiency: BG 75 mm (100 mm high-speed); MG 50 mm. Negative cant: on the turnout branch curve opposite to main line curve. Degree of curve: D = 1750 / R (30.5 m chord); D = 1146 / R (20 m chord). Max permissible speed (BG, transitioned curve): V = 0.27 √[(Ca + Cd) R]  (Ca, Cd in mm). Transition length = max of 0.008 Ca Vm, 0.008 Cd Vm, 0.72 Ca. Grade compensation on curves: BG 0.04% per degree; MG 0.03%; NG 0.02%. Ruling gradient: 1 in 150–200 (plains), 1 in 100 (hilly). Momentum & pusher gradients steeper. Gradient at stations (yards): max 1 in 400 (prevent runaway); min 1 in 1000 for drainage.

Turnout components: points (switches), lead rails, crossing (frog), check rails, heel block. Number of crossing N = cot α; methods: right-angle (Cole's), centre-line, isosceles triangle. Switch angle: angle between stock rail and tongue rail. Crossings: acute (V/frog), obtuse (diamond), square. Track junctions: diamond crossing, scissors crossover, gauntlet track, triangle (to reverse direction of engine). Signals: semaphore, colour light; absolute block system ensures one train per block section. Interlocking: prevents conflicting signal/point settings. Station yards: marshalling yard (sorting wagons, hump yard), loco yard, goods yard, passenger yard. Hauling capacity of locomotive = μ × W × n (μ coefficient of adhesion ≈ 0.2 dry rail). Train resistances: due to friction, wave action, speed, wind, gradient, curvature, starting/accelerating. Fig. 7.2 — Turnout: stock rail, tongue rails, lead rails, crossing (frog), check and wing rails. Pakistan Railways: Mostly broad gauge (1676 mm); ML-1 (Karachi–Peshawar, ≈ 1,726 km) is the main line planned for upgrading under CPEC; ML-2 and ML-3 are other main lines. Rail weight: Expressed in kg/m (e.g., 52 kg/m, 60 kg/m UIC rails); older in lb/yd. Long welded rails: Reduce joints, noise and maintenance; need de-stressing and good ballast. Airport site factors: regional plan, airspace, surrounding obstructions, ground accessibility, meteorology, soil, noise, future expansion. Runway orientation: along prevailing wind; determined by wind rose diagram (Type I: direction & duration; Type II: direction, duration & intensity). Crosswind component: max 25 km/h (large aircraft), 15 km/h (small); runway coverage ≥ 95% (ICAO). Basic runway length: at sea level, 15°C, zero gradient, no wind. Corrections (ICAO): elevation +7% per 300 m; temperature +1% per 1°C above standard (T = Ta + (Tm − Ta)/3); gradient +20% per 1% effective gradient. Combined elevation + temperature correction should not exceed 35%. Standard atmosphere temperature drops 6.5°C per km altitude. Runway configurations: single, parallel, open-V, intersecting. Taxiway: connects runway to apron/terminal; exit taxiway (high-speed) angle 30° (ideal), 45°. Apron: aircraft parking/loading area. Hangar: aircraft repair & housing. Holding apron: near runway end for final checks before take-off. Turning zone: provided at runway end when no parallel taxiway. Clearway: obstacle-free area beyond runway. Stopway: paved area beyond runway for aborted take-off. Runway markings: white; taxiway markings: yellow. Imaginary surfaces (obstruction clearance): approach, transitional, inner horizontal (45 m height), conical. Airport classification (ICAO aerodrome reference code): number 1–4 by field length; letter A–F by wingspan. Lighting: approach lighting, runway edge lights

Harbour: sheltered area for ships. Types — natural, semi-natural, artificial. Breakwater: protects harbour from waves (mound type, wall type, composite). Wet dock: water level maintained by lock gates. Dry dock: for ship repair (emptied of water). Jetty/pier: projects into water; wharf: parallel to shore; quay: wharf retaining land. Fender: absorbs ship impact. Dolphin: mooring structure away from shore. Littoral drift: sediment movement along coast. Tunnel shapes: circular (best for soft ground & water pressure), egg, horseshoe (rock), D-shape. Tunnelling in soft ground: shield method, needle beam, liner plate; in rock: full face, heading & bench, drift method; TBM for both. Tunnel ventilation: natural, mechanical (longitudinal, transverse, semi-transverse). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Pakistan ports: Karachi Port, Port Qasim, Gwadar Port (deep-sea, CPEC). Tunnel surveys: Alignment transferred through shafts; tunnels in Pakistan — Lowari, Kohat, Malakand, Attabad (KKH), Lahore Orange Line (cut-and-cover/elevated). NATM: New Austrian Tunnelling Method — shotcrete + rock bolts, uses the ground’s own strength; widely used in rock tunnels. Mound (rubble) breakwater for deep water/soft bed is costlier in material; wall-type breakwater needs a firm bed.

Competitive Exam Handbook — concise points (ACI 318, SI units; US values in brackets)

Working Stress Design (WSD / ASD): elastic behaviour; stresses under service loads ≤ allowable stresses. Uses modular ratio n = Es/Ec. Ultimate Strength Design (USD / LRFD): factored loads ≤ φ × nominal strength (φRn ≥ U). Basis of ACI 318. Limit State Design (LSD): checks both ultimate limit state (collapse) and serviceability limit state (deflection, cracking). Used by BS 8110 / Eurocode / IS 456. Partial safety factors in LSD: concrete γm = 1.5, steel γm = 1.15 (IS/BS). RCC: concrete takes compression, steel takes tension; works because of bond and nearly equal thermal expansion (≈ 10–12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Codes used in Pakistan: Building Code of Pakistan 2021 adopts ACI 318 for concrete design (BCP-2007 seismic provisions were aligned to ACI 318-05); IS 456 values often appear in MCQ books. WSD vs USD: WSD: elastic, service loads, permissible stresses (fc = 0.45f′c, fs ≈ 0.5fy); USD/LRFD: factored loads, nominal strength × φ. Limit state of collapse (strength) and limit state of serviceability (deflection, cracking) are both checked in modern design.

Deep beam: ℓn ≤ 4h or concentrated load within 2h from support; minimum distributed reinforcement 0.0025 each way. STM elements: Struts (compression, bottle-shaped or prismatic) fce = 0.85 βc βs f′c; ties (steel) Fnt = Ast fy; nodes CCC (βn = 1.0), CCT (0.8), CTT (0.6). Angle limit: Angle between strut and tie ≥ 25°. Corbels/brackets: a/d ≤ 1 and Nuc ≤ Vu; shear-friction plus flexural steel; closed stirrups Ah ≥ 0.5(As − An). Shear friction: Vn = μ Avf fy (μ = 1.4λ monolithic, 1.0λ roughened, 0.6λ smooth). STM is a lower-bound (plasticity) method — any equilibrium-satisfying truss with adequate element strengths is safe.

Equilibrium torsion: needed for equilibrium (e.g. cantilever slab on edge beam) — must be designed for full Tu. Compatibility torsion: arises from continuity; may be reduced (redistribution permitted) to cracking torque. Threshold torsion: Tth = 0.083λ√fc′ (Acp²/pcp) [US: λ√fc′ Acp²/pcp]; neglect torsion if Tu < φTth. Cracking torque Tcr = 4 × Tth. Space truss analogy; concrete core assumed to contribute nothing after cracking. Reinforcement: closed stirrups (135° hooks) + longitudinal bars distributed around perimeter. Transverse: At/s = Tn/(2Aofyt tanθ), Ao = 0.85Aoh, θ = 45°. Longitudinal: Al = (At/s)ph(fyt/fy)cot²θ. Stirrup spacing ≤ ph/8 or 300 mm; longitudinal bar spacing ≤ 300 mm; min bar dia ≥ 0.042s or #3 (10 mm). Shear and torsion combined: cross-section limit check prevents web crushing.
More on this topic — Advanced RC Design (MSc): Torsion, Redistribution & Serviceability (advanced)

Compatibility vs equilibrium torsion: Compatibility torsion (redistributes after cracking, e.g., spandrel beams) can be designed for cracking torque; equilibrium torsion must be resisted fully. Threshold torsion: Neglect if Tu < φ 0.083λ√f′c (Acp²/pcp). Moment redistribution: ACI 6.6.5: up to 1000εt % (max 20%) when εt ≥ 0.0075 at the section. Long-term deflection: λΔ = ξ/(1 + 50ρ′); ξ = 2.0 for ≥ 5 years. Crack control: Bar spacing s ≤ 380(280/fs) − 2.5cc ≤ 300(280/fs) mm; fs ≈ ⅔ fy.

Bond resistance from: chemical adhesion, friction, and mechanical interlock of ribs (main for deformed bars). Development length ld: length needed to develop fy in bar. Simplified tension ld (clear spacing ≥ db, cover ≥ db, min stirrups): #6 (19 mm) and smaller: ld = (fyψtψe / 2.1λ√fc′) db  [US: fyψtψe/(25λ√fc′)] #7 (22 mm) and larger: ld = (fyψtψe / 1.7λ√fc′) db  [US: /20λ√fc′] Rule of thumb (fc′ = 28, Gr 60): ld ≈ 40–50db. ld ≥ 300 mm (12 in) in tension. ψt (casting position) = 1.3 for top bars (> 300 mm fresh concrete below); 1.0 otherwise. ψe (coating) = 1.5 epoxy (cover < 3db or spacing < 6db); 1.2 other epoxy; 1.0 uncoated. ψtψe ≤ 1.7. Compression: ldc = max(0.24fy/λ√fc′, 0.043fy) db ≥ 200 mm (8 in). Shorter than tension (end bearing helps). Standard hook in tension: ldh ≥ 8db and ≥ 150 mm (6 in). Hooks not effective in compression. Standard hooks: 90° with 12db extension; 180° with 4db (≥ 65 mm) extension; stirrup hooks 135°/90° with 6db.

Splice Length Tension lap Class A (As,prov ≥ 2As,req and ≤ 50% spliced) 1.0 ld ≥ 300 mm Tension lap Class B (all other cases) 1.3 ld ≥ 300 mm Compression lap (fy ≤ 420 MPa) 0.071fy db ≥ 300 mm Compression lap (fy > 420 MPa) (0.13fy − 24) db ≥ 300 mm Bars larger than #11 (36 mm) shall not be lap spliced (except compression into footings). Other splice types: mechanical couplers and welded splices (must develop 1.25fy). Splice at points of minimum stress; stagger splices. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Standard hooks: 90° and 180° hooks; ldh ≈ 0.24 fy ψ /(λ√f′c) db (≥ 8db, 150 mm). Development length (simplified, #19 and smaller): ld = (fy ψt ψe /(2.1λ√f′c)) db; larger bars (fy/(1.7λ√f′c)) db. Top-bar factor ψt = 1.3 (more than 300 mm fresh concrete below); epoxy coating ψe up to 1.5.
Minimum thickness (deflection not computed), fy = 420 MPa

Member Simply supported One end continuous Both ends continuous Cantilever Solid one-way slab L/20 L/24 L/28 L/10 Beams / ribbed one-way slabs L/16 L/18.5 L/21 L/8 For other fy multiply by (0.4 + fy/700) [US: 0.4 + fy/100,000]. Lightweight concrete: multiply by (1.65 − 0.0003wc) ≥ 1.09.

Cracking moment Mcr = fr Ig / yt. Effective moment of inertia (Branson): Ie = (Mcr/Ma)³Ig + [1 − (Mcr/Ma)³]Icr ≤ Ig. (ACI 318-19 uses Bischoff equation.) Long-term deflection multiplier: λΔ = ξ / (1 + 50ρ′). Time factor ξ: 5 years or more = 2.0; 12 months = 1.4; 6 months = 1.2; 3 months = 1.0. Member condition Deflection limit Flat roofs not supporting damage-prone elements (immediate L) L/180 Floors not supporting damage-prone elements (immediate L) L/360 Roof/floor supporting elements likely to be damaged (long-term + L) L/480 Roof/floor supporting elements not likely to be damaged L/240

Max bar spacing: s = 380(280/fs) − 2.5cc ≤ 300(280/fs) mm; fs ≈ (2/3)fy. For Gr 60, cc = 50 mm: s ≈ 254 mm (10 in). Skin reinforcement on side faces when h > 900 mm (36 in). Use more small-diameter bars rather than few large bars to control crack width. Permissible crack width (IS/BS): 0.3 mm normal exposure; 0.2 mm aggressive; 0.1 mm water-retaining.

One-way if long span / short span (L/S) ≥ 2; bends mainly in short direction. Designed as 1 m (or 1 ft) wide beam strip. Shrinkage & temperature (S&T) steel (of gross area): 0.0020 for Gr 280/350; 0.0018 for Gr 420; 0.0018 × 420/fy for higher grades (≥ 0.0014). S&T steel spacing ≤ 5h or 450 mm (18 in). Main steel spacing ≤ 3h or 450 mm; As,min for flexure = S&T steel. Shear rarely governs; stirrups not provided in slabs. ACI moment coefficients (approx. analysis): +M end span = wl²/11 (discontinuous end unrestrained) or /14 (integral); interior +M = wl²/16; −M at exterior face of first interior support = wl²/9 (two spans) or wl²/10 (more than two spans); other interior support faces wl²/11. Conditions for ACI coefficients: ≥ 2 spans, adjacent spans differ ≤ 20%, uniform load, L ≤ 3D, prismatic members.

L/S < 2; load carried in both directions. Types: slab on beams, flat plate (no beams, no drops), flat slab (drop panels and/or column capitals), waffle slab. Methods: Direct Design Method (DDM), Equivalent Frame Method (EFM), yield line, strip method, FEM. DDM limitations: ≥ 3 continuous spans each way; successive spans differ ≤ 1/3 of longer; panel ratio long/short ≤ 2; column offset ≤ 10% of span; gravity load only, uniformly distributed; L ≤ 2D (unfactored). Total static moment: Mo = qu l2 ln² / 8; ln ≥ 0.65 l1 (clear span face to face). Interior span distribution: −M = 0.65Mo, +M = 0.35Mo. Column strip width each side of column centreline = 0.25 × smaller of l1, l2; middle strip = remainder. Column strip carries most negative moment (≈ 75% interior −M for flat plates). Min thickness (no interior beams, fy 420): without drop panels ln/30 (exterior panel, no edge beam) or ln/33 (interior) ≥ 125 mm; with drop panels ln/33 or ln/36 ≥ 100 mm. Drop panel: projects ≥ h/4 below slab; extends ≥ l/6 from column centre each way. Max bar spacing in two-way slabs ≤ 2h or 450 mm at critical sections.

Critical perimeter bo at d/2 from face of column / drop panel / concentrated load. Vc = least of (× bo d): 0.33λ√fc′  [4λ√fc′] 0.17(1 + 2/β)λ√fc′  — β = long/short side of column 0.083(αs d/bo + 2)λ√fc′ — αs = 40 interior, 30 edge, 20 corner column Remedies if inadequate: increase thickness, drop panel/capital, larger column, shear studs/stud rails, shear heads. Unbalanced moment transfer: γf = 1/[1 + (2/3)√(b1/b2)] by flexure; γv = 1 − γf by eccentric shear. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 10.1 — One-way vs two-way slab action. Shrinkage & temperature steel: ρ = 0.0018 (Grade 60) of gross area; spacing ≤ 5h or 450 mm. Two-way slab methods: Direct design method (DDM), equivalent frame method (EFM), moment coefficient (ACI old/Marcus) methods, yield-line theory. Flat plate / flat slab: No beams; drop panels/column capitals increase punching shear capacity. Ly/Lx > 2 → one-way; ≤ 2 → two-way. Punching shear is checked at d/2 from the column face.
More on this topic — Advanced RC Design (MSc): Two-Way Slabs — DDM, EFM, Flat & Waffle Slabs

Systems: Flat plate (no drops), flat slab (drop panels/column capitals), two-way slab with beams, waffle (two-way joist) slab — light & stiff for long spans. Minimum thickness (no interior beams): Without drop panels: ln/30 (exterior panels without edge beams) / ln/33 (interior); with drop panels ln/33 / ln/36 (fy 420 MPa); h ≥ 125 mm (≥ 100 mm with drops). Direct Design Method limits: ≥ 3 continuous spans each way; panels rectangular with long/short ≤ 2; successive spans differ ≤ ⅓ of longer; column offset ≤ 10%; gravity loads only; L ≤ 2D (unfactored). Interior span distribution: −0.65 Mo at supports, +0.35 Mo mid-span; end spans use ACI table (e.g., flat plate with edge beam: 0.30/0.50/0.70). Column & middle strips: Column strip width = each side 0.25 × smaller of ℓ₁, ℓ₂; interior negative moment: 75% to column strip (no beams); positive: 60%. Equivalent Frame Method: Slab–beam + equivalent column (torsional members) analysed by moment distribution; any span ratio and lateral loads (with limits). Punching (two-way) shear: Critical section d/2 from column face; vc = least of 0.33λ√f′c, 0.17(1 + 2/β)λ√f′c, 0.083(αs d/bo + 2)λ√f′c (MPa); αs = 40/30/20 interior/edge/corner; size effect factor λs (ACI 318-19). Unbalanced moment transfer: γf Msc by flexure within c₂ + 3h; γv Msc = (1 − γf) Msc by eccentric shear. Waffle slab: Rib width ≥ 100 mm, depth ≤ 3.5 × rib width, clear spacing ≤ 750 mm; solid heads around columns for punching shear. Mo = quℓ₂ℓn²/8; interior span: 65% nega

Column: vertical member with height > 3 × least lateral dimension carrying mainly axial load (pedestal if ≤ 3). Tied columns: φ = 0.65; less ductile. Spiral columns: φ = 0.75; more ductile, higher toughness. Steel ratio ρg = 1% – 8% (practical ≤ 4% to avoid congestion; ≤ 6% in seismic). Minimum longitudinal bars: 4 (rectangular/circular tied), 3 (triangular ties), 6 (spiral). Pure axial: Po = 0.85fc′(Ag − Ast) + fyAst. Max design load (accidental eccentricity): φPn,max = 0.80φPo (tied); 0.85φPo (spiral).

Tie bar: #3 (10 mm) for longitudinal bars up to #10 (32 mm); #4 (13 mm) for #11, #14, #18 and bundled. Tie spacing ≤ least of: 16db (longitudinal), 48 dtie, least column dimension. Every corner and alternate bar laterally supported; no bar > 150 mm clear from a supported bar. Spiral ratio: ρs = 0.45(Ag/Ach − 1)fc′/fyt; spiral dia ≥ 10 mm; clear pitch 25–75 mm (1–3 in).

Plot of Pn vs Mn; any (Pu, Mu) inside the φ-curve is safe. Key points: pure axial (Po), balanced point (Pb, Mb), pure moment, pure tension. P > Pb (e < eb): compression failure — concrete crushes first. P < Pb (e > eb): tension failure — steel yields first. Near balanced region, increasing axial load can increase moment capacity (below Pb).

Radius of gyration r = 0.3h (rectangular), 0.25D (circular). Slenderness neglected (short column) if: Unbraced (sway) frame: klu/r ≤ 22 Braced (non-sway) frame: klu/r ≤ 34 + 12(M1/M2) ≤ 40 (ACI 318-19: M1/M2 negative for single curvature, positive for double; older ACI wrote 34 − 12(M1/M2) with the opposite sign) k = 1.0 conservative for braced; k ≥ 1.0 for unbraced. Pin-pin k = 1, fixed-fixed 0.5, fixed-free 2.0. klu/r > 100: second-order (P-Δ) analysis required. Moment magnifier (non-sway): δns = Cm / (1 − Pu/0.75Pc) ≥ 1.0;  Pc = π²(EI)eff/(klu)². Cm = 0.6 − 0.4(M1/M2) with M1/M2 negative for single curvature (ACI 318-19) → Cm = 1.0 for equal single-curvature moments; older ACI: Cm = 0.6 + 0.4M1/M2 ≥ 0.4 (positive for single curvature). Cm = 1.0 with transverse loads. Minimum moment: M2,min = Pu(15 + 0.03h) mm [Pu(0.6 + 0.03h) in]. Biaxial bending — Bresler reciprocal method: 1/Pn = 1/Pnx + 1/Pny − 1/Po. Bresler load contour: (Mnx/Mox)^α + (Mny/Moy)^α = 1. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 11.1 — Column interaction (P–M) diagram: pure axial, compression-controlled, balanced point, tension-controlled. Fig. 11.2 — Detailing: beam stirrups, tied column and spiral column. Axial capacity (tied): φPn,max = 0.80φ[0.85f′c(Ag − Ast) + fyAst], φ = 0.65; spiral: 0.85 factor, φ = 0.75. Short column limit (braced): kLu/r ≤ 34 + 12(M₁/M₂) ≤ 40 (ACI 318-19 sign: M₁/M₂ negative in single curvature); unbraced: kLu/r ≤ 22. Longitudinal steel 1

Fig. 11.3 — P–Δ effect in a slender column and the moment-magnifier equations (ACI 318). Slenderness limits (ACI 6.2.5): Neglect slenderness if k lu/r ≤ 34 + 12(M1/M2) ≤ 40 for braced (non-sway) frames; ≤ 22 for sway frames. r = 0.3h (rectangular), 0.25D (circular). Effective length k: Braced frames 0.5–1.0 (often taken 1.0); sway frames > 1.0 — from Jackson–Moreland alignment charts using ψ = Σ(EI/l)columns / Σ(EI/l)beams. Non-sway magnifier: δns = Cm/(1 − Pu/0.75Pc) ≥ 1.0; Cm = 0.6 − 0.4(M1/M2) (ACI 318-19: M1/M2 negative for single curvature, positive for double curvature; Cm = 1 with transverse loads). M2,min = Pu(15 + 0.03h) mm. (EI)eff: 0.4 Ec Ig/(1 + βdns) or (0.2 Ec Ig + Es Ise)/(1 + βdns); βdns = factored sustained axial / total factored axial. Sway frames: δs = 1/(1 − ΣPu/(0.75ΣPc)) or Q-method; or second-order (P-Δ) analysis. Upper limit: Second-order moment ≤ 1.4 × first-order moment, otherwise revise sections. Double curvature (M1/M2 positive in ACI 318-19) gives smaller Cm and a higher slenderness limit — slender effects are less severe; single curvature is the critical case.

Types: isolated (spread), wall (strip), combined, strap/cantilever, mat/raft, pile cap. Area from service (unfactored) loads and allowable bearing pressure; reinforcement and depth from factored loads (net factored pressure qu). Depth above bottom reinforcement ≥ 150 mm (6 in) on soil; ≥ 300 mm (12 in) on piles. Cover: 75 mm (3 in) for concrete cast against earth. Critical section for moment: face of column/pedestal/wall (concrete); midway between centre and face for masonry wall; halfway between column face and edge of steel base plate. One-way (beam) shear: at d from face.  Two-way (punching) shear: at d/2 from face — usually governs depth. Rectangular footing: long-direction steel uniform; short-direction band width = short side, band steel = 2/(β + 1) × total, β = long/short. Bearing at column–footing interface: φ(0.85fc′A1) × √(A2/A1), with √(A2/A1) ≤ 2. Min dowel area across interface = 0.005Ag of the supported column. Combined footing: make centroid of area coincide with resultant of column loads for uniform pressure. Strap footing: strap beam does not bear on soil; transfers moment from eccentric (property-line) footing. Mat foundation: used when footings cover > 50% of plan area or for weak soil / differential settlement control. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 12.1 — Critical sections of an isolated footing: moment at face, one-way shear at d, punching at d/2. Worked sizing: Service load 1200 kN, qa = 200 kPa → area

Types: gravity (≤ 3 m), cantilever (up to ~6–7 m), counterfort (> 6–7 m), buttressed, crib, sheet pile. Counterforts on backfill (tension) side; buttresses on front (compression) side. Factors of safety: overturning ≥ 2.0 (1.5 granular), sliding ≥ 1.5, bearing ≥ 3 (on ultimate). Rankine active pressure: Ka = (1 − sinφ)/(1 + sinφ); passive Kp = 1/Ka; total Pa = ½Ka γH² acting at H/3. Shear key below base increases sliding resistance (mobilises passive pressure). Weep holes and drainage reduce hydrostatic pressure. Cantilever wall: main steel in stem on earth (tension) face; heel steel at top; toe steel at bottom. Preliminary: base width ≈ 0.4–0.7H; base thickness ≈ H/10–H/12. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 13.1 — Cantilever retaining wall: stem, toe, heel, shear key, weep holes. Main steel of the stem is on the earth (backfill) face; heel slab main steel at the top; toe slab main steel at the bottom.
Isolated Square Footing — Full Design Example

Procedure: (1) Area from service loads: A = (D + L)/q_net. (2) Factored soil pressure qu = Pu/A. (3) Depth from punching shear at d/2 from column face and one-way shear at d from the face. (4) Moment at column face → steel. (5) Check As,min = 0.0018bh, development length, bearing at column interface, dowels ≥ 0.005Ag. Punching shear (ACI 318-19, no shear reinforcement): vc = least of 0.33λs√f′c, 0.17(1 + 2/β)λs√f′c, 0.083(αs d/bo + 2)λs√f′c (MPa); αs = 40 interior, 30 edge, 20 corner; size-effect factor λs = √[2/(1 + 0.004d)] ≤ 1 (d in mm). φ = 0.75. One-way shear (ACI 318-19 Table 22.5.5.1, Av < Av,min): Vc = 0.66 λs λ (ρw)^(1/3) √f′c bw d. Because ρw in footings is small, this often needs a thicker footing than the older 0.17√f′c bw d expression (ACI 318-14 and earlier).

Column 400 × 400 mm; D = 600 kN, L = 400 kN; net allowable soil pressure 200 kPa; f′c = 25 MPa; fy = 420 MPa; #16 bars (199 mm²). Area: A = 1000/200 = 5.0 m² → use 2.3 m × 2.3 m (5.29 m²). Factored pressure: Pu = 1.2(600) + 1.6(400) = 1360 kN → qu = 1360/5.29 = 257 kPa. Trial d = 400 mm (h = 500 mm): Punching OK (Vu = 1,195 kN < φVc = 1,389 kN with λs = 0.877), but one-way shear fails: Vu = 257 × 2.3 × 0.55 = 325 kN > φVc = 267 kN (ρw = 0.0024). Increase depth. Adopt d = 500 mm (h = 600 mm): λs = √[2/(1 + 2.0)] = 0.816. Punching: bo = 4 × 0.9 = 3.6 m; Vu = 257 × (2.3² − 0.9²) = 1,152 kN; φVc = 0.75 × 0.33 × 0.816 × 5 × 3600 × 500 = 1,819 kN ✔.  Moment & steel: Cantilever 0.95 m → Mu = 257 × 2.3 × 0.95²/2 = 267 kN·m → As (required) = 1,430 mm²; As,min = 0.0018 × 2300 × 600 = 2,484 mm² governs → 13 #16 (2,587 mm²) each way. One-way shear check: Section at d: projection 0.45 m → Vu = 257 × 2.3 × 0.45 = 266 kN; ρw = 2,587/(2300 × 500) = 0.00225 → φVc = 0.75 × 0.66 × 0.816 × 0.00225^(1/3) × 5 × 2300 × 500 = 305 kN ✔. Bearing on column: φ(0.85f′c A1) = 0.65 × 0.85 × 25 × 160,000 = 2,210 kN > 1,360 kN ✔ (footing side higher with √(A2/A1) ≤ 2). Dowels ≥ 0.005 × 160,000 = 800 mm² (e.g., 4 #16). Area from SERVICE loads; depth from punching and one-way shear (under ACI 318-19 the size-effect factor λs and low ρw often make one-way shear govern); steel often controlled by 0.0018bh.

Trial proportions (height H): Base width B ≈ 0.4H–0.7H; toe ≈ B/3; stem top 200–300 mm, stem base ≈ H/10–H/12; base slab thickness ≈ H/10–H/12. Counterfort walls become economical above ≈ 6–7 m; counterfort spacing ≈ H/3–H/2. Earth pressure: Rankine active Ka = (1 − sinφ)/(1 + sinφ); Pa = ½KaγH² at H/3; surcharge q adds Ka·q·H at H/2. Passive resistance in front of toe usually ignored (or only partly counted). Checks: Overturning FOS ≥ 1.5 (2.0 commonly specified for granular backfill); sliding FOS = μΣV/ΣH ≥ 1.5 (add shear key if short); bearing qmax ≤ qa; e ≤ B/6 (no tension under base). Structural design: Stem = vertical cantilever, main steel on earth face; heel slab = cantilever loaded downward by soil — main steel at TOP; toe slab = cantilever loaded upward by soil pressure — main steel at BOTTOM. Weep holes (≈ 75–100 mm at 1.5–3 m c/c) + drainage filter behind wall.

H = 5.0 m (to base underside), level granular backfill γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 30°, μ = 0.5, γc = 24 kN/m³. Trial: B = 3.2 m, toe 0.9 m, stem 0.25 m (top) → 0.40 m (base) with vertical back face, base slab 0.45 m, heel 1.9 m. Fig. — Worked cantilever wall: dimensions, active pressure and position of main steel in stem, heel and toe. Pressure: Ka = 1/3; Pa = ½ × 1/3 × 18 × 5² = 75 kN/m at 1.67 m → MO = 125 kN·m/m. Vertical loads (lever arm from toe): Base 3.2 × 0.45 × 24 = 34.6 kN (1.60 m); stem rectangular 0.25 × 4.55 × 24 = 27.3 kN (1.175 m); stem triangle ½ × 0.15 × 4.55 × 24 = 8.2 kN (1.00 m); soil on heel 1.9 × 4.55 × 18 = 155.6 kN (2.25 m). ΣV = 225.7 kN; ΣMR = 445.7 kN·m. Overturning: FOS = 445.7/125 = 3.57 ✔. Sliding: FOS = 0.5 × 225.7/75 = 1.50 ✔ (just adequate; add a shear key for margin). Base pressure: x̄ = (445.7 − 125)/225.7 = 1.42 m; e = 1.6 − 1.42 = 0.18 m < B/6 = 0.53 m ✔; qmax = (225.7/3.2)(1 + 6 × 0.18/3.2) = 94 kPa, qmin = 47 kPa. Heel steel at TOP, toe steel at BOTTOM, stem steel on EARTH face. Sliding usually governs — a shear key below the base increases passive resistance.

Geometry: Riser R 150–190 mm, tread (going) T 250–300 mm; 2R + T ≈ 600–640 mm; R × T ≈ 40,000–45,000 mm²; max ≈ 12–15 risers per flight; headroom ≥ 2.1 m; landing width ≥ stair width. Types: Straight, dog-legged (most common in houses), open-well, quarter/half-turn, spiral, helical, free-standing (scissors) and cantilever (steps fixed into a wall/beam). Structural systems: Waist-slab stair spanning longitudinally (between landings/beams) or transversely (between stringer/wall); folded-plate (slabless) stair; cantilever steps. Loads: Self-weight of waist on plan = γc·t·√(R² + T²)/T; steps = ½·R·γc (on plan); finishes ≈ 1 kPa; live load ≈ 4.8 kPa (ASCE 7 stairs: 100 psf). Effective span: Horizontal span between supports; landings spanning in the same direction are included; when landings span transversely (supported on walls), ACI/BS allow reduced span — check the code.

R = 150 mm, T = 300 mm, simply supported horizontal span 3.6 m, waist t = 180 mm (≈ span/20), cover 20 mm, #12 bars. Fig. — Waist-slab stair: riser, tread, waist thickness and main steel along the soffit. Loads (per m² of plan): Waist = 0.18 × 24 × 1.118 = 4.83 kPa; steps = 0.5 × 0.15 × 24 = 1.80 kPa; finishes 1.0 kPa → D = 7.63 kPa; L = 4.8 kPa. wu = 1.2(7.63) + 1.6(4.8) = 16.8 kPa. Moment & steel: Mu = 16.8 × 3.6²/8 = 27.3 kN·m/m; d = 180 − 20 − 6 = 154 mm → As = 484 mm²/m → #12 @ 225 mm c/c (> As,min 324 mm²/m). Distribution steel 0.0018bh = 324 mm²/m → #10 @ 225 mm. Waist slab = inclined one-way slab: load on plan includes the slope factor √(R² + T²)/T; main steel along the going.

Types: By position: resting on ground, underground, elevated (overhead). By shape: circular (most economical for walls — pure hoop tension), rectangular, Intze (large elevated tanks). Codes: ACI 350 (Code requirements for environmental engineering concrete structures) — strength design with environmental durability factor Sd to keep service steel stresses low; IS 3370 (Parts 1–4); BS 8007 / EN 1992-3. Crack control: Design to limit cracking for water-tightness: BS 8007 crack width 0.2 mm (normal), 0.1 mm (severe/critical appearance). Use smaller bars at closer spacing. ACI 350 detailing: Minimum cover ≈ 50 mm for surfaces in contact with liquid; walls ≥ 3 m high at least 300 mm thick; shrinkage & temperature steel ratio 0.003–0.005 depending on distance between movement joints; waterstops at joints. Circular tank wall — hoop tension: Free (sliding) base: hoop tension at depth h, T = γw·h·D/2 per metre height (maximum at the base). Fixed base: hoop tension is zero at base and maximum somewhere above; vertical cantilever moment develops at the base. Worked hoop tension: D = 10 m, H = 4 m, free base: T = 9.81 × 4 × 10/2 = 196 kN/m at the bottom. Hoop steel As = T/fs (fs = permissible/service steel stress of the chosen code) placed as rings in both faces; check concrete tensile stress T/[A_c + (m − 1)A_s] where an uncracked design is required. Fig. — Left: hoop tension in a circular tank wall (free vs fixed base). Right: parts of an Intze tank. Rectangular tanks: Walls act as pla

Allowable stresses: concrete fc = 0.45fc′; steel fs = 140 MPa (Gr 40) / 170 MPa (Gr 60) [20 / 24 ksi]. Neutral axis factor: k = √(2ρn + (ρn)²) − ρn;  lever arm factor j = 1 − k/3. Stair: riser 150–190 mm, tread 250–300 mm; 2R + T ≈ 600–640 mm; waist slab designed as one-way slab along going. Effective span of beam: lesser of clear span + d and c/c of supports. Lintel load: masonry within 60° equilateral triangle above opening. Seismic (special moment frames): beam width ≥ 250 mm and ≥ 0.3h; ρ ≤ 0.025; hoops at ≤ d/4, 6db (318-19), 150 mm within 2h from joint face. Strong column – weak beam: ΣMnc ≥ (6/5)ΣMnb. Column hoops in plastic hinge zone lo ≥ max(h, lu/6, 450 mm). Seismic hooks: 135° with 6db (≥ 75 mm) extension. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Special moment frames: Strong column–weak beam: ΣMnc ≥ 1.2 ΣMnb; closely spaced hoops at beam ends & column ends (plastic hinge zones); 135° seismic hooks. Short-column effect: Columns partially restrained by walls/mezzanine attract high shear — avoid or detail with full-height hoops. Seismic hooks: 135° bend with 6db (≥ 75 mm) extension — prevents opening of ties during earthquakes.

Principle: Introduce internal compression (prestress) so that service tensile stresses are cancelled — whole section effective, no cracking at service. Three concepts: (1) Stress concept — concrete as elastic material; (2) Strength concept — internal couple of steel & concrete (like RC); (3) Load-balancing concept (T.Y. Lin) — tendon profile balances part of the load. Pre-tensioning: Tendons stressed before casting, released when concrete gains strength; force transferred by bond (Hoyer effect); for factory precast (hollow-core, railway sleepers, piles). Post-tensioning: Concrete cast with ducts, tendons stressed after hardening and anchored; bonded (grouted) or unbonded; for bridges, long-span slabs, in-situ work. Systems: Freyssinet (wedge cones), Magnel–Blaton (sandwich plates), Gifford–Udall, Lee–McCall (threaded bars), multi-strand wedge anchorages (VSL, Dywidag). Degree of prestress: Full (no tension at service), limited, partial prestressing (cracking allowed with control). Advantages: Smaller depth (L/d ≈ 25–35), crack-free, better durability & fatigue, lower deflection, efficient use of high-strength materials. Pre-tensioning: bond transfer; post-tensioning: end anchorages. Load balancing was introduced by T.Y. Lin (1963).

Pre-compression applied to counteract tensile stresses from loads → crack-free, slimmer sections. Pre-tensioning: tendons stressed before concreting; bond transfers force (factory products, sleepers, hollow-core). Post-tensioning: tendons in ducts stressed after concrete hardens; anchorages transfer force (bridges, long spans). High-strength steel: strands fpu ≈ 1860 MPa (270 ksi); concrete fc′ ≥ 35–40 MPa. Immediate losses: elastic shortening, anchorage slip, friction (post-tensioned). Time-dependent losses: creep, shrinkage, steel relaxation. Total ≈ 15–25%. Elastic shortening loss is absent in post-tensioning with single tendon / all tendons stressed together. Friction loss only in post-tensioning (curvature + wobble). Load balancing method: parabolic tendon with sag e balances w = 8Pe/L². Kern distance (rectangular) = h/6 from centroid. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Losses of prestress: Elastic shortening, shrinkage, creep, relaxation of steel (time-dependent); friction & anchorage slip (post-tensioning). Pre- vs post-tensioning: Pre-tensioning: tendons stressed before casting (factory, bond transfer); post-tensioning: after hardening via ducts & anchorages (site, large spans). High-strength concrete (≥ 35–40 MPa) and high-tensile steel (fpu ≈ 1860 MPa) are essential because losses can reach 15–25%.

Concrete: High strength: f′c ≥ 35 MPa (post-tensioned) and ≥ 40 MPa (pre-tensioned) typically; transfer strength f′ci ≈ 0.7–0.8 f′c. Prestressing steel: 7-wire low-relaxation strands (fpu = 1860 MPa, Grade 270 ksi; 12.7 & 15.2 mm), stress-relieved wires (1620–1720 MPa), high-strength bars (fpu ≈ 1035 MPa). Why high strength: Losses ≈ 200–300 MPa would cancel most of the prestress in mild steel (fy 250–420 MPa). Allowable jacking stress (ACI): ≤ 0.94 fpy and ≤ 0.80 fpu; immediately after transfer ≤ 0.82 fpy and ≤ 0.74 fpu; post-tensioning at anchorage after seating ≤ 0.70 fpu. Low-relaxation strand has relaxation loss ≈ ¼ of stress-relieved strand.

Fibre stresses: f = −P/A ∓ P e y/I ± M y/I → top: −P/A + Pe/Zt − M/Zt; bottom: −P/A − Pe/Zb + M/Zb (compression −). Kern points: kt = Zb/A (upper kern), kb = Zt/A (lower kern); prestress within kern → no tension anywhere; core = middle third for rectangle. Pressure line (C-line): Line of action of compressive force; shifts by M/P from tendon; must lie within kern for no tension. Stages: Transfer (Pi, self-weight only — critical for top tension) and service (Pe after losses, full load — bottom tension). Allowable concrete stresses (ACI 24.5): At transfer: compression 0.60 f′ci (0.70 at ends of simply supported), tension 0.25√f′ci (0.5√f′ci at ends). Service: compression 0.45 f′c (sustained) / 0.60 f′c (total); tension Class U ≤ 0.62√f′c, Class T 0.62–1.0√f′c, Class C > 1.0√f′c (MPa). Magnel's diagram: Graphical feasible zone for 1/P vs e from the four stress inequalities. Concentric prestress on a rectangle: P/A uniform. Eccentricity e = h/6 → zero stress at top and 2P/A at bottom.

Elastic shortening: Pre-tensioned: Δfp = n fcgp (n = Es/Ec). Post-tensioned with sequential stressing: ≈ half of that (first tendon loses most; last none). Anchorage slip: Δfp = Es Δ/L (more important for short members). Creep loss: Δfp = Cu n fcgp (Cu ≈ 1.6–2.0 for normal concrete). Shrinkage loss: Δfp = εsh Es (εsh ≈ 300–600 ×10⁻⁶; post-tensioned smaller as some shrinkage occurs before stressing). Typical totals: Pre-tensioned ≈ 20–25%, post-tensioned ≈ 15–20%; old AASHTO lump-sum ≈ 310 MPa (45 ksi) pre-tensioned and ≈ 220–230 MPa post-tensioned — use refined methods for design. Elastic-shortening loss is absent if all post-tensioned tendons are stressed simultaneously; friction loss exists only in post-tensioning.

Bonded tendons (ACI approx.): fps = fpu[1 − (γp/β₁)(ρp fpu/f′c)] when fse ≥ 0.5 fpu; γp = 0.28 low-relax, 0.40 stress-relieved, 0.55 bars. Unbonded tendons: fps = fse + 70 + f′c/(100ρp) (span/depth ≤ 35) — lower than bonded. Nominal moment: Mn = Aps fps (dp − a/2); a = Aps fps/(0.85 f′c b); tension-controlled if εt ≥ 0.005 (φ = 0.9). Minimum strength: φMn ≥ 1.2 Mcr (avoid brittle failure at cracking). Cracking moment: Mcr = (fr + P/A + Pe/Zb) Zb with fr = 0.62λ√f′c. φMn ≥ 1.2Mcr — minimum reinforcement rule for prestressed flexural members.

Shear: Vc = lesser of Vci (flexure-shear: 0.05λ√f′c bw dp + Vd + Vi Mcre/Mmax) and Vcw (web-shear: (0.29λ√f′c + 0.3fpc) bw dp + Vp). Inclined tendon gives vertical component Vp that relieves shear. Transfer length: Pre-tensioned: lt ≈ 50 db (strand); development length ld = (fse/21)db + ((fps − fse)/7)db (MPa) ≈ 100+ db. Anchorage zone (post-tensioned): High bursting (splitting) tensile stresses behind anchorages — end blocks & spiral/bursting reinforcement; Guyon/Magnel methods; zone extends ≈ one section depth. Deflection: Camber due to prestress (upward) − dead/live load deflection; camber for a parabolic tendon (e at midspan, zero at ends) = 5PeL²/(48EcI); for a straight tendon with constant e = PeL²/(8EcI). Long-term camber: Multipliers (PCI): erection ≈ 1.8 × initial camber, final ≈ 2.2–2.45. Inclined tendons provide a shear component Vp = P sin θ that reduces design shear.

Fig. 29.1 — Parabolic tendon: equivalent upward uniform load wb = 8Ph/L². Load balancing: Parabolic tendon with sag h exerts upward wb = 8Ph/L²; harped tendon exerts point load 2P sin θ. Choose wb ≈ dead load (+ part of live load) → beam under uniform axial stress P/A. Continuous beams: Prestress induces secondary (parasitic) moments; line of thrust ≠ tendon line. Concordant cable = no secondary moments; linear transformation keeps the pressure line unchanged. Applications: Bridge girders (AASHTO I, box), hollow-core & double-tee slabs, post-tensioned flat slabs, water tanks (circular prestressing), nuclear containments, railway sleepers, poles & piles. Post-tensioned slabs: Span/depth ≈ 40–48 (two-way); average precompression ≥ 0.9 MPa (ACI) typically 1–2 MPa; banded–distributed tendon layout. Concordant cable produces zero secondary moments in continuous prestressed beams.

Sequence: proportional limit → elastic limit → upper yield point → lower yield point → plastic range (yield plateau) → strain hardening → ultimate stress → necking → fracture Strain hardening starts at about 10–15 times the yield strain Elongation at fracture ≈ 20–25% (high ductility) Yield stress (Fy) is the basis of design; for high-strength steels without a clear yield point, use 0.2% offset method Ductility = ability to deform plastically before fracture; toughness = energy absorbed (area under curve)

Advantages: high strength-to-weight ratio, uniformity, elasticity, ductility, toughness, speed of erection, easy additions/alterations, reusable/recyclable Disadvantages: corrosion, fire weakness, buckling of slender members, fatigue, brittle fracture at low temperature, high maintenance cost

Fatigue – failure under repeated/cyclic stress below Fu; depends on stress range and number of cycles Brittle fracture – favoured by low temperature, thick plates, high strain rate, notches, triaxial stress Lamellar tearing – through-thickness separation in thick plates near welds Corrosion protection – painting, galvanizing (zinc coating), weathering steel, encasement Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Corrosion protection: Painting (primer + finish), hot-dip galvanising, weathering steel (ASTM A588), cathodic protection, encasement. Fire protection: Spray-applied fireproofing, intumescent paint, concrete/gypsum encasement — steel loses ≈ 50% strength at ≈ 550 °C. Steel: E = 200 GPa, G ≈ 77 GPa, ν = 0.3, density 7850 kg/m³, α ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C.

Designation: W 14×90 = nominal depth 14 in, 90 lb/ft; L 4×4×½ = equal angle 4 in legs, ½ in thick. Built-up sections: Plate girders, box sections, laced/battened columns (two channels with lacing or batten plates). W-shapes have parallel flange faces (S-shapes are tapered); HSS has the best torsional and buckling resistance for its weight.
