PART IV — DESIGN OF MASONRY STRUCTURES
Based on the MSc course Design of Masonry Structures (UET Peshawar, Drive folder) — TMS 402/602, BCP 2021 and UET/NED research on unreinforced masonry in Pakistan.

Units: Clay bricks (Pakistan: 228 × 114 × 76 mm, f ≈ 7–20 MPa), concrete masonry units (CMU — hollow blocks 190 × 190 × 390 mm), stone, AAC blocks. Mortar types (ASTM C270): M, S, N, O, K (decreasing strength: M ≈ 17.2, S 12.4, N 5.2, O 2.4 MPa) — mnemonic "MaSoN wOrK". Type S/N for structural masonry. Grout: Fine or coarse grout fills cells/cavities around reinforcement; f′g ≥ 14 MPa and ≥ f′m. Prism strength f′m: By unit-strength method (tables) or prism test (h/t = 2 standard); f′m < unit strength but > mortar strength. Elastic modulus: Em = 700 f′m (clay masonry) / 900 f′m (concrete masonry), TMS 402; Ev = 0.4 Em. Behaviour: Anisotropic, weak in tension (bond), failure under compression by lateral splitting due to mortar expansion (unit in biaxial tension). Masonry compressive strength lies between mortar and unit strengths; increases with unit strength more than mortar strength.

Design methods (TMS 402): Allowable stress design (ASD), strength design (LRFD), empirical design (prescriptive, low seismic), prestressed masonry, AAC masonry. Axial strength (URM, strength design): Pn = 0.80[0.80 An f′m (1 − (h/140r)²)] for h/r ≤ 99; Pn = 0.80[0.80 An f′m (70r/h)²] for h/r > 99; φ = 0.60 (URM axial/flexure). Flexural tension: Modulus of rupture (TMS table) perpendicular/parallel to bed joints — very small (≈ 0.2–1 MPa); URM walls sized to avoid tension. Load-bearing walls in Pakistan: Common 1–3 storey construction; vulnerable in earthquakes (2005 Kashmir) — confined masonry recommended. Slenderness: Effective height h/t limits; empirical design h/t ≤ 18–20 for load-bearing walls. Strength-reduction factor for URM is low (φ = 0.6) because tension strength is unreliable.
Reinforced Masonry Walls, Beams & Shear Walls

Fig. 47.1 — Reinforced (grouted) hollow concrete-block wall. Flexure: Rectangular stress block 0.80 f′m over depth a = 0.80c; εmu = 0.0025 (concrete masonry), 0.0035 (clay); φ = 0.90. Maximum reinforcement: Limited by strain compatibility (steel strain ≥ 1.5 εy for walls, higher for special shear walls) to ensure ductility. Bar limits: Bar ≤ No. 11 (36 mm), ≤ ⅛ wall thickness / ¼ cell dimension; area ≤ 4% of the cell area. Shear: Vn = Vnm + Vns; Vnm = [4.0 − 1.75(Mu/Vu dv)] An √f′m + 0.25Pu (US units); Vns = 0.5(Av/s) fy dv; φ = 0.80. Shear wall classes (seismic): Ordinary plain, detailed plain, ordinary reinforced, intermediate reinforced, special reinforced (SDC D+ requires special). Prescriptive seismic reinforcement: Special walls: vertical & horizontal spacing ≤ min(⅓ length, ⅓ height, 1.2 m); ρv + ρh ≥ 0.002, each ≥ 0.0007. Masonry crushing strain: 0.0025 for concrete masonry, 0.0035 for clay masonry (concrete uses 0.003).

Confined masonry: Wall built first, then RC tie-columns and tie-beams cast against it — integral action; preferred for low-rise housing in seismic zones (ERRA guidelines after 2005). Failure modes: In-plane: diagonal shear (X-cracks), sliding, rocking/toe crushing; out-of-plane: wall overturning (most dangerous), gable collapse. Good practice: Horizontal RC bands at plinth, lintel and roof; vertical bars at corners/junctions; openings ≤ 50% of wall length and away from corners; light roofs well connected. Building code: BCP 2021 (Chapter on masonry) & ERRA/NDMA guidelines; height limits for URM in high seismic zones. Lintel band is the most important seismic band in masonry buildings; RC tie-columns go at corners and wall intersections.

Based on the MSc course Bridge Engineering (UET Peshawar, Drive folder: lectures 2–14 on loads, superstructure, bearings, abutments, strut-and-tie models, FHWA abutment design & bearing-pad examples) — AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications and Pakistan Highway Bridge Code (CSI/NHA).

Fig. 49.1 — Main components of a girder bridge: superstructure, bearings and substructure. Superstructure: Deck slab, wearing surface, girders/stringers, diaphragms, parapets/railings, expansion joints. Substructure: Bearings, pier caps, piers, abutments with wing walls, foundations (spread, pile, well/caisson). Span classification (common): Culvert < 6 m; minor bridge 6–30 m (some codes 8–30 m); major bridge > 30 m; long span > 120 m. Structural types & typical spans: Slab (≤ 12 m), T-beam (10–25 m), PC I/box girders (25–60 m), steel plate/box girders (30–150 m), trusses (50–250 m), arches (≤ 500 m), cable-stayed (150–1100 m), suspension (≥ 400 m; record ≈ 2 km — Çanakkale 1915). Deck position: Deck bridge (deck on top), through bridge (deck at bottom between trusses), half-through. Other types: Causeway (submersible, flush with bed), bascule/swing/lift (movable), viaduct (series of spans over valley), Bailey (pre-fab military). Through bridge: deck at the level of the bottom chord. A causeway is a submersible road across a river bed.

Site selection: Straight reach, stable banks, narrow and well-defined channel, good foundation strata, minimal skew, approach alignment. Design flood: Usually 100-year (major bridges); check 500-year for scour (AASHTO/HEC-18). Waterway: Lacey regime width P = 4.75√Q; linear waterway ≈ regime width for alluvial rivers. Scour: Normal scour depth (Lacey) R = 1.35 (q²/f)^⅓; maximum scour = 1.25R (straight reach), 1.5R (moderate bend), 1.75R (severe bend), 2R (right-angled bend or at pier noses; abutments ≈ 1.27R); local pier scour by CSU/HEC-18. Foundation depth: Bottom of foundation ≥ 1.33 × max scour depth below HFL for wells/piles (Indian/Pakistani practice). Afflux & freeboard: Afflux by Molesworth/orifice formulas; freeboard ≥ 600 mm (more for debris-laden rivers). Bridge failures in Pakistan floods: 2010 & 2022 floods damaged hundreds of bridges, mainly due to scour, debris blockage and inadequate waterway in KP & Swat. Most bridge failures worldwide are due to scour, not structural overstress.

Fig. 51.1 — AASHTO HL-93 design truck (also checked with design tandem 2 × 110 kN at 1.2 m; plus 9.3 kN/m lane load). Permanent loads: DC (components), DW (wearing surface & utilities), EV/EH (earth), DD (downdrag). HL-93 live load: Design truck (35 + 145 + 145 kN) or design tandem (2 × 110 kN at 1.2 m) + lane load 9.3 kN/m (3 m wide). Dynamic load allowance (IM): 33% of truck/tandem (not lane); deck joints 75%; fatigue 15%. Multiple presence factors: 1 lane 1.20, 2 lanes 1.00, 3 lanes 0.85, > 3 lanes 0.65. Other loads: BR braking (25% of truck axle weights), CE centrifugal, WS/WL wind, EQ, TU temperature, CR/SH creep/shrinkage, WA water/stream pressure, CV vessel collision, IC ice. Limit states: Strength I (1.25DC + 1.5DW + 1.75LL+IM), Service I/II/III, Fatigue I/II, Extreme Event I (EQ) & II (collision, flood). Pakistan practice: Pakistan Highway Bridge Code / West Pakistan Code of Practice (Class A, Class AA, NLC military loading) and NHA adoption of AASHTO LRFD. Strength I: 1.25 DC + 1.50 DW + 1.75 (LL + IM). IM = 33% applies to truck/tandem only, not the lane load.

Deck slab: Approximate strip method or empirical design (AASHTO 9.7.2 — isotropic reinforcement, min 175 mm thick); cantilever overhang checked for vehicle collision. Live-load distribution factors: AASHTO formulas (girder spacing S, span L, Kg) for moment & shear in interior/exterior girders; lever rule for exterior girders. Influence lines: Used to position HL-93 truck for maximum moment (absolute max moment near mid-span under the middle axle) and shear. Composite steel girders: Shear connectors (studs) make slab act with girder; check constructibility (wet concrete on non-composite steel). PC girders: AASHTO/PCI I-girders, bulb-tees, box girders; continuity for live load via deck; time-dependent losses (see Prestressed chapter). Grillage & FE models: Grillage analogy for slab-on-girder decks; FE (CSiBridge, Midas, Abaqus — curved beam analysis assignment on your Drive). Exterior girder distribution factor is often found by the lever rule (pin at interior girder).

Bearings: Transfer loads & allow movements: elastomeric pads (plain/steel-reinforced), pot bearings, PTFE sliding, rocker & roller (steel), spherical, seismic isolation (LRB, friction pendulum). Fixed vs expansion: Fixed bearing allows rotation, restrains translation; expansion bearing allows both. Elastomeric pad design: Shape factor S = plan area/(perimeter × layer thickness); limits on compressive stress (Method A/B), shear strain ≤ 0.5 from thermal movement, rotation and stability. Expansion joints: Strip seal, finger plate, modular joints for large movements; movement from temperature, creep, shrinkage. Piers: Solid wall, hammerhead, multi-column bents, pile bents; checks for axial + biaxial bending, slenderness, ship/debris impact, stream pressure. Abutments: Stub, full-height cantilever, counterfort, integral & semi-integral, spill-through; design as retaining walls + bearing seat (FHWA design example on your Drive). Seat width: Minimum support length N = (200 + 0.0017L + 0.0067H)(1 + 0.000125S²) mm to prevent unseating in earthquakes. Integral abutments eliminate bearings and expansion joints — lower maintenance, but need flexible piles for thermal movement.

Arithmetic increase: Pn = P0 + n·x̄ — old, large, saturated cities (gives low values) Geometric increase: Pn = P0 (1 + r/100)^n — young, rapidly growing cities (gives high values) Incremental increase: Pn = P0 + n·x̄ + [n(n+1)/2]·ȳ — average cities (most realistic of the three) Others: decreasing rate of growth, simple graphical, comparative graphical, ratio/correlation, master plan/zoning, logistic (S-curve) Logistic saturation population: Ps = [2P0P1P2 − P1²(P0 + P2)] ÷ (P0P2 − P1²) Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Typical per-capita demand: ≈ 135 L/person/day is a common design value for towns with full flushing; ≈ 40–70 lpcd for stand-post/rural supplies; large cities 150–200+ lpcd. Pakistan WASAs often design with ≈ 150–250 L/c/d (incl. losses). Breakdown of domestic use: Drinking ≈ 5 L, cooking ≈ 5 L, bathing ≈ 55 L, washing clothes ≈ 20 L, utensils ≈ 10 L, house washing ≈ 10 L, flushing ≈ 30 L (≈ 135 L total). Non-revenue water (NRW): Leakage + theft + metering errors; often 30–50% in South-Asian cities — leak detection and metering reduce it.

Year Population Increase x Incremental y 1990 40,000 — — 2000 52,000 12,000 — 2010 66,000 14,000 +2,000 2020 82,000 16,000 +2,000 Arithmetic (2030): x̄ = 14,000 → P = 82,000 + 14,000 = 96,000. Incremental (2030): ȳ = 2,000 → P = 82,000 + 1(14,000) + (1×2/2)(2,000) = 98,000. Geometric: Growth rates ≈ 30%, 26.9%, 24.2% per decade → r̄ ≈ 27% → P ≈ 82,000 × 1.27 ≈ 1,04,000 (gives the highest value). Geometric method gives the HIGHEST forecast (young, growing cities); arithmetic the LOWEST (old, saturated cities); incremental lies between.

Pumps: Centrifugal (most common in water works), reciprocating (high head, small discharge), submersible (tube wells), jet, air-lift. Economical diameter of rising main: Lea’s formula D = (0.97–1.22)√Q (D in m, Q in m³/s). Pipe joints: Socket-and-spigot (CI), flanged (pumps), expansion, flexible, mechanical (Dresser) joints. Corrosion of pipes: Tuberculation in CI/steel; prevented by lining (cement mortar, bitumen), cathodic protection, pH control. Hazen-Williams C: new CI ≈ 130, old CI ≈ 100, PVC/HDPE ≈ 140–150. Water hammer pressure rise is controlled by surge tanks, slow valve closure and air vessels.

Turbidity: NTU; measured by Jackson candle turbidimeter, nephelometer (most accurate) Colour: platinum-cobalt scale (TCU); taste & odour: threshold odour number (TON) TDS: affects palatability; measured by evaporation or conductivity (TDS ≈ 0.55–0.7 × EC µS/cm)

pH: 6.5–8.5 for drinking water Hardness (mg/L as CaCO3): due to Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ Temporary (carbonate): bicarbonates of Ca, Mg — removed by boiling Permanent (non-carbonate): sulphates, chlorides, nitrates of Ca, Mg Soft 0–75 | Moderately hard 75–150 | Hard 150–300 | Very hard > 300 Fluoride: < 1 mg/L → dental caries; > 1.5 mg/L → fluorosis Nitrate: > 45 mg/L (as NO3) → methaemoglobinaemia (blue baby syndrome) Iron (0.3) & manganese (0.1 mg/L): staining of clothes and fixtures, taste Arsenic: skin lesions, cancer (major groundwater issue in Punjab/Sindh) Lead: plumbosolvency; neurological damage

Coliform bacteria (E. coli) = indicator of faecal contamination MPN test (multiple tube fermentation): presumptive → confirmed → completed Membrane filter technique: direct colony count Waterborne diseases: cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis A & E, polio, giardiasis

Parameter WHO Guideline Pakistan NSDWQ (2010) Turbidity < 5 NTU < 5 NTU pH 6.5–8.5 6.5–8.5 TDS < 1000 mg/L < 1000 mg/L Total hardness (CaCO3) — (500 often cited) < 500 mg/L Chloride < 250 mg/L < 250 mg/L Fluoride 1.5 mg/L ≤ 1.5 mg/L Nitrate (NO3) 50 mg/L ≤ 50 mg/L Arsenic 0.01 mg/L ≤ 0.05 mg/L Lead 0.01 mg/L ≤ 0.05 mg/L E. coli / faecal coliform 0 per 100 mL 0 per 100 mL Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Alkalinity: Due to OH⁻, CO₃²⁻, HCO₃⁻; phenolphthalein (P) & methyl orange (total, T) titration — P = 0 → only bicarbonate. Hardness conversion: Hardness (mg/L as CaCO₃) = Ca²⁺ × 50/20 + Mg²⁺ × 50/12. Chlorides: Mohr’s method (silver nitrate, potassium chromate indicator); sudden rise indicates sewage pollution. Indicator organism: E. coli / faecal coliforms; drinking water should have 0 per 100 mL. Arsenic in Pakistan: Groundwater in parts of Punjab and Sindh exceeds safe limits; WHO guideline 10 µg/L (Pakistan NSDWQ allows 50 µg/L). Methaemoglobinaemia (blue-baby) — nitrates; fluorosis — fluoride > 1.5 mg/L; Minamata — mercury; Itai-itai — cadmium; arsenicosis — arsenic.
Intake & screening → aeration → coagulation (flash mix) → flocculation → sedimentation → filtration → disinfection → storage & distribution
Removes CO2, H2S, taste & odour; oxidises Fe and Mn Types: spray aerators, cascade/multiple tray, diffused air

Stokes' law (d < 0.1 mm): Vs = g (Gs − 1) d² ÷ (18 ν) Surface overflow rate = Q/A; ideal tank efficiency depends on overflow rate, not depth Detention time = V/Q: plain sedimentation 4–8 h; with coagulation 2–4 h Overflow rate: plain 12–18 m³/m²/day; with coagulation 24–40 m³/m²/day Weir loading ≤ 300 m³/m/day Settling types: Type I discrete, Type II flocculent, Type III zone (hindered), Type IV compression

Alum Al2(SO4)3·18H2O — most common; effective pH 6.5–8.5 Ferrous sulphate (copperas): pH > 8.5; ferric chloride / ferric sulphate: wide pH range Coagulant aids: polyelectrolytes, activated silica, bentonite clay Optimum dose found by jar test Mechanisms: charge neutralisation, sweep floc, bridging Flash mixing 30–60 s; flocculation 20–40 min Velocity gradient G = √(P ÷ μV); flocculator G = 20–80 s⁻¹, Gt = 10⁴–10⁵

Feature Slow Sand Filter Rapid Sand Filter Rate of filtration 100–200 L/m²/h 3000–6000 L/m²/h Effective size (D10) 0.2–0.35 mm 0.45–0.7 mm Uniformity coefficient (D60/D10) 2–3 (up to 5) 1.3–1.7 Pre-treatment Plain sedimentation only Coagulation + sedimentation Cleaning Scraping top 1.5–3 cm sand Backwashing Bacteria removal 98–99% 80–90% Area required Large Small Main mechanism Biological (schmutzdecke) Straining, adsorption Pressure filter: closed steel vessel; small plants, industries, swimming pools Dual/multimedia: anthracite over sand — longer filter runs Operational troubles: mud balls, air binding (negative head), cracking of sand bed

Chlorine: Cl2 + H2O → HOCl + HCl ; HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻ HOCl is ~80 times more effective than OCl⁻; low pH (< 7.5) favours HOCl Chlorine demand = chlorine applied − residual chlorine Free residual chlorine: 0.2–0.5 mg/L at consumer end; contact time ≥ 30 min Break-point chlorination: chlorine added beyond point where all ammonia/organics are oxidised; residual is free chlorine Super-chlorination: excess dose during epidemics, followed by dechlorination (SO2, sodium thiosulphate, sodium bisulphite, activated carbon) Chlorine forms: liquid/gas chlorine, bleaching powder CaOCl2 (~30–35% available Cl), sodium hypochlorite, chloramines, chlorine dioxide Other disinfectants: ozone (strongest, no residual), UV rays, boiling, silver (Katadyn process), iodine/bromine (small supplies) Disinfection by-products: trihalomethanes (THMs) — carcinogenic

Softening: lime-soda process (lime → carbonate hardness; soda ash → non-carbonate); zeolite/base exchange (zero hardness, regenerated by NaCl brine); ion exchange demineralisation Fe & Mn removal: aeration + sedimentation + filtration Defluoridation: Nalgonda technique (alum + lime), activated alumina; fluoridation ~1 mg/L Desalination: reverse osmosis, distillation, electrodialysis Taste & odour: activated carbon, aeration, KMnO4; algae control: copper sulphate Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 4.1 — Sequence of units in a conventional water treatment plant with typical design values. Rapid sand filter design: Rate ≈ 5–7.5 m³/m²/h (≈ 3000–4800 L/m²/h); effective size 0.45–0.7 mm; uniformity coefficient 1.3–1.7; backwash when head loss ≈ 2.5–3 m. Slow sand filter: Rate ≈ 2.4–4.8 m³/m²/day (≈ 100–200 L/m²/h); schmutzdecke (biological layer) does the work; scraped, not backwashed. Alum dose: ≈ 10–30 mg/L typical; produces floc Al(OH)₃ and consumes alkalinity. Chlorine contact time: ≥ 30 min before consumers. Zeolite (base exchange): Removes both temporary & permanent hardness to zero hardness; regenerated with brine (NaCl). Rapid sand filter is ≈ 30–40 times faster than slow sand filter but needs coagulation; bacterial removal: slow sand 98–99%, rapid 80–90%.

Dead-end / tree system: old towns; simple, cheap; stagnation at dead ends Grid-iron system: no dead ends, water circulates; more valves & pipes; best for planned towns Ring / circular system: well-planned towns; any point fed from two directions Radial system: area divided into zones, each fed from a central reservoir — high pressure, quick service
Gravity, pumping without storage, combined pumping & storage (most common) Continuous supply preferred; intermittent supply causes contamination risk

Hardy Cross method: pipe networks (loops) — balancing head loss / flow corrections Equivalent pipe method: replace series/parallel pipes by single pipe Balancing/service reservoir capacity: mass curve method

Sluice/gate valve: stops/controls flow Check/reflux (non-return) valve: one-way flow, on pump delivery Air relief valve: at summits; scour/drain valve: at low points Pressure relief valve: protects against high pressure; butterfly valve: large pipes Fire hydrants: ~100–150 m spacing Residual pressure at ferrule: 7 m (1 storey), 12 m (2 storeys), 17 m (3 storeys) Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 5.1 — Distribution layouts: dead-end, grid-iron, ring and radial systems. Storage: Service reservoir capacity = balancing storage (from mass curve) + breakdown storage + fire storage. Overhead tanks: Elevated tanks (Intze tank for large capacity) provide pressure and balancing. Leak detection: Sounding rods, aqua-phones, district metered areas (DMA), pressure management. Hardy Cross: head-loss correction Δ = −Σ(kQⁿ)/(nΣkQⁿ⁻¹) applied loop by loop until losses balance.

Sewage: liquid waste including human excreta; sullage: kitchen & bath water without excreta Sewer: pipe carrying sewage; sewerage: entire system of collection, treatment, disposal Systems: separate (sanitary & storm separate), combined, partially separate

Dry weather flow (DWF) = 75–80% of water supplied Babbitt peak factor: M = 5 ÷ P^0.2 (P in thousands) Harmon peak factor: PF = 1 + 14 ÷ (4 + √P) (P in thousands) Storm water – Rational method: Q = C I A ÷ 360 (Q m³/s, I mm/h, A hectares) Time of concentration = inlet time + time of flow in drain Runoff coefficient C: roofs 0.7–0.95, paved roads 0.8–0.9, lawns/parks 0.05–0.35

Manning: V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2) — most used for sewers Self-cleansing velocity: 0.6–0.9 m/s (prevents deposition) Non-scouring (maximum) velocity: ~2.5–3 m/s (depends on pipe material) Shields/Camp: Vs = √[(8k/f)(G − 1) g d] Sanitary sewers designed running 1/2 to 3/4 full (never full) Minimum diameter: 150–225 mm Circular section most common; egg-shaped: combined sewers (better velocity at low flow)

Vitrified clay (stoneware): house sewers, smooth, corrosion resistant, weak in tension RCC/concrete: large sewers; suffer crown corrosion (H2S → H2SO4) Cast iron/ductile iron: under heavy loads, pressure mains, crossings PVC/HDPE, AC pipes: light, smooth

Manholes: at junctions, changes in direction/gradient/size; spacing ~30 m (small) up to 300 m (very large) Drop manhole: when incoming sewer is > 0.6 m above outgoing Lamp holes, clean-outs, street inlets/gully pits, catch basins, flushing tanks, grease & oil traps Inverted siphon (depressed sewer): crossing rivers/valleys; velocity ≥ ~1 m/s Testing of sewers: water test, smoke test, air test, ball test

Traps (water seal 25–75 mm): P, Q, S, nahani (floor), gully, intercepting trap Plumbing systems: one-pipe, two-pipe, single-stack, partially ventilated one-pipe Vent pipe: prevents loss of seal by siphonage/back pressure Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Minimum cover over sewers: ≈ 0.9–1.0 m under roads (protection from traffic loads and frost). Manhole spacing: ≈ 30 m for small sewers (≤ 0.9 m dia) up to ≈ 90–300 m for large sewers. Crown corrosion: H₂S → oxidised to H₂SO₄ on crown of concrete sewers; prevented by ventilation, adequate velocity, PVC/vitrified pipes, coatings. Storm sewers: Designed running full; flushing tanks and self-cleansing velocity prevent deposition in sanitary sewers. Self-cleansing velocity ≈ 0.6–0.9 m/s; maximum velocity ≈ 2.5–3 m/s. Sanitary sewers never designed to run full — ½ to ¾ full at peak.

Sewage ≈ 99.9% water, 0.1% solids Fresh sewage: grey, musty odour; stale/septic: dark/black, H2S smell Nitrogen forms: organic & ammonia (fresh) → nitrite (being oxidised) → nitrate (well oxidised, stable) Relative stability test: methylene blue

Oxygen required by microbes to stabilise biodegradable organic matter (aerobic) Standard: 5 days at 20 °C (BOD5) BODt = L0 (1 − 10^(−kt)), k ≈ 0.1/day (base 10) or 0.23/day (base e) at 20 °C BOD5 ≈ 68% of ultimate BOD (k = 0.1) Temperature correction: kT = k20 × θ^(T − 20), θ = 1.047 BOD = (DOinitial − DOfinal) ÷ P, P = dilution fraction Domestic sewage BOD5: ~200–300 mg/L Population equivalent = industrial BOD (kg/day) ÷ per capita BOD (~0.08 kg/person/day)

COD: chemical oxidation by potassium dichromate in acid; result in ~3 h; COD > BOD BOD/COD > 0.5 → readily biodegradable; ThOD > COD > BODu > BOD5 TOC: total organic carbon (instrumental) DO saturation ≈ 9.1 mg/L at 20 °C; fish need ≥ 4–5 mg/L

Disposal by dilution (rivers, sea) or on land (sewage farming/irrigation) Self-purification zones: degradation → active decomposition → recovery → clear water Streeter-Phelps equation: oxygen sag curve; critical point = minimum DO Factors: dilution, temperature, sunlight, current/turbulence, sedimentation, oxidation Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 7.1 — BOD curve: first-stage carbonaceous BOD and nitrification; BOD₅ ≈ 68% of ultimate (k = 0.1/day, base 10). Fig. 7.2 — Oxygen sag curve and zones of self-purification downstream of a sewage outfall. Worked BOD: Sample diluted 2% (P = 0.02); DO₀ = 8.5, DO₅ = 4.5 → BOD₅ = (8.5 − 4.5)/0.02 = 200 mg/L. Ultimate BOD from BOD₅: L₀ = BOD₅ / (1 − 10^(−5k)); for k = 0.1 → L₀ = BOD₅/0.684. Dilution method criteria: Dilution factor ratio — no treatment needed if river:sewage flow > 500; primary (plain sedimentation) if 300–500; sedimentation + chemical precipitation if 150–300; complete treatment if < 150 (classic Indian/US guidance). COD > BOD always (dichromate oxidises non-biodegradable organics). Fresh sewage is slightly alkaline, grey; septic sewage is black, smells of H₂S.

Screens (coarse/medium/fine), comminutors (shredders) Grit chamber: removes sand/grit (Gs ~2.65); horizontal velocity ~0.3 m/s kept constant by proportional flow weir or Parshall flume; detention 30–60 s Skimming tank: oil & grease; detention ~3–5 min
Primary sedimentation: detention 1.5–2.5 h Removes ~50–65% suspended solids and ~30–35% BOD

Activated Sludge Process (suspended growth): aeration tank + secondary clarifier + return activated sludge Conventional: MLSS 1500–3000 mg/L; F/M 0.2–0.4; HRT 4–8 h; SRT (mean cell residence time) 5–15 days BOD removal 85–95% SVI 50–150 mL/g = good settling; > 200 = sludge bulking (filamentous organisms) Variants: complete mix, step aeration, tapered aeration, contact stabilisation, extended aeration (HRT 18–36 h, low F/M), oxidation ditch, SBR, MBBR Trickling Filter (attached growth): biological oxidation, not true filtration Low-rate: 1–4 m³/m²/day; BOD removal 80–90% High-rate: 10–40 m³/m²/day with recirculation NRC formula: E = 100 ÷ [1 + 0.4432 √(W/VF)] Problems: ponding, filter flies (Psychoda), odour Rotating Biological Contactor (RBC): rotating discs with biofilm Waste Stabilisation Ponds: algae–bacteria symbiosis; anaerobic, facultative (1–2 m deep), maturation ponds; ideal for hot climates; low cost, large land Aerated lagoons; UASB (upflow anaerobic sludge blanket) reactors

Nitrogen removal: nitrification (aerobic) + denitrification (anoxic); ammonia stripping Phosphorus removal: chemical precipitation (alum, lime, ferric) or biological Filtration, activated carbon adsorption, membranes, final disinfection

Thickening (gravity, flotation) → digestion → conditioning → dewatering → disposal Anaerobic digestion stages: hydrolysis → acidogenesis → acetogenesis → methanogenesis Mesophilic 30–35 °C (20–30 days); thermophilic 50–55 °C Digester gas: ~65–70% CH4, ~30% CO2 Dewatering: sludge drying beds, vacuum filter, belt press, centrifuge Volume vs moisture: V1/V2 = (100 − p2) ÷ (100 − p1)

Septic tank: sedimentation + anaerobic digestion; detention ~24 h; desludging every 1–3 years; effluent to soak pit/drain field Imhoff tank: two-storey — sedimentation (upper), digestion (lower) Others: cesspool, pit latrine, soak pit Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 8.1 — Units of a sewage treatment plant and the sludge line. Fig. 8.2 — Activated sludge process: aeration tank, secondary clarifier, return and waste sludge. Fig. 8.3 — Two-compartment septic tank: scum, clear zone, sludge, baffle, T-pipe inlet and outlet. Sludge age (SRT): θc = mass of MLSS in system ÷ mass wasted per day; conventional ASP ≈ 5–15 days; extended aeration ≈ 20–30 days. Sludge volume index: SVI = (settled volume in 30 min, mL/L × 1000) ÷ MLSS (mg/L). Waste stabilisation ponds (Pakistan): Widely used for small and medium towns in Pakistan — cheap, low energy, but need large land area. Oxidation ditch: Extended-aeration ASP in a looped channel with rotors; small towns. Trickling filter = attached growth; ASP = suspended growth; RBC = attached growth on rotating discs; UASB = anaerobic sludge blanket.

Municipal (MSW), industrial, hazardous, biomedical, e-waste, construction & demolition Garbage: putrescible food waste; rubbish: non-putrescible (combustible paper/plastic, non-combustible glass/metal); ashes Developing countries generate ~0.3–0.6 kg/capita/day
Generation → on-site handling & storage → collection → transfer & transport → processing → disposal Collection is the costliest element (~70–80% of total cost)

Sanitary landfill: most common; waste spread, compacted, daily cover ~15 cm soil; liner + leachate collection + gas (CH4) venting Composting: aerobic (Indore, windrow, Bangalore is anaerobic); optimum C/N ratio 25–30; vermicomposting uses earthworms Incineration: 800–1000 °C; volume reduction 80–90%; energy recovery; air pollution concern Pyrolysis: thermal decomposition in absence of oxygen Open dumping: unsanitary, not acceptable Waste hierarchy: reduce → reuse → recycle → recover → dispose Biomedical waste: colour-coded segregation; incineration, autoclaving Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 9.1 — Sanitary landfill: liner, leachate collection, compacted waste cells, daily cover, final cap, gas vents. Composition (South Asia): High organic/food fraction (≈ 50–60%), moisture high, calorific value low — composting more suitable than incineration. C/N ratio for composting: Optimum ≈ 25–30 : 1; moisture ≈ 50–60%; temperature reaches 55–65 °C (kills pathogens). Leachate: Liquid percolating through waste — very high BOD/COD; collected & treated. Pakistan: Waste management companies (e.g., Lahore Waste Management Company, WSSP Peshawar, SWMB Karachi) handle collection; Lakhodair landfill (Lahore) is a well-known engineered site. Collection & transportation ≈ 70–80% of SWM cost; sanitary landfill is the final, unavoidable disposal step.
Composition: N2 78%, O2 21%, Ar 0.93%, CO2 ~0.04% Layers: troposphere (0–~12 km, weather) → stratosphere (ozone layer) → mesosphere → thermosphere

Primary: emitted directly — CO, SO2, NOx, hydrocarbons, particulates Secondary: formed in atmosphere — O3, PAN, smog, H2SO4/HNO3 aerosols Criteria pollutants (US EPA, 6): CO, Pb, NO2, O3, PM (PM10, PM2.5), SO2

CO: forms carboxyhaemoglobin; affinity for Hb ~210–250 times that of O2 SO2: respiratory irritation, acid rain; NOx: photochemical smog, acid rain PAN: eye irritation, plant damage; lead: neurological damage PM2.5: penetrates deep into lungs; most harmful particulate fraction

London (classical) smog: smoke + SO2, cold humid winter, reducing Photochemical (Los Angeles) smog: NOx + HC + sunlight → O3, PAN; oxidising Acid rain: pH < 5.6 (normal rain ~5.6 due to CO2) Greenhouse gases: CO2, CH4, N2O, CFCs, water vapour, O3 Ozone depletion: CFCs (chlorine radicals); ozone measured in Dobson units

Dry adiabatic lapse rate: 9.8 °C/km (~1 °C per 100 m) Super-adiabatic: unstable; sub-adiabatic: stable; inversion (temperature increases with height): very stable, traps pollutants Plume Type Atmospheric Condition Looping Super-adiabatic (strongly unstable) Coning Neutral / slightly stable Fanning Inversion (stable) at stack level Lofting Inversion below, unstable above stack — best for dispersion Fumigation Inversion above, unstable below stack — worst (pollutants brought to ground) Trapping Inversion both above and below stack Effective stack height H = h + Δh (plume rise); dispersion by Gaussian plume model

Device Use / Particle Size Remarks Gravity settling chamber > 50 µm Cheap, low efficiency, pre-cleaner Cyclone separator > 5–10 µm Centrifugal force; moderate efficiency Fabric filter (baghouse) < 1 µm possible ~99% efficiency; not for hot/humid gas Electrostatic precipitator (ESP) Fine particles > 99% efficiency; thermal power, cement plants Wet scrubber (venturi) Particles + gases Removes SO2 also; creates wastewater Gaseous control: absorption, adsorption (activated carbon), combustion/incineration SO2: flue gas desulphurisation (limestone scrubbing); vehicles: catalytic converter (CO, HC, NOx) Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Smog episodes in Pakistan: Winter smog in Lahore and other Punjab cities (Nov–Jan) from vehicle exhaust, industry, brick kilns and crop-residue burning combined with inversions. Particle collectors: Settling chamber (> 50 µm), cyclone (5–20 µm+), fabric (bag) filter (> 0.1 µm, ≈ 99%), electrostatic precipitator (0.1–1 µm, ≈ 99%), wet scrubber (gases + particles). Vehicles: Catalytic converter: CO → CO₂, HC → CO₂ + H₂O, NOx → N₂ (three-way). AQI: Air Quality Index combines PM2.5, PM10, O₃, NO₂, SO₂, CO concentrations into one number. Fanning plume — strong inversion (stable); looping — super-adiabatic (unstable); coning — neutral/slightly stable; lofting — inversion below stack (best); fumigation — inversion above stack (worst).

Sound level: L = 10 log(I/I0) = 20 log(P/P0); reference pressure P0 = 20 µPa Audible range: 20 Hz – 20 kHz; threshold of hearing 0 dB; threshold of pain ~120–140 dB Two equal sources combined: +3 dB; doubling distance (point source): −6 dB Measured with sound level meter in dB(A); Leq = equivalent continuous level WHO residential guideline: ~55 dB(A) day, ~45 dB(A) night Control: at source (silencers, maintenance), along path (barriers, green belts), at receiver (ear plugs/muffs) Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Adding sound levels: L = 10 log Σ10^(Li/10). Example: 80 dB + 80 dB = 83 dB; 80 + 70 dB ≈ 80.4 dB. Exposure limits: ≈ 85–90 dB(A) for 8 h occupational exposure; every +3 to +5 dB halves the allowed time. Doubling distance from a point source → −6 dB; from a line source (road) → −3 dB.

Plumbing, Rural Sanitation & Water in Buildings

Traps & seal: P, Q, S, gully, nahani (floor), intercepting traps; water seal 25–75 mm (≈ 50 mm common). Loss of trap seal: Self-siphonage, induced siphonage, back pressure, evaporation, capillarity, wind effect — prevented by anti-siphonage/vent pipes. Rural sanitation: Pit latrine, VIP (ventilated improved pit) latrine, pour-flush latrine, twin-pit latrine, septic tank with soak pit. Soak pit: Effluent percolation pit filled with brickbats/stone; ≥ 15–20 m away from wells. Rain-water harvesting: Roof-top collection → first-flush diverter → filter → storage/recharge wells; mandatory for large buildings in some Pakistani cities. Distance between a water well and a soak pit / septic tank should be ≥ 15 m (more in sandy soils).

Fluid: substance that deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small. Mass density (ρ): mass/volume. Water = 1000 kg/m³ at 4°C; air ≈ 1.225 kg/m³. Specific weight (γ): γ = ρg. Water = 9.81 kN/m³. Specific gravity (S): ρ_liquid/ρ_water. Mercury = 13.6. Specific volume: 1/ρ (volume per unit mass). Newton's law of viscosity: τ = μ (du/dy). Dynamic viscosity (μ): unit N·s/m² = Pa·s; CGS unit poise (1 poise = 0.1 Pa·s). Water at 20°C ≈ 1 centipoise. Kinematic viscosity (ν): ν = μ/ρ; unit m²/s; CGS unit stoke (1 stoke = 10⁻⁴ m²/s). Temperature effect: viscosity of liquids decreases with temperature (cohesion falls); of gases increases (molecular momentum exchange rises). Newtonian fluid: τ ∝ du/dy (water, air, oil). Non-Newtonian: dilatant (n > 1, e.g. quicksand), pseudoplastic (n < 1, e.g. blood, paint), Bingham plastic (yield stress, e.g. toothpaste, sewage sludge), thixotropic (printer ink). Ideal fluid: incompressible and inviscid (μ = 0). Real fluid: has viscosity. Bulk modulus K = −dp/(dV/V). Water ≈ 2.1 × 10⁹ N/m². Compressibility = 1/K. Isothermal: K = p. Adiabatic: K = kp (k = 1.4 for air). Surface tension (σ): force per unit length (N/m). Water–air at 20°C ≈ 0.073 N/m. Decreases with temperature. Pressure inside droplet: Δp = 4σ/d. Soap bubble (two surfaces): Δp = 8σ/d. Liquid jet: Δp = 2σ/d. Capillary rise: h = 4σ cosθ/(γd). Water–glass θ ≈ 0° (rise); mercury–glass θ ≈ 130–140° (depression). Cohesion > adhesion → depression (mercury). Adhesion > cohesion → ri

Mass density ρ = m/V; water = 1000 kg/m³ (at 4 °C). Specific weight γ = ρg = 9.81 kN/m³ for water. Specific gravity S = ρ/ρ(water at 4 °C). Mercury S = 13.6. Viscosity of liquids decreases with temperature (cohesion falls); of gases increases (molecular momentum exchange rises). Newtonian fluids: τ ∝ du/dy (water, air). Non-Newtonian: dilatant (shear thickening), pseudoplastic (shear thinning), Bingham plastic (yield stress, e.g. toothpaste, sewage sludge). Ideal fluid: incompressible and zero viscosity. Surface tension σ: unit N/m; water–air ≈ 0.073 N/m at 20 °C. Decreases with temperature. Vapour pressure: pressure at which liquid boils; rises with temperature. Cavitation occurs when local pressure drops below vapour pressure. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Pascal's law: pressure at a point in a static fluid is equal in all directions. Hydrostatic law: dp/dz = −ρg; p = γh. Absolute = gauge + atmospheric. Vacuum pressure = atmospheric − absolute. Standard atmosphere = 101.325 kPa = 760 mm Hg = 10.33 m of water. Pressure head: h = p/γ. Barometer: measures atmospheric pressure. Piezometer: simple gauge pressure; not for gases or high/negative pressure. Simple U-tube manometer: gauge and vacuum pressure. Differential manometer: pressure difference between two points. Inverted U-tube: small differences with lighter fluid. Micromanometer: very small pressure differences. Inclined manometer: improves sensitivity. Bourdon gauge: mechanical; measures gauge pressure (high pressures). Differential manometer reading (venturi, same liquid): h = x (S_m/S − 1). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Manometer rules: Move from one end to the other: add γh going down, subtract going up; in a U-tube differential manometer for same liquid in pipes: h = x(Sm/S − 1). Inverted U-tube: Used for small pressure differences between two points of a liquid (lighter manometric fluid on top). Pressure in units: 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa ≈ 10.2 m of water; 1 kg/cm² ≈ 98.1 kPa ≈ 10 m water. Mercury: S = 13.6; 1 atm = 760 mm Hg = 10.33 m of water. Bourdon gauge reads gauge pressure.
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Fluid Pressure and Measurement

Hydrostatic law: dp/dz = −ρg → p = ρgh. Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure. Vacuum = negative gauge pressure. Pressure head h = p/(ρg). Piezometer: measures gauge pressure of liquids only; not for gases or negative pressure. Simple U-tube manometer: measures positive and negative pressures. Differential manometer: pressure difference between two points. Inverted U-tube for small differences. Micromanometer / inclined manometer: very small pressure differences (higher sensitivity). Mechanical gauges: Bourdon tube (most common), diaphragm, dead-weight gauge (used for calibration). Barometer measures atmospheric pressure (mercury or aneroid).

Total pressure on plane surface: F = γ A h̄ (h̄ = depth of centroid). Centre of pressure (vertical/inclined): h* = h̄ + I_G sin²θ/(A h̄). For vertical plane: h* = h̄ + I_G/(A h̄). Centre of pressure always lies below centroid (except horizontal surface, where they coincide). Vertical rectangle with top at free surface: h* = 2H/3 from surface. Vertical triangle, apex at surface, base down: h* = 3H/4. Base at surface: h* = H/2. Curved surface: horizontal component = force on vertical projection; vertical component = weight of liquid above (real or imaginary). Lock gates: P = force on gate; reaction between gates R = P/(2 sin α). Dam: resultant must lie in middle third to avoid tension. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. — Hydrostatic force on a vertical plane: pressure diagram, centroid G and centre of pressure P.

Given: Vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide × 3 m high, top edge 1 m below water surface. Force: x̄ = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 m; F = 9.81 × (2 × 3) × 2.5 = 147 kN. Centre of pressure: I_G = 2 × 3³/12 = 4.5 m⁴; h* = 2.5 + 4.5/(6 × 2.5) = 2.8 m below the surface. As depth of immersion increases, the centre of pressure moves closer to the centroid.
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Hydrostatic Forces on Surfaces
I_G: rectangle bd³/12; circle πd⁴/64; triangle bh³/36. Applications: dams, lock gates, sluice gates, tank walls.

Archimedes' principle: buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced; acts at centre of buoyancy (centroid of displaced volume). Metacentric height: GM = BM − BG, where BM = I/V (I = moment of inertia of waterline area about longitudinal axis). Floating body: stable if M above G (GM > 0); neutral if GM = 0; unstable if M below G. Time period of rolling: T = 2π √(k²/(g·GM)). Larger GM → more stable but uncomfortable (shorter period). Typical GM: passenger ships 0.3–1.2 m (small for comfort); warships/cargo higher. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. — Stability of floating bodies: M above G (stable) and M below G (unstable). Experimental GM: GM = w x / (W tan θ) — shift weight w by distance x, measure heel angle θ. Large GM: Very stable but uncomfortable (quick rolling); small GM → slow rolling, comfortable — passenger ships keep small GM. Floating body: stable if M above G. Fully submerged body (submarine, balloon): stable if B above G.
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Buoyancy and Floatation

Centre of buoyancy (B): centroid of displaced volume. Metacentre (M): point where line of buoyant force of slightly tilted body cuts the original vertical axis. Metacentric height GM = BM − BG, where BM = I/V (I = moment of inertia of waterplane area about tilting axis, V = displaced volume). Submerged body stability: stable if B above G; neutral if coincide; unstable if B below G. Time period of rolling T = 2π √(k² / (g·GM)). Larger GM → quicker, uncomfortable roll; passenger ships have small GM, warships larger GM.

Horizontal linear acceleration a: free surface slope tanθ = a/g. Vertical acceleration a (upward): p = ρ h (g + a); downward: p = ρ h (g − a); free fall → p = 0. Forced vortex (rotating container): paraboloid free surface, z = ω²r²/(2g). Velocity v = ωr. Rise at wall = fall at centre (for cylinder initially at rest), each = ω²R²/(4g). Free vortex: vr = constant; no external torque (e.g. whirlpool, flow in sink drain).

Steady flow: properties at a point do not change with time (∂/∂t = 0). Uniform flow: no change with distance (∂/∂s = 0). Laminar vs turbulent; rotational vs irrotational; compressible vs incompressible; 1-D, 2-D, 3-D flow. Streamline: tangent gives velocity direction; no flow across it. Pathline: path of one particle. Streakline: locus of particles passing through a point (dye). Steady flow: streamline, pathline and streakline coincide. Continuity (1-D, incompressible): Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂. General: ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂. 3-D continuity (incompressible): ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y + ∂w/∂z = 0. Acceleration = local (∂V/∂t) + convective (V·∂V/∂s). Convective exists in steady non-uniform flow. Rotation ωz = ½(∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y). Vorticity = 2ω. Irrotational if ω = 0. Velocity potential (φ): u = −∂φ/∂x, v = −∂φ/∂y; exists only for irrotational flow; satisfies Laplace equation. Stream function (ψ): u = −∂ψ/∂y, v = ∂ψ/∂x (sign convention varies); exists for 2-D continuous flow; difference of ψ = discharge per unit width. Equipotential lines and streamlines intersect orthogonally → flow net. Flow net not valid for: rotational flow, near solid boundaries (viscous effects), separation zones. Free vortex: V·r = constant, irrotational (whirlpool, flow into drain). Forced vortex: V = ωr, rotational (rotating cylinder, impeller). Forced vortex: free surface is paraboloid; rise above centre z = ω²r²/(2g). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Checks: Flow possible if continuit
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Fluid Kinematics

Steady flow: properties at a point do not change with time (∂/∂t = 0). Unsteady: they do. Uniform flow: velocity does not change with distance along flow (∂V/∂s = 0). Non-uniform: it does. Laminar: fluid moves in layers. Turbulent: random mixing. Rotational vs irrotational: irrotational if rotation (ω) = 0 everywhere. Pathline: path traced by a particle over time. Streakline: locus of particles passing through a fixed point (dye/smoke). In steady flow streamlines, pathlines and streaklines coincide. Continuity (incompressible): A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ = Q. 3D: ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y + ∂w/∂z = 0. Stream function ψ: u = −∂ψ/∂y, v = ∂ψ/∂x (sign conventions vary); exists for 2D continuous flow (rotational or not). Acceleration = convective (spatial change) + local (time change). Circulation Γ = ∮ V·ds; vorticity = 2 × rotation.

Euler's equation (along streamline): dp/ρ + V dV + g dz = 0. Bernoulli's equation: p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant. Bernoulli assumptions: steady, incompressible, inviscid (no friction), irrotational, along streamline, no shaft work/heat. Terms: pressure head, velocity (kinetic) head, datum (potential) head. Sum = total head. Hydraulic gradient line (HGL) = p/γ + z. Energy gradient line (EGL) = HGL + V²/2g; EGL always above HGL by V²/2g. Kinetic energy correction factor α: laminar pipe = 2.0; turbulent ≈ 1.03–1.1. Momentum correction factor β: laminar pipe = 4/3; turbulent ≈ 1.01–1.05. Impulse–momentum: F = ρQ(V₂ − V₁). Force of jet on stationary flat plate (normal): F = ρaV². On moving plate: ρa(V − u)². Series of moving flat plates (wheel): F = ρaV(V − u); max efficiency 50% at u = V/2. Curved vane, jet deflected 180°: theoretical efficiency 100% at u = V/2. Moment of momentum: torque = ρQ(V₂r₂ − V₁r₁) → basis of turbines, sprinklers. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Applications of Bernoulli: Venturimeter, orifice meter, pitot tube, flow from orifices, siphons, lift on aerofoils. Jet on hinged/inclined plate: Force normal to inclined plate F = ρaV² sin θ. Moving curved vane: Work done/s = ρaV(V − u)(1 + cos φ)u for symmetric vane — basis of Pelton wheel. HGL lies below EGL by V²/2g; HGL can go below pipe centreline (negative pressure — siphon); EGL always slopes down in direction of flow.
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Fluid Dynamics

Euler equation (along streamline): dp/ρ + g dz + V dV = 0. Assumes ideal, steady flow. Bernoulli's equation: p/ρg + V²/2g + z = constant (pressure head + velocity head + datum head). Assumptions: steady, ideal (inviscid), incompressible, along a streamline, irrotational (for across streamlines). Real fluid: p₁/ρg + V₁²/2g + z₁ = p₂/ρg + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_L. Kinetic energy correction factor α: laminar pipe flow = 2; turbulent ≈ 1.03–1.1. Momentum correction factor β: laminar pipe flow = 4/3; turbulent ≈ 1.01–1.04. Impulse–momentum equation: ΣF = ρQ(V₂ − V₁). Used for pipe bends, nozzles, jets. Moment of momentum equation: basis of turbines, sprinklers, centrifugal pumps. Jet on series of moving flat vanes: max efficiency 50% at u = V/2. Curved vanes (Pelton) max theoretical efficiency 100% at u = V/2 with 180° deflection.

Venturimeter: Q = Cd·a₁a₂√(2gh)/√(a₁² − a₂²). Cd ≈ 0.95–0.99. Convergent cone ~ 20–22°, divergent 5–7° (avoids separation). Orificemeter: cheaper, more head loss; Cd ≈ 0.6–0.65. Flow nozzle: Cd between venturi and orifice meter. Pitot tube: measures point velocity, V = Cv√(2gh). Pitot-static tube measures stagnation − static. Rotameter: variable-area meter. Current meter: velocity in open channels/rivers. Orifice coefficients: Cd = Cc × Cv. Typical Cc ≈ 0.64, Cv ≈ 0.97–0.98, Cd ≈ 0.62. Vena contracta: section of minimum jet area, about d/2 from orifice. Small orifice: Q = Cd·a√(2gH). Large rectangular orifice: Q = ⅔ Cd b√(2g)(H₂^1.5 − H₁^1.5). Time to empty tank (orifice at bottom): T = 2A(√H₁ − √H₂)/(Cd·a√(2g)). Hemispherical tank emptying and other shapes — derive from A·dh = −Cd·a√(2gh)dt. External cylindrical mouthpiece: Cd = 0.855. Convergent–divergent: Cd = 1.0. Borda's (re-entrant) running free: Cd = 0.5; running full: 0.707. Mouthpiece length should be 2–3 × diameter. Rectangular notch/weir: Q = ⅔ Cd L√(2g) H^1.5. Triangular (V) notch: Q = (8/15) Cd tan(θ/2)√(2g) H^2.5. 90° V-notch: Q ≈ 1.417 H^2.5 (Cd = 0.6). Best for low discharges; error in H affects Q more (2.5 × %). Error in Q from error in H: rectangular dQ/Q = 1.5 dH/H; triangular = 2.5 dH/H. Trapezoidal (Cipolletti) weir: side slopes 1H:4V; compensates end contractions. Francis formula: Q = 1.84 (L − 0.1nH) H^1.5 (n = number of end contractions). Broad-crested weir: Q_max = 1.705 Cd L H^1.5 (critical depth = ⅔
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Flow Measurement

Venturimeter: Q = C_d A₁A₂ √(2gh) / √(A₁² − A₂²). C_d ≈ 0.95–0.98. Convergent cone ≈ 20–22°, divergent 5–7° (long, to avoid separation). Throat diameter ≈ 1/3 to 3/4 of pipe diameter. Orifice meter: cheaper, compact, higher head loss; C_d ≈ 0.6–0.65. Pitot-static (Prandtl) tube: stagnation minus static pressure → velocity. Rotameter: variable-area meter; float position indicates flow rate. Current meter: velocity in rivers/open channels. Hot-wire anemometer: velocity fluctuations in turbulent flow (gases). Head loss order (highest → lowest): orifice meter > flow nozzle > venturimeter. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Torricelli: theoretical velocity V = √(2gH). C_c = jet area at vena contracta / orifice area ≈ 0.61–0.69. C_v = actual velocity / theoretical ≈ 0.95–0.99. C_d = C_c × C_v ≈ 0.61–0.65 (sharp-edged orifice). C_v from jet trajectory: C_v = x / √(4yH). Large rectangular orifice: Q = (2/3) C_d b √(2g) (H₂^1.5 − H₁^1.5). External cylindrical mouthpiece: C_d ≈ 0.855; requires length ≈ 3d; vacuum at vena contracta ≈ 0.89H. Convergent–divergent mouthpiece: highest C_d (≈ 1.0 based on throat). Borda (internal/re-entrant) mouthpiece: running free C_d = 0.5; running full C_d ≈ 0.707. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Notches and Weirs

Notch: small opening in tank side; weir: larger structure across river/channel. Rectangular: Q = (2/3) C_d L √(2g) H^1.5. Triangular (V-notch): Q = (8/15) C_d tan(θ/2) √(2g) H^2.5. For 90°: Q ≈ 1.417 H^2.5 (C_d = 0.6). Most accurate for low flows. Trapezoidal: rectangular + triangular parts. Cipolletti weir: trapezoidal with side slopes 1H:4V (14°); slope compensates end contractions. Q = 1.86 L H^1.5. Francis' formula (end contractions): L_eff = L − 0.1nH (n = number of end contractions). Broad-crested weir: Q_max = 1.705 C_d L H^1.5 (critical depth = 2H/3 on crest). Ogee weir: crest shaped to lower nappe profile; used as dam spillway. Submerged weir: downstream water above crest; treat as free part + drowned part. Velocity of approach increases discharge; include head ha = Va²/2g. Error in discharge due to error in head: rectangular dQ/Q = 1.5 dH/H; triangular dQ/Q = 2.5 dH/H. Ventilation of weir required to keep nappe free (prevent pressure drop under nappe).

Fundamental dimensions: M, L, T. Force = MLT⁻². Viscosity μ = ML⁻¹T⁻¹. ν = L²T⁻¹. Surface tension = MT⁻². Power = ML²T⁻³. Rayleigh's method: suitable for up to 3–4 variables. Buckingham π theorem: n variables, m fundamental dimensions → (n − m) π terms. Repeating variables must not form a π term themselves and should include geometry, flow and fluid property. Reynolds number Re = ρVL/μ = inertia/viscous. Model law for pipe flow, submarines, aircraft (subsonic), flow around fully submerged bodies. Froude number Fr = V/√(gL) = inertia/gravity. Model law for open channels, spillways, weirs, ships, waves, hydraulic jump. Weber number We = V/√(σ/ρL) = inertia/surface tension. Capillary flows, droplets, very shallow flows. Mach number M = V/C = inertia/elastic. Compressible flows, aircraft at high speed. M < 1 subsonic, = 1 sonic, > 1 supersonic, > 5 hypersonic. Euler number Eu = V/√(p/ρ) = inertia/pressure. Cavitation, pressure-dominated flow. Froude model scale ratios (Lr): Vr = Lr^½, Tr = Lr^½, Qr = Lr^2.5, Fr (force) = Lr³, Pr (power) = Lr^3.5. Reynolds model (same fluid): Vr = 1/Lr. Similitude: geometric (shape), kinematic (velocity/flow pattern), dynamic (force ratios). Distorted models: different horizontal and vertical scales; used for rivers and harbours. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Model / phenomenon Governing law Pipe flow, submarines, aircraft at low speed, flow meters Reynolds Spillways, open channels, ships (wave resistance), weirs, river models Froude Capillary flow, small weirs/jets, droplets Weber High-speed aircraft, projectiles, water hammer Mach Cavitation, pressure-driven flows Euler Froude model example: Spillway model 1:25; prototype Q = Qm × Lr^2.5 = Qm × 3125. Froude scale ratios: Vr = Lr^½, Qr = Lr^(5/2), Tr = Lr^½, Fr(force) = Lr³, Pr(power) = Lr^(7/2).

Fundamental dimensions: M, L, T (and θ for temperature). Rayleigh's method: suits ≤ 4 variables. Buckingham π theorem: n variables, m fundamental dimensions → (n − m) π terms. Repeating variables: should not form a π term by themselves; usually one geometric, one flow, one fluid property (e.g. D, V, ρ). Reynolds number (inertia/viscous): pipe flow, submarines, aircraft at low speed, flow meters. Euler number (pressure/inertia): flow with pressure dominance, cavitation studies. Froude model laws (scale ratio Lr): Vr = Lr^0.5, Qr = Lr^2.5, Tr = Lr^0.5, Fr(force) = Lr³, Pr(power) = Lr^3.5. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Pipe flow: laminar Re < 2000; transition 2000–4000; turbulent > 4000. Open channel (Re based on R): laminar < 500, turbulent > 2000 (approx.). Hagen–Poiseuille: velocity profile parabolic; Vmax = 2 Vavg. Head loss: hf = 32μVL/(γD²). Loss ∝ V (laminar). Friction factor (Darcy): f = 64/Re. (Fanning f′ = 16/Re = f/4.) Shear stress varies linearly: zero at centre, maximum at wall. Between fixed parallel plates: Vmax = 1.5 Vavg; hf = 12μVL/(γB²). Couette flow: one plate moving, linear velocity profile (no pressure gradient). Stokes' law (sphere, Re < 1): Drag F = 3πμDV; Cd = 24/Re. Terminal velocity V = D²(γs − γ)/(18μ) → falling-sphere viscometer, settling of particles. Dashpot, capillary tube viscometer (Poiseuille), rotating cylinder viscometer. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. — Velocity distribution in pipes: laminar (parabolic) and turbulent (flatter). Hagen–Poiseuille: Q = πD⁴Δp/(128μL); head loss ∝ V (laminar) but ∝ V² (turbulent). Power to overcome viscous resistance: In a journal bearing P ∝ μ N² D³ L / t. Laminar: f = 64/Re, Vmax = 2 Vavg, α = 2, β = 4/3. Between parallel plates: Vmax = 1.5 Vavg.
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Laminar Flow

Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν (ratio of inertia to viscous forces). Open channel (Re based on hydraulic radius R): laminar < 500, turbulent > 2000 (approx.). Hagen–Poiseuille (circular pipe): h_f = 32 μ V L / (ρ g D²). Velocity profile parabolic; V_max = 2 × V_avg. Viscometers: capillary tube, falling sphere, rotating cylinder, orifice type (Saybolt, Redwood).
Turbulent Flow and Flow Through Pipes

Darcy–Weisbach: hf = fLV²/(2gD) = fLQ²/(12.1 D⁵). Loss ∝ V² (fully turbulent); ∝ Q²/D⁵. Chezy: V = C√(RS). Relation C = √(8g/f). Manning: V = (1/n) R^⅔ S^½. Hazen–Williams: V = 0.849 C R^0.63 S^0.54 (SI). Hydraulic mean depth R = A/P. Pipe flowing full: R = D/4. Blasius (smooth pipes, Re < 10⁵): f = 0.316/Re^0.25. Hydraulically smooth: roughness k < laminar sublayer δ′; rough: k > 6δ′ (f independent of Re). Laminar sublayer thickness δ′ = 11.6ν/V*. Shear velocity V* = √(τ₀/ρ). Turbulent velocity profile: logarithmic (Prandtl). Vmax ≈ 1.2–1.25 Vavg; shear stress = laminar + turbulent (Reynolds stress). Prandtl mixing length theory; eddy viscosity. Moody diagram: f vs Re and relative roughness k/D; Colebrook–White equation. Minor losses: sudden enlargement hL = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g (Borda–Carnot). Sudden contraction: hL = (1/Cc − 1)² V₂²/2g with Cc = 0.62 this gives ≈ 0.375 V₂²/2g; taken as 0.5 V₂²/2g when Cc is not given. Entrance loss = 0.5 V²/2g; exit loss = V²/2g; bend/fitting loss = kV²/2g. Pipes in series: Q same; losses add. Equivalent pipe (Dupuit): L/D⁵ = ΣLi/Di⁵. Pipes in parallel: head loss same; discharges add. Power transmission through pipe: P = γQ(H − hf). Maximum when hf = H/3 → max efficiency 66.7%. Nozzle at end of pipe: max power when head loss in pipe = H/3; optimum nozzle diameter d = (D⁵/(2fL))^¼ with Darcy f [= (D⁵/(8fL))^¼ if hf = 4fLV²/2gD is used]. Siphon: summit should not be more than about 7.6 m above the supply water level, to avoid vapour/air separation.

Given: D = 0.3 m, L = 500 m, Q = 0.1 m³/s, f = 0.02. Velocity: V = Q/A = 0.1/0.0707 = 1.41 m/s. Loss: hf = 0.02 × 500 × 1.41²/(2 × 9.81 × 0.3) ≈ 3.4 m. Shear velocity: V* = √(τ₀/ρ) = V√(f/8). Smooth pipe: f depends on Re only; fully rough: f depends on k/D only; transition zone: on both (Colebrook). Siphon limit: Summit not more than ≈ 7.5–8 m above the HGL/inlet level (vapour pressure, dissolved air). Three-reservoir problem: Solve by assuming the junction head; continuity at junction must balance. Series: Q same, hf adds. Parallel: hf same, Q adds. Dupuit equivalent pipe: L/D⁵ = ΣLi/Di⁵. Wave speed in elastic pipe: c = √[(K/ρ)/(1 + KD/(Et))] — thinner/elastic pipe walls reduce c and hence surge pressure. Surge tank types: Simple, restricted-orifice, differential (Johnson), closed (air) surge tanks. Rapid closure (t < 2L/c): pressure rise = ρcV (Joukowski) — independent of pipe length.
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Turbulent Flow and Boundary Layer

Turbulent shear: Boussinesq eddy viscosity; Prandtl mixing length theory τ = ρ l² (du/dy)². Velocity profile is flatter (logarithmic); V_max ≈ 1.2 V_avg in pipes. Colebrook–White equation and Moody diagram give f for commercial pipes. In fully rough zone f depends only on relative roughness k/D, not Re. Boundary layer: thin region near wall where velocity rises from 0 to 99% of free stream. Laminar BL thickness (Blasius): δ = 5x / √Re_x. Turbulent: δ = 0.37x / Re_x^0.2. Transition on flat plate at Re_x ≈ 5 × 10⁵. Displacement thickness δ* > momentum thickness θ > energy thickness. Shape factor H = δ*/θ (laminar flat plate ≈ 2.59). Separation occurs under adverse pressure gradient (dp/dx > 0) where (du/dy) at wall = 0. Separation control: streamlining, suction, blowing, rotating cylinder, slots. Drag = pressure (form) drag + friction (skin) drag. Lift via circulation (Kutta–Joukowski: L = ρVΓ per unit length). Magnus effect: rotating body in a stream. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Thickness relations (laminar, Blasius): δ = 5x/√Rex; δ* ≈ δ/3; θ ≈ δ/7.5; shape factor H = δ*/θ ≈ 2.6 (laminar), ≈ 1.3–1.4 (turbulent). Turbulent BL: δ = 0.37x/Rex^(1/5); grows faster than laminar BL. Separation occurs where ∂u/∂y = 0 at the wall (wall shear zero) under adverse pressure gradient.
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Flow Through Pipes

Darcy–Weisbach: h_f = f L V² / (2gD) (f = Darcy friction factor = 4 × Fanning f'). Chezy: V = C √(R S); Hazen–Williams: V = 0.849 C R^0.63 S^0.54 (water supply design). Minor losses: sudden expansion h = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g (Borda–Carnot). Sudden contraction h = (1/C_c − 1)² V₂²/2g ≈ 0.5V²/2g at entry. Fittings/bends: h = k V²/2g. Equivalent length method: minor loss expressed as extra pipe length. Equivalent pipe (Dupuit): L/D⁵ = L₁/D₁⁵ + L₂/D₂⁵ + … Siphon: pipe rising above hydraulic gradient; summit pressure must stay above vapour pressure (practical limit ≈ 7.6 m of water below atmosphere). Nozzle at pipe end for maximum power: d = (D⁵ / (2fL))^0.25 with Darcy f [= (D⁵/(8fL))^0.25 if h_f = 4fLV²/2gD is used]. Pipe networks: Hardy Cross method (loop corrections ΔQ = −Σh / (n Σ h/Q)). Branching pipes: three-reservoir problem — continuity at junction plus energy along each pipe.

Water hammer: pressure surge from sudden valve closure in pipe. Wave velocity c = √(K/ρ) (rigid pipe); elastic pipe: c = √(K/ρ) / √(1 + KD/(Et)). Critical time = 2L/c. Closure faster than this is "rapid". Rapid closure (rigid pipe): pressure rise p = ρ c V (Joukowsky). Gradual closure (t > 2L/c): p = ρ L V / t. Protection: surge tank, slow-closing valves, relief valves, air chambers. Surge tank located between reservoir and turbine/valve on penstock; types: simple, restricted orifice, differential.

Boundary layer: thin region near wall where velocity rises from 0 to 99% of free stream (Prandtl, 1904). Displacement thickness δ*, momentum thickness θ, energy thickness δ**. Shape factor H = δ*/θ (laminar flat plate ≈ 2.6, turbulent ≈ 1.3–1.4). Laminar boundary layer over flat plate (Blasius): δ = 5x/√Re_x. Turbulent: δ = 0.37x/Re_x^0.2. Separation control: streamlining, suction, blowing, rotating cylinder, slotted wing, vortex generators. Drag = pressure (form) drag + friction (skin) drag. Streamlined bodies: mainly friction drag; bluff bodies: mainly pressure drag. F_D = ½ Cd ρ A V²; F_L = ½ CL ρ A V². Golf ball dimples: trigger turbulent boundary layer → delayed separation → lower pressure drag. Magnus effect: lift on rotating cylinder/sphere in flow (spin of balls). Kutta–Joukowski: lift per unit span L = ρVΓ (Γ = circulation). Drag crisis: sudden drop in Cd of sphere/cylinder at Re ≈ 2–5 × 10⁵. Aerofoil stall: at high angle of attack flow separates → lift drops.

Free surface at atmospheric pressure; driving force is gravity. Classification: steady/unsteady; uniform/non-uniform (GVF, RVF); subcritical/critical/supercritical. Froude number Fr = V/√(gD) (D = hydraulic depth A/T). Fr < 1 subcritical (tranquil), = 1 critical, > 1 supercritical (rapid/shooting). Specific energy E = y + V²/2g. Minimum specific energy at critical depth. Rectangular channel: yc = (q²/g)^⅓; Emin = 1.5 yc; Vc = √(g yc). Triangular: Emin = 1.25 yc. Parabolic: Emin = 4/3 yc. Alternate depths: same E, different depths (sub and supercritical). Sequent (conjugate) depths: same specific force (before and after jump). Most economical section (max Q for given A): Rectangular: b = 2y; R = y/2. Trapezoidal: half regular hexagon; R = y/2; sloping side = half top width; side slope 60° to horizontal. Triangular: vertex 90° (side slopes 1:1); R = y/(2√2). Circular (max velocity): y = 0.81D; (max discharge): y ≈ 0.938D (Manning; ≈ 0.95D with Chezy). Hydraulic jump: supercritical to subcritical. Rectangular: y₂/y₁ = ½(−1 + √(1 + 8Fr₁²)). Energy loss in jump: ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4y₁y₂). Jump types (Fr₁): undular 1–1.7; weak 1.7–2.5; oscillating 2.5–4.5; steady 4.5–9 (best for energy dissipation); strong > 9. Length of jump ≈ 5–7 (y₂ − y₁); commonly 6(y₂ − y₁). Uses of jump: energy dissipation below spillways, mixing chemicals, raising water level, aeration. GVF equation: dy/dx = (S₀ − Sf)/(1 − Fr²). Slopes: Mild (M) yn > yc; Steep (S) yn < yc; Critical (C) yn = yc; Horizontal (H)

Given: Rectangular channel 4 m wide, Q = 12 m³/s → q = 3 m²/s. Critical depth: yc = (q²/g)^(1/3) = (9/9.81)^(1/3) = 0.97 m; Emin = 1.5 × 0.97 = 1.46 m; Vc = q/yc = 3.09 m/s. Classify: If actual depth = 1.5 m > yc → subcritical (Fr < 1). Critical flow: Fr = 1, minimum specific energy for given Q, maximum Q for given E; rectangular: yc = ⅔ Ec. Location: Below spillways, sluice gates and falls where supercritical flow meets subcritical tail water. Efficiency of jump: E₂/E₁ — lower for stronger jumps; relative loss ΔE/E₁ rises with Fr₁. Steady jump Fr₁ 4.5–9 (best for stilling basins); oscillating jump 2.5–4.5 should be avoided (waves).
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Open Channel Flow — Basics and Uniform Flow

Types: steady/unsteady; uniform/non-uniform (gradually varied GVF, rapidly varied RVF). Hydraulic radius R = A/P (wetted perimeter). Hydraulic depth D = A/T (top width). Chezy: V = C√(RS). Manning: V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2) (SI). Relation C = R^(1/6)/n. Bazin and Kutter formulae give Chezy C in terms of roughness. Most economical (efficient) section: maximum Q for given A, i.e. minimum P. Trapezoidal: half-regular hexagon; R = y/2; sloping sides tangent to semicircle centred on free surface; side slope 1V:√3H (60°) optimal. Circular: max discharge at y ≈ 0.938D (Manning); max velocity at y ≈ 0.81D. Normal depth y_n: depth at uniform flow.

Specific energy E = y + V²/2g (measured from channel bed). Critical depth: minimum specific energy for a given discharge; Fr = 1. Rectangular channel: y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3); E_min = 1.5 y_c; V_c = √(g y_c). General: Q²T/(gA³) = 1 at critical. Alternate depths: two depths with same E for given q (one sub-, one supercritical). Specific force (momentum function) M = Q²/(gA) + A z̄; conjugate (sequent) depths have equal M. Critical slope S_c: slope giving normal depth = critical depth. Mild: y_n > y_c; steep: y_n < y_c. Critical depth meters: venturi flume, Parshall flume, broad-crested weir (flow passes through critical depth). Hump in subcritical flow: water surface drops; in supercritical: rises. Contraction in width: similar behaviour.

Sudden rise from supercritical to subcritical flow; large energy dissipation. Sequent depth (rectangular): y₂/y₁ = ½ (−1 + √(1 + 8Fr₁²)). Energy loss: ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³ / (4 y₁ y₂). Length of jump ≈ 5 to 7 × (y₂ − y₁) (≈ 6.9(y₂ − y₁) commonly used). Height of jump = y₂ − y₁. Classification by Fr₁: undular 1–1.7; weak 1.7–2.5; oscillating 2.5–4.5; steady 4.5–9 (best for stilling basins); strong > 9. Uses: energy dissipation below spillways/sluices, raising downstream water level, mixing chemicals, aeration, removing air pockets. Jump is a rapidly varied flow (RVF); momentum (not energy) is conserved across it.

Dynamic equation: dy/dx = (S₀ − S_f) / (1 − Fr²). Assumptions: hydrostatic pressure, uniform-flow friction formula applies locally, small slope, constant n. Slope classes: Mild (M), Steep (S), Critical (C), Horizontal (H), Adverse (A). Zones: 1 = above both y_n and y_c; 2 = between them; 3 = below both. M1 (backwater curve): upstream of dam/weir — most common. M2 (drawdown curve): upstream of a free overfall/drop. M3: downstream of sluice gate on mild slope (ends in jump). S1: upstream of dam on steep slope (begins with jump). S2: downstream of slope change mild→steep. S3: below sluice on steep slope. No H1 and A1 curves exist (normal depth infinite/undefined). Computation: direct step method (prismatic channels), standard step method (natural channels), graphical integration. Control sections: where depth–discharge relation is fixed (critical depth at free overfall, weirs, gates).

Impulse turbine (Pelton): high head (> 250 m), low discharge, tangential flow; jet at atmospheric pressure; no draft tube. Pelton: max efficiency at bucket speed u = V/2; jet ratio m = D/d ≈ 12 (10–14); deflection ≈ 165°. Speed ratio ku ≈ 0.43–0.47. Number of buckets Z = 15 + D/(2d). Reaction turbines: Francis (medium head 60–250 m, mixed/radial-inward flow); Kaplan (low head < 60 m, high discharge, axial flow, adjustable blades); Propeller (fixed blades). Degree of reaction: Pelton = 0; Francis ≈ 0.5–0.9; Kaplan high. Draft tube: in reaction turbines; recovers kinetic energy and allows turbine above tailrace. Types: conical (efficiency ~90%), elbow, Moody spreading, simple elbow. Specific speed Ns = N√P/H^(5/4) (P in metric horsepower; in SI with P in kW: Pelton 8.5–30, Francis 50–340, Kaplan 255–860): Pelton 10–35 (single jet); Francis 60–300; Kaplan/Propeller 300–1000. Unit speed Nu = N/√H; unit discharge Qu = Q/√H; unit power Pu = P/H^1.5. Hydraulic efficiency = runner power/water power; overall η = mechanical × hydraulic. Governing: Pelton by spear (needle) valve and deflector; Francis by wicket (guide) gates; Kaplan by guide vanes + runner blades. Thoma's cavitation factor σ = (Ha − Hv − Hs)/H; used to fix turbine setting above tail water. Surge tank: protects penstock from water hammer. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. — Choice of turbine by specific speed and head. Pakistan hydropower: Tarbela & Mangla — Francis turbin

Turbine converts hydraulic energy into mechanical energy. Impulse turbine (Pelton wheel): all available head converted to kinetic energy in nozzle; runs at atmospheric pressure; high head (> 250 m), low discharge. Reaction turbines: part pressure, part kinetic; runner full of water; draft tube required. Francis: mixed/radial inward flow; medium head (≈ 30–250 m). Kaplan: axial flow, adjustable runner blades; low head (< 30 m), high discharge. Propeller turbine: fixed blades. Pelton: jet ratio m = D/d ≈ 12 (min 6); bucket speed ratio u/V ≈ 0.46; bucket deflection ≈ 165°; number of buckets ≈ 15 + D/(2d). Specific speed N_s = N√P / H^(5/4). Pelton (single jet) ≈ 8.5–30; Francis ≈ 50–340; Kaplan ≈ 255–860 (SI, P in kW). Efficiencies: hydraulic, mechanical, volumetric; overall = mechanical × hydraulic (× volumetric). Unit quantities (unit speed, unit discharge, unit power) predict performance at different heads. Draft tube: recovers kinetic energy at exit, allows turbine above tail race; types — conical (most efficient, ≈ 90%), elbow, Moody spreading. Cavitation in turbines: assessed by Thoma cavitation factor σ; most likely at runner exit (reaction turbines). Governing of turbines: speed kept constant by adjusting flow (spear valve in Pelton, guide vanes in Francis/Kaplan). Penstock: pipe carrying water from reservoir to turbine.

Centrifugal pump: converts mechanical energy to pressure energy via centrifugal action; casing types: volute, vortex, diffuser (turbine pump). Priming: required before starting centrifugal pump (fill casing and suction pipe with liquid). Manometric head Hm = Hs + Hd + losses + Vd²/2g. Manometric efficiency = gHm/(Vw₂u₂). Minimum starting speed: N = 120 ηman Vw₂D₂/(π(D₂² − D₁²)). Specific speed of pump Ns = N√Q/H^(3/4). Low Ns → radial flow (high head); high Ns → axial flow (low head, high Q). Pumps in series → increase head; in parallel → increase discharge. Backward-curved vanes: most common, stable characteristic, non-overloading. Affinity laws: Q ∝ ND³, H ∝ N²D², P ∝ N³D⁵. NPSH available must exceed NPSH required to avoid cavitation. Reciprocating pump: positive displacement; for small Q, high head; no priming needed. Slip = Q_th − Q_act. Negative slip when delivery pipe short, suction long, high speed. Air vessels: reduce acceleration head, make flow uniform, save power (single-acting saves ~84.8%, double-acting ~39.2%). Other: jet pump, hydraulic ram (uses water hammer), air lift pump, submersible pump. Hydraulic ram efficiency (D'Aubuisson / Rankine). Hydraulic press, accumulator, intensifier, lift, coupling, torque converter: hydraulic devices. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. — Pump H–Q and efficiency curves with system curve and operating point. Cavitation in pumps: Occurs at impeller eye when suction pressure < vapou
More on this topic — Hydraulics: Pumps

Centrifugal pump: converts mechanical energy to pressure energy by centrifugal action; high discharge, moderate head. Priming: filling casing and suction pipe with liquid before start — essential for centrifugal pumps. Manometric head H_m = head imparted by pump = static head + losses + exit velocity head. Manometric efficiency = gH_m / (V_w2 u₂). Overall efficiency = ρgQH_m / shaft power. Minimum starting speed: u₂² − u₁² ≥ 2gH_m (centrifugal head must exceed manometric head). Specific speed N_s = N√Q / H^(3/4). Radial (low N_s), mixed flow, axial (high N_s). Vane shape: backward-curved vanes (most common, stable characteristics); forward-curved rarely used. Casings: volute, vortex (whirlpool chamber), diffuser (guide vanes). Pumps in series: same Q, heads add (high head). In parallel: same head, discharges add (high flow). Multistage pump: impellers in series for high head. NPSH (Net Positive Suction Head): available must exceed required to avoid cavitation. Affinity laws (same pump): Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³. Slip = theoretical − actual discharge; negative slip possible with a long suction pipe, short delivery pipe and high speed. Air vessels on reciprocating pumps: smooth flow, reduce acceleration head, save power (≈ 84.8% saving in single-acting). Other machines: hydraulic ram (uses water hammer to lift water), hydraulic press, accumulator, intensifier, jack, crane, torque converter, fluid coupling, jet pump, air-lift pump, gear pump.

Speed of sound C = √(kRT) (gas) or √(K/ρ) (liquid). In air at 20°C ≈ 343 m/s; in water ≈ 1480 m/s. Mach cone angle: sin α = 1/M. Stagnation temperature T₀ = T(1 + (k − 1)M²/2). Choked flow: max discharge through nozzle when throat M = 1. Critical pressure ratio (air, k = 1.4): p*/p₀ = 0.528. Subsonic: diverging section decelerates flow. Supersonic: diverging section accelerates flow (De Laval nozzle). Normal shock: supersonic → subsonic; irreversible; entropy increases. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Regimes: M < 0.3 incompressible; 0.3–0.8 subsonic; 0.8–1.2 transonic; 1.2–5 supersonic; > 5 hypersonic. In supersonic flow a diverging passage ACCELERATES the flow (opposite of subsonic) — principle of the convergent-divergent (de Laval) nozzle.

g = 9.81 m/s²; ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³; γ_water = 9.81 kN/m³. 1 atm = 101.325 kPa = 10.33 m water = 760 mm Hg. Laminar pipe: Re < 2000, f = 64/Re, V_max = 2V_avg, α = 2, β = 4/3. Rectangular weir L = 2 m, H = 0.4 m, Cd = 0.62: Q = 0.93 m³/s. 90° V-notch H = 0.3 m, Cd = 0.6: Q = 0.070 m³/s.
