Irrigation: artificial application of water to soil to meet crop water needs. Need: inadequate/uneven rainfall, commercial crops, multiple cropping, controlled water supply. Benefits: higher yield, famine protection, hydropower, navigation, domestic water, revenue. Ill effects: waterlogging, salinity/alkalinity, mosquito breeding, cold & damp climate.

Flow irrigation: water flows by gravity. (a) Perennial – continuous supply from weir/barrage/storage; (b) Inundation/flood – canals run only in high river stages, no headworks. Lift irrigation: water lifted by pumps/wells/tube wells. Storage irrigation: dam built to store water, released as needed. Direct irrigation: water diverted directly from river by weir/barrage (no storage).

Surface: free/wild flooding (cheapest, least efficient), border strip, check basin, basin (orchards), furrow (row crops: maize, cotton, potato). Subsurface: water applied below ground; water table raised to root zone. Sprinkler: water sprayed like rain; for undulating land, sandy soils; efficiency ≈ 70–80%. Drip / trickle: water at root zone drop by drop; highest efficiency ≈ 90%+; suits saline water, orchards, vegetables, arid areas. Efficiency order: Drip > Sprinkler > Furrow/Border > Flooding.

Kharif (summer): Apr–Sep — rice, cotton, maize, sugarcane (sown), millets. Rabi (winter): Oct–Mar — wheat, gram, barley, mustard, oilseeds. Perennial crops: sugarcane, orchards (need water whole year). Cash crops: cotton, sugarcane, tobacco. Fodder: berseem, jowar. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Sprinkler system: Pump + main + laterals + risers + nozzles; application efficiency ≈ 70–80%; suits sandy/undulating land, closely spaced crops; not good in high wind. Drip system: Mains, sub-mains, laterals, emitters (≈ 2–8 L/h); efficiency ≈ 90%; needs filters (screen/sand/disc) against clogging; ideal for orchards, vegetables, saline water. Furrow / border / basin: Furrows for row crops (cotton, maize); borders (strips) for wheat, fodder; check basins for orchards. Inundation canals: Take off from river without weir; flow only when river is high (flood season); Sindh had many before barrages. Water-use priority: Pakistan agriculture uses ≈ 90%+ of withdrawals — hence efficiency improvement (lining, laser levelling, drip) matters most. Efficiency order: drip > sprinkler > furrow/border > flooding. Lift irrigation = tube wells/pumps; storage irrigation = dams.

Saturation capacity: all pores filled with water. Gravity water: drains freely after saturation; not useful to plants. Field capacity (FC): water held after gravity drainage stops (≈ 1–3 days after irrigation). Permanent wilting point (PWP): moisture below which plants cannot extract water and wilt permanently. Available moisture = FC − PWP (also called capillary water available to plants). Readily available moisture (RAM): ≈ 75–80% of available moisture; irrigation applied before this is used up. Hygroscopic water: thin film held tightly on particles; not available to plants. Optimum moisture content: moisture at which crop gives maximum yield.

Quantity Formula Depth of water held in root zone d_w = (γd/γw) · d · (FC − m) Available water depth d_w = (γd/γw) · d · (FC − PWP) Irrigation frequency (days) f = d_w / Cu (Cu = daily consumptive use) Volume of water V = A · d_w

Consumptive use (Cu): water used by plant (transpiration) + evaporation from soil + water in plant tissue. Effective rainfall: part of rainfall useful for crop needs. Consumptive irrigation requirement (CIR) = Cu − effective rainfall. Net irrigation requirement (NIR) = CIR + leaching requirement + other needs. Field irrigation requirement (FIR) = NIR / application efficiency. Gross irrigation requirement (GIR) = FIR / conveyance efficiency. Methods: Blaney–Criddle (Cu = k·f; f = Σ p(1.8t+32)/100, inches), Penman (energy balance, most accurate), Hargreaves, Thornthwaite, lysimeter (direct measurement).

Efficiency Definition Conveyance (ηc) Water delivered to field / water diverted from source Application (ηa) Water stored in root zone / water delivered to field Storage (ηs) Water stored in root zone / water needed in root zone before irrigation Distribution / uniformity (ηd) 1 − y/d (y = avg deviation from mean depth d) Water use efficiency Crop yield / water used Overall (project) ηc × ηa Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Depth of water stored in root zone: d = (γd/γw) · D · (FC − m) — where D = root-zone depth, m = moisture content before irrigation. Frequency of irrigation: Interval (days) = depth of readily available water ÷ daily consumptive use. Penman / modified Penman: Most accurate ETo method (radiation + wind + humidity + temperature); Hargreaves and Thornthwaite are simpler temperature-based methods. Pan evaporation method: ETo = Kp × Epan (Class-A pan; pan coefficient ≈ 0.7). Crop coefficient: ETcrop = Kc × ETo; Kc is low at the initial stage, maximum at mid-season (flowering), falls at maturity. Available moisture = FC − PWP. Readily available moisture ≈ 75–80% of it. Irrigate before moisture falls to the readily-available limit.

Duty (D): area (hectares) irrigated by 1 cumec flowing continuously for the base period. Unit: ha/cumec. Delta (Δ): total depth of water required by a crop during its base period (m or cm). Base period (B): time between first and last watering before harvest (days). Crop period: time from sowing to harvest (crop period ≥ base period; usually taken equal). Relation: Δ = 8.64 B / D (Δ in m, B in days, D in ha/cumec). Kor watering: first watering after crop grows a few cm; most critical. Kor depth (wheat ≈ 13.5 cm, rice ≈ 19 cm). Kor period: time in which kor watering must be done (wheat 3–4 weeks, rice 2–3 weeks). Paleo: first watering before sowing to give moisture for germination.
Crop Delta (cm) Crop Delta (cm) Rice 120 Cotton 50 Sugarcane 90 Vegetables 45 Tobacco 75 Wheat 40 Garden fruits 60 Fodder 22.5 Rice has the highest delta; wheat/fodder among lowest.

Type of crop, climate & season, rainfall, soil type, base period, method of irrigation, canal condition (lined/unlined), water quality, skill of cultivator. Duty increases downstream due to losses: Duty at field > head of watercourse > head of distributary > head of main canal. Improving duty: lining, proper ploughing, crop rotation, efficient methods (sprinkler/drip), volumetric water charges.

Gross command area (GCA): total area that can be irrigated by a canal, including roads, villages, ponds. Culturable command area (CCA): GCA − unculturable area. CCA = culturable cultivated + culturable uncultivated. Intensity of irrigation: % of CCA irrigated in a season. Can exceed 100% annually (e.g., Rabi + Kharif). Time factor = days canal actually ran / days it was supposed to run. Capacity factor = mean supply / full design supply. Outlet factor: duty at the head of the watercourse (outlet). Canal capacity: Q = (CCA × intensity) / duty, then adjusted for time factor & losses. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Given: Wheat: base period 120 days, delta 40 cm; CCA 10,000 ha; intensity 50%. Duty: D = 8.64 B/Δ = 8.64 × 120 / 0.40 = 2592 ha/cumec. Area irrigated: 10,000 × 0.50 = 5000 ha → Q = 5000/2592 ≈ 1.93 cumec at the field (increase for losses at head). Outlet factor (kor): Duty during kor period = 8.64 × kor period (days) / kor depth (m). Kor periods (typical): Wheat ≈ 3–4 weeks (kor depth ≈ 13.5 cm); rice ≈ 2–3 weeks (kor depth ≈ 19 cm); sugarcane ≈ 4 weeks (≈ 16.5 cm). Duty at field > duty at outlet > duty at head of canal (losses increase upstream). Rice has the highest delta (≈ 120 cm).

Salinity hazard: measured by Electrical Conductivity (EC). Classes C1 (low) to C4 (very high). Sodium hazard: measured by SAR = Na⁺ / √[(Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺)/2] (meq/L). Classes S1 to S4. Residual sodium carbonate (RSC) = (CO₃ + HCO₃) − (Ca + Mg); RSC > 2.5 meq/L unsuitable. Boron: toxic above ~0.3–4 ppm depending on crop sensitivity.

Soil EC (dS/m) ESP pH Remedy Saline (white alkali) > 4 < 15 < 8.5 Leaching with good water + drainage Sodic / alkali (black alkali) < 4 > 15 > 8.5 Gypsum, then leaching Saline–sodic > 4 > 15 ≈ 8.5 Gypsum + leaching Leaching requirement: LR = EC_iw / EC_dw (irrigation water EC / drainage water EC).

Definition: land is waterlogged when water table rises into root zone, reducing soil aeration & yield (rule of thumb: water table within ≈ 1.5–2 m of surface). Causes: seepage from unlined canals, over-irrigation, poor natural drainage, obstruction of drainage by roads/railways, flat topography, impervious subsoil. Effects: lack of aeration, fall in soil temperature, salt rise by capillarity (salinity), weed growth, malaria, reduced yield. Remedies: canal lining, intercepting drains along canals, lowering FSL of canals, efficient irrigation, surface & subsurface drainage, vertical drainage by tube wells, crop rotation, reduced intensity. SCARP (Pakistan): Salinity Control and Reclamation Project; began 1960s (SCARP-I in Rechna Doab); used tube wells for vertical drainage.

Surface drains: open ditches removing excess surface water. Subsurface drains: tile/perforated pipe drains in trenches; spacing by Hooghoudt or ellipse equation S = √[4K(b² − a²)/q]. Tile drain min slope ≈ 0.05–0.3%; usual depth 1–2 m. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Waterlogging & salinity in Pakistan: Large areas of the Indus plains were affected by rising water tables after canal irrigation; SCARP tube wells (from 1960s), surface drains and the Left Bank Outfall Drain (LBOD) in Sindh were built to control it. Reclamation of saline soil: Leaching with good-quality water + good drainage. Reclamation of sodic (alkali) soil: Gypsum (CaSO₄) to replace Na⁺, followed by leaching; also sulphur, acid-forming amendments, organic matter. Biological drainage: Eucalyptus and other high-transpiration trees planted to lower the water table. Drain spacing: Hooghoudt’s equation is commonly used for spacing of subsurface drains. Saline soil → leaching. Sodic soil → gypsum + leaching. SAR measures the sodium hazard; EC measures the salinity hazard.

By function: irrigation, carrier (irrigates + carries water to another canal), feeder (only feeds another canal), navigation, power canal. By discharge/hierarchy: main canal → branch canal → major distributary → minor distributary → watercourse (field channel; farmer-owned). Direct irrigation is normally not done from main canal; branch canals irrigate partly; distributaries feed outlets. By alignment: (a) Watershed/ridge canal – runs along ridge; no cross-drainage works needed; irrigates both sides. (b) Contour canal – follows contour; irrigates one side; needs CD works. (c) Side-slope canal – perpendicular to contours; parallel to natural drainage; no CD works but steep slope (needs falls). By soil: alluvial canal (in silt; design by regime theories), non-alluvial canal (hard soil/rock). By lining: unlined, lined.

Full supply level (FSL): water level at full design discharge. Freeboard: vertical distance between FSL and top of bank (≈ 0.3–0.9 m, depending on discharge). Berm: horizontal strip between inner toe of bank and top of cutting; strengthens banks, protects from erosion; silt deposit forms 1/2:1 regime slope. Balancing depth: depth of cutting at which earthwork in cutting = earthwork in filling (most economical). Spoil bank: excess excavated earth dumped along canal. Borrow pit: pit dug to get earth for filling. Service road / inspection road on bank top; dowla – small bank on road side for safety. Side slopes: cutting ≈ 1:1 (H:V), filling ≈ 1.5:1 to 2:1.

Evaporation: small (≈ 2–3% of total losses). Seepage: major loss — (a) percolation (water table close; direct connection) and (b) absorption (water table deep; wetted zone only). Typically 30–45% of diverted water may be lost in unlined systems. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 5.1 — Canal in partial cutting & filling: FSL, freeboard, berm, banks, service road, side slopes. Canal alignment types: Watershed (ridge) canal — no cross-drainage works, irrigates both sides; contour canal — irrigates one side, needs CD works; side-slope canal — at right angle to contours, parallel to drainage, no CD works but steep slope. Berm functions: Strengthens banks, protects against erosion, room for future widening, deposit of silt forms lining (in time). Seepage formulas: Losses in cumec per million m² of wetted area (e.g., ≈ 2.5 for unlined canals in Punjab practice). Hierarchy in Pakistan: Main canal → branch canal → distributary (disty) → minor → watercourse (farmers’ channel) via outlet (mogha). Balancing depth = depth of cutting for which cut = fill. Freeboard ≈ 0.5–0.75 m for main canals.

Based on observations on Upper Bari Doab Canal (UBDC), Punjab. Silt kept in suspension by eddies generated from the bed only (sides ignored). Critical velocity (V₀): velocity that neither silts nor scours: V₀ = 0.55 m D^0.64 (metric; D = depth of flow, m). Critical velocity ratio (CVR, m) = V/V₀; m = 1 for UBDC silt; >1 for coarser silt, <1 for finer silt. Mean velocity from Kutter's formula (later Manning's). Design by trial; Garret's diagrams used. Limitations: no concept of silt charge or grade; B/D ratio not fixed; trial & error; Kutter's formula limitations; eddies from sides ignored.

Lindley first gave regime concept (1919); Lacey developed it fully. Regime channel: neither silting nor scouring; bed & sides in equilibrium. Conditions: constant discharge, constant silt charge, incoherent alluvium of same grade, unlimited incoherent alluvium. Types of regime: initial regime (bed slope & depth adjust, width fixed), final regime (all variables adjusted), true regime (theoretical ideal). Silt supported by eddies generated from the entire wetted perimeter; normal to perimeter. Regime section is a semi-ellipse; in practice trapezoidal with side slopes ½ : 1 (H:V). Lacey equation Formula (SI) Silt factor f = 1.76 √d_mm Velocity V = (Q f² / 140)^(1/6) Hydraulic mean radius R = (5/2) · V² / f Wetted perimeter P = 4.75 √Q Area A = Q / V Bed slope S = f^(5/3) / (3340 Q^(1/6)) Regime flow equation V = 10.8 R^(2/3) S^(1/3) Scour depth (wide channel) R = 1.35 (q² / f)^(1/3) Scour depth (general) R = 0.473 (Q / f)^(1/3) Defects of Lacey: true regime rarely achieved; silt factor not truly constant; ignores silt concentration; semi-ellipse not practical; equations empirical.

Kennedy Lacey Eddies from bed only Eddies from whole perimeter Trapezoidal section Semi-elliptical section Kutter's formula Own regime flow equation Trial & error Direct design B/D ratio not given P (≈ width) fixed by Q Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Given: Q = 30 cumec, silt factor f = 1.0. Velocity: V = (Q f² / 140)^(1/6) = (30/140)^(1/6) ≈ 0.77 m/s. Area, perimeter, R: A = Q/V ≈ 39 m²; P = 4.75√Q ≈ 26 m; R = 5V²/(2f) ≈ 1.48 m. Bed slope: S = f^(5/3) / (3340 Q^(1/6)) ≈ 1 / 5900. Kennedy’s CVR (m): m = 1.0 standard silt; coarser silt m > 1 (1.1–1.2); finer silt m < 1 (0.8–0.9). Kennedy: eddies from the BED only keep silt in suspension; Lacey: eddies from the whole wetted PERIMETER. Lacey’s regime section ≈ semi-ellipse.

Advantages: seepage control (saves water), prevents waterlogging, higher velocity → smaller section, less maintenance, weed control, stable banks, better command (higher FSL possible), reduced breaches. Disadvantages: high initial cost, repair is difficult, berms/outlets shifting difficult.

Hard surface: cement concrete (most common), shotcrete/gunite, brick/tile, stone masonry, asphalt concrete, precast slabs. Earth type: compacted earth, soil–cement, bentonite/clay, buried membranes (plastic/asphalt). Lined canal sections: triangular (small discharge, < ~55 cumec) and trapezoidal (larger discharge); corners rounded. Uplift/hydrostatic pressure behind lining relieved by drainage: filter layers, pressure relief valves, longitudinal & cross drains. Economics: Benefit–cost ratio = annual benefit / annual cost; lining justified if B/C > 1. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Concrete lining thickness: ≈ 75–100 mm for small canals, 100–150 mm for large canals; joints with bitumen/PVC water stops. Brick-tile lining: Two layers of brick tiles in cement mortar — widely used in Pakistan for watercourses and small channels. Pressure-relief: Drains/weep holes and pressure-release valves behind lining in high water-table areas. Watercourse lining (Pakistan): On-Farm Water Management programmes line watercourses and laser-level fields to cut conveyance and field losses. Benefits of lining: less seepage, no waterlogging, higher velocity (smaller section), less weed growth, lower maintenance.

Purpose: raise water level in river, divert into canal, regulate supply, control silt entry, reduce river fluctuation. Weir: raised barrier across river; water level raised mainly by solid crest; shutters small/none. Pond level depends on crest. Barrage: water level raised mainly by gates; crest at low level. Better control of pond level, silt and floods; costlier.

Weir/barrage proper – main body raising water level. Undersluices (scouring sluices): deep pocket near canal head; keep channel clear of silt, provide still pond, scour silt. Divide wall: separates undersluices from weir; creates still pocket; prevents cross flow. Fish ladder: allows fish migration; located near divide wall. Canal head regulator: controls supply into canal; excludes silt. Silt excluder: in river bed upstream of head regulator; separates bottom silt-laden water. Silt ejector (extractor): in canal downstream of head regulator; removes silt that already entered canal. River training works: guide banks (Bell's bunds), marginal bunds, spurs/groynes.
Masonry weir with vertical drop wall; dry stone (rockfill) slope weir; concrete weir with sloping glacis (based on Khosla's theory; modern).
Causes of failure of weirs on permeable foundation

Subsurface flow: (a) Piping / undermining – exit gradient too high, soil particles washed out at tail; (b) Uplift pressure – floor too thin, bursts. Surface flow: (a) hydraulic jump suction – lifts floor; (b) scour on u/s and d/s. Remedies: adequate creep length, sheet piles/cut-offs (esp. d/s end), sufficient floor thickness, inverted filter, launching aprons, deep cut-offs. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 8.1 — Layout of diversion headworks: weir/barrage, undersluices, divide wall, fish ladder, silt excluder, head regulator, guide banks. Pond level: Water level maintained upstream of weir/barrage for diversion into the canal. Afflux: Rise in the high-flood level upstream caused by the weir/barrage; kept small (≈ 0.3–1.0 m). Barrage advantages: Better control of pond level, less afflux, less silting, gates can be fully opened during floods. Silt excluder is placed in the RIVER (upstream of the head regulator); silt ejector/extractor is placed in the CANAL (downstream of the head regulator).

Percolating water creeps along contact of base profile with soil (both vertical & horizontal equally). Head loss is uniform (proportional to creep length) along path. Creep length L = b + 2(d₁ + d₂ + …) (vertical cut-offs counted on both faces). Hydraulic gradient = H_L / L; safe if H_L/L ≤ 1/C → L ≥ C · H_L (C = Bligh's creep coefficient). Floor thickness: t = h / (G − 1); with safety factor t = (4/3) · h / (G − 1) (h = residual uplift head). Limitations: no distinction between horizontal & vertical creep; exit gradient not considered; outer & inner faces of piles treated same; failed for some actual weirs.
Vertical creep given full weight; horizontal creep 1/3 weight: L = ΣL_v + (1/3) ΣL_h. Slopes steeper than 45° → vertical; flatter than 45° → horizontal.

Based on potential flow theory (Laplace equation) & failures of Punjab weirs; flow net concept. Outer faces of end sheet piles more effective than inner faces & floor. Undermining starts at the tail end; a downstream end cut-off is essential to prevent piping. Exit gradient must be within safe limit: G_E = (H/d) · 1/(π√λ), where λ = [1 + √(1 + α²)]/2, α = b/d. Method of independent variables: complex profile split into simple standard profiles (pile at end, pile in middle, depressed floor); pressures φ_E, φ_D, φ_C found from Khosla's curves. Corrections: (1) mutual interference of piles, (2) floor thickness, (3) slope of floor (+ for down slope, − for up slope). Soil Safe exit gradient Shingle 1/4 – 1/5 Coarse sand 1/5 – 1/6 Fine sand 1/6 – 1/7 Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 9.1 — Weir on permeable soil: creep path along the floor and cut-offs, hydraulic gradient line, exit point.
Bligh’s creep coefficient C (safe hydraulic gradient = 1/C)

Soil Bligh’s C Lane’s weighted C Fine micaceous sand 15 8.5 Fine sand ≈ 15 7 Coarse-grained sand 12 5 Gravel & sand 9 3.5–4 Boulders, gravel & sand 4–6 2.5–3 Khosla’s safe exit gradient: Shingle 1/4–1/5; coarse sand 1/5–1/6; fine sand 1/6–1/7. Bligh: L = b + 2(d₁ + d₂); uniform head loss. Lane: horizontal creep counted as ⅓. Khosla: exit gradient GE = (H/d)·(1/π√λ) must be within safe limits.

Hydraulic jump: sudden rise of water when supercritical flow (F > 1) changes to subcritical flow (F < 1); dissipates energy. Sequent (conjugate) depth: y₂/y₁ = ½ [−1 + √(1 + 8F₁²)]. Energy loss: ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³ / (4 y₁ y₂). Length of jump ≈ 5 to 7 × (y₂ − y₁) (≈ 6 × height of jump). Froude number F₁ Type of jump 1.0 – 1.7 Undular 1.7 – 2.5 Weak 2.5 – 4.5 Oscillating (avoid; waves) 4.5 – 9.0 Steady (best, efficient) > 9.0 Strong (rough) Energy dissipators: stilling basins (USBR Type I–IV, SAF), hydraulic jump basin, ski-jump (trajectory) bucket, roller bucket (solid/slotted), baffle blocks, chute blocks, end sill, friction blocks. Ski-jump: used where tailwater is low & rock bed is good; roller bucket: tailwater depth high. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 10.1 — Hydraulic jump: y₁ (supercritical) → y₂ (subcritical), roller, length ≈ 6 (y₂ − y₁). Uses of jump: Energy dissipation below spillways/falls, mixing of chemicals, raising d/s water level, aeration. Tail-water rating curve: Jump forms at the toe only when tail-water depth = y₂; otherwise jump is repelled (TW < y₂) or drowned (TW > y₂). Froude 4.5–9 = steady, well-balanced jump (best). F < 1.7 = undular; 2.5–4.5 = oscillating (avoid); > 9 = strong, rough.

Need: when natural ground slope is steeper than designed canal bed slope; bed lowered by a fall to avoid excessive filling. Power can be generated at large falls. Types: Ogee fall (old), rapids (long glacis, used where stone cheap), stepped fall, trapezoidal notch fall (Reid), vertical drop / Sarda fall (developed on Sarda canal, UP), straight glacis fall, Montague fall (parabolic glacis), Inglis fall (baffle wall), baffle fall, cylinder/well fall (high drop, small discharge), pipe fall. Meter falls: used to measure discharge (e.g., glacis fall, notch fall). Non-meter falls: no measurement.

Head regulator: at head of off-taking canal; regulates supply into it; controls silt; can measure discharge. Cross regulator: across parent canal just downstream of off-take; heads up water for off-take when parent canal runs low; helps close canal for repair; absorbs fluctuations. Canal escape: disposes surplus water; types: weir type (surface), sluice type, tail escape (at end of canal). Distributary head regulator = head regulator for distributary. Canal outlet: small structure feeding watercourse from distributary.

Non-modular: discharge depends on difference of levels in distributary and watercourse (submerged pipe outlet, open sluice). Semi-modular (flexible): discharge depends on distributary water level only, independent of watercourse level (free fall). Examples: pipe outlet with free fall, Kennedy's gauge outlet, open flume outlet, Crump's Adjustable Proportional Module (APM). Modular (rigid): discharge constant within limits regardless of both levels. Examples: Gibb's module, Khanna's rigid module, Foote module. Outlet term Meaning Flexibility (F) (dq/q) / (dQ/Q) = (m/n)·(y/H); m = outlet index, n = channel index (≈ 5/3) Proportional outlet F = 1 (outlet draws share proportional to distributary flow) Hyper-proportional F > 1 Sub-proportional F < 1 Setting H/y = depth of outlet crest below FSL / full supply depth Proportional setting H/y = m/n → open flume (m = 3/2): 0.9; pipe/orifice (m = 1/2): 0.3 Sensitivity Rate of change of outlet discharge with change in distributary water level Minimum modular head Min working head needed for outlet to remain semi-modular Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Common falls: Sarda fall (vertical drop, UP/Sarda canal), straight glacis fall, Montague fall (parabolic glacis), Inglis fall, notch fall, pipe fall (small discharge), stepped fall. Outlet terms: Flexibility = ratio of rate of change of outlet discharge to rate of change of distributary discharge; proportional outlet when flexibility = 1. Rigid m

Built where canal crosses a natural drain/stream. Avoided by watershed alignment. Type Arrangement / condition Aqueduct Canal over drain; drain HFL well below canal bed; drain flows freely Siphon aqueduct Canal over drain; drain HFL above canal bed → drain flows under pressure (siphon action) below canal Super passage Drain over canal; canal FSL below drain bed; canal flows freely Canal siphon (syphon) Drain over canal; canal FSL above drain bed → canal flows under pressure below drain Level crossing Canal & drain at nearly same level; large drain discharge; regulators on both Inlet / outlet Small drain admitted into canal (inlet) and released (outlet) Selection factors: relative bed levels & FSL/HFL, discharges, foundation, cost. Aqueduct types: Type I – canal banks continued, drain waterway enclosed; Type II – canal sides as retaining walls; Type III – canal trough flumed (most economical). Uplift on barrel floor of siphon aqueduct is critical (worst when drain empty & canal at FSL with water table high). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 12.1 — Cross-drainage works: aqueduct, siphon aqueduct, super-passage and canal siphon. Level crossing: Canal and drain at about the same level; regulators on canal and drain; used when the drain discharge is large and short-duration. Inlet & outlet: For small drains: drain water admitted into the canal (inlet) and released downstream (outlet). Canal over drain (drain free) = aqueduct; canal

By function: storage, diversion, detention (flood control), debris, coffer dam (temporary, to keep work area dry). By material: rigid (concrete/masonry: gravity, arch, buttress) and non-rigid (earth, rockfill). By hydraulic design: overflow (spillway) dam, non-overflow dam.

Resists water pressure by its own weight. Forces: self weight (main resisting force), water pressure (main external force), uplift, silt pressure, wave pressure, ice pressure, earthquake forces (horizontal & vertical), wind. Modes of failure: overturning, sliding, compression (crushing), tension (cracking). No tension condition: resultant must lie within middle third of base (e ≤ b/6). Stress at toe/heel: p = (ΣV/b)(1 ± 6e/b). Elementary profile: right-angled triangle; base width b = H/√(S_c − c) with uplift (c = uplift coefficient); b = H/√S_c without uplift; for sliding b = H/[μ(S_c − c)]. Limiting height (low vs high dam): H = f / [γ_w (S_c + 1)] ≈ 88 m for usual concrete; dams higher than this = high gravity dams. FOS against overturning = ΣM_R / ΣM_O (≥ 1.5). Sliding = μΣV/ΣH (≥ 1, usually 1–1.5). Shear friction factor = (μΣV + b·q)/ΣH (≥ 3–5). Galleries: for inspection, drainage, grouting; drainage holes reduce uplift.

Types: homogeneous (single material; needs drainage), zoned (impervious core + pervious shells; most common), diaphragm (thin impervious diaphragm of concrete/steel/clay). Causes of failure: (a) Hydraulic (≈ 40%) – overtopping (most common), wave erosion, toe erosion, gullying; (b) Seepage (≈ 30%) – piping, sloughing; (c) Structural (≈ 30%) – foundation slide, slope slide (u/s on sudden drawdown, d/s at steady seepage), earthquake. Phreatic line: top seepage line; approximately a base parabola (Casagrande) with focus at toe of filter/drain. Seepage discharge (flow net): q = k H (N_f / N_d). Seepage control: impervious core, cut-off trench, grouted curtain, upstream impervious blanket, relief wells. Drainage filters: toe filter / rock toe, horizontal blanket, chimney drain. Critical conditions for stability: u/s slope – sudden drawdown; d/s slope – steady seepage; both – construction (end of construction pore pressure).

Arch dam: curved in plan, transfers load to abutments by arch action; narrow gorge with strong rock (width/height < ~5). Constant-radius, constant-angle (most economical), variable radius. Buttress dam: sloping deck supported by buttresses; less concrete; types: deck (Ambursen), multiple arch, massive head. Rockfill dam: rock with impervious membrane (concrete face – CFRD) or core.

Narrow valley with wide basin upstream, sound foundation, availability of materials, spillway site, low land acquisition/submergence, minimal sediment, access, cost. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 13.1 — Forces on a gravity dam: water pressure, self weight, uplift; resultant in the middle third. Fig. 13.2 — Zoned earth dam: clay core, pervious shells, cut-off, rock toe, phreatic line. Other forces on gravity dam: Silt pressure, wave pressure (Molitor/Stevenson), ice pressure, earthquake (horizontal & vertical inertia + hydrodynamic pressure — Zanger/Westergaard). Principal stresses: Maximum principal stress occurs at the toe; minimum (possible tension) at the heel. Earth dam piping: Prevented by filters (Terzaghi’s criteria), cut-offs, relief wells and adequate seepage path. Pakistan examples: Tarbela — earth & rockfill (one of the world’s largest by volume); Mangla — earth-fill (later raised to add storage); Mohmand — concrete-face rockfill (CFRD); Diamer-Bhasha — roller-compacted concrete (RCC). Gravity dam no-tension: e ≤ b/6. FOS overturning ≥ 1.5; sliding FOS (μΣV/ΣH) ≥ 1–1.5; shear friction factor ≥ 3–5.

Spillway: passes surplus flood water safely to downstream; prevents overtopping. Discharge: Q = C L H^(3/2) (L = effective length, H = head over crest). Effective length: L = L′ − 2(N K_p + K_a) H. Type Key point Free overfall (straight drop) Water falls freely; low heads, thin arch dams Ogee (overflow) Most common; crest shaped to lower nappe of sharp-crested weir (WES profile); used in gravity dams Chute (trough) Steep open channel; used with earth dams Side channel Flow over crest then turns 90°, flows parallel to crest; narrow gorges Shaft (morning glory / bell-mouth) Circular crest, vertical shaft + tunnel; where no space for others Siphon Primed by air removal; automatic, maintains near-constant level; limited capacity Conduit / tunnel Closed conduit through or around dam Cavitation: occurs if pressure falls below vapour pressure (negative pressure on crest when head > design head). Gates: vertical lift (fixed wheel, slide), radial (Tainter) gate – most common on spillways/barrages, drum gate, rolling gate, stop logs, needles, flash boards. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Spillway types: Free overfall (straight drop), ogee (most common), chute/trough, side-channel (narrow valleys), shaft/morning-glory (bell-mouth), siphon (automatic, constant pool), labyrinth/piano-key. Spillway capacity: Designed for the inflow design flood after routing through the reservoir (PMF for large dams). Aerators: Slots/ramps on chute surface intr
Gravity Dam — Design Checks & Worked Example

Forces (per metre length): Self-weight W (main stabilising force), water pressure P = ½γwH² at H/3, uplift U = ½·c·γw·H·B (c = 1 without drains; reduced with drainage gallery), silt pressure, wave pressure, ice, earthquake (horizontal & vertical inertia + Zangar/Westergaard hydrodynamic pressure). Elementary profile: Triangle with zero top width and vertical upstream face, height H, base B. No tension (resultant in middle third): B ≥ H/√(Sc − c); without uplift B = H/√Sc. Sliding: B ≥ H/[μ(Sc − c)]. Stability checks: Overturning FOS = ΣMR/ΣMO ≥ 1.5; sliding FOS = μΣV/ΣH ≥ 1.0–1.5; shear-friction factor SFF = (μΣV + B·q)/ΣH ≥ 3–5; no tension (e ≤ B/6); compressive stress ≤ allowable. Base pressures: p = (ΣV/B)(1 ± 6e/B); e = B/2 − x̄, where x̄ = (ΣMR − ΣMO)/ΣV measured from the toe. Load combinations (USBR): Usual (normal pool + uplift + silt + ice), unusual (maximum flood), extreme (usual + maximum credible earthquake).

Fig. — Forces on the elementary profile of the worked example: water pressure, self-weight, uplift and resultant in the middle third. Given: H = 30 m, B = 26 m, vertical upstream face, γc = 24 kN/m³, γw = 9.81 kN/m³, full uplift (c = 1, triangular), μ = 0.75; reservoir full to the top. Forces: W = ½ × 26 × 30 × 24 = 9,360 kN (acts B/3 = 8.67 m from heel → 17.33 m from toe). P = ½ × 9.81 × 30² = 4,414.5 kN at 10 m. U = ½ × 9.81 × 30 × 26 = 3,825.9 kN at B/3 from heel (17.33 m from toe). Moments about toe: ΣMR = 9,360 × 17.33 = 162,240 kN·m; ΣMO = 4,414.5 × 10 + 3,825.9 × 17.33 = 110,461 kN·m. Overturning: FOS = 162,240 / 110,461 = 1.47 → just below 1.5 (marginal). Resultant & stresses: ΣV = 9,360 − 3,826 = 5,534 kN; x̄ = (162,240 − 110,461)/5,534 = 9.36 m from toe; e = 13 − 9.36 = 3.64 m < B/6 = 4.33 m → no tension. p = (5,534/26)(1 ± 6 × 3.64/26) → 392 kPa (toe) and 34 kPa (heel). Sliding: FOS = 0.75 × 5,534 / 4,414.5 = 0.94 < 1 → unsafe by pure friction; needs shear-key / bond (SFF check), a wider base (B ≥ H/[μ(Sc − c)] = 28.6 m) or drainage to cut uplift. Uplift is what makes the elementary profile fail in sliding — drainage galleries and grout curtains reduce c and are the cheapest fix.

Types: Homogeneous (with toe drain/filter), zoned (impervious core + pervious shells — most common for high dams; Tarbela, Mangla), diaphragm (thin core of concrete/asphalt). Phreatic line (Casagrande / Kozeny): Basic parabola with focus at the start of the toe filter: y² = 2xy₀ + y₀², y₀ = √(h² + d²) − d (h = water depth, d = horizontal distance from focus to the point 0.3 × upstream wetted projection). Seepage q = k·y₀ per metre. Seepage by flow net: q = k·h·(Nf/Nd) per metre length (Nf = flow channels, Nd = equipotential drops). Worked seepage: h = 20 m, d = 40 m, k = 1 × 10⁻⁷ m/s → y₀ = √(400 + 1600) − 40 = 4.72 m; q = 1 × 10⁻⁷ × 4.72 = 4.7 × 10⁻⁷ m³/s per metre (≈ 0.04 m³/day/m). Fig. — Zoned earth dam: impervious core, pervious shells, chimney filter and drain; the phreatic line ends in the filter. Filter criteria (Terzaghi): D15(filter)/D85(base) ≤ 4–5 (piping); D15(filter)/D15(base) ≥ 4–5 (permeability). Critical conditions: Upstream slope — sudden drawdown; downstream slope — steady seepage at full reservoir; both slopes — end of construction (pore pressure). Failures: Hydraulic (overtopping, wave erosion, toe erosion, gullies); seepage (piping, sloughing); structural (slides, foundation shear, earthquake). Freeboard prevents overtopping. Typical slopes: Upstream 2.5H:1V–3H:1V (flatter, drawdown), downstream 2H:1V–2.5H:1V; top width (USBR) = H/5 + 3 m (H in m) or empirical. Upstream slope is critical in sudden drawdown; downstream slope in steady seepage. Phreatic li

Ogee spillway discharge: Q = C·L·He^(3/2); C ≈ 2.2 (SI) at design head (≈ 4.0 in ft-units). Effective length L = L′ − 2(N·Kp + Ka)He (pier & abutment contractions). WES crest profile (vertical upstream face): x^1.85 = 2·Hd^0.85·y (downstream of crest). Hydraulic jump in stilling basins (USBR): Fr₁ 1.7–2.5: no baffles (pre-jump); 2.5–4.5: oscillating jump → Type IV basin; Fr₁ > 4.5 with V₁ < 18 m/s → Type III (chute blocks, baffle piers, end sill); V₁ > 18 m/s → Type II (no baffle piers). Fig. — Ogee spillway discharging into a USBR Type III stilling basin with chute blocks, baffle piers and end sill. Other dissipators: Roller bucket (solid / slotted) where tail water is high; ski-jump / flip bucket where tail water is low and rock is sound; plunge pool. Spillway design flood: Large dams → PMF (probable maximum flood); medium → 100–1000-yr flood; check freeboard against wave run-up. Outlets & gates: Low-level outlets/sluices for irrigation and sediment flushing; radial (Tainter) gates (least hoisting force, most common on spillways); vertical lift gates; stop logs for maintenance. Ski-jump bucket = low tail water; roller bucket = high tail water; hydraulic-jump basin = tail water matching sequent depth.

Power: P = η·γw·Q·H = 9.81·η·Q·H kW (Q in m³/s, H = net head in m). Energy (kWh) = P × hours. Overall η ≈ 0.80–0.90. Worked example: Q = 100 m³/s, Hnet = 80 m, η = 0.88 → P = 9.81 × 0.88 × 100 × 80 = 69,062 kW ≈ 69 MW. Annual energy at 50% capacity factor ≈ 69 × 8760 × 0.5 ≈ 302 GWh. Heads: Gross head = headwater − tailwater level; net (effective) head = gross − losses (trash rack, intake, penstock friction, bends, valves). Classification by head (Garg): Low head < 15 m (Kaplan/propeller/bulb), medium 15–60 m (Francis, Kaplan), high > 60 m (Pelton, Francis). Other books use < 30 m / 30–300 m / > 300 m — note the book used in the paper. Classification by operation: Run-of-river without pondage, run-of-river with pondage (daily regulation), storage (seasonal), pumped storage (peak-load; pumps at off-peak, generates at peak; cycle efficiency ≈ 70–80%), tidal. Classification by load: Base-load plants (large storage & run-of-river with steady flow) vs peak-load plants (pumped storage, pondage plants). Components: Reservoir/headworks → intake with trash rack → headrace (tunnel/canal) → forebay (open-channel systems) or surge tank (pressure systems) → penstock → powerhouse (turbine, generator, governor) → draft tube (reaction turbines) → tailrace. Fig. — Layout of a high-head scheme: intake, headrace tunnel, surge tank, penstock, powerhouse, draft tube and tailrace. Surge tank: Absorbs water-hammer pressure rise on load rejection and supplies water on sudden load demand; protects th

Load factor: Average load ÷ peak load over a period (always < 1). Fig. — Daily load curve: peak demand 100 MW, average ≈ 65 MW, so load factor ≈ 0.65. Capacity (plant) factor: Average output ÷ installed capacity = actual energy ÷ (installed capacity × hours). Utilisation (plant use) factor: Actual energy produced ÷ (capacity actually used × hours) — always ≥ capacity factor. Diversity factor: Sum of individual maximum demands ÷ maximum demand of the system (≥ 1). Firm (primary) power: Power available at all times (based on minimum flow, or 90–95% dependable flow). Secondary (surplus) power — available only part of the time; sold at lower rates. Flow-duration curve: Discharge vs % time equalled or exceeded — used to fix firm power and installed capacity of run-of-river plants. Power-duration curve = same with power ordinate. Mass curve / sequent-peak: Storage required for a given demand (Rippl method) — used for storage plants. Pondage factor: Total inflow hours in a period ÷ hours of plant operation in the same period. Load factor = average/peak demand; capacity factor = average output/installed capacity. Firm power is fixed from the minimum (or 90–95% dependable) flow.

Project River / Location Installed capacity (MW) Notes Tarbela Indus, KP 4,888 Earth & rock-fill; 4th ext. 1,410 MW (2018); 5th ext. +1,530 MW under construction → 6,418 Mangla Jhelum, AJK 1,000 (upgrading to ≈ 1,310) Earth-fill; raised 2009 (Mangla raising) Ghazi-Barotha Indus (d/s Tarbela), Attock 1,450 Run-of-river, 52 km power channel (2003) Neelum–Jhelum Neelum → Jhelum, AJK 969 Run-of-river, long headrace tunnels (2018) Suki Kinari Kunhar, KP 884 CPEC, run-of-river Karot Jhelum, Punjab/AJK 720 CPEC, run-of-river Warsak Kabul River, KP 243 Concrete gravity (1960) Chashma Indus, Punjab 184 Low-head, bulb turbines at barrage Dasu Indus, Kohistan 4,320 (Stage-I 2,160) Run-of-river, under construction Diamer-Bhasha Indus, GB 4,500 RCC dam ≈ 272 m high, storage ≈ 8.1 MAF, under construction Mohmand Swat River, KP 800 CFRD; flood control + water supply, under construction Pakistan hydropower share: Total installed capacity ≈ 49,000+ MW (2024), of which ≈ 11,500 MW hydro; identified potential ≈ 60,000 MW (mostly the Indus cascade in KP & GB). Tarbela is the largest hydropower station of Pakistan (4,888 MW); Ghazi-Barotha and Neelum–Jhelum are run-of-river; Diamer-Bhasha is designed as an RCC (roller-compacted concrete) dam.

Dead storage: below minimum pool level; for silt; cannot be released by gravity. Live (useful) storage: between minimum pool level and normal pool (conservation) level. Surcharge storage: between normal pool level and maximum pool level (flood storage; uncontrolled). Bank storage: water absorbed into banks; valley storage: natural river channel storage before dam. Mass curve (Rippl) method: used to find required storage capacity / safe yield. Safe (firm) yield: max quantity guaranteed in critical dry period. Secondary yield: water available in excess of safe yield. Reservoir sedimentation: trap efficiency depends on capacity–inflow ratio (Brune's curve). Life of reservoir = time to fill dead storage (or capacity reduced to set %). Control of silting: catchment treatment (afforestation, check dams), sluicing, flushing, venting density currents, dredging, selecting site with low sediment. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 21.1 — Reservoir storage zones: dead, live (useful) and surcharge storage; minimum, normal and maximum pool levels. Trap efficiency: Brune’s curve — trap efficiency vs capacity/inflow ratio; large reservoirs trap ≈ 90–100% of sediment. Sediment in Pakistan reservoirs: Tarbela and Mangla have lost a significant part of their original storage to sediment, a key reason for new storages. Life of reservoir: Usually taken as the time until ≈ 50–80% of capacity is silted (depends on purpose). Mass curve (Rippl) method

Storage zones: Dead storage (below minimum drawdown — sediment), live/useful storage (between MDDL & normal pool), flood storage/surcharge (between normal pool and maximum water level), freeboard above MWL. Mass curve (Rippl) method: Storage required = maximum cumulative deficiency between demand line and inflow mass curve; sequent-peak algorithm for computation. Reservoir sedimentation: Trap efficiency vs capacity/inflow ratio (Brune's curve); Tarbela & Mangla losing live storage to silt — reason for raising Mangla (2009) and for new dams. Yield: Firm (safe) yield — guaranteed in the critical dry period; secondary yield — available in wetter years. Droughts: Meteorological, hydrological, agricultural; indices SPI, PDSI. Mass-curve method: draw demand lines tangent at the peaks of the inflow mass curve — the largest vertical gap to the next trough = required storage.

Rivers by stage: rocky/mountain (incised), boulder, alluvial (trough), tidal/delta. Alluvial rivers: aggrading (silting), degrading (scouring), meandering (single sinuous channel), braided (multiple channels, wide shallow). Meander ratio = meander belt / meander length. Tortuosity = curved length / straight length (> 1). Objectives of training: high flood protection, safe passage of flood, sediment control, navigable depth, stable course near structures.

Guide banks (Bell's bunds): confine river to approach bridge/barrage; length ≈ 1.1–1.5 × Lacey's waterway u/s, 0.1–0.25 d/s. Marginal embankments / levees: parallel to river to prevent spill. Groynes / spurs: transverse structures. Attracting spur points downstream, repelling spur points upstream, deflecting spur is perpendicular & short. Pitching & launching apron: stone protection of slopes; apron settles into scour hole. Artificial cut-offs: shorten meander loops. Pitched islands, bank revetment, closure dykes. Lacey's waterway: P = 4.75 √Q. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Lacey’s scour depth: R = 0.47 (Q/f)^(1/3); maximum scour depth below HFL ≈ 1.25R (straight reach), 1.5R (moderate bend), 1.75R (severe bend), 2R (right-angled bend); larger (≈ 2–2.75R) at noses of guide banks/spurs. Guide bank length: Upstream ≈ 1.0–1.5 × waterway length; downstream ≈ 0.25 × waterway (Spring’s/Gales’ practice). Spur types (by action): Attracting (points d/s), deflecting (normal to flow), repelling (points u/s); also by construction — permeable / impermeable, submerged / non-submerged. Repelling spur points UPSTREAM and pushes the river away; attracting spur points DOWNSTREAM and attracts the river towards the bank.

Aquifer: stores & transmits water (sand, gravel). Aquitard: stores, transmits slowly (sandy clay). Aquiclude: stores, does not transmit (clay). Aquifuge: neither (solid rock). Unconfined (water table) aquifer: upper surface at atmospheric pressure. Confined (artesian): between impervious layers; under pressure. Perched aquifer: above main water table on local impervious lens. Porosity = specific yield + specific retention. Storage coefficient: volume released per unit area per unit head decline (confined: 10⁻⁵–10⁻³; unconfined ≈ specific yield). Transmissivity T = K·b (b = aquifer thickness). Darcy's law: V = K i; valid for laminar flow (Re < 1). Well (Dupuit–Thiem) Discharge Unconfined aquifer Q = πK (H² − h²) / ln(R/r) Confined aquifer Q = 2πKb (H − h) / ln(R/r) Open wells: shallow (in unconfined aquifer) / deep; yield by recuperation test; specific capacity. Tube wells: strainer type, cavity type, slotted type; well development removes fines around screen; gravel pack well. Cone of depression, radius of influence, drawdown – key well terms. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Specific capacity: Well discharge per unit drawdown (m³/day per m). Pumping tests: Theis (non-equilibrium), Jacob’s straight-line method, recovery test — give T and S. Well development: Surging, back-washing, over-pumping, compressed air — removes fines and increases yield. Interference: Overlapping cones of depression reduce yields of nearby wells; maintain s
More on this topic — Engineering Hydrology: Groundwater Hydrology

Aquifer types: Aquifer (stores & yields), aquitard (leaky, low permeability), aquiclude (stores but does not transmit — clay), aquifuge (neither — solid granite). Confined vs unconfined: Unconfined: water table at atmospheric pressure; confined (artesian): between impermeable layers, piezometric surface above top; flowing well if piezometric surface is above ground. Properties: Porosity n, specific yield Sy (+ specific retention Sr = n), storativity S (confined ≈ 10⁻⁵–10⁻³; unconfined ≈ Sy), transmissivity T = K b. Darcy's law: Q = K i A; valid for laminar flow (Re < 1–10). Steady well flow (Thiem/Dupuit): Confined: Q = 2πKb(h₂ − h₁)/ln(r₂/r₁); unconfined: Q = πK(h₂² − h₁²)/ln(r₂/r₁). Unsteady (Theis): s = Q W(u)/(4πT), u = r²S/(4Tt); Cooper–Jacob approximation for u < 0.01. Pakistan: Indus Basin aquifer is one of the largest in the world; over-pumping lowers water tables (Lahore, Quetta). Waterlogging & salinity tackled by SCARP tubewells. Specific yield + specific retention = porosity. Cone of depression extends to the radius of influence R.

One of the largest contiguous gravity irrigation systems in the world. Indus Waters Treaty: signed 19 Sept 1960 in Karachi between Pakistan (Ayub Khan) and India (Nehru), brokered by World Bank. Eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) → India. Western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) → Pakistan. Indus Basin Project (replacement works): Mangla Dam (Jhelum, 1967), Tarbela Dam (Indus, 1976; one of world's largest earth/rockfill dams), 5 barrages, 1 siphon and 8 link canals. System has 3 major reservoirs (Tarbela, Mangla, Chashma), 12 inter-river link canals, ~45 canal commands and 100,000+ watercourses. Water Apportionment Accord: 1991 (between provinces). IRSA (Indus River System Authority) set up 1992 to implement it.

River Barrages / Headworks (u/s → d/s) Indus Jinnah (Kalabagh), Chashma, Taunsa, Guddu, Sukkur, Kotri (Ghulam Muhammad) Jhelum Rasul Chenab Marala, Khanki, Qadirabad, Trimmu, Panjnad Ravi Balloki, Sidhnai Sutlej Sulemanki, Islam Sukkur Barrage (1932): formerly Lloyd Barrage; feeds 7 canals; among the largest single barrage irrigation systems. Panjnad: confluence of five eastern/central rivers before joining Indus. Other dams: Warsak (Kabul River), Hub Dam, Khanpur Dam (Haro River), Rawal Dam (Korang), Simly Dam; Diamer-Bhasha & Mohmand dams (under construction). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 24.1 — Schematic of the Indus Basin rivers with main dams and barrages (not to scale). New storages (2026): WAPDA is executing Mohmand Dam (Swat River), Tarbela 5th Extension, Diamer-Bhasha Dam and the Dasu Hydropower Project, besides the K-IV Karachi water scheme. Diamer-Bhasha Dam: ≈ 272 m high — the highest RCC dam in the world; gross storage ≈ 8.1 MAF; ≈ 4,500 MW; Indus diverted in December 2023; still under construction. Dasu Hydropower Project: 4,320 MW run-of-river project on the Indus, built in two stages; river diverted in February 2023. Mohmand Dam: Concrete-face rockfill dam on the Swat River; ≈ 1.2–1.29 MAF storage, 800 MW; flood relief for Peshawar, Charsadda and Nowshera; completion expected around 2027-28. Tarbela extensions: 4th and 5th extensions raise installed capacity from 4,888 MW to 6,418 MW. Indus Waters Treaty —

Duty is expressed in ha/cumec; delta in cm or m. Δ = 8.64 B/D — Δ (m), B (days), D (ha/cumec). Crop with highest delta: rice. Most efficient irrigation method: drip. Kennedy's theory based on Upper Bari Doab Canal. Kennedy critical velocity: V₀ = 0.55 D^0.64. Lacey silt factor: f = 1.76 √d (mm). Lacey wetted perimeter: P = 4.75 √Q. Lacey regime section shape: semi-ellipse. Bligh: horizontal and vertical creep given equal weight. Lane: horizontal creep weighted 1/3. Khosla: failure (piping) starts at downstream end — d/s cut-off essential. Cross regulator is built in the parent canal d/s of off-take. Gibb's module is a rigid module; open flume is semi-modular. Drain over canal with canal running free: super passage. Watershed canal needs no cross-drainage works. Sarda fall is a vertical drop type fall. Gravity dam no-tension: resultant in middle third. Most common cause of earth dam failure: overtopping. Phreatic line in earth dam: base parabola (Casagrande). U/s slope of earth dam critical during sudden drawdown. Most common spillway in gravity dams: ogee. Spillway with automatic action and constant pool: siphon spillway. Steady (best) hydraulic jump: Froude number 4.5 – 9. Most accurate method of average rainfall: isohyetal. Non-recording rain gauge: Symon's gauge. Channel flood routing: Muskingum. Aquiclude: clay (stores but does not transmit). Sodic soil reclaimed with gypsum. Saline soil: EC > 4 dS/m, ESP < 15, pH < 8.5. Attracting spur points downstream; repelling spur p

Fig. 28.1 — The hydrologic cycle: precipitation, interception, infiltration, runoff, evaporation and transpiration. Hydrology: Science of the occurrence, circulation and distribution of water on Earth; engineering hydrology deals with estimating design flows, yields and storages. Water budget: P − R − G − E − T = ΔS (precipitation − runoff − groundwater outflow − evaporation − transpiration = change in storage). Catchment (watershed / drainage basin): Area draining to a single outlet, bounded by the water divide (ridge line). Global distribution: ≈ 97% of Earth's water is in oceans; ≈ 2% in ice caps/glaciers; < 1% is fresh liquid water (mostly groundwater). Applications: Design floods for spillways, bridges, culverts and drains; reservoir capacity; irrigation & water-supply yield; flood forecasting; drought studies. Residence time: atmosphere ≈ 8–10 days, rivers ≈ 2 weeks, oceans ≈ 3,000+ years, deep groundwater ≈ up to 10,000 years.
More on this topic — Irrigation Engineering: Hydrology (Brief)

Hydrological cycle: evaporation → condensation → precipitation → infiltration/runoff → back to sea. Rain gauges: non-recording – Symon's gauge; recording – tipping bucket, weighing bucket, float (natural siphon) type. Average rainfall: arithmetic mean (flat, uniform), Thiessen polygon (weights by area), isohyetal (most accurate). Infiltration: Horton's equation f = f_c + (f₀ − f_c) e^(−kt); φ-index (avg rate above which rainfall = runoff); W-index. Rational formula: Q = CIA/3.6 (Q m³/s, I mm/h, A km²); for small catchments. Hydrograph: rising limb, crest (peak), recession limb; base flow + direct runoff. Unit hydrograph (Sherman, 1932): hydrograph of 1 cm direct runoff from rain of unit duration uniformly over catchment. S-curve used to change duration. Flood routing: reservoir – Modified Puls / Goodrich method; channel – Muskingum method. Return period: T = 1/P. Risk: R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ over n years. Gumbel's method for flood frequency. Design floods: PMF (probable maximum flood) for large dams; SPF (standard project flood). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 28.2 — Flood hydrograph: rising limb, crest, recession limb, base flow and direct runoff. Runoff estimation: Rational formula (small catchments), Dickens / Ryves (empirical), unit hydrograph (medium), SCS-CN method (curve number). S-curve: Used to change the duration of a unit hydrograph. Double-mass curve: Checks consistency of rain-gauge records. Network design: Minimum

Forms: Rain (> 0.5 mm drops), drizzle (< 0.5 mm, intensity < 1 mm/h), snow, sleet, hail (> 8 mm ice balls), glaze. Types by lifting mechanism: Convective (local heating, thunderstorms), orographic (forced over mountains — monsoon in northern Pakistan), cyclonic/frontal (warm & cold fronts; western disturbances in winter). Non-recording gauge: Symon's (standard) gauge — 127 mm funnel, read daily at 8:30 AM (IMD/PMD practice). Recording gauges: Tipping-bucket (0.25 mm buckets, electronic pulses), weighing-bucket (records snow too), natural-siphon/float (Hellmann) — give the mass curve and intensity. Gauge siting: Distance from obstruction ≥ 2 × its height (preferably 4×); level ground, fenced enclosure. Optimum number of gauges: N = (Cv/ε)², Cv = coefficient of variation of existing gauge records, ε = allowable error (%; usually 10%). Missing data: Arithmetic mean if normal annual rainfalls differ < 10%; otherwise normal-ratio method: Px = (Nx/n) Σ(Pi/Ni). Consistency check: Double-mass curve: cumulative station rainfall vs cumulative group mean; a break in slope shows a change (correct by slope ratio). Mean areal rainfall: Arithmetic mean (flat, dense network); Thiessen polygon (area-weighted, most common); Isohyetal (most accurate, uses orography). DAD curves: Depth–Area–Duration: average depth decreases exponentially with area for a given duration (P = P₀ e^(−kAⁿ)). Fig. 29.1 — Intensity–Duration–Frequency curves: intensity falls with duration and rises with return period. I

Evaporation factors: Vapour-pressure difference (Dalton's law E = C(ew − ea)), temperature, wind, atmospheric pressure, dissolved salts (salinity reduces evaporation). Measurement: Class-A pan (USWB, 1210 mm dia, 255 mm deep); pan coefficient ≈ 0.7 (lake evaporation = 0.7 × pan). Colorado sunken pan coefficient ≈ 0.78. Evaporation reduction: Cetyl alcohol (hexadecanol) monomolecular films, wind breaks, floating covers, reducing surface area. Evapotranspiration: PET (water not limiting) vs AET; estimated by Penman / Penman–Monteith (FAO-56), Blaney–Criddle, Thornthwaite, Hargreaves; measured with lysimeters. Infiltration: Entry of water into soil surface; percolation = downward movement below the root zone. Infiltration capacity fc depends on soil type, moisture, cover, compaction and temperature. Horton equation: f = fc + (f₀ − fc) e^(−kt) — capacity decays exponentially to a constant rate. Other models: Philip: F = S t½ + K t; Green–Ampt (physically based); Kostiakov. Infiltration indices: φ-index = constant rate above which rainfall volume = runoff volume; W-index = φ excluding initial losses (W ≤ φ). Measurement: Double-ring (flooding) infiltrometer — outer ring prevents lateral spreading; rainfall simulators. φ-index: rainfall above φ = runoff. For a storm, total rain − runoff = losses; find φ by trial so that Σ(i − φ)·Δt = runoff depth.

Stage: Water-surface elevation; measured by staff gauge, wire gauge, float recorder, bubble gauge, radar/pressure sensor. Area–velocity method: Q = Σ (a_i v_i). Current meter (cup type — Price; propeller type) with rating V = a N + b (N = revolutions/time). Velocity sampling: Single point at 0.6 d (shallow, < 3 m) or mean of 0.2 d & 0.8 d (deep). Surface velocity × 0.85 ≈ mean velocity. Section computation: Mid-section method or mean-section method; segments should carry ≤ 10% of total discharge. Other methods: Float method (rough), dilution/tracer (mountain streams), ultrasonic (ADCP), electromagnetic, slope-area (Manning) for past floods, weirs & flumes (Parshall) for small channels. Rating curve: Stage–discharge relation Q = Cr (G − a)^β fitted by log regression; extended by log-log or Stevens method; loop rating under unsteady flow. Mean velocity ≈ velocity at 0.6 depth from surface ≈ average of velocities at 0.2 d and 0.8 d.

Fig. 32.1 — Components of a flood hydrograph and base-flow separation. Runoff components: Surface (overland) flow, interflow (subsurface storm flow) and base flow (groundwater). Direct runoff = surface + prompt interflow. Stream types: Perennial (always flows — base flow), intermittent (flows in wet season), ephemeral (only after storms; arid areas). Hydrograph parts: Rising limb (concentration curve), crest/peak, falling limb (recession), inflection point (end of direct-runoff inflow). Base-flow separation: Straight-line method; fixed-base length N = 0.83 A^0.2 (N in days, A in km²); variable-slope method. Factors affecting shape: Climatic (intensity, duration, storm movement — storms moving downstream give higher peaks) and physiographic (area, shape — fan-shaped basins give sharp peaks, slope, drainage density, land use). Time of concentration tc: Time for runoff from the hydraulically most remote point to reach the outlet. Kirpich: tc = 0.01947 L^0.77 S^−0.385 (min; L in m, S in m/m). Rational method: Qp = C i A / 3.6 (Qp m³/s, i mm/h, A km²) or Q = 0.278 C i A; i for duration = tc; for small catchments (< 50 km², urban drains, culverts). Fig. 32.2 — SCS-CN runoff equation for different curve numbers. SCS Curve Number: Q = (P − 0.2S)² / (P + 0.8S) for P > 0.2S; S = 25400/CN − 254 (mm). CN depends on hydrologic soil group (A–D), land use/cover and antecedent moisture (AMC I dry, II normal, III wet). Runoff coefficient C (typical): Roofs/pavement 0.7–0.95; lawns 0.05–0.35;

Definition: D-h unit hydrograph: DRH from 1 cm (or 1 mm/1 inch) of effective rainfall uniformly distributed over the basin in D hours (Sherman, 1932). Assumptions: Time invariance and linear response — principle of proportionality (ordinates ∝ rainfall excess) and superposition; uniform rainfall in space and time. Derivation: Separate base flow → DRH; effective rain depth = DRH volume / area; UH ordinates = DRH ordinates / effective depth. Volume check: Σ UH ordinates × Δt = 1 cm × A → for 1-cm UH: Σ Q (m³/s) × Δt (h) × 0.36 = A (km²). Multiple storms: Successive storms: lag and add (superposition); complex storms: matrix method or successive subtraction (as in the CE-323 final paper: UH3 from three 3-h storms). Fig. 33.1 — S-curve method to change unit-hydrograph duration. Changing duration: Lagging method if T = n·D (add n UHs lagged by D, divide by n); S-curve method for any T: UH_T = (S(t) − S(t − T)) × D/T. S-curve equilibrium discharge: Qe = 2.778 A / D (Qe m³/s, A km², D h). IUH: Instantaneous unit hydrograph: D → 0; Nash model (cascade of n linear reservoirs), Clark model (time-area + linear reservoir). To convert UH3 to UH6: lagging method works (6 = 2 × 3); add UH3 and UH3 lagged by 3 h, divide by 2.

Need: Ungauged catchments — UH derived from basin characteristics. Snyder (1938): Basin lag tp = Ct (L·Lc)^0.3 (h; L, Lc in km, Ct 1.35–1.65); peak Qp = 2.78 Cp A / tp; standard duration tr = tp/5.5; base T = 3 + 3(tp/24) days. SCS dimensionless UH: tp = D/2 + tlag; tlag ≈ 0.6 tc; Qp = 2.08 A / tp (A km², tp h, Qp m³/s per cm); base ≈ 2.67 tp (triangular). Others: Gray, Espey, Clark time-area method, geomorphological IUH. SCS triangular UH: time base = 2.67 tp, recession = 1.67 tp; peak factor 484 (US units) ↔ 2.08 (SI with A in km²).

Return period: T = 1/P; probability of at least one exceedance in n years: R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ (risk). Reliability = (1 − 1/T)ⁿ. Plotting position: Weibull: T = (N + 1)/m (m = rank in descending order). Chow's general equation: x_T = x̄ + K σ. Gumbel (EV-I): K = −(√6/π)[0.5772 + ln ln(T/(T − 1))]; reduced variate y = −ln ln(T/(T − 1)); for finite N use ȳn, Sn tables. Log-Pearson Type III: Used in US (Bulletin 17C); applied to log Q with skew coefficient. Empirical formulas: Dickens Q = C A^¾; Ryves Q = C A^⅔; Inglis Q = 124 A/√(A + 10.4) (A km²). Design floods: Spillways of major dams — PMF (probable maximum flood); barrages/major bridges — 100–1000-yr flood; culverts — 25–50 yr; urban drains — 2–10 yr. PMP: Probable maximum precipitation — by storm maximisation/transposition or Hershfield statistical method (K ≈ 15). Risk of a 100-yr flood being exceeded at least once in 100 years = 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 63%.

Fig. 36.1 — Reservoir routing: peak attenuation and lag; the outflow peak occurs where outflow equals inflow. Purpose: Determine the outflow hydrograph at a downstream point from the inflow hydrograph — attenuation (peak reduction) and translation (lag). Continuity: I − O = dS/dt → ((I₁ + I₂)/2)Δt − ((O₁ + O₂)/2)Δt = S₂ − S₁. Reservoir (level-pool) routing: Modified Puls / storage-indication: (2S₂/Δt + O₂) = (I₁ + I₂) + (2S₁/Δt − O₁); Goodrich method. Linear reservoir: S = K O → O₂ = C₁ I₁ + C₂ I₂ + C₃ O₁ with routing coefficients from K and Δt (CE-323 final: K = 2 h, Δt = 1 h). Channel routing — Muskingum: S = K[x I + (1 − x) O]; O₂ = C₀I₂ + C₁I₁ + C₂O₁; C₀ = (−Kx + 0.5Δt)/(K − Kx + 0.5Δt), C₁ = (Kx + 0.5Δt)/(K − Kx + 0.5Δt), C₂ = (K − Kx − 0.5Δt)/(K − Kx + 0.5Δt); C₀ + C₁ + C₂ = 1. Muskingum x: 0 (reservoir) to 0.5 (pure translation); natural channels 0.1–0.3; K ≈ travel time; stability needs 2Kx ≤ Δt ≤ 2K(1 − x). Hydraulic routing: Saint-Venant equations; kinematic & diffusion wave approximations; Muskingum–Cunge. In level-pool routing the outflow peak lies on the falling limb of the inflow hydrograph (I = O at that instant, storage is maximum).

Experiments: Rainfall–runoff on hydrology bench (lag time, hydrograph shape), infiltration with double-ring infiltrometer, scour around bridge piers in a flume, stream gauging with current meter. Scour: Local scour depth at piers increases with flow velocity, pier width and is reduced by pier nose shape/collar; Lacey normal scour depth R = 0.473 (Q/f)^(1/3). Data handling: Plot contour/surface (Surfer) of scour bed; compare observed vs predicted using RMSE and R².

Symon's gauge = non-recording; tipping-bucket gives intensity; Thiessen polygons = area weights. Horton: f = fc + (f₀ − fc)e^(−kt); φ-index ≥ W-index. Unit hydrograph = 1 cm effective rain in D hours; S-curve changes duration; Qe = 2.778A/D. Rational method for small areas; SCS-CN with S = 25400/CN − 254 mm. Gumbel EV-I and Log-Pearson III for flood frequency; Weibull plotting T = (N + 1)/m. Aquiclude stores but does not transmit; aquifuge neither stores nor transmits.

Surveying: art of determining relative positions of points on, above or below the earth's surface by measuring distances, directions and elevations. Two basic principles: (1) work from whole to part (prevents accumulation of errors); (2) locate a new point by at least two independent measurements from known points. Plane surveying: earth treated as flat; curvature ignored; areas < 250 km² (or ~195.5 km² per some texts). Geodetic surveying: curvature considered; large areas; done by Survey of Pakistan / national agencies. Difference between arc and chord over 18.5 km ≈ 1 cm; sum of angles of a spherical triangle exceeds 180° by 1″ per ~196 km² (spherical excess).

By instrument: chain, compass, plane table, theodolite, tacheometric, EDM/total station, GPS, photogrammetric. By purpose: engineering, military, mine, geological, archaeological. By object/nature of field: land (topographic, cadastral, city), marine/hydrographic, astronomical. Cadastral survey: fixes property boundaries. Topographic survey: natural and man-made features with relief.

Representative Fraction (RF) = map distance ÷ ground distance (same units). Plain scale: two dimensions (e.g. m and dm). Diagonal scale: three dimensions (m, dm, cm). Vernier: reads finer than smallest division. Least count = 1 MSD – 1 VSD = s/n (s = value of 1 MSD, n = no. of vernier divisions). Direct (forward) vernier: n VSD = (n–1) MSD. Retrograde vernier: n VSD = (n+1) MSD. Shrunk scale = shrinkage factor × original scale. Shrinkage factor = shrunk length ÷ original length. Large scale: 1 cm = 10 m or less (building sites). Small scale: 1 cm = 50 m or more (topographic maps). Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Survey of Pakistan: National mapping agency (HQ Rawalpindi) — topographic sheets (1:50,000 standard), geodetic control; heights are referred to mean sea level (Karachi tide gauge). Scale conversions: 1 cm = 10 m → RF 1:1000; 1 inch = 1 mile → RF 1:63,360. Diagonal scale: Reads three units (e.g., m, dm, cm) — based on similar triangles. Principle 1: work from whole to part (prevents accumulation of errors). Principle 2: locate a point by at least two independent measurements.

Mistakes (blunders): carelessness; detected by checks. Systematic (cumulative) errors: same sign and magnitude under same conditions; can be computed and corrected; vary directly with L. Accidental (compensating) errors: random; follow probability laws; vary with √L. Positive error: measured length > true length (e.g. tape too short). Negative error: tape too long. Most probable value: arithmetic mean of equal-weight observations; weighted mean otherwise. Weight ∝ 1/(variance); weight ∝ number of observations; for levelling weight ∝ 1/distance. Probable error of mean = probable error of single observation ÷ √n. Standard error ≈ 1.4826 × probable error (PE = 0.6745σ). Precision: closeness of repeated measurements. Accuracy: closeness to true value. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Accuracy vs precision: Accuracy = closeness to the true value; precision = closeness of repeated observations to each other. Systematic (cumulative) errors ∝ number of observations (or length); accidental errors ∝ √n.
Suitable for small, open, fairly level areas with simple details. Basis: triangulation (network of triangles). Well-conditioned triangle: no angle < 30° or > 120°; ideal equilateral (60°).

Bearing: horizontal angle of a line with a reference meridian. Meridians: true (geographic), magnetic, grid, arbitrary. Whole Circle Bearing (WCB): 0°–360° clockwise from north. Used in prismatic compass. Quadrantal / Reduced Bearing (QB/RB): 0°–90° from N or S towards E or W. Used in surveyor's compass. Back bearing = Fore bearing ± 180° (WCB). In QB: same value, change N↔S and E↔W. Feature Prismatic Compass Surveyor's Compass Graduations WCB, 0° at S end, inverted figures QB, 0° at N & S, E–W interchanged Ring Graduated ring fixed to needle (rotates with needle) Graduated ring fixed to box Reading Through prism; sighting & reading together Directly from top; separate Tripod May be held in hand Tripod essential Included angle = difference of bearings of the two lines (computed from bearings). Magnetic declination: angle between true and magnetic meridians. True bearing = Magnetic bearing + declination (E) / – declination (W). Isogonic lines: equal declination. Agonic line: zero declination. Isoclinic lines: equal dip. Aclinic line: zero dip (magnetic equator). Declination variations: secular (largest, ~250-year cycle), annual, diurnal (daily, more in summer), irregular (magnetic storms). Dip: angle of needle with horizontal; 0° at magnetic equator, 90° at magnetic poles. Balanced by rider on needle. Local attraction: deviation due to nearby iron, rails, cables. Detected when FB – BB ≠ 180°. Correct by starting from a station free of attraction (where difference is exactly 18

Rule: A line whose FB and BB differ by exactly 180° is free from local attraction; start corrections from its stations. Declination: True bearing = magnetic bearing + declination (E) or − declination (W). Prismatic compass: graduated ring rotates with needle, WCB, readings taken through prism; surveyor’s compass: ring fixed to box, QB, readings taken directly (inverted E–W).

Level surface: parallel to mean spheroidal surface of earth (e.g. still lake). Datum: reference surface (MSL in Pakistan: Karachi; India: Mumbai). Reduced Level (RL): height of a point above/below datum. Bench Mark (BM): fixed point of known RL. Types: GTS (Great Trigonometrical Survey), permanent, arbitrary, temporary. Line of collimation: line through intersection of cross hairs and optical centre of objective. Back Sight (BS): first reading after setting up (on known RL point; plus sight). Fore Sight (FS): last reading before shifting (minus sight). Intermediate Sight (IS): between BS and FS. Change point (turning point): point where both FS and BS are taken. Height of Instrument (HI) = RL of BM + BS.

Dumpy level: telescope rigidly fixed to vertical spindle; simple and stable. Tilting level: telescope tilts about horizontal axis with fine screw; main bubble centred each sighting. Wye (Y) level: telescope removable from Y-supports; easy adjustment but wear. Automatic (self-levelling) level: compensator; most common now. Digital level: reads bar-code staff. Levelling staff: self-reading (telescopic/Sopwith, folding) and target staff. Folding staff 4 m; 5 mm graduations. Temporary adjustments: setting up, levelling up, elimination of parallax (focus eyepiece first, then objective). Permanent adjustment of dumpy level: two-peg test (axis of bubble tube ⊥ vertical axis; line of collimation ∥ bubble tube axis).

Item HI (Collimation) Method Rise & Fall Method Arithmetic check ΣBS – ΣFS = Last RL – First RL ΣBS – ΣFS = ΣRise – ΣFall = Last RL – First RL Check on IS No check on intermediate RLs Complete check on all RLs Speed Faster; less calculation Laborious Best for Profile levelling, construction, contouring Fly levelling / accurate work

Simple, differential (compound/fly), profile (longitudinal section), cross-sectioning, reciprocal, precise, trigonometric, barometric, hypsometric (boiling point). Fly levelling: rough levelling to check BM or carry RL to work site. Check levelling: run at end of day to check the day's work. Reciprocal levelling: across rivers/valleys; eliminates collimation, curvature and refraction errors. True difference h = [(ha – hb) + (ha′ – hb′)]/2.

Correction Formula (d in km) Sign Curvature Cc = d²/(2R) = 0.0785 d² (m) – Refraction Cr = Cc/7 = 0.0112 d² (m) + Combined C = 0.0673 d² (m) – Distance to visible horizon d = 3.855 √C (km, C in m) — Refraction coefficient m ≈ 0.07 (about 1/7 of curvature). Refraction is maximum near ground and at sunrise/sunset. Equal BS and FS distances eliminate collimation error and curvature-refraction effects.

Sensitivity of bubble tube = angle (in seconds) per one division of tube; α″ = (s/(nD)) × 206265 (s = staff difference, n = divisions moved, D = distance). Sensitivity increases with radius of curvature of tube, length, larger diameter, low viscosity liquid (spirit/alcohol). Permissible closing error (K in km): rough 0.100√K, ordinary 0.025√K, accurate 0.012√K, precise 0.006√K m. Error in levelling ∝ √(distance).
