HI method has no check on IS.

Contour: imaginary line joining points of equal elevation. Contour interval: vertical distance between consecutive contours; constant on a map. Depends on scale, nature of ground, purpose, time & funds. Horizontal equivalent: horizontal distance between two consecutive contours. Contour gradient: line on ground maintaining constant inclination (set with Abney level/tangent clinometer/ghat tracer).

Close together = steep slope; widely spaced = gentle slope; uniformly spaced = uniform slope. Equal spacing straight & parallel = plane surface. Closed contours with higher values inside = hill; lower values inside = depression (pond). Two contours never cross except at overhanging cliff; they may merge at vertical cliff. Contours cross ridge and valley lines at right angles. V-shape with apex towards higher ground = valley; towards lower ground = ridge. A contour cannot end abruptly; it closes on itself (within or outside map). Methods: direct (tracing contours on ground; accurate, slow) and indirect (grid of squares, cross sections, tacheometric, spot levels). Interpolation: estimation, arithmetic, graphical. Uses: intervisibility, catchment area, reservoir capacity, route alignment, earthwork estimation, sections. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 6.1 — Contour shapes for a hill, depression, ridge and valley. Choice of contour interval: Depends on scale, purpose, nature of ground and time/funds: ≈ 0.5 m flat ground, 1–2 m for buildings/roads, 5–10 m for hilly terrain at small scales. Interpolation: By estimation, arithmetic calculation or graphical method between spot levels. A contour cannot split or end inside the map; overhanging cliff is the only case where contours cross; vertical cliff → contours merge.

Field work and plotting done simultaneously; graphical method; suitable for small scale and details; not for wet climate or high accuracy. Accessories: drawing board, alidade (plain or telescopic), spirit level, trough compass (orientation to magnetic north), U-frame with plumb bob, drawing paper. Setting up: levelling, centring, orientation. Orientation (most important): by back-sighting (most accurate) or by magnetic needle (compass).

Radiation: from one station; small areas, all points visible. Intersection (graphic triangulation): two stations; locate inaccessible points; well-conditioned rays. Traversing: like compass/theodolite traverse; for roads, rivers. Resection: locate the station occupied by the table from known points.

Two-point problem: two visible known points; needs an auxiliary station; less accurate, more time. Three-point problem: three visible known points. Solved by: mechanical (tracing paper), graphical (Bessel's method), trial & error (triangle of error / Lehmann's method). Lehmann's rules: point lies on same side of all three rays; distance from each ray proportional to distance of the station; if station is outside great triangle, point lies outside the triangle of error. Great circle (danger circle): circle through the three known points; if station lies on it, solution is indeterminate. Errors: instrumental, manipulation & sighting, plotting. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Orientation methods: By compass (quick), by back-sighting (most accurate), by resection. Plane table errors: Non-horizontal board, bad centring, defective alidade, incorrect orientation, drawing errors. Three-point problem methods: mechanical (tracing paper), graphical (Bessel’s), trial & error (Lehmann’s); two-point problem needs an auxiliary station.

Most precise instrument for horizontal and vertical angles; also used for prolonging lines, levelling, traverse. Transit theodolite: telescope can revolve 360° about horizontal axis. Non-transit: cannot. Size: diameter of graduated lower circle (e.g. 10 cm, 12 cm). Least count of vernier theodolite usually 20″.

Levelling head (tribrach with foot screws), lower plate (scale plate) with lower clamp, upper plate (vernier plate) with upper clamp, standards (A-frame), telescope, vertical circle, plate levels, altitude bubble, plumb bob.

Centring: placing vertical axis over station. Transiting (plunging/reversing): turning telescope through 180° in vertical plane. Swinging: turning telescope in horizontal plane. Right swing = clockwise. Face left (normal): vertical circle on left of observer. Face right (inverted). Changing face: transit + swing 180°. Vertical axis, horizontal (trunnion) axis, line of collimation (line of sight), axis of plate level, axis of altitude level.
Axis of plate level ⊥ vertical axis. Line of collimation ⊥ horizontal (trunnion) axis. Axis of altitude level ∥ line of collimation (vertical circle index error).

Repetition method: angle measured cumulatively n times on the circle; eliminates graduation errors, improves accuracy beyond least count. Used for single angles. Reiteration method (direction method): several angles at one station measured successively; closing the horizon; sum should be 360°. Used in triangulation. Face left + face right mean eliminates: collimation error, trunnion axis error, index error of vertical circle, eccentricity of verniers. Errors NOT eliminated by face change: plate level error (vertical axis not truly vertical). Eccentricity of circles eliminated by reading both verniers (A and B). Deflection angle: angle a line makes with prolongation of previous line (R or L, 0°–180°); used for roads, railways. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Least count of vernier theodolite: Commonly 20″ (vernier) — modern digital theodolites read 1″–5″. Errors eliminated by face left/face right: Line of collimation not ⊥ horizontal axis, horizontal axis not ⊥ vertical axis, index error of vertical circle, eccentricity of verniers. Repetition method eliminates errors of graduation and improves accuracy for single angles; reiteration (direction) method for many angles from one station (triangulation).

Traverse: series of connected lines whose lengths and directions are measured. Closed traverse: forms a closed polygon or starts and ends at known points; check available. Open traverse: no check (roads, rivers, pipelines). Methods: chain angle, compass (free needle), theodolite (fast needle / included angle / deflection angle), plane table. Sum of interior angles = (2n – 4) × 90°. Sum of exterior angles = (2n + 4) × 90°. Sum of deflection angles = 360° (algebraic).

Latitude L = l cos θ (N +, S –). Departure D = l sin θ (E +, W –). θ = reduced bearing. Closed traverse: ΣL = 0 and ΣD = 0. Closing error e = √[(ΣL)² + (ΣD)²]. Direction: tan δ = ΣD/ΣL. Relative precision = e/(perimeter). Typical: compass 1:300–1:600; theodolite 1:1000–1:5000 or better.

Bowditch (compass) rule: correction ∝ length of line. CL = ΣL × (l/Σl). Used when angular and linear measurements are equally precise. Transit rule: correction ∝ latitude/departure. CL = ΣL × (L/ΣL_arith). Used when angles are more precise than lengths. Graphical method: compass traverse adjustment by Bowditch principle. Axis method: when angles are accurate and linear errors are along a particular line. Consecutive coordinates: L and D of each line. Independent (total) coordinates: referred to a common origin; used for plotting. Gale's traverse table: tabulation of computations for coordinates. Omitted measurements: max two unknowns (one length + one bearing, two lengths, two bearings, etc.) can be computed. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 9.1 — Closed traverse: latitudes, departures, closing error and balancing rules.

Given: Line AB = 200 m, WCB = 60°. Answer: Latitude = 200 cos60° = +100 m (N); departure = 200 sin60° = +173.2 m (E). Relative precision: Closing error / perimeter, e.g., 0.5 m / 2000 m = 1 in 4000. Bowditch rule when angles and lengths are equally precise; transit rule when angles are more precise than lengths.

Horizontal and vertical distances obtained optically (no chaining); fast; for hilly/broken ground, contouring, route surveys. Instrument: tacheometer = theodolite with stadia diaphragm (3 horizontal hairs).

Horizontal line of sight: D = (f/i)s + (f + d) = Ks + C. K = multiplying constant = f/i = 100 (usually). C = additive constant = f + d (≈ 0 with anallactic lens). Anallactic lens: convex lens between objective and eyepiece in external-focusing telescope; makes C = 0. Internal-focusing telescopes have C ≈ 0 naturally. Inclined sight, staff vertical: D = Ks cos²θ + C cos θ;  V = (Ks sin 2θ)/2 + C sin θ. RL of staff station = RL of instrument axis ± V – h (h = central hair reading). Other methods: movable hair (subtense), tangential method (two vertical angles), subtense bar (2 m bar, D = cot(α/2)). Accuracy of stadia: about 1 in 300 to 1 in 500. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 10.1 — Stadia tacheometry: staff intercept s and horizontal distance D = Ks + C. Worked example: s = 1.50 m, K = 100, C = 0, horizontal sight → D = 150 m. Subtense bar: 2 m invar bar; D = (b/2) cot(α/2) — tangential/subtense methods for difficult terrain. Anallactic lens makes the additive constant C = 0 (multiplying constant K = 100).

Horizontal curves: simple circular, compound (two arcs, same direction), reverse (two arcs, opposite directions), transition (spiral). Vertical curves: summit (crest) and valley (sag); usually parabolic.
Simple Circular Curve – Elements (R = radius, Δ = deflection angle)

Element Formula Tangent length T R tan(Δ/2) Length of curve l πRΔ/180 Long chord L 2R sin(Δ/2) External distance E R[sec(Δ/2) – 1] Mid-ordinate M (versine) R[1 – cos(Δ/2)] Chainage of T1 Chainage of PI – T Chainage of T2 Chainage of T1 + l Degree of curve D: angle subtended at centre by a standard chord/arc. For 30 m arc: R = 1719/D; for 20 m arc: R = 1146/D (m). For 100 ft chord: R ≈ 5730/D (ft). Smaller radius = sharper curve = larger degree. Apex angle (intersection angle) = 180° – Δ.

Linear (chain & tape): offsets from long chord, offsets from tangents (radial/perpendicular), successive bisection of arcs, offsets from chords produced (best linear method). Offset from chord produced: O1 = C1²/(2R); On = Cn(Cn-1 + Cn)/(2R). Angular (instrumental): Rankine's method of tangential (deflection) angles — one theodolite + tape; most common. δ (minutes) = 1718.9 C/R. Two-theodolite method: no tape needed; for rough ground. Tacheometric method also possible.

Purpose: gradual introduction of curvature and super-elevation; radius varies from ∞ (at tangent) to R (at circular curve). Ideal: clothoid (Euler spiral) — radius × length = constant. Railways: cubic parabola. Highways: lemniscate (Bernoulli) / spiral. Shift S = L²/(24R).  Spiral angle φ = L/(2R) radians. Length of transition: by rate of change of centrifugal acceleration L = v³/(CR); by rate of super-elevation; by time rate. Super-elevation (cant): e = v²/(gR) (theoretical); railways e = GV²/(127R) (G = gauge, V km/h); roads e + f = V²/(127R).

Parabola used: constant rate of change of grade; offsets ∝ square of distance from tangent point. Length L = (g1 – g2)/r, where r = rate of change of grade. Sight distance governs summit curve length; headlight distance governs valley curve. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 11.1 — Elements of a simple circular curve: PC, PI, PT, R, Δ, tangent length, long chord, mid-ordinate.

Given: R = 300 m, Δ = 40°, chainage of PI = 1250.00 m. Tangent length: T = 300 tan 20° = 109.19 m → chainage PC = 1140.81 m. Curve length: l = π × 300 × 40/180 = 209.44 m → chainage PT = 1350.25 m. Rankine’s deflection angle: δ (minutes) = 1718.9 c/R for chord length c. Rankine’s method (theodolite + tape) is most accurate for long curves; offsets from long chord / tangents suit short curves.

From field notes: division into triangles, squares, trapezoids. Mid-ordinate rule: A = d × (O1 + O2 + … + On) (mid-ordinates). Average ordinate rule: A = L × (ΣO)/(n + 1). Trapezoidal rule: A = (d/2)[O1 + On + 2(O2 + … + On-1)]. Any number of ordinates. Simpson's 1/3 rule: A = (d/3)[O1 + On + 4(even ordinates) + 2(remaining odd ordinates)]. Needs odd number of ordinates (even number of divisions). More accurate (parabolic boundary). By coordinates: A = ½|Σ(xi yi+1 – xi+1 yi)|. Also by double meridian distance (DMD) and latitudes/departures. Planimeter (Amsler polar): A = M(F – I ± 10N + C). M = multiplier, N = zero-mark passings, C = constant (added when anchor inside figure).

Trapezoidal (end-area) rule: V = (d/2)[A1 + An + 2(A2 + … + An-1)] — overestimates. Prismoidal (Simpson's) rule: V = (d/3)[A1 + An + 4(even) + 2(odd)]; for single prismoid V = (L/6)(A1 + 4Am + A2). Most accurate. Prismoidal correction = difference between end-area and prismoidal volumes. Curvature correction applied when section lies on a curve (Pappus theorem). Volume from spot levels: borrow pits (grid of squares/triangles). Volume from contours: reservoir capacity. Mass diagram: cumulative volume vs. chainage; rising = cutting, falling = filling; max ordinate = balance point; used for haul, lead and economical earthwork. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Simpson’s rule condition: Needs an ODD number of ordinates (even number of strips); more accurate than trapezoidal rule. Planimeter: Area = M (F − I ± 10N + C); zero circle constant C used when anchor is inside. Prismoidal correction: Volume by prismoidal formula is more accurate; trapezoidal (end-area) formula over-estimates. Mass-haul diagram: Rising line = cut, falling = fill; balancing line gives free-haul and over-haul for earthwork. Trapezoidal: A = d[(O₁ + On)/2 + O₂ + … + On₋₁]; Simpson: A = (d/3)[(O₁ + On) + 4Σ even + 2Σ odd].

Network of triangles with one base line measured accurately and all angles measured; other sides computed by sine rule. Used for large areas, geodetic and control surveys; more economical than traversing in hilly terrain. Order Base line accuracy Avg triangle closure Side length Primary (1st) 1 in 300,000 < 1″ 16–150 km Secondary (2nd) 1 in 150,000 3″ 8–65 km Tertiary (3rd) 1 in 75,000 6″ 1.5–10 km Figures: single triangles chain (fast, least check), braced quadrilaterals (best for accuracy), centred polygons, chain of quadrilaterals. Strength of figure: angles near 60°; avoid < 30°. Braced quadrilateral strongest. Satellite (eccentric) station: when main station cannot be occupied (e.g. church spire); reduction to centre correction applied. Intervisibility: height of signal/tower computed using curvature & refraction (h = 0.0673 d²). Signals: luminous (heliotrope — sun's rays; Gauss), opaque (pole, tripod). Phase error in opaque cylindrical signals. Base line correction & extension; base net to expand base. Trilateration: all sides measured (EDM) instead of angles. Station adjustment, figure adjustment; least squares used for adjustment. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 13.1 — Triangulation figures: chain of triangles, braced quadrilateral and centred polygon. Satellite station: Used when the true station cannot be occupied; reduction to centre applied to observed angles. Spherical excess: ≈ 1″ per 196 km² of triangle area —

Measures distance by phase difference of modulated electromagnetic waves. Microwave EDM (tellurometer): long ranges up to 100 km; two instruments. Infrared EDM (distomat): 3–5 km; reflector (prism) required. Visible light (geodimeter, laser): up to 25 km (laser longer). Accuracy expressed as ±(a mm + b ppm).

Electronic theodolite + EDM + microprocessor + data collector; measures horizontal angle, vertical angle and slope distance; computes coordinates, RL, area. Reflectorless total stations use laser; robotic total stations can be operated by one person.

Satellite-based positioning: minimum 4 satellites for 3D position + time (3 for 2D). GPS (USA, ~31 satellites, 6 orbital planes, ~20,200 km altitude), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU), BeiDou (China). Segments: space, control, user. Positioning by trilateration from satellite pseudo-ranges. DGPS (differential): uses base station correction; sub-metre accuracy. RTK: real-time kinematic; cm-level accuracy. Errors: ionospheric/tropospheric delay, multipath, clock, orbital, PDOP/GDOP (geometry).

Photogrammetry: measurements from photographs. Terrestrial (ground) and aerial. Scale of vertical photo S = f/(H – h) (f = focal length, H = flying height above datum, h = ground elevation). Relief displacement d = r h/H (displacement radial from principal point). Overlap: forward (longitudinal) ≈ 60%; side (lateral) ≈ 25–30%. Stereoscopic vision requires overlap. Tilted photo: tilt < 3°. Oblique: high (horizon visible) and low. Parallax bar: measures heights from stereo pairs. Stereoscope: lens or mirror type. Remote sensing: data from sensors without contact. Passive (uses sun energy) vs active (RADAR, LiDAR). GIS: system to capture, store, analyse and display spatial data; raster and vector models. LiDAR: laser pulses from aircraft/drone to produce DEMs. Drones (UAVs) used for rapid mapping. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) GNSS systems: GPS (USA), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU), BeiDou (China); RTK-GNSS gives cm-level accuracy using a base station or CORS. Total station functions: Angle + distance + coordinates; stake-out, resection, area, remote elevation measurement; data downloaded to CAD. LiDAR & drones: Airborne/UAV laser scanning and photogrammetry produce DEMs/point clouds for roads, dams and mining. GIS: Stores spatial data in vector (points, lines, polygons) and raster (cells) formats; used in urban planning, irrigation command areas, flood mapping. EDM types: microwave (long range), infrared/light-wave (most total sta

Hydrographic survey: water bodies; soundings to find depth; used for navigation, dredging, harbours. Sounding equipment: sounding rod (shallow), lead line, echo sounder (fathometer; most used). Locating soundings: cross-rope, range & time intervals, two angles from shore (theodolites), sextant (three-point problem), total station, GPS. Tide gauges: staff, float (self-registering), weight gauge. Mean sea level from long-term tide records (19-year cycle). Setting out works: buildings (centre line method), culverts, bridges, tunnels (transfer of alignment underground through shafts). Mine surveying: weisbach triangle for transferring meridian down a shaft. Barometric levelling: aneroid barometer; rough heights in hilly regions. Hypsometry: boiling point of water to find altitude.

Abney level (clinometer): measures slopes, heights; sets out gradients. Ceylon ghat tracer: sets out gradients in hilly areas. Indian pattern clinometer, tangent clinometer: vertical angles and gradients. Box sextant: measures horizontal and vertical angles (up to 120°); hand-held; used in hydrography. Hand level: rough levelling. Pantagraph: enlarging or reducing maps. Eidograph: same purpose. Planimeter: area of plan. Opisometer: length of curved lines on maps. Optical square: two mirrors at 45°; sets right angles. Prism square: same principle with prism. Line ranger: locating intermediate point on a line. Hypsometer: elevation from boiling point.

Agate cap: used in compass needle pivot. Prismatic compass: 0° marked at south end of ring (because prism is at opposite side). In surveyor's compass, E and W are interchanged on the ring. Sum of interior angles of 6-sided closed traverse = 720°. Bubble of level tube moves towards the higher end. Parallax: image not formed in plane of cross hairs; removed by focusing. HI method preferred for profile and construction work; rise & fall more accurate checks. Normal tension: pull at which sag and pull corrections cancel. Sag correction is always negative; slope correction always negative; MSL correction negative for points above MSL. Error due to bad ranging and bad straightening: cumulative and positive. Best chain line arrangement: few main lines, well-conditioned triangles, check lines provided. Contours of different elevations cannot unite to form one contour except at vertical cliff. Zero dip at magnetic equator; 90° dip at magnetic poles. Anallactic lens provided in external-focusing tacheometer to make additive constant zero. Multiplying constant of tacheometer usually 100. Rankine's method: deflection angles; most accurate for setting out long curves. Simpson's rule needs odd number of ordinates; trapezoidal rule assumes straight boundaries. Prismoidal formula gives most accurate earthwork volume. Danger circle in three-point problem: circle through three known points. A 30 m steel tape (standard at 20 °C, 100 N; A = 8 mm²; E = 200 GPa; α = 11.6 × 10⁻⁶/°C; w = 0.2 N/m) measures 240 m in catenary (8 spans) at 32 °C with 150 N pull. Ct = 11.6e−6 × 12 × 240 = +0.0334 m; Cp = 50 × 240/(8 × 200,000) = +0.0075 m; Cs = 8 × (6² × 30)/(24 × 150²) = −0.0160 m. Net = +0.0249 m → true length = 240.025 m.
Sight of 2 km: combined correction = 0.0673 × 2² = 0.269 m (subtract from staff reading).

Instrument near A: A = 1.625, B = 2.545. Instrument near B: A = 0.725, B = 1.695. True difference = [(2.545 − 1.625) + (1.695 − 0.725)]/2 = 0.945 m (B lower). Combined collimation/curvature error = [(0.920) − (0.970)]/2 = −0.025 m.

Closed traverse, perimeter 1000 m, ΣL = +0.30 m, ΣD = −0.40 m. e = √(0.30² + 0.40²) = 0.50 m; precision = 1 in 2000. For a 200 m line: correction to latitude = −0.30 × 200/1000 = −0.06 m; to departure = +0.40 × 200/1000 = +0.08 m.
Staff intercept 1.20 m, angle of elevation 8°, K = 100, C = 0: D = 100 × 1.2 × cos²8° = 117.68 m; V = 100 × 1.2 × sin 16°/2 = 16.54 m.
Sections 20 m apart: 20, 32, 50 m². Prismoidal (L = 40 m) = (40/6)(20 + 4 × 32 + 50) = 1,320 m³; end-area = (20/2)(20 + 2 × 32 + 50) = 1,340 m³ (end-area over-estimates).
f = 150 mm, flying height 3000 m above datum, ground at 500 m: S = 0.15/(3000 − 500) = 1 : 16,667.

Plan (noun): a physical representation (drawing/map) OR an orderly arrangement of parts of an objective. Planning: deliberately achieving an objective by assembling actions into an orderly sequence. Planning as general activity: making an orderly sequence of action leading to stated goals; techniques = written statements, statistical projections, mathematical representations, quantified evaluations, diagrams; may (not must) include physical blueprints. Urban planning: planning with a spatial/geographical component; aims at a spatial structure of activities (land uses) better than without planning. Also called: physical planning; "spatial planning" is the more neutral, precise term. Urban/regional planning is a special case of general planning that includes the plan‑making (representational) component (Hall, 2002). Urban planning integrates land use planning + transportation planning to improve built, economic and social environments. Regional planning: larger environment, less detailed level. Urban renewal: applying planning methods to existing cities suffering decay and lack of investment. Planned city: planned from inception, usually on previously undeveloped land; fewer land‑use conflicts.

Communities constantly change through development and population growth — planning controls rather than reacts. Planners prepare socio‑economic and physical design plans based on residents’ felt needs. Aims: preserve/enhance quality of life, protect physical & natural environment, promote economic growth. Stakes: planning decisions involve large sums of public/private money; deliver large gains to some and losses to others. Challenges: in a democratic society planning is tied to politics, law, economics and ideology. Best planners: master the technical side AND have "peripheral vision" — understand links with political, social, demographic and economic forces.

Term Meaning Hamlet Rural settlement too small to be a village Town Larger than a village, smaller than a city City Relatively large, permanent settlement; complex sanitation, utilities, land use, housing, transport; often has legal/administrative status Suburb Separate residential community within commuting distance of a city Exurbs Ring of prosperous communities beyond the suburbs; commuter towns Commuter town Mainly residential; most workforce commutes out Metropolitan area Dense urban core + less‑populated surroundings sharing industry, infrastructure, housing Urban area Higher population density and human features than surroundings (cities, towns, conurbations) Conurbation Several cities/towns merged by growth into one continuous urban‑industrial area Megalopolis Term by geographer Jean Gottmann (1961) for cities of the US northeast seaboard growing into one urban region Edge city Joel Garreau (1991): commercial centres growing far outside the old central city (e.g., Tysons Corner)

Cities grow outward from the centre in a series of rings. Context: 1920s, class‑conscious society, housing segregated by income, poor transport. Assumptions: older buildings in centre, newer at edge; land values highest in centre; strong economic/ethnic segregation; low‑income groups lack transport so live near centre; flat plain with equal access. Five zones: (1) CBD; (2) Transition & industry — low income, oldest housing, ghettos; (3) Low‑income residential; (4) Middle‑income residential — suburban estates, gardens; (5) High‑income residential/commuter — small towns & villages. Criticism: old; ignores car ownership, landscape, effect of industry & transport; zones never so clear‑cut.

Sectors radiate out from the CBD along transport routes. Context: late 1930s; income/status‑divided society; housing reflects social segregation. Assumptions: growth along transport routes; low‑income and industrial areas lie next to each other; wealthy choose best sites. Criticism: old, too general; most zones have mixed uses; ignores urban renewal. Burgess vs Hoyt: Hoyt based on statistical data → less open to criticism.

City develops around several business centres (nuclei), each a growth point; growth spreads until nuclei merge. Modern cities more complex than earlier models; a mixture of Burgess and Hoyt. Some uses attract similar uses (industry); some repel others (housing away from industry). Criticism: not an exact fit for all cities; too complex.

Some relevance only; urban renewal puts high‑income housing near CBD. Modern cities expand beyond these models → urban sprawl. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 2.1 — Burgess concentric zone, Hoyt sector and Harris–Ullman multiple-nuclei models. Burgess 1925 (concentric, Chicago), Hoyt 1939 (sectors along transport routes), Harris & Ullman 1945 (multiple nuclei).
History of City Design & Urban Growth
Five pre‑industrial ideas of city design

Wall: defence/fortification; later the idea of limits to the city. Grid: easy to map and subdivide land; Greeks in Asia Minor (~500 BC); Spanish colonial cities (e.g., Lima). Axis: emphasises important places/people (Beijing imperial axis; Pope Sixtus V in Rome linking monuments). City square: "living room" of the city; began as markets; green squares in England/N. Europe. Cloister: sacred spaces (monasteries, temples, churches) in prominent locations.

Chang’an (Xi’an), China: largest city c. 800 AD (>1 million), Tang capital; walls ≈ 9.7 × 8.6 km, 11 gates, central axis, grid; prototype for Beijing. Bastides (France, 12–13th c.): fortified grid new towns; market square at centre (e.g., Monpazier). Rome (16th c.): Sixtus V — axes, view corridors, piazzas (Piazza del Popolo); led to St Peter’s Square — icon of Baroque planning. London fire 1666: Wren & Evelyn plans not used, but influenced the New World. Philadelphia (William Penn / Thomas Holme): grid, two main streets, five squares; "green country town". Savannah (Oglethorpe, 1733): nearly every house faces a square. Adelaide (Col. William Light): surrounded by a greenbelt; North Adelaide added as separate town. Washington DC (L’Enfant): grid + monumental axes; later best example of City Beautiful movement.

Growth sequence (Kansas City): riverboats & wagons → railway → street railways (suburbs along lines) → automobile (spread anywhere). By 1950 three of four US households owned cars. Metropolis split into old city (pre‑1950) and new suburban city with its own offices/shopping (edge cities). Sprawl became dysfunctional: congestion, long commutes, car dependence → revival of walkable downtowns. Remedy: transit linking new‑city centres to old CBD; multi‑city "mega‑regions" forming worldwide.
Sustainable Development & Urban Planning in Pakistan

Brundtland Report (Our Common Future): development that meets present needs without compromising future generations’ ability to meet theirs. Three pillars: environmental, economic, social sustainability. UN‑Habitat (1996) sustainability measures: quality of life, scale of non‑renewable resource use, recycling/re‑use, renewable resource use, waste produced and its environmental impact. Pakistan system: planning & housing departments at federal, provincial, local level; development authorities in big cities (CDA, RDA, LDA, KDA); 3‑tier local government under PLGO 2001. Islamabad master plan prepared by Doxiadis Associates (1960).

Housing schemes developed without approval; mere land subdivision into residential/commercial. Green area 0.85–2.19% vs prescribed ≥7%; public buildings 0–0.41% vs 5–10%; graveyard 0% vs ≥2%. Green standard fell: 3 acres/1000 persons (1970 plan) → 1 acre/1000 (1996 plan); actual 0.69 acre/1000 (1996). Amenities 2–7 km away → more car trips, fuel, emissions. Water shortage and poor quality (diarrhoea, stomach infection); untreated sewage into nullahs; sewers in only ~35% of city. Open dumping of solid waste; non‑conforming uses (schools, clinics, parlours in houses). National figures cited: housing shortage 7.57 million units (2011); ~25% urban population in squatter settlements; sewerage for only 48%.

Local bodies to prepare and approve urban & environmental development plans; strong development control. Uniform planning & environmental standards; simplify EPA clearance. Public participation; independent periodic evaluation of plans. Comprehensive solid waste management; engineered landfill + composting; source segregation (kitchen vs other waste). Sewage treatment plants; water metering and conservation; use of solar energy. Walkable/cycleable neighbourhoods; green areas at sub‑neighbourhood level; public‑private partnership and cross‑subsidy for projects. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Planned cities of Pakistan: Islamabad — master plan by Constantinos Doxiadis (1960s), grid of sectors (e.g., F-6, G-9) with a dynapolis concept; Lahore Development Authority, CDA, KDA (Karachi), PDA (Peshawar) control planning. Urbanisation: Pakistan’s urban population ≈ 37–40% (census-based), with rapid growth of Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad, Rawalpindi–Islamabad and Peshawar; informal settlements (katchi abadis) are common. Islamabad’s master plan: Doxiadis; Chandigarh: Le Corbusier; Brasília: Lúcio Costa & Oscar Niemeyer.
Role of Transportation in Urban Planning

Transportation = mobility of people and goods; a basic human need; shaped human civilisation and settlement (recall land‑use theories). Planner’s inputs: solution must be analytically based, economically sound, socially credible, environmentally sensitive, practically acceptable. Outputs: safe, rapid, comfortable, convenient, economical, eco‑friendly.

Demand: changes with population, income, land‑use pattern. Technology: from bus/rail only to LRT, MRT (e.g., Manila LRT, Jakarta/Singapore MRT). Operational policy: car‑pool incentives, fares, road tolls. Public values: identify target groups (rich, poor, young, work/leisure trips).

Transportation planning: current and future system. Geometric design: cross‑section, horizontal & vertical alignment, intersections. Pavement design: flexible (bituminous) and rigid (concrete). Traffic engineering: signals, signs, markings.

Suburbanisation complicates collection (getting rider to vehicle) and distribution (vehicle to destination). Trade‑off: wider stop spacing → higher speed but poorer access. Ideal environment: jobs concentrated in core + apartments near stops (large, older cities); high density discourages car use. Demand‑response (para‑transit, e.g., Dial‑a‑Ride): vehicle sent on call; no fixed route or schedule; biggest growth area. BRTS: highly efficient public transport concept.

Forecasting: estimating future vehicles/people using a facility (road, rail line, airport, seaport). Purpose: infrastructure capacity (e.g., number of lanes), financial & social viability, project impact. Classical Four‑Stage Model (FSM): Trip generation → Trip distribution → Modal split → Traffic assignment.

Street network: connected roads made of nodes and segments. Node: intersection of two or more streets, or end of a street. Segment: line connecting two nodes; Link = segment with direction (Lij from i to j). Traffic Analysis Zone (TAZ): study area divided into zones instead of points. Trip: movement >300 m from origin to destination with a purpose; vehicle trip vs person trip; two trip ends. Travel Time Index (TTI): peak‑hour time ÷ off‑peak time (e.g., 40/25 = 1.6). Design capacity: max vehicles passing end of a link per time without delay (veh/h). Design speed: max speed on a link with no delay; higher on flat than steep roads.

Rows = origins; last column = total trips produced by each zone. Columns = destinations; last row = total trips attracted to each zone. Diagonal = intra‑zonal trips. Zone attracting most trips likely an employment/shopping centre.

LOS Condition A Free flow; low volume, high speed B Reasonably free / stable flow; some speed restriction C Stable flow; speed and lane changes controlled by volume D Approaching unstable flow E Unstable flow (~25 mph); stoppages possible F Forced flow / breakdown; queuing; volume exceeds capacity

Predicts total trips produced by and attracted to each zone ("how many trips?"). Depends on: zone population, income, vehicle ownership; also household size, age distribution, education, occupied dwelling units. Expressed as trips/employee, trips/unit land area, trips/occupied dwelling unit. Methods: growth factor model, regression model, category (cross‑classification) analysis. Growth factor: Ti = fi × ti; fi = f(Pd, Id, Vd) / f(Pc, Ic, Vc) (d = design year, c = current year). Growth factor overestimates → used mainly for external trips; regression preferred for internal trips. Regression: Y = a + b1X1 + b2X2 + … (multiple linear regression), coefficients by regression analysis. Worked example (growth factor): 275 households with car (5 trips/day) + 275 without (2.5 trips/day). Current trips = 1375 + 687.5 = 2062.5. If all get cars: fi = 550/275 = 2.0 → future = 4125 trips/day. Realistic estimate = 550 × 5 = 2750 trips/day → shows growth factor over‑estimates.

Trip distribution: where trips go; gravity model based on Newton’s law of gravitation; growth factor method responds only to relative growth rates at origins and destinations. Modal split: share of trips by mode (public vs private); logit — equal utilities give equal probability (0.5 each). Traffic assignment: selection of routes between origin and destination in the network. Urban transportation planning: the process leading to decisions on transport policies and programmes. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 6.1 — Four-step travel demand model. Gravity model: Tij = Pi Aj f(cij) / Σ Aj f(cij) — trips decrease with travel impedance (distance/time/cost). Order: trip generation → trip distribution → modal split → traffic assignment.

LUA studies where and what human activities take place on land; tells if land suits an activity and the consequences of change. Land cover: natural and human‑altered land surface on which activities take place. Land utilisation (land use): the activity/action on the land. LUA is carried out where change is expected. Answers: what to build, where, when & how, and what impact. In short: how land is used now, what changes are allowed under rules, impacts of those changes.

Location (spatial coordinates) Activity (use) Natural qualities (surface, subsurface, vegetation) Improvements (levelling, filling, drainage, buildings) Intensity of use (activity per unit area) Land tenure (ownership) Land price (market activity) Interrelations (access affects use; links to employment, income, investment)

Market: owners, builders, realtors, bankers — seek profit. Government: elected/appointed officials — public interest. Special interest groups: environment, economic development, farming — analyse impacts on their interests.

Suitability = land has the features to support a proposed use (social, physical, spatial, economic factors). Factor categories: Physical constraints: slope, soil, aquifers, flood plains. Access: distance to roads, surface water, sewer and water lines. Costs and benefits of development. Eight steps: Select land use type. Select factors and their attribute values. Score each factor attribute. Weigh the factors. Calculate composite (weighted) score. Rank scores into suitability levels. Identify available land from existing uses. Compare with comprehensive plan/zoning to remove unavailable land. GIS is used to overlay factor maps and compute weighted suitability (Assignment 4 topic).

Cities occupy ~2% of land but use ~75% of resources and produce ~70–80% of CO₂/GHG emissions. Largest CO₂ emitters: buildings, energy and transport — hence greatest mitigation potential. Six investments for green cities: low‑carbon transport, green industry, energy‑efficient buildings, city greening, green resilient infrastructure, intelligent systems. Compact, dense, mixed‑use cities are most resource‑efficient (e.g., Singapore); low‑density sprawl raises energy use and excludes the poor. Four spatial models: monocentric (radial trips, needs mass transit), polycentric (random trips), "urban village" (live near work), composite (most common). WHO: 9 m² green space per capita within 15‑minute walk. Tools: 3R (reduce–reuse–recycle), TOD (transit‑oriented development), BRT, rainwater harvesting, green roofs, LEED rating. Land‑use regulation types: minimum plot size, FSI/FAR limits, zoning, subdivision rules.

Art and science of designing and erecting buildings and other physical structures. Style and method of design and construction; buildings and large structures; orderly arrangement of parts. Practice of the architect (professional services for built environment). Vitruvius (Roman, ~25 BC): firmitas, utilitas, venustas → "Commodity, Firmness and Delight" (Sir Henry Wotton, 1624). More than shelter — a cultural artifact; "a projection of a society on the ground".

Form: shape, size, solid/open. Function: building type (temple, palace, tomb). Material: depends on resources; shape linked to technology and workforce. Place: urban/rural, climate, site specifics. Time: period, style, cultural associations. Meaning: why (priorities), who (power/authority).
Le Corbusier — "A house is a machine for living in" (Villa Savoye)

Five Points of Architecture: Free plan — structure separated from walls; rooms flow. Free façade — uninterrupted windows. Pilotis — building raised on columns; away from damp, open to light and air. Ribbon windows — continuous horizontal windows, broad views. Roof terrace — flat roof as usable outdoor space.

Idea precedes object; communicated by sketches, plans, sections and elevations. Examples: BMW Central Building (Zaha Hadid — "nerve centre"); Jewish Museum Berlin (Libeskind). Famous works cited: Pyramids of Giza, Step Pyramid of Zoser, Parthenon, Acropolis, Stonehenge, Chartres Cathedral, Machu Picchu. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Classical orders: Doric (plain, sturdy), Ionic (scroll/volute capitals), Corinthian (acanthus leaves); Tuscan and Composite are Roman additions. Mughal & Islamic architecture in Pakistan: Badshahi Mosque & Lahore Fort (Mughal), Shalimar Gardens (charbagh layout), Wazir Khan Mosque (kashi tile work), Faisal Mosque (modern, by Vedat Dalokay). Principles of design: Unity, balance (symmetrical/asymmetrical), proportion & scale, rhythm, emphasis, contrast, harmony; Le Corbusier’s Modulor based on golden ratio (≈ 1.618). ‘Form follows function’ — Louis Sullivan; ‘Less is more’ — Mies van der Rohe; Fallingwater — Frank Lloyd Wright.

By level: national, regional, master/comprehensive, local/neighbourhood, site plan. By duration: short‑term (≤5 yr), medium (5–10 yr), long‑term/perspective (20+ yr). Planning elements: land use, transport, housing, utilities, community facilities, open space, economy, environment. Related professions: architecture, civil engineering, economics, law, sociology, geography, environmental science. Planner’s functions: survey & analysis, plan preparation, development control, public consultation, policy advice, implementation & monitoring.
Garden city, satellite town, squatter settlements

Garden City: Ebenezer Howard (1898/1902); self‑contained town ~32,000 people surrounded by a greenbelt; combines town and country (Letchworth, Welwyn). Satellite town: smaller town near a big city to absorb its overflow, partly dependent on it (e.g., Rawalpindi’s Satellite Town). Squatter settlement (katchi abadi): informal housing on land not owned by occupants; upgrading = regularising tenure + providing water, sanitation, roads.

Climate change: long‑term change in climate due mainly to GHG emissions; responses = mitigation (cut emissions) and adaptation (cope with impacts). Urban heat island: city hotter than surroundings due to paving, buildings, less vegetation, waste heat; remedy — trees, green/cool roofs, water bodies. Renewable energy: solar, wind, hydro, biomass, geothermal. Rainwater harvesting: collect roof/surface runoff for storage or groundwater recharge.

Sources: residential, commercial, institutional, industrial, construction & demolition, municipal services. Functional elements: generation → storage → collection → transfer & transport → processing/recycling → disposal (sanitary landfill). ISWM: integrated hierarchy — reduce, reuse, recycle, recover (compost/energy), then dispose. Pakistan: mostly open dumping, low collection efficiency, large organic fraction suitable for composting.

Influences: geographical, climatic, religious, social, historical. Principles: truth/purpose and beauty. Qualities: strength, vitality, grace, breadth, scale. Factors: proportion, colour, balance, use of materials. Features: domes, minarets, arches, courtyards, geometric and calligraphic ornament (e.g., Badshahi Mosque, Taj Mahal).

Sheet Size (mm) A0 841 × 1189 (area 1 m²) A1 594 × 841 A2 420 × 594 A3 297 × 420 A4 210 × 297 Each A-size is half of the previous one; sides in ratio 1 : √2. Title block: bottom-right corner of the sheet. Pencils: H series = hard (9H hardest), B series = soft (9B softest), HB = medium. Typical use: 2H construction lines, H dimension lines, HB outlines & lettering. T-square: horizontal lines. Set squares (45° and 30°–60°): vertical/inclined lines; together give angles in multiples of 15°. Divider: transfers distances / divides lines. French curves: irregular curves. Mini-drafter: replaces T-square, set squares and protractor. Clinograph: adjustable set square. Protractor: measures/sets angles.

Line type Use Continuous thick Visible outlines and edges Continuous thin Dimension, extension, leader, hatching (section) lines, short centre lines, imaginary intersection lines Continuous thin freehand Short break lines Thin zig-zag (ruled) Long break lines Dashed (thin/thick) Hidden outlines and edges Chain thin (long dash–dot) Centre lines, axes, lines of symmetry, pitch circles Chain thin, thick at ends & bends Cutting plane lines Chain thick Surfaces needing special treatment Chain thin double-dashed Adjacent parts, extreme positions of moving parts, centroidal lines Thick : thin thickness ≥ 2 : 1 (e.g. 0.7/0.35 or 0.5/0.25 mm). Precedence when lines coincide: visible > hidden > cutting plane > centre line > break line > dimension/extension > hatching. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 14.1 — Types of lines and their uses. Visible outlines: continuous thick; hidden edges: dashed; centre lines: thin chain; cutting plane: chain thick at ends & bends.

Single-stroke letters, vertical or inclined at 75° to the horizontal. Type A: stroke thickness = h/14. Type B: stroke thickness = h/10. Standard heights: 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm (each ≈ √2 × previous). Main title 7–10 mm; sub-titles 5–7 mm; dimensions and notes 3.5–5 mm. Lower-case letter height ≈ 0.7 h; spacing between characters ≈ 2 × stroke thickness.

Elements: dimension line, extension (projection) line, arrowhead, leader line, dimension figure/note. All drawn thin. Extension line: small gap (~1 mm) from object, extends ~3 mm beyond dimension line. Arrowhead: length : width = 3 : 1, closed and filled. First dimension line ~10 mm from outline; next ones ~8 mm apart. Aligned system: figures parallel to dimension line, readable from bottom or right side, placed above the line. Unidirectional system: all figures read from the bottom; dimension line is broken for the figure. Arrangement: chain (continuous), parallel, progressive (from a common datum), combined. Rules: units in mm (unit not written); each feature dimensioned once; avoid dimensioning hidden lines; never use an outline or centre line as a dimension line; place dimensions outside the view; smaller dimensions inside, larger outside. Symbols: Ø diameter, R radius, SØ sphere diameter, SR sphere radius, □ square.

Representative Fraction (RF): drawing length ÷ actual length (same units). RF > 1 enlarging, = 1 full size, < 1 reducing. Length of scale = RF × maximum length to be measured. Area RF = (linear RF)²; volume RF = (linear RF)³. Example: 1 cm = 1 km → RF = 1/100 000. Scale Key point Plain Reads two units (e.g. m & dm) or one unit and its fraction Diagonal Reads three units (e.g. m, dm, cm); based on similar triangles; reads to 1/100 of main unit Vernier Reads two units; small divisions read using least count Comparative Two scales with same RF but different units (e.g. km & miles) Scale of chords Measures/sets angles; chord of 60° = radius Shrinkage scale Used by pattern makers (allows for metal shrinkage) Least count (vernier): 1 MSD − 1 VSD = MSD ÷ number of vernier divisions. Direct vernier: VSD < MSD (n VSD = n−1 MSD). Retrograde vernier: VSD > MSD (n VSD = n+1 MSD). BIS reducing scales: 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20, 1:50, 1:100, 1:200, 1:500, 1:1000. Enlarging: 2:1, 5:1, 10:1, 20:1, 50:1. Typical civil scales: building plan/elevation/section 1:100 or 1:50; details 1:20, 1:10, 1:5; site plan 1:200–1:500; key/location plan smaller.
Conic sections (cone cut by a plane)

Cutting plane Curve Eccentricity e Perpendicular to axis Circle 0 Inclined to axis, cuts all generators Ellipse < 1 Parallel to one generator Parabola = 1 Parallel to axis (cuts both nappes) Hyperbola > 1 Through apex Triangle — Eccentricity: distance of point from focus ÷ distance from directrix. Ellipse: sum of distances from the two foci = major axis. Distance from focus to end of minor axis = half major axis. Ellipse methods: concentric circles, rectangle (oblong), arcs of circles, trammel, eccentricity, parallelogram, four-centre (approximate; used in isometric). Parabola methods: rectangle, tangent, eccentricity. Uses: arches, reflectors, projectile path, BM diagram of simply supported beam under UDL, cable under UDL. Hyperbola uses: cooling towers, PV diagram. Rectangular hyperbola (asymptotes at 90°): xy = constant, e.g. Boyle’s law PV = C.

Cycloid: path of a point on a circle rolling on a straight line; base length = πD. Epicycloid: circle rolls outside another circle. Hypocycloid: rolls inside; becomes a straight line when rolling circle Ø = ½ directing circle Ø. Trochoid: point inside (inferior) or outside (superior) the rolling circle. Involute: path of the end of a string unwound from a circle/polygon; used for gear tooth profiles (cycloids also). Archimedean spiral: equal radial movement for equal angular movement (cams, scroll chucks). Logarithmic spiral: ratio of successive radius vectors constant (equiangular). Helix: point moving around a cylinder/cone and along its axis uniformly; pitch = axial advance per turn. Uses: screw threads, springs, spiral staircases. Regular polygon: interior angle = (n − 2) × 180° / n. Hexagon side = radius of circumscribing circle. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 18.1 — Conic sections: ellipse, parabola and hyperbola. Other curves: Cycloid (point on rolling circle), epicycloid/hypocycloid (circle rolling outside/inside another), involute (gear teeth), Archimedean spiral (cams), helix (springs, screw threads). Eccentricity: e < 1 ellipse, e = 1 parabola, e > 1 hyperbola; rectangular hyperbola (asymptotes ⊥) describes Boyle’s law pV = constant.

Projectors parallel to each other and perpendicular to the plane of projection; observer at infinity. Planes: HP (horizontal), VP (vertical), PP (profile, ⟂ to both). XY line = intersection of HP and VP (reference line). Views: Front view/Elevation on VP; Top view/Plan on HP; Side/End view on PP. Quadrant Position I Above HP, in front of VP II Above HP, behind VP III Below HP, behind VP IV Below HP, in front of VP First angle: object between observer and plane. Top view below front view; left side view on the right of front view. Used in Pakistan, India (BIS), UK, Europe. Third angle: plane between observer and object. Top view above front view; left side view on the left. Used in USA, Canada. 2nd & 4th angles not used: front and top views overlap. Projection symbol: two views of a truncated cone (frustum). Two views usually enough for simple objects; three for most; cylinder can be shown in one view with Ø. Auxiliary views: AVP (⟂ HP, inclined to VP) gives auxiliary front view; AIP (⟂ VP, inclined to HP) gives auxiliary top view. Used to get true shape of inclined surfaces. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Fig. 19.1 — Arrangement of views in first-angle and third-angle projection. First angle: object between observer and plane (top view BELOW front view); third angle: plane between observer and object (top view ABOVE front view).

Point h above HP and d in front of VP (1st quadrant): front view a′ is h above XY; top view a is d below XY; aa′ ⟂ XY. Point on HP: front view on XY. Point on VP: top view on XY. Line ∥ to both HP & VP: both views true length (TL), ∥ to XY. Line ⟂ HP: top view is a point; front view TL, ⟂ XY. Line ⟂ VP: front view is a point. Line ∥ VP, inclined θ to HP: front view = TL showing true θ; top view shorter, ∥ XY. Line inclined to both planes: neither view TL; apparent angles α > θ and β > φ. θ + φ ≤ 90°; θ + φ = 90° when the line lies in a profile plane. Finding TL & true inclinations: rotating line method, trapezoid method, auxiliary plane method. Traces: HT = point where line (extended) meets HP; VT = meets VP. A line ∥ to a plane has no trace on it.

Plane ∥ HP: top view = true shape; front view = line ∥ XY. Plane ∥ VP: front view = true shape; top view = line ∥ XY. Plane ⟂ both HP & VP (profile plane): both views are lines ⟂ XY; side view true shape. Plane inclined θ to HP, ⟂ VP (AIP): front view = line at true θ; top view = reduced shape. Oblique plane (inclined to both): no view shows true shape; solved by change-of-position (2/3 stage) or auxiliary plane method.

Platonic solids (5): tetrahedron (4 △), cube (6 □), octahedron (8 △), dodecahedron (12 pentagons), icosahedron (20 △). Euler’s formula: F + V − E = 2. Solids of revolution: cylinder (rectangle about one side), cone (right triangle about one ⟂ side), sphere (semicircle about diameter). Right solid: axis ⟂ base. Oblique solid: axis inclined to base. Frustum: part left after cutting by a plane ∥ base. Truncated: cutting plane not ∥ base. Axis ⟂ HP: start with top view (true shape of base). Axis ⟂ VP: start with front view. Sphere: every view is a circle of the same diameter. Cone slant height L = √(r² + h²).

Cutting plane line: thin chain, thick at ends and bends, arrows show viewing direction, labelled (A–A). Hatching: thin lines at 45° to main outline, ~1–3 mm apart; adjacent parts hatched in opposite direction or different spacing. Not sectioned when cut lengthwise: shafts, bolts, nuts, rivets, keys, pins, ribs, webs, spokes, balls. Types: full, half (¼ removed; symmetric objects), offset (stepped cutting plane), broken-out/partial, revolved, removed, aligned, auxiliary. True shape of section: obtained on a plane ∥ to the cutting plane. Section of cylinder by inclined plane = ellipse; any section of a sphere = circle. Material hatching (civil): brick masonry 45° lines; concrete dots + small stones; earth irregular strokes; timber grain lines; stone masonry irregular blocks; glass thin diagonal strokes.

Unfolding all surfaces of a solid onto one plane in true size; always uses true lengths. Uses: sheet-metal work (ducts, hoppers, chimneys, funnels, tanks, trays). Methods: parallel-line (prisms, cylinders), radial-line (pyramids, cones), triangulation (transition pieces), approximate (sphere — zone/lune method). Cylinder lateral surface: rectangle πD × H. Cone lateral surface: sector of radius L (slant height) and angle θ = 360° × r / L. Pyramid: triangles about apex, radius = true length of slant edge. Sphere and doubly curved surfaces: non-developable (only approximate).

Curve/line where two solids interpenetrate; found by line (generator) method or cutting-plane method. Two equal cylinders with axes intersecting at 90°: intersection appears as straight lines in front view. Uses: pipe T-joints, ducts, dome-and-wall junctions.
Classification: parallel (orthographic, axonometric, oblique) vs converging/central (perspective).

Three axes at 120°; on paper two axes at 30° to horizontal, one vertical. Each axis inclined 35°16′ to plane of projection. Isometric scale: isometric length = √(2/3) × TL = 0.816 TL (≈ 82%, ≈ 9/11). Isometric projection: uses isometric scale. Isometric drawing/view: uses true lengths (≈ 22.5% larger). Only isometric lines (∥ to axes) show measured lengths; non-isometric lines are located by end points. Circles appear as ellipses (four-centre method). Sphere: circle of radius = true radius in isometric projection, 1.22 × radius in isometric drawing. Hidden lines normally omitted. Axonometric types: isometric (3 equal angles), dimetric (2 equal), trimetric (all different).

Front face ∥ to picture plane shown in true shape; receding lines at 30°, 45° or 60° (usually 45°). Cavalier: receding lines full scale. Cabinet: receding lines half scale (more realistic). Keep circular features and longest dimension ∥ to picture plane.

Projectors converge to the observer’s eye (station point); most realistic; used by architects. Terms: Station Point (SP), Picture Plane (PP), Ground Line (GL), Horizon Line (HL), Vanishing Point (VP), Centre of Vision. Types: one-point (parallel), two-point (angular), three-point (oblique). Objects farther away appear smaller; parallel lines meet at vanishing points. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Isometric scale: Isometric length ≈ 0.816 × true length (cos 35°16′); isometric drawing uses true lengths, isometric projection uses reduced lengths. Oblique: Cavalier: receding lines full scale at 45°; cabinet: receding lines half scale. Isometric axes are 120° apart (30° to horizontal); perspective uses vanishing points (one-, two-, three-point).

Plan: horizontal section through doors/windows (around sill–lintel level, ~1–1.5 m above floor) viewed from above. Elevation: exterior views — front, rear, sides. Section: vertical cut from foundation to roof; usually taken through staircase, doors, windows and WC. Drawing order: plan first → elevation projected from plan → section. Site plan: plot boundary, building position, roads, services, north direction. Key/location plan: site relative to surroundings. North line usually shown on plan; levels shown as RL. Other drawings: foundation plan, working drawings, detail drawings, structural (RCC detailing, bar bending schedule), plumbing, electrical layout. Openings notation: D door, W window, V ventilator, CW clerestory window. Plumbing symbols: WC, wash basin, sink, floor trap, gully trap, inspection chamber, manhole. Electrical symbols: switch, socket, light point, fan, distribution board (DB). Abbreviations: RCC, PCC, DPC (damp-proof course), GL (ground level), NGL (natural ground level), PL (plinth level), FFL (finished floor level), RL (reduced level), BM (bench mark), c/c (centre to centre), NTS (not to scale).

Coordinates: absolute (x,y); relative (@x,y); polar (@distance<angle). Angles measured anticlockwise from +X (east = 0°). Diagonal scale → three units; plain and vernier → two units. Eccentricity: circle 0, ellipse < 1, parabola 1, hyperbola > 1. Cooling tower → hyperbola; gear teeth → involute/cycloid; screw thread → helix. Profile plane is ⟂ to both HP and VP. First angle → plan below elevation; third angle → plan above elevation. Development: cylinder → rectangle; cone → sector; sphere → not developable. Isometric scale = 0.816; angle between isometric axes = 120°. Perspective → converging projectors; orthographic → parallel projectors ⟂ to plane. Half section is used for symmetrical objects. Ribs, shafts, bolts are not hatched when cut lengthwise.

Hazard: process/phenomenon that may cause loss of life, injury, property damage, social or environmental disruption. Natural: geophysical (earthquake, tsunami, volcano, landslide), hydro-meteorological (flood, cyclone, drought, heatwave), biological (epidemic). Man-made / technological: industrial accidents, fire, explosions, chemical leaks, dam failure, nuclear. Socio-natural: hazards made worse by human activity (e.g. floods due to deforestation, urban flooding). Disaster: serious disruption of a community's functioning that exceeds its capacity to cope using its own resources. Vulnerability: susceptibility to harm (physical, social, economic, environmental). Exposure: people, property and systems located in hazard zones. Capacity: strengths and resources available to manage risk. Coping capacity: ability to manage adverse conditions with available resources. Resilience: ability to resist, absorb, accommodate, adapt to and recover from a hazard in a timely manner. Risk formula: Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability (expanded: R = H × E × V / C). Rapid-onset: earthquake, flash flood, tsunami. Slow-onset: drought, desertification, sea-level rise. Secondary / cascading hazards: e.g. earthquake → landslide, tsunami, fire, liquefaction. Build Back Better (BBB): use recovery to reduce future risk. Phase Timing Activities Prevention Before Avoid hazard/risk entirely (e.g. no construction in floodplain) Mitigation Before Reduce impact: building codes, embankments, retrofitting, land-use zoning Preparedness Before Plans, early warning, drills, stockpiles, training, evacuation routes Response During / immediately after Rescue (SAR), evacuation, first aid, relief, shelter Recovery After Rehabilitation (short-term restoration) → Reconstruction (long-term rebuilding) Classic 4 phases: Mitigation, Preparedness, Response, Recovery. Paradigm shift: reactive relief-centric approach → proactive Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR).

Focus/hypocenter: point of origin underground. Epicenter: point on surface directly above. Body waves: P-wave (primary, longitudinal, fastest, through solids & liquids); S-wave (secondary, shear/transverse, solids only). Surface waves: Love (horizontal shear, faster surface wave); Rayleigh (rolling, elliptical motion). Surface waves cause most damage. Magnitude (energy released): Richter (ML, 1935), Moment magnitude (Mw) — preferred. +1 magnitude = 10× amplitude, ≈ 32× energy. Intensity (effects/damage at a place): Modified Mercalli (MMI), I–XII; MSK scale. Seismograph records ground motion; accelerograph records acceleration → PGA (peak ground acceleration). Pakistan tectonics: Indian plate colliding with Eurasian plate (north); Arabian plate subducting under Eurasian at Makran (south-west).
Building Code of Pakistan — Seismic Provisions 2007 (BCP-SP 2007)

Ductility; strong column – weak beam; regular & symmetric plan/elevation. Avoid: soft storey, short-column effect, torsional irregularity, heavy roofs, re-entrant corners. Seismic gap between buildings to prevent pounding. Shear walls, bracing, base isolation, dampers (viscous, friction, tuned mass damper). Detailing: closely spaced stirrups near joints, 135° hooks, confinement, proper lap splices. Masonry: seismic bands (plinth, lintel, roof/gable), confined masonry, vertical bars at corners. Liquefaction: loose, saturated sandy soils lose strength in shaking. Remedies: compaction, drainage, stone columns, grouting, deep (pile) foundations. Tsunami: caused by vertical seafloor displacement (subduction earthquakes), submarine landslides, volcanoes; speed ≈ 700–800 km/h in deep ocean.

Types: riverine (fluvial), flash flood, urban (pluvial), coastal / storm surge, GLOF, dam-break. Return period: T = 1/P.  Probability of at least one exceedance in n years: R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ. Rational formula: Q = CIA/360 (Q in m³/s, I in mm/h, A in hectares) — small catchments. Spillways designed for PMF (Probable Maximum Flood) for large dams. Structural measures: dams & reservoirs, levees/embankments (bunds), flood walls, spurs/groynes, channel improvement, diversion channels, retention basins, check dams. Non-structural measures: floodplain zoning, flood forecasting & warning, flood insurance, flood-proofing, watershed management/afforestation, relocation. Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources) Structural measures: Embankments/levees, spurs, dams & reservoirs, flood bypasses (e.g., Head Marala–Ravi), river training, drainage. Non-structural: Flood forecasting & early warning (FFD Lahore, PMD), floodplain zoning, flood insurance, community preparedness, evacuation plans. GLOF = glacial lake outburst flood — a major threat in Gilgit-Baltistan & Chitral (thousands of glacial lakes).

Weak sustainability: natural capital can be replaced by man-made capital. Strong sustainability: critical natural capital cannot be substituted. Carrying capacity: maximum population an environment can support indefinitely. Ecological footprint: land/water area needed to supply resources and absorb waste; unit = global hectare (gha). Earth Overshoot Day: date humanity uses up the year's renewable resources. Precautionary principle (Rio Principle 15): lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to delay preventive action. Covers the BSc mathematics courses on your Drive — Linear Algebra (1st sem), Differential Equations & Probability and Statistics (3rd sem), Numerical Analysis (4th sem) and MATLAB — at the level asked in engineering competitive tests (NTS/PPSC/FPSC/WAPDA, GATE-style).

Types: Symmetric (A = Aᵀ), skew-symmetric (A = −Aᵀ, diagonal zero), orthogonal (AᵀA = I, det = ±1), singular (det = 0), idempotent (A² = A), nilpotent (Aᵏ = 0), Hermitian. Determinant facts: det(AB) = det A·det B; det(kA) = kⁿ det A; det(Aᵀ) = det A; swapping two rows changes sign; triangular → product of diagonal. Inverse: A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A|; (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹; exists only if |A| ≠ 0. Rank: Number of non-zero rows in echelon form; Ax = b consistent iff rank(A) = rank([A|b]); unique if rank = n; infinite solutions if rank < n. Eigenvalues: det(A − λI) = 0; Σλ = trace(A); Πλ = det(A); symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues & orthogonal eigenvectors; eigenvalues of triangular matrix = diagonal entries. Cayley–Hamilton: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation (used to find A⁻¹ & powers). Engineering use: Stiffness matrices (symmetric, positive definite), eigenvalue problems for natural frequencies & buckling, principal stresses. Sum of eigenvalues = trace; product = determinant. A matrix is singular iff one eigenvalue is zero.

Numerical Analysis — Errors & Roots of Equations

Errors: Round-off (finite digits), truncation (series/step approximation); absolute, relative, percentage error; significant figures. Bisection: Bracketing, always converges, linear (halves interval each step): n ≥ log₂((b − a)/ε). Regula falsi (false position): Bracketing with linear interpolation; faster than bisection but one end may stagnate. Fig. 5.1 — Newton–Raphson iterations converge quadratically near a simple root. Newton–Raphson: xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ)/f′(xₙ); quadratic convergence; fails if f′ ≈ 0. Square root of N: xₙ₊₁ = ½(xₙ + N/xₙ). Secant: Uses two previous points, no derivative; order ≈ 1.618. Fixed-point iteration: x = g(x) converges if |g′(x)| < 1 near the root. Orders of convergence: bisection 1 (linear), secant 1.618, Newton–Raphson 2 (quadratic).
Numerical Analysis — Linear Systems, Interpolation, Integration & ODEs

Direct methods: Gauss elimination (with partial pivoting), Gauss–Jordan (→ identity; gives inverse), LU decomposition (Doolittle, Crout), Cholesky (symmetric positive definite — stiffness matrices). Iterative methods: Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel (uses latest values, faster); converge if matrix is diagonally dominant; SOR for acceleration. Interpolation: Newton forward/backward differences (equal spacing), Lagrange (unequal spacing), Newton divided differences; cubic splines. Curve fitting: Least squares (linear, polynomial, exponential via log transform). Fig. 6.1 — Trapezoidal rule vs Simpson's 1/3 rule. Numerical integration: Trapezoidal: (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ] (error O(h²)); Simpson 1/3: (h/3)[y₀ + 4Σodd + 2Σeven + yₙ] (n even, O(h⁴)); Simpson 3/8 (n multiple of 3); Gauss quadrature (n points exact to degree 2n − 1). Numerical differentiation: Forward difference O(h); central difference (y₁ − y₋₁)/2h is O(h²). ODE solvers: Euler (first order, O(h)), modified Euler/Heun (2nd order), Runge–Kutta 4th order (most used, O(h⁴)), predictor–corrector (Milne, Adams). Engineering use: Simpson's rule for areas/volumes (earthwork — prismoidal formula is Simpson's rule), Newton–Raphson in nonlinear analysis, Gauss quadrature in FEM, RK4 in dynamics & routing. Simpson's 1/3 rule needs an even number of intervals; it is exact for polynomials up to degree 3.

BCP Seismic Provisions 2007 — Zones & Key Rules

Design earthquake: Ground motion with 10% probability of exceedance in 50 years (≈ 475-year return period). Zoning: Pakistan divided into five seismic zones by peak ground acceleration (PGA), following UBC-97 zoning. Zone PGA range Hazard 1 0.05 – 0.08 g Low 2A 0.08 – 0.16 g Moderate 2B 0.16 – 0.24 g Moderate 3 0.24 – 0.32 g Severe 4 > 0.32 g Very severe (e.g., Quetta region) Site (soil) profile types: SA hard rock, SB rock, SC very dense soil/soft rock, SD stiff soil, SE soft soil, SF special soils needing site-specific study. If soil properties are not known, use type SD. Seismic coefficients: Ca and Cv depend on zone and soil profile type; they define the design response spectrum (as in UBC-97). Structural systems: Where PGA ≥ 0.2 g, high-ductility systems such as special moment-resisting frames are required; ordinary systems are allowed only where PGA < 0.2 g and the building is low (height ≈ 15 m or less). Base shear (UBC-97 form): V = Cv·I·W/(R·T), not more than 2.5·Ca·I·W/R and not less than 0.11·Ca·I·W. I = importance factor, R = response modification factor, T = fundamental period, W = seismic weight. Approximate period: T = Ct·hn^(3/4); Ct = 0.0853 (steel moment frames), 0.0731 (RC moment frames and eccentrically braced frames), 0.0488 (all other buildings), with hn in metres. Unknown soil → profile SD. Zone 4 is the highest (PGA > 0.32 g). Return period of design earthquake ≈ 475 years (10% in 50 years).

Basis: International Building Code (IBC) approach in place of UBC-97: mapped spectral accelerations at short period (Ss) and 1 second (S1), site classes A–F, design spectral values SDS and SD1, and seismic design categories (SDC A–F) instead of zones 1–4. Site classes: Classified by average shear-wave velocity Vs30 (or SPT N / undrained strength) in the top 30 m, as in ASCE 7. Load combinations & design: Strength design with ASCE 7–type load combinations; concrete to ACI 318 and steel to AISC (editions referenced in the code). If a question says "seismic design category" or "Ss and S1" it refers to BCP 2021/IBC; "Zone 2B, Ca, Cv" refers to BCP 2007/UBC-97.

NEQS for municipal and liquid industrial effluents were first approved by the Pakistan Environmental Protection Council in 1993 and revised in 2000 (SRO 549(I)/2000). Values in mg/L unless stated; three columns: into inland waters / into sewage treatment / into sea. Pakistan Environmental Protection Act (PEPA): 1997 — created Pak-EPA and the Environmental Protection Council; Section 12 requires an IEE or EIA before construction of a project (outer limit for the agency decision: four months). IEE & EIA Regulations: 2000 — Schedule I projects need an IEE (initial environmental examination), Schedule II projects need a full EIA; the agency decides within 45 days (IEE) and 90 days (EIA) of a complete application. After 18th Amendment (2010): Environment became a provincial subject: Punjab EPA Act (amended 2012), Sindh EPA Act 2014, KP EPA Act 2014, Balochistan EPA Act 2012 — each with its own standards and review procedure. IEE = smaller projects (Schedule I); EIA = major projects (Schedule II) such as large dams, highways and power plants.

PSQCA: Pakistan Standards & Quality Control Authority (Act VI of 1996) issues Pakistan Standards (PS) and runs compulsory certification for items such as cement. PS 232: Ordinary Portland cement. The 2008 edition uses grades 43 and 53 (like IS); the 2015 revision uses strength classes 32.5, 42.5 and 52.5 N/R (like EN 197-1). Chemical limits quoted by makers: MgO ≤ 6%, SO₃ ≤ 3%. PS 5313: Common cements per EN 197-1 (CEM I, CEM II blended types) — printed on many local bags (e.g., CEM II/A-M 42.5N). Reinforcing bars: Pakistan standard for deformed bars is aligned with ASTM A615; local mills sell Grade 40 (280 MPa) and Grade 60 (420 MPa). Bricks: Standard first-class burnt clay brick in Pakistan ≈ 9 × 4.5 × 3 in. (nominal). Cement bag "PS 232 Grade 53" = OPC; "PS 5313 CEM II" = blended cement.

NHA General Specifications (1998): Standard technical specification for national highways; contract BOQs refer to its item numbers. NHA item (common) Work 108 Formation of embankment 201 Granular subbase 202 Aggregate base course 203 Asphaltic base course (plant mix) 305 Asphaltic concrete wearing course (plant mix) Marshall criteria commonly specified for wearing course (Item 305): 75 blows each face; stability ≥ 1000 kg; flow 8–14 (units of 0.25 mm); air voids 4–6% (some contracts 4–7%); loss of stability after immersion ≤ 20–25%. Check the project special provisions — values are set per contract. Compaction (typical): Embankment and subgrade ≥ 95% of modified AASHTO (T-180) maximum dry density; subbase and base ≥ 98–100% of modified AASHTO. Bitumen grades in Pakistan: Penetration grades 60/70 (hot plains — most common) and 80/100 (cooler northern areas); performance grades (PG) used on newer motorways. Design references: AASHTO 1993 Guide for pavement thickness (structural number SN), Asphalt Institute MS-2 for Marshall mix design, AASHTO Green Book for geometric design. Item 305 = AC wearing course; Item 203 = asphalt base; Item 202 = aggregate base; Item 201 = subbase.

Islamabad: CDA Building Regulations and the Islamabad Capital Territory zoning regulations. Lahore: LDA Building and Zoning Regulations 2019 (amended since). Karachi / Sindh: Karachi Building & Town Planning Regulations 2002, enforced by the Sindh Building Control Authority (SBCA). Punjab (other cities): Punjab Private Housing Schemes and Land Sub-division Rules; Punjab Land Use (Classification, Reclassification and Redevelopment) Rules 2009. Common items in by-laws: Setbacks (front, rear, side), floor area ratio (FAR), ground coverage, maximum height, parking, structural-stability certificate by a PEC-registered engineer, completion certificate before occupation. FAR = total covered area of all floors ÷ plot area. Ground coverage = ground-floor covered area ÷ plot area.

PEC Standard Form of Bidding Documents: Based on FIDIC conditions of contract; mandatory for many public-sector civil works contracts. PEC contractor categories: Constructors are licensed in categories C-A (no cost limit), C-B, and C-1 to C-6 (decreasing contract-value limits); limits are revised by PEC. Procurement rules: Federal: Public Procurement Rules 2004 (PPRA Ordinance 2002). Punjab: Punjab Procurement Rules 2014 (PPRA Punjab). Sindh: SPP Rules 2010. KP: KPPRA Rules 2014. Market Rate System (MRS): Punjab Finance Department publishes district-wise market rates of materials and labour twice a year; used with the Schedule of Rates to prepare estimates. Schedule of Rates: Composite Schedule of Rates (CSR) — Punjab and other provinces; Pak PWD Schedule of Rates for federal works. Estimates in Punjab = CSR item rates updated with the current MRS rates.

Setting ≠ hardening: setting = loss of plasticity (C₃A); hardening = strength gain (C₃S, C₂S). Early strength → C₃S; later strength → C₂S; flash set & highest heat → C₃A; least strength role → C₄AF. Gypsum controls setting (added at grinding); not a strength contributor. Unsoundness is due to free lime, MgO, excess SO₃ — not due to fineness. Finer cement: faster strength & more heat, but more shrinkage and cracking risk. Abrams' law: strength depends on w/c (for full compaction) — not on cement content alone. Bleeding is a form of segregation (Type 3). Laitance is the result of bleeding. Air entrainment ↑ workability but ↓ strength; entrapped air is accidental and harmful. Retarders increase bleeding; they do not cool concrete. Calcium chloride is not an anti-freeze and is banned in prestressed concrete. Creep = deformation under sustained load; shrinkage = deformation without load. Young concrete creeps more; high humidity reduces both creep and shrinkage. Compacting factor test suits low-workability concrete; slump test unsuitable for very dry or very wet mixes; Vee-Bee for very dry mixes. Cube strength > cylinder strength (≈ 1.25×) because of platen restraint and lower height/width ratio. Sulphate attack → ettringite & gypsum; best defence low-C₃A cement (Type V) + low w/c; MgSO₄ is the worst. ASR needs all three: reactive silica + alkalis + moisture; sign = map cracking. Carbonation lowers pH (danger to steel), it does not attack concrete strength directly; detected by ph

Framework: PPRA Ordinance 2002 and Public Procurement Rules 2004 (federal); provinces have their own: Punjab PPRA Rules 2014, KPPRA Rules 2014, Sindh SPPRA Rules 2010, Balochistan BPPRA Rules 2014. Response time (Rule 13): Not less than 15 days for national competitive bidding and 30 days for international competitive bidding, counted from first publication. Advertisement: Above the threshold: PPRA website + newspapers (one English, one Urdu national daily); e-PADS for e-procurement. Bid security: Not more than 5% of the estimated value (fixed amount, so as not to reveal the estimate). Performance security: Commonly up to 10% of contract price, valid until completion/defects liability. Bid validity extension: May be extended once, by not more than the original validity period; bidders refusing may withdraw without forfeiting bid security. Repeat order: Not to exceed 15% of the original order value. Bidding procedures: Single-stage one-envelope (simple works), single-stage two-envelope (technical + financial, opened separately), two-stage, two-stage two-envelope (complex/turnkey). Evaluation: Lowest evaluated bid (not necessarily lowest price) is awarded; evaluation report published before award; grievance redressal committee for complaints. PPRA: 15 days national / 30 days international; bid security ≤ 5%; repeat order ≤ 15%.
